en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Birth Stories in the Minor Collection.
(Seventh Division) 22.
Mahānipāta [543] 6.
The Exposition of the Bhūridatta Jātaka
The Section on the City:
"Whatever jewel there is..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana near Sāvatthī, concerning lay followers who had observed the Uposatha.
It is said that on the Uposatha day, they would resolve upon the Uposatha as early as morning and give alms.
Having given [the offerings] after the meal, they went to Jetavana with perfumes, garlands, and other items in their hands, and sat to one side at the time for hearing the Dhamma.
The Teacher, having arrived at the Dhamma hall and sat upon the adorned Buddha-seat, surveyed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
then, together with those concerning whom a discourse on the Dhamma arose—whether among the bhikkhus or others—the Tathāgata [proceeded].

They were conversing; therefore, knowing that a discourse on the Dharma connected with former conduct would arise concerning the lay followers today, he addressed the lay followers while conversing with them, asking, "Are you observing the Uposatha, lay followers?
When they replied, "Yes, venerable sir," he said, "Excellent, lay followers! You have done well. However, it is not surprising..."
“Indeed, it is because you have obtained such a Buddha as I, a teacher who gives exhortation, that you should observe the Uposatha.
But even the ancient wise ones, though they had no teacher, abandoned great fame and observed the Uposatha nonetheless.
Having said this, being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, while King Brahmadatta was reigning, he gave the vice-regency to his son.
Seeing the great glory of the prince, he became apprehensive, thinking, "He might even seize my kingdom. Thus, filled with suspicion, he said: "Dear son, depart from here;
dwell wherever you please, and after my passing, take the hereditary kingdom."
Having accepted this with the words "Very well," he paid homage to his father and departed. Traveling by stages, he reached the Yamunā River;
there, between the Yamunā and the ocean, and near a mountain, he constructed a leaf-hut and lived there, subsisting on forest roots and fruits.
At that time, in a nāga-realm beneath the ocean, a certain nāga-maiden whose husband had died was [among] others...
Having observed the glory of those with husbands, and driven by defilement, she departed from the Nāga realm and wandered along the seashore.
Seeing the footprints of the prince, she followed their tracks and beheld that leaf-hut.
At that time, the prince had gone out to gather fruits. She entered the leaf-hut and [saw] the bedding of wood-shavings as well as the remaining requisites.
Seeing this, he thought: "This is the dwelling place of a renunciant; I shall test him to see whether or not he has gone forth out of faith.
For if he has gone forth out of faith and is intent on renunciation, he will not accept my decorated bed.
But if he is devoted to sensual pleasures and has not gone forth out of faith, [he will]."
"He will lie down right upon my bed; then, taking him and making him my husband, I shall dwell right here.

Having gone to the Naga realm, she brought celestial flowers and celestial perfumes, prepared a bed of celestial flowers, made an offering of flowers at the leaf-hut, scattered fragrant powders, and adorned the leaf-hut.
She had gone straight to the abode of the Nāgas.
When the prince returned in the evening and entered the leaf-hut, he saw that situation and thought, "By whom has this bed been prepared?
After partaking of various fruits, he remarked, "Oh, how fragrant these flowers are!"
Thinking, "Oh, how pleasant this bed has been prepared! he, having become joyful because of his state of having gone forth out of faith, turned over and lay down upon the flower-bed.
Having fallen asleep, he rose at sunrise on the following day;
without sweeping the leaf-hut, he went out for the sake of various fruits. At that moment, the young woman Nāgamaṇavikā arrived and [found] the flowers withered.
Seeing the flowers, he realized, "This man is devoted to sensual pleasures; he has not gone forth out of faith. It is possible to win him over.

Having removed the old flowers and brought other flowers, he prepared a bed of fresh flowers just as before, decorated the leaf-hut, scattered flowers along the walking path, and returned to his own abode in the Nāga realm. On that very day, he...
Having lain upon his bed of flowers, on the following day he thought, "Who indeed is decorating this leaf-hut?
Without going out for fruit, he remained hidden not far from the leaf-hut.
The other woman also, taking many perfumes and flowers, went to the hermitage. The prince saw the Naga maiden of supreme beauty.
Upon seeing her, his heart was bound with passion. Without revealing himself, he entered her leaf-hut;
and when it was time for her to prepare the bed, he entered and asked, "Who are you? "I am a young Naga maiden, my lord," she replied. "Are you married or unmarried?
"My lord, formerly I had a husband, but now I am a widow without a husband. "And where do you live? he asked.
“I am Prince Brahmadatta, the son of the King of Bārāṇasī. “Why have you come here, abandoning the abode of the Nāgas?
“Sir, having seen the splendor of the young Nāga maidens who have husbands there, I became distressed by defilement;
I left that place and am wandering about seeking my husband. “In that case, blessed lady,” he said.
“Excellent! I too did not go forth out of faith; rather, I live here because my father sent me away.
Do not worry; I shall be your husband, and we both shall live here in harmony.
She accepted this, saying, “Very well. From then on, they both lived there in harmony. She...
By his own supernatural power, he caused a magnificent house to be built, brought a costly couch, and prepared a bed.
From that time forth, he no longer ate roots or wild fruits; instead, he sustained his life by consuming only divine food and drink.
Later, the Naga maiden conceived and gave birth to a son. Because he was born on the shore of the ocean, [he was named Sāgara].
They gave him the name Sāgarabrahmadatta. While he was traveling on foot, the Nāga maiden gave birth to a daughter;
because she was born on the seashore, they gave her the name Samuddajā.
Then a forest-dweller from Bārāṇasī, having reached that place and exchanged greetings with him, recognized the prince and stayed there for several days.
Having stayed there, he said, "Your Majesty, I shall inform the royal court of your residence here," and after paying homage to him, he departed and went to the city.

At that time, the king passed away. The ministers performed the funeral rites for his body and, having assembled on the seventh day, declared, "A kingdom without a king cannot endure; [we must find] the dwelling place of the prince."
“Or, if we do not know his whereabouts, we shall release Phussa-ratha and seize the king,” they deliberated.
At that moment, a forest-dweller who had reached the city heard this conversation;
he went to the ministers and reported the news, saying, “I stayed in the presence of the prince for three or four days before returning.”
The ministers, having paid him honor and gone there with that guide, exchanged greetings and informed him of the king’s death,
saying, “Your Majesty, please take over the kingdom. He replied,
“I shall first ascertain the mind of the maiden Nāgā,” and approaching her, he said, “Bhadde, my father has passed away.”
"My ministers have come to raise the royal parasol over me; come, my dear, let us both rule the kingdom of Bārāṇasī, twelve yojanas in extent.
You shall be the chief among sixteen thousand women," he said.
"My lord, I cannot go," she replied. "For what reason? he asked. "Because we are of fierce venom, quick to anger, and even at the slightest provocation—"

“I am angry, and one who is full of resentment toward an enemy is indeed burdensome. If I were to look upon anyone while feeling anger after seeing or hearing something, he would be scattered like a handful of ashes.
For this reason, it is not possible for me to go. On the following day, the prince requested her once more. Then she said to him: “As for me, I will not go by any means whatsoever.”
"Moreover, these sons of mine, the Nāga princes, are of human birth because they were born from your own body.
If you have any affection for me, be diligent regarding them. Furthermore, these delicate water-born ones might die from exhaustion caused by the wind and heat while traveling along the road;
therefore, have a boat excavated, fill it with water, and [place them] therein."
"Having had your two little sons play in the water, you should have a lotus pond constructed right here within the city grounds;
in this way, they will not grow weary.
Having spoken thus, she paid homage to the prince, circumambulated him to the right, embraced her two sons, and [placed them] between her breasts.
Having laid her down, kissed her on the head, and entrusted her to the prince, she wept and wailed, then vanished right there and went to the Naga realm.
The prince, overcome with grief and his eyes filled with tears, departed from his residence;
having wiped his eyes, he approached his ministers. They consecrated him right there, saying, "O Lord, for us..."

"Let us go to the city," they said. "In that case, quickly have a boat dug out, load it with carts, fill it with water, and scatter various flowers endowed with beautiful colors and fragrances upon the surface of the water. My sons are 'water-seeds';
playing there, they will travel in comfort. The ministers did exactly as instructed. The king, having reached Benares—
Having entered the decorated city, surrounded by sixteen thousand female dancers and his ministers, he sat upon the great terrace and drank the great draught for seven days.
For the sake of his sons, he had a lotus pond constructed. They played there constantly.
Then one day, as water was being poured into the pond, a certain tortoise entered it, but found no way out.

Not seeing him, he lay down on the surface of the lotus pond; then, at the time when the children were playing, he rose from the water, lifted his head out, looked at them, and submerged back into the water again.
Seeing this, the children were terrified and went to their father, saying, "Father, a certain *yakkha* in the lotus pond is frightening us. The king commanded his men, "Go and seize him!"
Having cast the net and caught the tortoise, they presented it to the king. When the princes saw it, they cried out, "Father, this is a *pisāca*!
Out of affection for his sons, the king became angry with the tortoise and commanded, "Go, inflict punishment upon him!
Thereupon, some said, "This man is an enemy of the king; let us grind him to powder in a mortar with pestles."
Some said, "It is permissible"; others said, "It is permissible to cook it over three fires and eat it"; others said, "It is permissible to roast it over coals";

yet others said, "It is permissible to cook it right inside the husk. But one minister, who was afraid of water, said, "It is permissible to throw this into an eddy in the Yamunā; there he will meet with great destruction. Such as this..."
“There is no punishment for him,” he said. Hearing his words, the tortoise poked out its head and spoke thus:
“Sir, what offense have I committed against you that you subject me to such a punishment?
I could endure other forms of punishment, but this one is exceedingly harsh; do not speak thus. To him—
Having heard this, the king thought, "It is fitting to have him executed right here," and he had him thrown into an eddy of the Yamunā River.
The man did as he was told. Upon reaching a watercourse leading to the Nāga realm, he entered the Nāga world.
Then, while playing in that waterway, the Nāga youths—the sons of King Dhatarattha—saw him and said, "Seize him!"
They said, "He is a slave. He thought, "Having escaped from the hands of the King of Bārāṇasī, I have now fallen into the hands of such cruel elephants. By what means might I be released?
Thinking, "There is this means," he uttered a falsehood and said, "Since you belong to Dhataraṭṭha, the king of the nāgas, why do you speak thus? I am Cittacūḷa..."
The tortoise named Nāma, a messenger from the King of Bārāṇasī, arrived in the presence of Dhatarattha and said, "Our king wishes to give his daughter to you, Dhatarattha;

he has sent me, so please grant me an audience. They were filled with joy, and taking him with them, they went into the presence of the king and reported the matter. The king said, "Bring him here," and having summoned him and seen him, he—
Being displeased, he said, "One with such a wretched body as this is not capable of performing the work of an envoy.
Hearing that, the tortoise replied, "But what, Great King, must envoys necessarily be the size of palm trees?
For whether a body is small or large, it is of no measure; the only standard is the accomplishment of the task in every place one goes. Great King, for us..."
“The king has many messengers: men perform their work on land, birds in the sky, and I alone in the water.
For I am a turtle named Cittacūḷa, who has attained a high station and is a favorite of the king;
do not despise me,” he said, praising his own virtues. Then Dhatarattha asked him, “For what purpose have you been sent by the king? “Great King,” [he replied].
The king said this to me: "I have established a bond of friendship with all the kings throughout Jambudīpa;
now, in order to establish a bond of friendship with Dhatarattha, the lord of the Nagas, I am giving my daughter Samuddajā to him.
Having said this, he sent me. "Without making any delay, you should send a man along with me, and having fixed the day, [proceed]."
“Take the girl! He was pleased and, having paid him honor, sent four young nāgas with him, saying, “Go;
having heard the king’s word, determine a day and come back.
They said, “Very well,” took the tortoise, and departed from the nāga realm.
Seeing a lotus pond between the Yamunā and Benares, a tortoise, wishing to escape by a certain stratagem, said:
"O young Nāgas, our king and his wives, because we feed in the water, see us as soon as we come to the royal palace and beg, saying, 'Give us lotuses!
Give us lotus roots and bulbs! For their sake, I [take them]."
“I will take it; release me here and go first to the presence of the king even without seeing me, for I shall see you right there.
Believing him, they released him. He hid himself there in a secluded spot.
The others, not seeing him, thought, “He must have gone into the presence of the king,” and [they approached] the king in the guise of young brahmins.
They approached him. The king, having offered them hospitality, asked, "From where have you come?
"From the presence of Dhatarattha, Great King. "For what purpose have you come here? "Great King, we are his messengers; Dhatarattha asks after your health.
If there is anything you desire, tell us. It is said that he wishes for your daughter..."
"Give us Samuddajā to serve as a handmaid to our king," they said, proclaiming this purpose, and spoke the first verse:
"Whatever jewels there are in the abode of Dhatarattha, let them all be yours;
give your daughter to the king."
In that regard, "May all those come to your home" means: "May all those jewels come to your residence.
Having heard this, the king spoke the second verse:
"Never before has a marriage with the Nāgas been performed by us."
"How can we perform that marriage, which is improper?

In this context, "improper" (asaṃyutta) means unsuitable, an inappropriate association with animals. "How can we," meaning "we who are of human birth, how can we form a connection with those belonging to the animal realm?
Having heard that, the young Nāgas said, "If a connection with Dhatarattha is unsuitable for you, then..."
"Why did he send a turtle named Cittacūḷa, our own attendant, to our king with the message: 'I give you my daughter, named Samuddajā'?
Having sent him thus, we shall now know what is appropriate to do for you who insult our king.
For we are young Naga princes," they said, threatening the king.
They spoke these two verses:
“Surely you have renounced your life, or perhaps your kingdom, O lord of men;
for when the Naga is enraged, such as these do not live long.”
“O King, you who are a mere human being, lacking supernatural power, you have shown contempt for Yāmuṇa, the son of Varuṇa’s sister.
In that context, “the kingdom or” means that either your life or the kingdom has been utterly abandoned by you. “Such as you” means those like you.
When a nāga of such great power is provoked, they are unable to live long; they vanish even midway.
"O King, you who are a human" means, O King, you who are a human being. "Of Varuṇa" means of the nāga king Varuṇa.
"His own son" means his biological son. "Born of the Yamunā" means born beneath the Yamunā River.
Then the king spoke these two verses:
“I do not despise King Dhatarattha, the illustrious one;
for Dhatarattha is indeed the lord of many nāgas.”
“Though he is of great power, he is not worthy of my daughter;
for Samuddajā is of noble birth, a kshatriya of the Videhas.
In this context, the phrase “even though many” was said with reference to his lordship over the Naga realm extending five hundred yojanas.
"He is not worthy of my daughter"—even though he possesses such great power, because he is of the snake species (*ahijātika*), he is not fit for my daughter.
By saying, "And a Khattiya among the Videhas," he spoke thus to show the kinsmen on his mother's side.

He was born of the sea (*samuddaja*) and was the son of the King of Videha, while my daughter was also born of the sea (*samuddajā*); thus both were of noble birth (*abhijāta*). They [were] united with one another.
“They are worthy,” he said, for she was not suitable for a snake that feeds on frogs.
Although the young Nāgas desired to kill her right there with the blast of their nostrils, they thought, “They were sent for the purpose of determining our day;
it is not right to go and kill her. We shall go, inform the King, and then find out. And so, right there—
Having vanished, she was asked by the king, "What is it, dear ones? Have you obtained the king’s daughter?
Becoming angry, she replied, "Why, Your Majesty, have you sent us here or there for no reason? Even if you wish to kill us, kill us right here!
He reviles and insults you, and exalts his own daughter out of pride in her birth. Thus she spoke.
Having spoken what was improper, they provoked the king’s anger. Commanding his own retinue to assemble, he said:
“Let the Kambalassatara elephants rise up; announce all the other elephants!
Let them set out for Bārāṇasī, and let no one cause them harm.”
In that context, "let the Kambalassataras arise" means: the Kambalassataras are the nāgas dwelling at the foot of Sineru who belong to his mother’s side;
let them arise. And as for others in the four quarters and intermediate directions, however many are obedient to my word—inform all those nāgas, go and make it known, and command them:
"Gather quickly, it is said! Thus he spoke while giving this order.
Then, when they had all assembled quickly and asked, "What shall we do, Your Majesty?", he said, "Let all those nāgas go forth to Benares.

When they replied, "Having gone there, what should be done, Sire? We shall reduce them to ashes by means of a blast from our nostrils," he—being attached in heart to the princess and not wishing for her destruction—said, "Do not..."
He said, "Do not harm anyone," meaning, "Let no one among you harm another. Or this is simply the reading.
Then the Nāgas asked, "If no human being is to be harmed, what shall we do by going there? Then, explaining to them, "Do this and that, and I too will do such-and-such," he spoke these two verses:
"In dwellings, in pits, on roads, and in crossroads..."
"Let them hang from the treetops and be spread across the gateways. I too,
with a great, all-white [elephant],
shall surround the city with my coils, striking fear into the people of Kāsi."
In that context, "in the ponds" means in lotus-pools (*pokkharaṇī*). "On the carriage-roads" means on the carriage-roads.
"Spread out" means having their bodies spread out, having become large-bodied, let them hang from these very dwellings and so forth, and from the gate-arches; let the *nāgas* do this much.
And while doing so, let them [hang] beneath and above the couches and seats in the dwelling first, and within and outside the inner and outer rooms, and in the lotus-pool.

Having fashioned massive bodies upon the surfaces of the water, along the sides of the streets and other thoroughfares, and on dry land as well, and having spread out great hoods, they hissed like blacksmiths’ bellows, making the sound "susū," and said: "Hang down!
Lie down! But for themselves, [they were not to be approached] by young children, the elderly, pregnant women, and those afflicted by sea-sickness.
"Do not show yourself to the four [kings]. I too, traveling with my entirely white and massive body, will surround the great city of Kāsi seven times with my coils;
covering it with my great hood and turning it into total darkness, I shall produce fear among the people of Kāsi and let out the sound 'Sussū!'"
Then all the nāgas did accordingly. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having heard those words of his, the many-colored uragas departed for Bārāṇasī, and they harmed no one at all.”
“In dwellings, in pits, on the streets, and in courtyards;
they hung from the tops of trees and were spread across gateways.
Seeing them hanging there, many women cried out.”
Seeing the elephant being treated as a butcher’s prize, breathing repeatedly again and again, [the people cried out]:
“Bārāṇasī is in turmoil; it has fallen into distress!
Raising their arms, they wailed: ‘Give the daughter to the king!’”
In this context, "of many colors" means they were of various colors such as blue and so forth;
for it was such forms that they fashioned. "They set out" means they entered at the time of midnight.
"They hung down" means that, according to the very method prescribed by Dhatarattha, they hung down, cutting off the movement of people at all those places. But those who had come as messengers...
Four young nāgas encircled the four legs of the king’s bed;
spreading their great hoods over his head and baring their fangs as if striking at his head with their snouts, they stood there glaring.
Dhatarattha, too, protected the city according to the method he had prescribed. When the men were about to wake, wherever they reached out their hand—
Or they stretched out their feet; having been touched by snakes here and there, they cried out, "A snake! A snake!

"They wailed in great numbers" means that in those houses where lamps were burning, the women woke up, looked at the door-frames, gateways, and rafters, and seeing the nagas hanging there, many of them wailed all at once. Thus, the entire city was filled with a single tumultuous uproar.
*Soṇḍikataṃ* means with their hoods spread out.

*Pakkandanti* means that when the night had turned to dawn, as the entire city and the royal palace were being tossed about by the breath of the nāgas as if they were blowing, the terrified people said, "Nāga kings, why do you harass us? and [said] to your king, "Your daughter..."
Having sent a messenger to Dhatarattha saying, "I will give her," and being told again by his messengers who had come back, "Give her," he reviled and abused our king.
When it was said, "If you do not give our king's daughter, there is no life for the entire city," he replied, "In that case, my lord, grant us leave; we shall go and entreat the king."
Having obtained leave to speak, they went to the king’s gate and cried out with a great clamor.
Even his wives, while still lying within their respective wombs, cried out all at once: "O King, give your daughter to King Dhatarattha!
Those four young nāgas, as if striking their heads with silence, bared their fangs, crying: "Give her!"
They stood watching.

While still lying down, he heard the sound of lamentation from the city-dwellers, his own wives, and [the others], and being terrified by the fear of death due to being threatened by the four young nāgas, he said:
"My daughter Samuddajā [I shall give] to Dhatarattha..."

"I give her," he said three times. Hearing this, all the Naga kings retreated by the measure of three gavutas and, having constructed a city there like a celestial city, they remained there and sent a gift, saying, "Let him indeed send us his daughter.
The king, having received the gifts brought by them, said, "You may go; as for me, I shall [give] my daughter to the ministers..."
Having dismissed them with the words, "I shall send him by hand," he summoned his daughter, led her up to the upper terrace of the palace, opened the lion-window, and said:
"My child, look at this adorned city! You shall become the chief queen of this king here.
That city is not far from here; whenever you feel weary, you will be able to come here, and you must go back there."
Having consoled her, bathed her head, adorned her with all manner of ornaments, and seated her in a covered carriage, he placed her in the hands of his ministers and sent her forth.
The Nāga kings came out to meet her and paid her great honor.
The ministers entered the city, delivered her to him, and returned taking much wealth with them. They [brought] the princess...
Having led her up to the palace, they laid her down upon a decorated celestial couch.
At that very moment, Nāga-maidens, assuming the guise of hunchbacks and other attendants, surrounded her like human female companions.
As soon as she lay down upon the celestial couch, she experienced a divine touch and fell into sleep.
Dhatarattha took her and, together with his retinue of nāgas, vanished from that place and appeared right there in the nāga realm.

Upon waking, the princess saw the decorated celestial bed, as well as other golden palaces, jewel palaces, and so forth, along with the park lotus ponds and the nāga realm adorned like a city of the gods;
she then asked her female attendants, such as the hunchbacked woman: "What city is this?"
“It is exceedingly well-adorned; it is not like our city. To whom does this belong? “O Queen, this belongs to your husband.
Those of little merit do not obtain such prosperity; it was obtained by you because of your great merit.
Dhatarattha also caused a drum to be beaten throughout his naga-abode, which extended five hundred yojanas, [proclaiming]: “Whoever [desires] Samuddaja in her snake-form...”
“[If] he shows [it], he shall suffer the king’s punishment. Therefore, not even a single person was able to show her the form of a snake.
With the perception that it was the human world, she lived there with him in pleasant companionship, exchanging friendly greetings.
The *Nagarakaṇḍa* is finished.
In the *Uposathakaṇḍa*:
Later on, she conceived a child by Dhataraṭṭha and gave birth to a son;
because he was beautiful to behold, they gave him the name Sudassana. Furthermore, she gave birth to another son, and they named him Datta.
Now, the Bodhisatta gave birth to another son, and they named him Subhoga. She gave birth to yet another son, and they named him Ariṭṭha.
Thus, although she had given birth to four sons, she did not know her state as a nāga-dweller.
Then one day, the young nāgas informed Ariṭṭha: "Your..."

“The mother is a human woman, not a female nāga. Thinking, “I shall test her,” one day while drinking from her breast, Ariṭṭha transformed himself into the body of a snake and struck his mother on the back of her foot with a piece of his tail.
Seeing his snake-body, she was terrified and shrieked a great cry; throwing him down upon the ground, she pierced his eye with her fingernail.
Then blood flowed out. Hearing her cry, the king asked, "What is this sound?
and upon hearing what Ariṭṭha had done, he came forward threateningly, saying, "Seize him! Take that slave and put him to death!
The princess, perceiving his anger, spoke out of maternal affection for her son: "Your Majesty, my son’s eye..."
“Since he has caused a rift, forgive his offense,” she said. The king, thinking, “What can be done about one who speaks thus?
forgave her. On that day, she realized, “This is the abode of the Nāgas. From then on, Ariṭṭha became known as Kāṇāriṭṭha.
All four sons reached the age of discretion.
Then their father, having divided the kingdom into portions of one hundred leagues each, gave it to them; thus they attained great glory.
Each was surrounded by sixteen thousand Naga maidens. Their father’s kingdom alone remained at one hundred leagues.
The three sons came to see their parents every month, but the Bodhisatta, however, came every half-month.
He comes. Only the Bodhisatta explains the questions that arise in the Nāga realm.
He also goes to attend upon the Great King Virūpakkha along with his father, and he alone explains the questions that arise in his presence.
Then one day, having gone to the city of the Thirty-three together with the assembly of Virūpakkha’s Nāgas and sitting surrounding Sakka, among the gods—
In the meantime, a question arose that no one was able to answer; however, having sat cross-legged upon his excellent throne, the Great Being himself explained it.
Then the King of the Devas, having honored him with divine fragrant flowers, said:
"Datta, you are endowed with vast wisdom equal to the earth; from this day forth, you shall be known as Bhūridatta. Thus he became "Bhūridatta."

He gave him a name. From then on, as he went to attend upon Sakka, he beheld Sakka’s magnificent prosperity—the exquisitely beautiful Vejayanta Palace adorned with celestial maidens—and having conceived a longing for the world of the gods, he thought:
"What use have I for this body of mine that feeds only on frogs? I shall go to the abode of the Nāgas and dwell there observing the Uposatha."

Thinking, "I shall perform the deeds that cause rebirth in this world of the devas," he went to the abode of the nāgas and asked his parents, "Mother and father, I wish to perform the observance-day rites. "Very well, dear son, do so;
but while performing them, do not go outside, but perform them right here in this nāga-abode in an empty celestial mansion (*vimāna*), for those who have gone outside..."
"But there is great fear for the nāgas.
Having agreed, saying "Very well," he dwelt right there in the empty celestial mansion within the royal park, observing the Uposatha vows.
Then, nāga maidens with various musical instruments in their hands surrounded him. He thought, "While I am dwelling here, my Uposatha practice..."

Thinking, "I shall reach the summit; having gone to the path of men, I will perform [my duties]," and fearing that his parents would prevent him, he did not inform them, but addressed his wives, saying: "Ladies, I am going to the world of men.
There is a banyan tree on the bank of the Yamunā; not far from it, upon the top of an anthill, I shall coil my coils and, endowed with the four factors..."
"I shall lie down after resolving upon the Uposatha and perform the Uposatha rite.

When I have performed the Uposatha rite while lying down throughout the entire night, at the very moment of sunrise, you ten women each, taking ten women with you, shall come to me in turn with musical instruments in hand;
having honored me with perfumes and flowers, you shall sing and dance."
"Take me and come right to the abode of the Nāgas," she said; and having gone there, she coiled her body upon the top of an anthill and,

having resolved upon the Uposatha endowed with its four factors, saying, "Whoever desires my skin, sinew, bone, or blood, let him take it," she lay down, manifesting a body as large as the head of a plough.
He performed the Uposatha ceremony. As soon as the dawn broke, that Nāga maiden would come, carry out his instructions exactly as they had been given, and lead him back to the Nāga realm.
While he was observing the Uposatha in this manner, a long period of time passed.
The Uposatha Section is concluded.
At that time, in the Garuḷakhaṇḍa section, a certain brahmin living in a village at the gate of Bārāṇasī went into the forest with his son named Somadatta;
having set snares, nets, and traps, he killed deer, carried the meat back on a shoulder-pole, and sold it.
He made his living. One day, having failed to obtain even as much as a lizard, he said, "Dear Somadatta, if we go with empty hands, your mother will be angry; let us take something with us.
Having said this, he went toward the place where the Bodhisatta lay in his burrow, [and saw] those who were descending into the Yamunā river to drink water.
Seeing the tracks of the deer, he said, "Father, the path of the deer is visible;
you stand back and wait, while I shall shoot the deer that has come for water. Taking up his bow, he stood at the foot of a tree, watching for the deer.
Then, at evening time, a certain deer came to drink water. He shot it.
The deer, unable to leap over it there and driven by the force of the arrows, fled with blood streaming from him.
The father and son pursued him, took some meat at the spot where he fell, and having departed from the forest, reached that banyan tree at the time of sunset.
Thinking, "Now it is not the right time; we cannot go further; let us stay right here," they placed the meat aside.
Leaving the tree, they climbed up and lay down among the branches. At dawn, the brahmin woke up and lent his ear to listen for the sound of wild animals.
At that moment, the young female nāgas arrived and prepared a flower seat for the Bodhisatta. He [climbed] onto the body of the snake...
Having made his celestial body, adorned with every ornament, vanish, he manifested it once more and sat upon a flower-seat with Sakka’s grace.
The young Naga maiden also worshipped him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings; they played celestial instruments and began dancing and singing.
Hearing that sound, the Brahmin thought, "Who could this be? I shall find out."
Having cried out, "Son! Son!", and being unable to awaken his son, he thought, "Let him sleep;
he must be exhausted. I alone shall go. Descending from the tree, he went into his presence.
Seeing him, the young Nāga maiden, together with her musical instruments, sank into the earth and returned to her own Nāga abode. The Bodhisatta was left all alone.
It came to pass. A brahmin went into his presence and, inquiring, spoke these two verses:
“In the midst of this grove where flowers are offered, who is this with blood-red eyes and broad shoulders?
And who are these ten women, well-dressed and wearing shell-bracelets and armlets, standing there in worship?”
“Who are you, O long-armed one, shining in the midst of the forest like a fire fed with ghee?
Are you some powerful *yakkha* of great influence, or perhaps a *nāga* of great majesty?
In this context, “with the offering of flowers” refers to the presentation of divine flowers brought for the purpose of worshipping the Bodhisatta.
[To one] thus endowed. Who indeed are you? "Lohitakkho" means red-eyed. "Vitatantaraṃso" means broad-shouldered.
"Kambukāyūradharā" means wearing golden ornaments. "Brahābāhū" means long-armed.
Having heard that, the Great Being thought: "Even if I were to say, 'I am one among the Sakka and others,' this person would surely believe it."
Thinking, "Today, however, it is right for me to speak only the truth," the brahmin spoke, revealing his own nature as a Nāga king:
"I am a Nāga, possessed of supernormal power, majestic and difficult to overcome;
if angered, I could consume even a prosperous kingdom with my fiery energy."
“Samuddajā was indeed my mother, and Dhatarattha was my father;
I am the youngest, Sudassana, and I am known as Bhūridatta.
In that context, *tejassī* means possessing splendor through the splendor of one’s own power. *Duratikkamo* means impossible for another to overcome.
"He would bite" means: "If I were angry, I could even bite down on a prosperous country;
by the mere falling of my fang upon the earth, through my fiery power, that entire country would be reduced to ashes," he says.
"I am the younger brother of Sudassana" means: "I am the younger brother of my elder brother, Sudassana. "The wise one" means: [he refers to] me in this way.
“They know [me] in the Nāga abode five hundred yojanas away.
Having said this, the Great Being thought: “This brahmin is fierce and harsh;
having informed the snake-charmer, he might even create an obstacle to my observance of the Uposatha. What if I were to lead him to this Nāga abode and [show him] the great...”
“By giving you glory, I shall make the Uposatha ceremony enduring. Then he said to him, “Brāhmaṇa, I will give you great glory;
the Nāga abode is delightful, come, let us go there. [The brāhmaṇa replied], “Master, I have a son;
I will come when he has gone there. Then the Great Being said to him, “Go, brāhmaṇa, bring him.”
Having said "No," he spoke while pointing out his own dwelling:
"That deep, ever-swirling, and fearsome lake you see—
this is my divine abode, many hundreds of fathoms in height."
“Do not enter the Yamunā in fear from the midst of the Nīloda forest, which resounds with the cries of peacocks and cranes; it is secure and auspicious for those who speak of safety.
Therein, *sadāvattaṃ* means a whirlpool that constantly occurs. *Bhesmaṃ* means terrifying. *Pekkhasi* refers to that which is of such a nature.
"You see the lake. It resounds with peacocks and cranes" means it is filled with the cries and warbling of peacocks and cranes dwelling in the forest thickets on both banks.
"It flows dark blue" means its water is blue. "Flowing through the middle of the forest" means flowing by way of the center of the forest.
"Enter without fear" means enter such a Yamunā river without being afraid. "As one who has done his duty" means...
“Enter the dwelling place of those who are perfected in their duties and possessed of good conduct; go, brahmin, and bring your son.
The brahmin went and, having informed his son of this matter, brought him back. Taking both of them with him, the Great Being went to the bank of the Yamunā river and, standing on the shore, said:
“O Brahmin, you have arrived there with your followers, together with your son.”
"Honored by my sensual pleasures, O Brahmin, you shall dwell in happiness.

Therein, "having arrived" means that you have reached our Nāga-abode. "By me" means honored with the sensual pleasures belonging to me. "You shall dwell" means you will live happily there in that Nāga-abode.
Having spoken thus, the Great Being, through his own supernatural power, brought both father and son to the Nāga-abode. Of them—
There, a divine body manifested. Then the Great Being, having granted them divine prosperity, gave four hundred nāga maidens to each of them.
They enjoyed that great prosperity. The Bodhisatta, too, remained heedful and performed the observance of the Uposatha.
Every half-month he went to attend upon his parents, and after delivering a discourse on the Dhamma, he departed.
Then, having gone into the presence of the brahmin and inquired after his health, he said, "Speak whatever you require;
remain here without longing and enjoy yourself. Having thus exchanged greetings with Somadatta, he returned to his own residence.
After the brahmin had lived in the Naga realm for one year, he became weary due to his meager merit.
He desired to go to the human world. To him, the nāga abode appeared like a hellish intermediate space between worlds;
his decorated palace appeared like a prison; and the decorated nāga maidens appeared like yakkhinīs.
Thinking, "I am weary of this life; I shall find out Somadatta’s mind as well," he went to him and said, "What is it, dear father?"
“Are you weary? “Why should I be weary? I am not weary; it is you who are weary, father.
“Yes, father. “For what reason? “I am weary because I do not see your mother, nor your brother and sister.
Come, dear Somadatta, let us go. Although he said, “I will not go,” he was entreated again and again by his father.
“Excellent,” he replied, accepting the proposal.
The brahmin thought, “I have already won my son’s mind;
however, if I tell Bhūridatta that I am weary, he will grant me even greater honor, and thus my departure will not take place. But by one [means]…”

Having praised his prosperity by means of skillful means, he asked, "For what reason do you abandon such prosperity and go to the world of men to perform the Uposatha observance? When he replied, "For the sake of heaven," [the teacher said],
"If even you abandon such prosperity to perform the Uposatha for the sake of heaven, how much more so should we, who live on the wealth of others?

Thinking, "I shall persuade him, saying, 'We shall maintain our livelihood; I too, having gone to the human world and seen my kinsmen, will go forth and practice the duty of a recluse,' and then he will grant me permission to depart," one day he approached him and was asked, "Brāhmaṇa, why are you dissatisfied?
He replied, "From your presence, nothing [of benefit] has come to us."
Without saying anything regarding his departure, [the Buddha] first spoke in praise of its excellence:
“The earth, level on all sides and covered with abundant tagara,
shines with its supreme greenness, strewn with *indagopaka* insects.”
“Delightful are the forest groves, delightful with the cries of swans;
there stand lotus ponds, well-constructed, with rows of blossoming flowers.
The pillars are well-fashioned into eight facets, all made of beryl.”
Palaces with a thousand pillars shine, filled with maidens.
"You have been reborn in a celestial mansion, [attained] through your own merits;
it is unconfined, auspicious, delightful, and endowed with ultimate happiness."
“I think you do not desire the celestial mansion of the Thousand-Eyed One;
for this power of yours is vast, like that of the radiant Sakka.
Therein, *samā samantapari* means all around, on every side, in all directions and quarters within this abode of yours, O Nāga.
The earth was strewn with gold, silver, gems, and pearls, and its surface was level. "The earth abounding in *tagara*" means it was endowed with many *tagara* shrubs.
"Covered with *indagopaka* insects" means covered with golden *indagopaka* insects.
"It shines with the finest green" means it shines, being covered with green-colored *dabba* grass. "Forest shrines" (*vanacetyāni*).
*Vanaghaṭā*: Forest clusters. *Opupphapaddhāti*: Water surfaces covered with lotus petals that have fallen after flowering.
*Sunimmitāti*: Well-constructed by means of the excellence of your merit. *Aṭṭhaṃsāti*:
In your residential palaces, well-fashioned octagonal pillars made of beryl were fashioned; by those pillars, your palaces possess a thousand columns along with the Naga maidens.
"They shine forth. "You have been reborn" means you have been produced in such a celestial mansion (*vimāna*).

"The mansion of the Thousand-Eyed One" refers to Sakka’s Vejayanta Palace. "For this power of yours is vast" means that because this power of yours is so extensive, you did not even aspire to Sakka’s mansion by virtue of that *uposatha* deed, let alone anything else beyond it.
“I think you are aspiring for a greater place.

Hearing this, the Great Being said, “Do not speak thus, Brahmin. Compared to the glory of Sakka, our own glory is like a mustard seed beside Mount Sineru; we are not even worth a servant of his. Having said this, he spoke the verse:
“Even by mind one cannot attain the majesty of the Radiant One;”
“While they are attending upon him, together with the gods led by Indra and exercising mastery over the Vasus.

The meaning of this is: O Brahmin, Sakka’s glory cannot be attained even by one who thinks in his mind for one, two, three, or four days, “It might be this much. Even the Four Great Kings attend upon him.
"Even the glory of the four world-protectors— the glorious ones who possess power over the Vasus and dwell with Indra as their leader while they serve those kings of the gods—
does not equal even a sixteenth part of our glory as animals.
Having spoken thus, and having heard the words, "I believe this is the palace of the Thousand-Eyed One," I [addressed] him.
I recollected: "For I perform the Uposatha observance desiring the Vejayanta Palace. Thus, declaring his own aspiration, he said:
"Longing for that celestial mansion, seeking the bliss of the immortals, I dwell upon the summit of the anthill while observing the Uposatha."
Therein, "coveting" means having longed for. "Of the immortals" means of the long-lived deities. "Seeking happiness" means those who have sought happiness and are established in happiness.
Having heard this, the brahmin, filled with joy, thinking, "Now I have found my opportunity," spoke these two verses while asking permission to depart:
"And I, seeking deer, entered the forest together with my son."
"Whether dead or alive, our kinsmen do not recognize me.
'I call upon Bhūridatta, the illustrious son of Kāsī:
permitted by you, may we at least see our kinsmen.'"

In that context, "they do not understand" means they do not know; even when it is explained to them, they have no comprehension. "I address" means I am addressing [you]. "Son of Kāsī" means the son of the daughter of the King of Kāsī.
Then the Bodhisatta said:
"Indeed, such is my desire that you should dwell in my presence."
“Indeed, such pleasures as these are not easily obtained among humans.
‘If you desire a dwelling honored by my pleasures,
and if you are permitted by me, may you see your kinsmen in safety.’”

Having spoken these two verses, the Great Being thought: "This man, living happily by means of this jewel, will not tell anyone [of its power]. I shall give him this jewel that grants all desires. Then, as he was giving it to him, he said:
"Maintain this divine jewel; you will find cattle and sons.
You will be healthy and happy; go, O Brahmin, taking it with you."
In that regard, "he finds cattle and sons" means that by wearing this jewel, through its power, he obtains cattle, sons, and whatever else he desires—all of it.
Then the brahmin spoke this verse:
"I welcome your skillful words, Bhūridatta."
“I am old; I shall go forth into homelessness; I do not long for sensual pleasures. The meaning of this is:
“Bhūridatta, your words are wholesome and blameless; I welcome them and do not reject them. However, I am old, therefore I shall go forth; I do not long for sensual pleasures.
What use have I for a jewel? Thus spoke the Bodhisatta.
“If there is a failure in the holy life, it must be remedied with wealth;
come without wavering, and I will give you much money.
In this context, “if there is a failure” means that living the holy life is difficult, and for one who finds no delight in the holy life...
"When there is a collapse [of the kingdom], then it must be dealt with by one who has become a householder through his wealth;
at such a time, you may come to me without hesitation, and I will give you much wealth.
The brahmin said:
“I welcome your words, Bhūridatta, which are wholesome;
I shall come again, if there should be need.
In this context, *punapi* means “again indeed,” or rather, this is simply the reading.
Then, knowing his desire not to remain there, the Great Being commanded the young nāgas and sent the brahmin back to the human world. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having said this, Bhūridatta dispatched four men, saying:
‘Come, go! Arise! Quickly send the brahmin back.’”
“Having heard those words of his, four men rose up;
sent by Bhūridatta, they quickly brought [the Brahmin] there, O Brāhmaṇa.

In this context, “they brought him” means that after bringing him out from the Yamunā river, they led him onto the road to Bārāṇasī. And having led him there, they said, “You may go,” and returned once more to the Nāga realm.
The Brahmin also, pointing out to his son, "Dear Somadatta, we have shot a deer at this spot,
and a boar at that one," saw a lotus pond along the way and said, "Dear Somadatta, let us bathe. When the other replied, "Very well,
father," they both removed their celestial ornaments and celestial garments, folded them into a bundle, and [proceeded].
Having set them down on the bank of the lotus pond, they descended and bathed. At that moment, those [weapons] vanished and returned to the Nāga realm itself.
First, the saffron-colored rags they had been wearing were fastened back onto their bodies, and their bows, arrows, and spears also became as they were before.
Somadatta lamented, "We have been ruined by you, father! Then his father said to him, "Do not..."
He thought, "While deer are present in the forest, we shall make our living by killing deer," and thus he reassured him.
When Somadatta’s mother heard of their arrival, she went out to meet them, led them home, and refreshed them with food and drink.
After the brahmin had eaten, he fell asleep. The other woman asked her son, "Dear one, where have you been for all this time?"
“Mother, we were led to the Naga realm by the Naga king Bhūridatta;
having grown weary of that, we have now returned. “But did you bring back any treasure? “We brought nothing back, Mother.
“Was nothing given to you by him? “Mother, Bhūridatta gave my father a jewel that grants all desires, but by this—”
“He has not taken it. “For what reason? “It is said he will go forth into homelessness.

She, becoming angry—thinking, “After living in the Naga palace bearing the burden of these children for so long, he is now reportedly going to go forth!”—struck him on the back with a rice-husking ladle and cried, “Hey, you wicked Brahmin! ‘I am going to go forth,’ you say, yet you do not take the jewel-treasure!”
Then he rebuked her, saying, "Why have you not gone forth [into homelessness] but come here? Leave my house at once!

Then he said to her, "My dear lady, do not be angry; since there are deer in the forest, I shall support you there," and having gone to the forest with his son, he maintained his livelihood according to their former custom.

At that time, in the direction of the great southern ocean, a certain garuḷa dwelling in a *simbali* tree stirred up the water of the sea with the wind of his wings and seized a nāga king by the head. For at that time, the supaṇṇas did not yet know how to seize a nāga;
it was only later, in the *Paṇḍara-jātaka*, that they learned. Having seized him by the head, he lifted him up without even letting the water overflow.

Taking the one who was hanging down, he set out across the slopes of the Himālaya. At that time, a certain brahmin living in the kingdom of Kāsi had gone forth into the ascetic life and was dwelling in a leaf-hut built in a region of the Himālaya.
At the edge of his walking path stood a great banyan tree; he would spend his midday rest beneath its root. A supaṇṇa [flew] over the top of the banyan tree...
He seized the nāga. As the nāga hung there, seeking liberation, he coiled his tail around a branch of a banyan tree.
The supaṇṇa, unaware of this, flew up into the sky by virtue of his great strength. The banyan tree was uprooted along with its roots.
The supaṇṇa led the nāga to a forest of *simbali* trees, struck him with his beak, tore open his belly, and ate the nāga’s fat.
He cast his body into the belly of the ocean. As the *nigrodha* tree fell, it made a great sound.
The supaṇṇa, wondering, "What is this sound?", looked down and saw the *nigrodha* tree.
Thinking, "From where was this uprooted by me?", he realized its true nature: "This is the *nigrodha* at the edge of the ascetic’s walking path; this tree has been of great benefit to him."
“‘Have I been intent upon what is unwholesome, or not? I shall find out by asking him myself.
Thinking thus, he went into his presence in the guise of a young brahmin.
At that moment, the ascetic was leveling that spot of ground. The king of the supaṇṇas paid homage to the ascetic and stood to one side.
Sitting there as if he did not know, he asked, "Venerable sir, what is this place? [The Buddha replied:
"Lay follower, a certain garuḍa, while carrying off a nāga for food, was encircled by the nāga’s tail around a banyan branch so that he might escape;
yet, because of his own great strength, he flew away. Then the banyan tree was uprooted—this is its [remains]."
“...the place where it was plucked out. “But, venerable sir, what unwholesome kamma does that supaṇṇa possess, or does he not?

“If he did not know [what he was doing], then an action performed without awareness is not called unwholesome. “And what about the nāga, venerable sir? “He did not seize him for the purpose of destroying him;
he seized him for the sake of his release. Therefore, that [unwholesome kamma] does not exist for him either. Thus spoke the supaṇṇa.
Pleased with the ascetic, he said, “Venerable sir, I am that king of the supaṇṇas. I am indeed satisfied by your explanation of the question.
You dwell in the forest, and I know a certain Alampāyana spell; it is a priceless spell.
I give it to you as the teacher’s fee; please accept it. [The ascetic replied,] “I have no need for the spell; go.”
"to you. Having entreated him again and again, and having obtained his consent, he gave him the mantra, explained the medicinal herbs, and departed.
The Chapter on the Garuḷas is finished.
The Chapter on Play.
At that time in Bārāṇasī, there was a certain poor brahmin who, having contracted a great debt and being pressed by his creditors, thought, "What is the use of my living here?
It would be better for me to enter the forest and die.
Having departed and entered the forest, he eventually reached that hermitage and won over the ascetic through the perfection of his service. The ascetic [thought], "This brahmin..."
Thinking, "He has been of great assistance to me; I shall give him the divine spell granted by the King of Supaṇṇas," he said, "Brāhmaṇa, I know the Alampāyana spell; I will give it to you, take it.
Although [the brāhmaṇa] replied, "Enough, venerable sir, I have no need for the spell," [the teacher] spoke again and again, pressing him until he finally consented.
He gave it to him. He then explained all the medicinal herbs suitable for that mantra as well as the entire ritual procedure for its application.
The brahmin, thinking, "I have found the means to my life," stayed for a few days. Then, making the pretext, "Venerable sir, a wind ailment afflicts me," he was dismissed by the ascetic;
having paid homage and asked for forgiveness, he departed from the forest and proceeded by stages.
Having reached the bank of the Yamunā, he proceeded along the great highway reciting that mantra.

At that time, about a thousand young female nāgas who were attendants of Bhūridatta emerged from the nāga-abode, took that wish-fulfilling jewel (maṇiratana), and having set it down upon a heap of sand on the bank of the Yamunā, [they departed]. For him—
Having spent the entire night playing in the water, they emerged at the rising of the sun, adorned with all their ornaments;
surrounding the jewel-treasure, they sat down as if ushering in prosperity. The brahmin also arrived at that place while reciting his mantras.
Hearing the sound of the mantras, the women thought, "This must be the Supaṇṇa," and were struck with the fear of death.
Without taking the jewel-treasure, they sank into the earth and went to the abode of the Nāgas.
The brahmin, too, having seen the jewel-treasure, thought with a joyful heart, "My spell has succeeded this very moment," and taking the jewel-treasure, he set out.
At that moment, the hunter-brahmin Somadatta, who was entering the forest with him for the purpose of hunting deer, [saw it] in his hand.
Seeing that jewel-gem, he said to his son, "Dear son, was this not the gem given to us by Bhūridatta?
"Yes, father, this is the gem. "Therefore, having spoken of its defects and deceived this brahmin, take this jewel-gem.
"Father, previously when it was being given by Bhūridatta, I did not accept it; but now, as for this brahmin—"
"He will surely deceive him; remain silent. The brahmin said, "Let it be, my son;
you see the deceptive nature of either him or me," and while conversing with Alampāyana, he spoke:
"Having taken up this auspicious gem, so excellent, wealthy, and delightful..."
“Whose is this jewel, flawless and endowed with beauty? Who has found this gem?
Therein, “auspicious” means it is regarded as auspicious and grants all desires. “Who has found this? means: where have you obtained this gem?
Then Alampāyana spoke this verse:
“Surrounded on all sides by a thousand red-eyed women, today as I was going along the road at the time of daybreak, I obtained this jewel.
The meaning of this is: today, while I was going along the path—the way—at the very time of dawn, surrounded by about a thousand red-eyed women...
"He has obtained this jewel while surrounded on all sides by Naga maidens. For upon seeing me, they were all terrified with fear and fled, leaving it behind.
Desiring to deceive him and wishing to take the jewel for himself, the Brahmin Nesāda spoke these three verses, proclaiming the jewel’s lack of merit:
“This stone has been well-prepared, always honored and revered;
well-maintained and properly placed, it shall succeed in every undertaking.
But for one whose conduct is impaired, whether in the placing or the maintaining [of the stone],”
“This rock, having been improperly cultivated, leads to destruction.
‘This unskilled man is not worthy to wear this divine gem;
follow the path of the virtuous, give me this jewel.’”

In this context, "in all respects" means that for one who knows how to properly attend to, honor, cherish as one's own life, maintain, and store away this rock, it is well-attended to, honored, cherished, maintained, and stored;
the meaning is that this rock accomplishes every purpose for him alone. However, for one whose attendance has failed...
"He has failed in his conduct; this [jewel] of his, having been handled by an improper means, leads only to destruction," he says. "It is worthy to be kept" means it is fit to be preserved.
"Accept a hundred *nikkhas*": "There are many jewels in our house; we know how to handle them.
I will give you a hundred *nikkhas*; accept that, and give me this precious jewel."
Indeed, there was not even a single gold coin in his house; however, he knew that the jewel had the power to grant all desires.
Therefore, it occurred to him: "I shall bathe with my head, sprinkle the jewel with water, and say, 'Give me a hundred coins.
Then it will give them to me, and I shall give them to him. Thus, being resolute, he spoke as follows.
Then Alampāyana spoke this verse:
“This gem of mine is not for sale, Neither for cows nor for jewels;
This stone, perfect in its markings, Is no gem to be sold by me.”
In that regard, "nor do they beg from me" means: "This jewel is mine; it is not something that can be sold by anyone.
"Nor is it to be bartered" means: "This jewel of mine is endowed with auspicious marks; therefore, it is not to be bartered or sold for anything whatsoever.
The Nesāda brahmin said:
“If that jewel is not to be sold for cattle or for treasures, then for what is that jewel to be sold? Tell me that when I ask you.
Alampāyana replied:
“Whoever has praised me as a Great Naga, radiant and difficult to overcome—
to him I would give this rock, as if blazing with radiance.
In that context, “as if blazing with radiance” means as if blazing with light.
The Brahmin hunter said:
“Who indeed, in the guise of a brahmin, is this supreme of winged creatures as he flies?
Seeking to seize a nāga, he searches for his own food.”
In this context, "Who indeed?"—this was said by the Nisāda-brāhmaṇa after he thought, "He must be a Garuḍa searching for his own food.
Alampāyana spoke thus:
"I am not the lord of birds; I have never seen a Garuḍa."
"O Brahmin, the wise know me as a physician who has been bitten by a venomous snake.
Therein, "the wise know me" means they know me thus: "This physician named Alampāyana has been bitten by a venomous snake.
The Nesāda Brahmin said:
“What fruit do you have? What craft is yours?
Or upon what are you so haughty that you do not show reverence to the serpent?

In this context, “Or upon what are you so haughty? means: being supported by what, relying on what support, do you not show reverence—that is, do you disregard—the serpent, the venomous snake, failing to treat it as your elder? Thus he asks.
Thus, demonstrating his own power, he said:
“To the forest-dwelling seer, long practiced in austerity,
the Supaṇṇa Kosiyasakkha taught the unsurpassed science of poisons.”
“On another occasion, that one of developed self was wandering correctly among the mountains;
I attended upon him with care, untiring by day and night.
At that time, he was well-served by me, living the holy life according to his instructions.”
“The Blessed One has revealed to me the divine mantra for the sake of my desires.
“Arrogant on account of those mantras, I do not fear the serpents;
I am known as Alampāna, the teacher of those who destroy poison.”
Therein, "Kosiya's son" refers to the Supaṇṇa who declared [the mantra] to the seer of the Kosiya clan.
The entire account of how it was declared should be related in detail. "A certain one of those with developed minds" means a certain one among the seers whose minds were developed.
"Dwelling" means residing there. "By his own desire" means according to his own wish. "To me" means he revealed that mantra to me.
"Relying on those mantras, O Brahmin, I am supported by them"—meaning I depend upon those mantras. "Bhogins" refers to the nāgas.
"Visaghātānaṃ" refers to physicians who destroy poison.
Having heard this, the Nesāda Brahmin thought: "This Alampāyana [must have] the jewel-treasure of that one who shows him the nāga."
“Having shown Bhūridatta to him, we shall take the jewel,” he thought. Then, consulting with his son, he spoke this verse:
“Let us take the jewel, dear father; O Somadatta, understand this!
Let us not abandon our fortune, which has come to us by chance, for the sake of punishment.”
In that context, "let us seize" means let us take hold. "By our own will" means let us not let him go, having struck him with a staff according to our own desire.
Somadatta said:
"O Brahmin, he who honors one who has reached his own home..."
“Why do you, out of delusion, desire misfortune for one who acts so virtuously?
‘If you desire wealth, Bhūridatta will see you;
go to him and beg, and he will give you much wealth.’”
In that context, "he worshipped" means he worshipped with divine sensual pleasures. "Do you wish to betray? means, "O dear one, do you wish to commit an act of betrayal against such a friend?
The brahmin said:
"It is better to eat what has come into one's hand, what has come into one's bowl, or what is scattered on the ground."
“May the visible benefit not elude us, Somadatta!”— therein,
“that which has come into my hand,” dear Somadatta, you are young and do not understand the ways of the world.
For whatever has come into my hand, or has come into my bowl, or has been placed before me and set out— that alone is for me to eat.
“Better [not to see] one standing nearby than one standing far away.
Somadatta said:
“One is cooked in the terrible hell; even the great earth opens up.”
“Betraying friends and abandoning those who are well-wishers, he withers away even while still living.
‘If you desire wealth, Bhūridatta will show it to you;
I think you will experience before long the enmity you have wrought against yourself.’”
"In that regard, 'he opens even the earth' means, dear one, that for a betrayer of friends, the earth itself splits open and provides a fissure while he is still alive.
'One who abandons his own welfare' means one who gives up his own well-being. 'He withers even while living' means that while still alive, he withers away and becomes a hungry ghost (manussapeta).
'Enmity created by oneself' refers to the evil committed by oneself. 'Not long' means I believe you will experience the result very soon."
The brahmin said:
"Having performed a great sacrifice, thus are the brahmins purified;
we shall perform a great sacrifice, thus shall we be released from evil."
"In this regard, they say they are purified, dear Somadatta; you are young and know nothing. The brahmins, having committed whatever evil, speak thus to show that they are purified by sacrifice.
Somadatta said:
"Come now, I shall depart; I will not stay with you today."
“I shall not go to the place of execution, being such an evildoer. Having spoken thus,
the wise young man, unable to persuade his father to accept his words, [departed] with great...
Having caused the deity to be distressed by his noise, she thought, "I will not go with such an evildoer," and even as her father looked on, she fled, entered the Himalayas, and went forth.
Having attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), she was reborn in the Brahma-world without falling away from her jhāna.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having said this to his father, the learned Somadatta, having reproached the spirits, departed from that place.
The Brahmin Nesāda, thinking, “Where will Somadatta go, other than to his own home? [approached] Alampāyana...
Seeing him somewhat dejected, he said, "Alampāyana, do not worry; I shall show Bhūridatta to you.
Taking him with him, he went to the place where the Naga king was observing the Uposatha.
Seeing the Naga king lying there with his coils folded upon the summit of an anthill, he stood nearby, extended his hand, and spoke these two verses:
“Seize this Great Naga! Bring me that jewel, which has the luster of an *indagopaka* insect and a crimson head.
This body appears like a heap of cotton pods.”
“He lies at the top of an anthill; seize him, O Brahmin!

Therein, “shining with the color of an *indagopaka* insect” means it appears like the color of an *indagopaka*. “Like a heap of well-arranged *kappāsa* pods” means like a pile of well-ordered cotton pods.
Then the Great Being, opening his eyes and seeing the hunter-Brahmin, thought: “This man will create an obstacle for my Uposatha.”
"Should he do so? [I replied: "Having led him to this abode of the Nāgas, I established him in great prosperity.
He did not wish to accept the jewel being offered by me. But now he is coming, having taken the snake-charmer with him.
If I were to become angry with this betrayer of friends, my virtue would be broken. For I have already, from the very beginning, been endowed with the four factors..."
Having thought, "The Uposatha has been undertaken; let it remain exactly as it was undertaken.

Whether Alampāyana cuts me, cooks me, or pierces me with a stake, I shall not be angry with him," he closed his eyes, thinking, "If I were to look at these men, they would turn to ashes. Even while they strike me, I will not be angry and I will not look."
Having made the perfection of resolve his forerunner, he thrust his head into the midst of the wealth and lay down perfectly motionless.
The Brahmin Nesāda said, "O Alampāyana, seize this Nāga and give me the jewel.
Seeing the Nāga, Alampāyana was delighted; disregarding anything else, he placed the jewel in the Brahmin's hand, saying, "Take it, Brahmin!"
He threw it. It slipped from his hand and fell upon the earth. As soon as it had fallen, it entered the earth and went straight to the abode of the Nāgas.
Thus the brahmin was deprived of three things: the jewel-treasure, his friendship with Bhūridatta, and his son.
Thus lamenting, "I am born without my son; I have not done as my son’s word bade," he went home.
Alampāyana, too, having smeared his own body with divine medicines, having eaten a little and sprinkled them over his frame, approached the Bodhisatta while reciting a divine mantra;
seizing him by the tail, he dragged him and [reached] his head.
Seizing him firmly, he opened the dragon king’s mouth, administered the medicine, and spat phlegm into it.
Out of fear of breaking his virtue, the Naga king Sucijātaka did not become angry and did not even open his eyes.
Then, having made the medicine effective with mantras, he seized him by the tail, turned him upside down, shook him, made him vomit up the food he had taken, and [threw him] onto the ground.
Having laid him out lengthwise, he crushed him with his feet as if kneading a cushion; the bones became as if ground into powder.
Then, seizing him by the tail, he thrashed him as if beating a cloth.
Even while experiencing such suffering, the Great Being did not become angry. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“With divine medicinal herbs, with chanting, and with mantra-words—thus he was able to take hold of the Teacher by performing a protective rite for himself.
In this context, *asakkhi* means “was able”; *satthuṃ* means “to take hold of.”
Thus, having weakened the Great Being, he prepared a chest with creepers and cast the Great Being inside; however, because of the Great Being’s great size, he could not fit within it.

Then, striking him with his heel, he forced him in, took the chest, went to a certain village, set it down in the middle of the village, and cried out: "Let those who wish to see the dance of the Naga come!"
He made a sound. All the inhabitants of the village gathered together. At that moment, Alampāyana said, "Come out, Great Nāga!
The Great Being thought: "Today it is fitting for me to play so as to delight the assembly.
In this way, Alampāyana will obtain much wealth and, being satisfied, will release me. Whatever he makes me do, I shall do it."
Then, having pulled it out from the basket, he said, "Become great! It became great:
small, round, shelled, with one hood, two hoods, three hoods, four hoods, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty hoods, a hundred hoods; tall, short, with a visible body.
“Be invisible-bodied; be visible-bodied with only half your form; be blue, yellow, red, or white; be like a flame of saffron;
emit flames of fire; emit water and smoke. The Great Being, manifesting his physical form in each of these modes as they were described, performed a dance.
Upon seeing this, no one was able to restrain their tears.
People gave him much gold, silver, clothing, ornaments, and so forth. Thus, he received about a thousand pieces of money in that village.

Although he had said, "When I have caught the Great Being, I will release him after receiving a thousand," once he had obtained that wealth, he thought, "Even in this small village I have already received such great wealth; they say that in the city..."
Thinking, "I shall obtain much," he did not release him out of greed for wealth.
Having established a household in that village, he had a casket made of jewels, placed the Great Being inside it, and mounting a comfortable carriage with a great retinue, he set out.
Entertaining him as they traveled through villages, market towns, and other places, he eventually reached Benares.
He gave honeyed cakes to the Nāga king, and having killed frogs, he gave them to him; yet the Nāga did not take his food out of fear of not being released.
Even though he would not take his food, the king had him play here and there for about a month, beginning from the four gate-villages.
Then, on the fifteenth day of the Uposatha, the king said, "Today I shall have you play in your presence."
He caused it to be announced. The king, having had a drum beaten throughout the city, assembled the great multitude. They constructed tiered platforms in the royal courtyard.
The section on the games was concluded.
Now begins the section on the entry into the city.

On the very day Alambāyana took the Bodhisatta, the mother of the Mahāsatta saw in a dream a dark man with red eyes who, having severed her right arm with a sword, was carrying it away while blood flowed profusely.
Terrified and trembling, she rose up, touched her right arm, and realized it was a dream. Then, for her—
He thought: "I have seen a harsh and evil dream; there must be some obstacle for either my four sons, or for King Dhatarattha, or for myself.
However, he reflected even more intensely concerning the Great Being alone.
For what reason? Because the others dwell in their own naga-abodes, whereas the other [the Great Being] possesses a disposition toward virtue (*sīla*).
Having gone to the human world, he performs the Uposatha rites. Therefore, he thought even more intensely:
"I wonder if a snake-charmer or a Supaṇṇa might have seized my son? Then, when half a month had passed, [he thought]:
"My son cannot endure being apart from me for more than half a month; surely some danger has befallen him."
Thinking, "He will come now," she became overcome with grief. After the passing of a month, there was no longer even time for tears to flow from her due to her sorrow;
her heart grew parched and her eyes became sealed shut.
Thinking, "He will arrive now, he will arrive now," she sat watching the very path by which he would come. Then her eldest son, Sudassana—
At the end of a month, he arrived with a large retinue to visit his parents.
Setting the assembly outside, he ascended the palace, paid homage to his mother, and stood to one side.
Grieving for Bhūridatta, she did not speak anything at all with him. He thought: "In the past, when I arrived, my mother was pleased."
“[Usually] she offers me hospitality, but today she has fallen into dejection; what indeed could be the reason? Then, questioning her, he said:
“Having seen me approaching, though I am one who has all desires fulfilled, my faculties are unexcited and your face has become sorrowful.”
“Just as a foot is placed in the hand and rubbed by the palm, so has your face become discolored upon seeing me in such a state.
In this context, *ahaṭṭhāni* means not clear or bright. *Sāvaṃ* means your face has become yellowish-black, like the color of a golden mirror.
"Born. "In hand" means cut by the hand. "'Such as this'—having seen me, who have come for the purpose of being seen by you, possessing such great glory and splendor.

Even when this was said, she did not speak at all. Sudassana thought, "Could it be that she is angry with someone, or perhaps bound by some obligation? Then, questioning her, he spoke the following verse:
“Are you not being reviled? Are you in pain?
For what reason has your face become so dejected upon seeing me?
In this context, “Are you not being reviled? means: are you not being assailed by anyone with abuse or reproach?
Or he asks, "Have you been harmed? He asks, "Tuyhaṃ" means: "This face of yours was not like this when you came before seeing me;
tell me the reason why your face has become so pale today.
Then, as she explains it to him, she says:
“Father, I saw a dream this month ago:
‘A man, having cut off my right arm as it were and smeared it with blood, departed while I was weeping.’”
“Since I saw that dream, Sudassana, understand this:
from that time on, whether by day or by night, no happiness has been found for me.
In this context, “a month has passed since then” means a month has elapsed from below that point; today is the month of the dream I saw.
This shows that [it] occurs. "A man" refers to a certain dark-skinned man with red eyes. "While she was weeping" means while she was in the state of weeping.
"'Happiness is not found for me' means that what is called my happiness does not exist.
Having spoken thus, she lamented, saying: "Dear father, my beloved little son is not seen; surely some danger must have arisen for him. Thus she spoke.
“He whom those maidens of radiant form once surrounded,
now hidden by a golden net— Bhūridatta is not seen.
He whom those who bear the finest diadems once surrounded...”
"The kaṇikāra trees are in full bloom, yet Bhūridatta is not to be seen.
Come now, let us go to Bhūridatta’s residence;
let us see your brother, who stands firm in the Dhamma and is perfected in virtue."

Therein, "in full bloom" means like *kaṇikāra* trees in full flower because she was adorned with garments and ornaments of gold. "Handa" is a particle used for emphasis; he said, "Come, dear one, let us go to Bhūridatta’s dwelling.
Having spoken thus, he went there together with him and his own retinue.
But Bhūridatta’s wives, not seeing him at the top of the anthill, were unconcerned, thinking, "He will be staying at his mother’s dwelling."
Hearing that their mother-in-law was coming because she could not find her son, they went out to meet her,
wailing with great lamentation, "Noble lady, a month has passed today since your son disappeared," and fell at her feet.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
Seeing Bhūridatta’s mother approaching,
the women of Bhūridatta raised their arms and wailed aloud: “O lady,
we have not seen your son for a month since he went down from here.”
“Whether dead or alive, the illustrious Bhūridatta.
In this context, “Putta teyya” refers to their lamentation.

Having lamented in the middle of the street together with her daughters-in-law, Bhūridatta’s mother took them and ascended his palace; there, looking upon her son’s bed and seat, she spoke while lamenting:
“Like a bird whose young have been killed, seeing her nest empty,
I shall brood for a long time in sorrow, not seeing Bhūridatta.
Like a kurarī bird whose chicks have been killed, seeing her nest empty...”
“I shall long brood in sorrow, not seeing Bhūridatta.
Surely like a female cakravāka bird in a pond without water,
I shall long brood in sorrow, not seeing Bhūridatta.”
“Just as the forge-fire of smiths glows within but not without, so do I burn with grief, not seeing Bhūridatta.
In this context, *apassatī* means “not seeing. *Hatachāpāvā* means “like those whose young have been killed.”
Thus, while Bhūridatta’s mother was lamenting, the entire residence became as silent as the interior of the ocean;
not even a single person was able to remain composed in their own nature.
The whole dwelling became like a grove of *sāla* trees struck by the winds from Mount Yugandhara. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Crushed like a sala tree and trampled by a māluva creeper, children and wives lie there in the dwelling of Bhūridatta.

Having heard that sound, both brothers Ariṭṭha and Subhoga went to attend upon their parents; entering the dwelling of Bhūridatta, they comforted their mother. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having heard this cry at the residence of Bhūridatta, Ariṭṭha and Subhoga ran out immediately.
‘Mother, take heart, do not grieve; for such is the nature of living beings.’”
“They pass away and they are reborn; this is his transformation.

Regarding that, “this is his transformation” means that this passing away and rebirth is the transformation of this world, for it is in this way that the world transforms. They say that there is no one who is exempt from these two factors.
Samuddajā said:
“I too know this, dear father: for such is the nature of living beings;
when one is overcome by grief, one does not see Bhūridatta.
If you would know it, Sudassana, even as I pass this night today,” he said.
"If I do not see Bhūridatta, I think I shall give up my life.
Therein, "If today, dear Sudassana," means: "If today, during this night, Bhūridatta does not come into my sight, then I think that not seeing him, I shall abandon my life.
The sons said:
“Mother, take heart and do not grieve; we shall bring back our brother.
We will go in every direction, wandering in search of our brother.
We shall search among the mountains, in inaccessible crags, in villages, and in market towns.”
