“Wait for seven days; see your brother returned.
Thereupon they comforted him, saying, “Mother, we three shall go in every direction, wandering about in search of our brother.
Then Sudassana thought: “If all three of us go in one direction, it will cause delay. By the three of us—”
"It is fitting to go to three places: one to the world of the gods, one to the Himalayas, and one to the human world.
But if Kāṇāriṭṭha goes to the human world, he will go wherever he sees Bhūridatta;
having burned that village or town, he will depart. He is cruel and harsh; it is not possible to send him there."

Having reflected thus, he sent Ariṭṭha to the world of the gods, saying, "Dear Ariṭṭha, you go to the world of the gods; if Bhūridatta has been led there by the deities who wish to hear the Dhamma, then bring him back from there.
To Subhoga, however, he said, "Dear one, go to the Himālaya mountains, search for Bhūridatta among the five great rivers, and then return."
He sent [his son] to the Himālayas. But he himself, desiring to go to the world of men, thought:
"If I go in the guise of a young brahmin, people will not hold me dear; it is better that I go in the dress of an ascetic, for among men, those who have gone forth are beloved and pleasing.
Having assumed the dress of an ascetic and paid homage to his mother, he departed.
Now, the Bodhisatta had a half-sister named Ajamukhī, who felt an exceeding affection for him.
Seeing him going to Sudassana, she said, "Brother, I am very weary; I too will go with you.
"Mother, it is not possible for you to go; I am going as one who has gone forth into homelessness."
"But I shall go by becoming a small female frog and lying within your matted hair. "In that case, come," he said.
That little female frog became a tiny frog and lay within his matted hair.
Sudassana, thinking, "I will go searching from the very roots," asked the Bodhisatta’s wives where they went to observe the Uposatha.

Having first gone there, and seeing the blood and the place where the basket had been made from creepers at the spot where the Great Being had been seized by Alampāyana, he realized, "Bhūridatta has been captured by the snake-charmer.
Filled with grief, his eyes brimming with tears, he followed the very path taken by Alampāyana back to the village where he had first played, and asked Manassa: "Was such a one..."
“Was the nāga named Nāma being made to play by some snake-charmer here? “Yes, he was made to play by Alampāyana about a month ago.
“Did he receive any money for it? “Yes, he received about a thousand [pieces] right here.
“Where has he gone now? “To a village called Such-and-such. From that point on, asking his way, he eventually arrived at the king’s gate.
At that moment, Alampāyana, having bathed and anointed himself and put on a polished robe, had a casket of jewels carried and went straight to the palace gate.
A great crowd gathered, and a seat was prepared for the king. While still standing within his residence, he sent word:
"I am coming; let them play with the Nāga king. Alampāyana placed the casket of jewels upon a spread of cloth.
Setting it aside and opening it, he gave the signal, "Come, Great Nāga! At that time, Sudassana was also standing within the assembly.
Then the Great Being extended his head and surveyed the entire assembly. For Nāgas survey an assembly for two reasons:
either to anticipate an obstacle from a Supaṇṇa or to see their kinsmen. They [saw] the Supaṇṇa...
Seeing this, they did not dance out of fear; nor did they dance when seeing their kinsmen, out of shame.
But the Great Being, looking about, saw his brother within the assembly. Taking up tears that filled his eyes, he emerged from the chest and set out toward his brother.
When the great multitude saw him approaching, they were terrified and retreated, except for Sudassana alone, who remained standing there.
Having gone there, he placed his head upon the elephant's hind feet and wept; Sudassana also lamented.
The Great Being, having wept, turned back and entered the very same box. Alampāyana also approached, thinking, "This ascetic must have been bitten by this elephant;
I shall comfort him," and said:
“The serpent, released from its hand, has fallen heavily at your feet;
did it perhaps bite you, dear one? Do not fear, may you be well.
Therein, “Do not fear”: “Dear ascetic, I am named Alampāyana; do not fear, for the care of you is my burden.”
Sudassana, wishing to converse with him, spoke this verse:
“This serpent is not mine; it is enough for anyone’s suffering.
As long as there is grasping at a self, nothing more exists than that.”
In this regard, he thought: "I am incapable of producing even the slightest bit of physical pain for anyone. Indeed, there is no snake-charmer equal to me.
Not knowing that it was someone named Alampāyana, the latter became angry and said:
"Who is this who has entered the assembly, arrogant and disguised as a brahmin?"
"Let them challenge me with fair combat; let the assembly hear me!
In this context, "proud" (ditta) means arrogant, a fool whose knowledge is blind. "Let them challenge" (avhāyantu) means challenging; or rather, this very reading [avhāyanto] is the correct one.
This is what is meant: "What fool is this, like a madman, challenging me to fair combat while [speaking] to himself?"
"Acting with impartiality, I have come to this assembly: 'Let the assembly hear my words; I have no fault; do not be angry with me.
Then Sudassana addressed him in verse:
"You seized me by the trunk, O elephant; I seized you by the tail, O frog."
"Let there be a wonder for us there, even with five thousand!"—in this regard, "with a nāga" means:
"You fight with me as a nāga; I shall fight with you as a frog-catcher. "Even with five thousand" means: "In that battle of ours, let there be a wonder [lasting] up to five thousand [years].
Thus spoke Alampāyana.
“I am indeed wealthy, O Vasumā, while you, young man, are poor.
Who then could be your guarantor, and what could be your stake?
If I were to have both a stake and such a guarantor as you, [I would play].”
"Let there be no wonder for you there, even with five thousand.
In this context, "Who indeed is yours? means: who indeed is there as a guarantor (*pāṭibhoga*) for you who have gone forth?
And "the stake in the game" (*upajūtaṃ*): what kind of wealth could you possibly have as a deposit in this game of dice? He says, "Show it to me. And "the stake in the game" (*upajūtaṃ*).
"But as for me, I have either a deposit of wealth to be given, or a guarantor of such a kind;
therefore, let there be no ordeal for us there, even with five thousand [pieces of gold].

Having heard his words, Sudassana, undaunted by the thought, "Let there be an ordeal for us with five thousand," ascended the royal palace, stood before his maternal uncle the king, and spoke this verse:
“Listen to my words, O Great King; may it be well with you!
For I am the renowned guarantor for five thousand [men].
In this context, “renowned” (*kittima*) means endowed with the renown of virtues—the renown of various virtuous qualities and conduct.
The king, thinking, "This ascetic asks me for an excessive amount of wealth; what could be the reason? spoke this verse:
"Is it a debt from your ancestors, or is it something you have done yourself?
Why do you ask me for such a great deal of wealth, O Brahmin?"

In that regard, "paternal" means either what was taken and consumed by one's father, or a debt contracted by oneself. [The other asks: "What is it that my father took from your hand? Or was it by me? For what reason do you ask me for so much wealth?
When this was said, Sudassana spoke these two verses:
"Alampāyana indeed seeks to overcome me with his elephant."
“O Brahmin, with the help of this female frog, I shall bite the brahmin.
Therefore, O Great King, Increaser of the Realm, go forth today to see the snake,
escorted by the assembly of kshatriyas.”
In this context, "he desires to conquer" means he wishes to win in battle.
In that case, if he is defeated, he will give me five thousand [pieces of gold]; if I am defeated, I shall give it to him; therefore, I ask for that great wealth.
"Therefore" (taṃ) means: "For that reason, O Great King, you should go today to see the snake."
The king said, "In that case, let us go," and set out together with the ascetic.
Seeing this, Alampāyana thought, "This ascetic has gone and returned having taken the king; he will become a courtier of the royal family. Fearing this, he followed along and spoke this verse:
"I do not despise you, young man, on account of your craft."
“You are too proud of your craft; you do not show respect to this serpent.

Therein, “by way of your craft” means: “Young man, I do not despise you because of my own craft, but you, being excessively proud of your craft, do not honor this serpent; you pay no homage to the Nāga.
Then Sudassana spoke two verses:
“I too do not despise you on account of your craft, O brahmin;
yet with your ‘non-venomous’ serpent, you greatly deceive the people.
If the people knew this as I know it, [they would not be deceived].”
“You do not obtain even a handful of chaff, Ālampāyana, let alone wealth.
Then Alampāyana, becoming angry, said:
“A man with a rough hide, matted hair, and foul-smelling, arrogant as he enters the assembly;”
“You who thus despise this Naga who has gone forth, saying,
‘He is not venomous’— having attacked him, you shall know Puṇṇa’s fierce majesty;
I think he will quickly reduce you to a heap of ashes.”

In this context, "dummī" means one who has no other way of seeing. "Aviso atimaññasī" means you despise [him], thinking he is venomless. "Āsajja" means having approached. "Jaññāsī" means you would know.
Then Sudassana, playing with him, spoke this verse:
"There might be venom in a stone-eating lizard, in a *deḍḍubha* snake that feeds on stones;"
“Even for a red-headed serpent, no poison is found.

In this context, *siluttassa* means “of the house-snake”; *deḍḍubhassa* means “of the water-snake”; *silābhu* means “of the blue-colored snake. Having thus pointed out that these snakes might be without poison, he said: “But for the red-headed snake, there is none at all.
Then Alampāyana addressed him with two verses:
“This has been heard from the Arahants, the self-restrained ascetics:
‘Having given gifts here in this world, donors go to heaven.
Give gifts while you are living, if there is something for you to give.’”
“This nāga is of great psychic power, majestic, and difficult to overcome;
with him I shall bite you, and he will reduce you to ashes.
In this context, “if there is anything to be given by you, give it,” means: if you have anything that ought to be given, give that.
“I have heard this, my friend, from self-restrained ascetics:
‘Having given gifts here, donors go to heaven.
You yourself should give while you are still alive, if there is anything for you to give.”
“This one is named Ajamukhī, full of fierce, burning power;
with her I shall bite you, and she will reduce you to ashes.
She is the daughter of Dhatarattha, my half-sister.”
“She, whose face is that of a goat, is full of fierce poison”—these verses are the words of Sudassana. In this context, “full of fierce poison” means she is filled with virulent venom.
Having spoken thus, he said: “O mother, goat-faced one, emerge from within my matted hair and settle upon my hand.”
Right in the midst of the great multitude, he called out to his sister and stretched forth his hand. Hearing his voice, she remained seated within the matted locks;

she croaked three times like a frog, then emerged, sat upon his shoulder, leaped up, and let fall three drops of poison onto the palm of his hand, after which she entered back into the matted locks once more.
Sudassana, having taken the poison, while still standing there, cried out three times with a great cry: "This country will perish! This country will perish!
That sound remained, covering the twelve-league city of Bārāṇasī.
Then the king, hearing that sound, asked: "For what purpose will the country perish? "Great King," [he replied].
“I do not see a place to pour out this poison. “Dear son, this earth is vast; pour it out upon the earth.
Then, refusing him by saying, “It is not possible to pour it out upon the earth, Great King,” he spoke this verse:
“If I were to pour it out upon the ground, O Brahmadatta, understand this well;”
“Grasses, creepers, and herbs would surely wither away.
Therein, “grasses, creepers, and herbs” means that all grasses, creepers, and herbs rooted in the earth would dry up; therefore, it is not possible to pour [the poison] upon the earth.
Then, showing that it is likewise impossible even if one were to throw it upwards into the sky, he spoke this verse:
“If I cause it to fall upwards, O Brahmadatta, you should know this:
for seven years the deva will not rain, nor will snow fall.
In this context, “nor will snow fall” means that for seven years not even a single drop of snow will fall.
"In that case, dear father, sprinkle it with water. To show that even there he was not able, he spoke this verse:
"If I were to sprinkle it in water, O Brahmadatta, know this:
as many creatures born of water as there are—fish and turtles—they would all die."
Then the king said to him, “Dear son, we know nothing; you alone must know the means by which our kingdom shall not perish.
“In that case, Great King, have three pits dug here in succession,” he replied.
The king had them dug. Sudassana filled the first pit with various medicinal herbs.
The second [hole] was filled with cow dung, and the third with divine medicinal herbs. Then, he dropped drops of poison into the first pit.
At that very moment, it smoked and flames burst forth. The fire went and took hold of the pit of cow dung;
from there, too, flames arose, seized the other pit filled with divine medicinal herbs, and having consumed the herbs, the fire was extinguished. Thus spoke Alampāyana.
He stood not far from that pit. Then a poisonous snake struck him;
its skin having peeled away, he became afflicted with white leprosy. Terrified by fear, he uttered these words three times: "I release the Naga King!
Hearing this, the Bodhisatta emerged from his jeweled casket, adorned with every ornament.
Having manifested his physical form, he stood there with the grace of a king of the gods. Sudassana and Ajamukhī likewise remained standing in that same manner.
Then King Sudassana said to the king, "Great King, do you know whose children these are? "I do not know," [the king replied].
"If even you do not know, then how can you not know that Samuddajā, the daughter of the King of Kāsi, was given in marriage to Dhatarattha?"
"Do you know her? "Yes, I know her; she is my younger sister. "We are her sons;
you are our maternal uncle. Upon hearing this, the king trembled; he embraced them, kissed their heads, wept, and having led them up into the palace, he had great honors performed for them.
Then, while exchanging greetings with Bhūridatta, he asked: "Dear one, how did you come to have such fierce power as this?"
“How did Alampāyana take it? He related everything in detail and, advising the king, taught his uncle the Dhamma, saying:
“Great King, it is fitting for a king to exercise sovereignty according to this method.
Then Sudassana said to him: “Uncle, my mother is suffering because she does not see Bhūridatta; we cannot [remain here].”
“Do not indulge in such elaboration. “Very well, dear ones, you may go for now.
But I wish to see my sister; how shall I see her? “Uncle, where is our grandfather, the King of Kāsi?
“Dear ones, being unable to live apart from my sister, he has renounced his kingdom, gone forth into homelessness, and is living in a certain grove named Asuka. “Uncle,” [he said].
“My mother wishes to see both you and my grandfather. You should go to my grandfather’s presence on such-and-such a day;
we shall take our mother and come to my grandfather’s hermitage. There you will see her as well.
Having thus fixed the date with their maternal uncle, they descended from the royal palace. The king—
Having sent his nephew away, he turned back after weeping. They too, having sunk into the earth, went to the abode of the nāgas.
The section on the entry into the city is finished.
Now begins the section on the search for the Mahāsatta.
When the Great Being arrived, the entire Nāga realm was filled with a single sound of lamentation.
He too, exhausted from having lived in the casket for a month, lay down upon his sickbed. There was no end to the number of Nāgas who came into his presence;
he grew weary of conversing with them. Kāṇāriṭṭha, having gone to the world of the gods, [saw] the Great Being...
Having seen him, he arrived first. Then, thinking, "This one is fierce and harsh; will he be able to restrain the assembly of nāgas?
they appointed him as the gatekeeper at the place where the Great Being was seated.
Subhoga, too, having searched throughout the entire Himavat, and then having examined the great ocean and the remaining rivers, came along examining the Yamunā. The Brahmin hunter also—
Seeing the leper Alampāyana, he thought: "This man has become a leper after tormenting Bhūridatta;
however, out of greed for the jewel, I gave him to Alampāyana, who was so very helpful to me. That evil deed will come back to me.
Before it reaches me, I shall go to the Yamunā and perform a ritual for the washing away of my sin at the Payāga ford."
Having gone there, he said, "I have committed an act of treachery against Bhūridatta;
I shall wash away that evil deed," and proceeded to perform the ritual of descending into the water. At that very moment, Subhoga arrived at that place.
Hearing those words of his, [Bhūridatta thought], "By this wicked man, my brother—who was the bestower of such great glory—[has been treated thus] with the jewel-treasure..."
“I have shown him to Alampāyana; I will not let him live,” he said. Wrapping his tail around the man’s feet, he dragged him down and submerged him in the water.
When the man was on the verge of suffocating, the hunter relaxed his grip slightly. The man raised his head.
Then the hunter dragged him down again and submerged him once more. Thus, being tormented by him many times, the Nesāda-brāhmaṇa—
Raising his head, he spoke this verse:
“The water that flows through the world, established at Payāga—
what being has swallowed me as I plunged into the river Yamunā?”

In this context, it is "honored by the world" (*lokasammata*) because people regard it as capable of carrying away evil in such a manner. "Anointing" (*sajanta*) means sprinkling themselves with water of such a kind. "At Payāga" means at the Payāga bathing-place.
Then Subhoga addressed him with a verse:
"When the illustrious lord of the world had cleared Bārāṇasī on all sides..."
“O Brahmin, they declare me to be Subhoga, the son of that bull among serpents.

Therein, *yad esa* means "this one who. *Pakiriya samantato* means having spread out all around; because he was capable of warding off enemies from every direction, he completely surrounded [them] and covered them above with his hood.
Then the Brahmin thought: "This is the brother of Bhūridatta; he will not spare my life. What if I were now to..."
“Having softened his heart by praising his parents, he should beg for his own life,” he thought,
and spoke this verse:
“If indeed the son of the serpent-like bull among men, the King of Kāsi, the lord of the immortals;”
“One of your fathers was of great power, and among mortals your mother was peerless;
such a one of great majesty does not deserve even to be made a slave to a brahmin.
In this context, *kāsissa* refers to one of that name by another title; they also read it as “of the king of Kāsi. [It refers to] the daughter of the king of Kāsi.
Because it was seized by him, he praises even the kingdom of Kāsi as belonging to him alone.
"Of the lord of the immortals" means of the lord of the *nāgas*, who are called "immortals" because of their long life-span. "Of great power" means of great majesty.
"A certain one" means one among those of great power. "Even as a gift" means that such a person of great majesty [could give] even a mere gift of water to a brahmin, devoid of majesty.
“He does not deserve to be killed, much less one of such great majesty as this brahmin.
Then Subhoga, addressing him, said—revealing the deed he had committed: “O wicked brahmin, you think that by deceiving me you will escape with your life;
I shall not let you live! You shot at a deer that had come to drink, while it was resting by a tree.”
Thus pierced, he fled far away with the speed of an arrow, swift of foot.
You saw him fallen there in the vast forest of the wilderness;
taking his roasted meat, you returned to the banyan tree in the evening.
“Resounding with the cries of parrots and mynahs, tawny-hued and carpeted with grass,
echoing with the songs of cuckoos, delightful and ever-green with lush turf—
there he appeared to you, blazing with supernatural power and glory.”
“My brother is of great power, surrounded by maidens.
You were attended by him and satisfied with all his desires;
yet you have wronged him who was innocent toward you—thus has this enmity come upon you here.”
“Quickly stretch out your neck! I will not give you your life!
Let your enmity toward your brother be appeased; I shall cut off your head!
Therein, “he approached the banyan tree at evening” means that he had gone to the banyan tree at the wrong time. “Tawny” refers to the color of his cooked [flesh].
*Piṅgalaṃ*: tawny. *Santhatāyutaṃ*: covered with spreading creepers. *Kokilābhirudaṃ*: resounding with the cries of cuckoos. *Dhuvaṃ haritasaddalaṃ*:
always green and lush, because it was grown on a watery ground; that portion of the earth was perpetually verdant. *Pāturahū*:
while he stood at that banyan tree, my brother became visible to me. *Iddhiyā*: by means of his psychic power (*puññateja*).
"So then" means: "But you, having been led by him to your own Nāga-abode, were served there.
"Recalling" means: "recalling and remembering the evil deed—the enmity committed against my brother by you.
"I shall cut off your head" means: "I shall sever your neck."
Then the brahmin, thinking, “He will not grant me my life; however, it is right to strive for my release by saying something,” recited this verse:
“A brahmin who is a scholar, one devoted to begging, and one who maintains the sacrificial fire—by these three grounds, a brahmin is exempt from being slain.”

In this context, "by these" means that for these three reasons—being a reciter (*ajjhāyaka*), and so forth—a Brahmin is inviolable; it is not permitted to kill a Brahmin. What do you say? For whoever kills a Brahmin is reborn in hell.
Having heard this, Subhoga became filled with doubt and, thinking, "I will take him to the Naga-abode, consult my brothers, and find out," he spoke two verses:
"The city of Dhatarattha, which has plunged into the Yamunā River..."
“Shine forth all the golden splendor, reaching as far as the Yamunā River!
There, those tigers among men, my own uterine brothers, will speak;
O Brahmin, you shall become exactly as they tell you.”
In that context, "Puram" refers to Nāgapura. "Ogāḷham" means entered.
"Girimāhacca yāmunaṃ" means it shines, having reached the Himalayas situated not far from the Yamunā river. "Tattha te" means "there in that city those brothers of mine dwell";
when you have been brought there, you will become exactly as they tell you. For if you speak the truth, [you will be released].
"You still have your life! Otherwise, I shall cut off your head right there!
Having said this, Subhoga seized him by the neck, shaking him and reviling and abusing him, as he went to the gate of the Great Being’s palace.
The section on the Great Being’s search is concluded.
**Wrong Speech** Then, having sat there as a gatekeeper, Kāṇāriṭṭha saw him being brought along after having been thus exhausted. Going out to meet him on the road, he said:
"O Subhoga, do not harass him! Brāhmaṇas are indeed the sons of Mahābrahmā. For if Mahābrahmā..."
"He will think, 'She is harming my son,' and in his anger, he will destroy our entire Nāga realm.
For in this world, brahmins are indeed the most excellent and possess great power; you do not know their power, but I do," he said.
It is said that in the immediately preceding past life, Kaṇāriṭṭha had been a brahmin who performed sacrifices; therefore—
He spoke thus. Having spoken, and being by nature a performer of sacrifices due to his past experiences, he addressed Subhoga and the assembly of Nāgas, saying:
"Come, sirs! I shall proclaim the virtues of those who perform sacrifices. Then, beginning the praise of sacrifice, he said:
"Sacrifices and the Vedas in this world, O Subhoga, are not supreme when associated with what is limited."
"By disparaging that which is most excellent, one abandons both wealth and the Dhamma of the virtuous.
In this context, "not inferior" (*anittara*) means: O wealthy one, the sacrifices and the Vedas in this world are not inferior; they are not base, but are of great power.
Since they are associated with those [Vedas], the Brahmins too have indeed been born as not inferior. "That which is most excellent" (*tadaggarayaṃ*)...
Therefore, by reviling a Brahmin who is beyond reproach, one loses both the wealth and the Dhamma of the wise.
It is said that he spoke thus so that the assembly of Nāgas would not be able to say, "By this man, an act of treachery against his friend Bhūridatta was committed.

Then Kaṇāriṭṭha said to him, "Subhoga, do you know by whom this world was created? When he replied, "I do not know," Kaṇāriṭṭha spoke the following verse to show that it was created by Mahābrahmā, the grandfather of the Brahmins:
“The nobles attained the recitation [of the Vedas], the lords of the earth the [ruling] power; the merchants agriculture, and the laborers service;
each approached according to their respective station. It is said that these were made by Him who is called the Controller.
In this context, “upāgu” means they approached. It is said that after Brahmā had fashioned the four castes, beginning with the brahmins, he first [addressed] the nobles...
To the brahmins he said: “You should devote yourselves solely to Vedic study; do not do anything else. To the kshatriyas he said:
“You should conquer the earth alone. To the vaiśyas he said: “You should engage solely in agriculture. To the śūdras he said:
“You should devote yourselves solely to service for the three castes. From that time forth, the nobles (ariyas) [pursued] Vedic study, and the kshatriyas...
They say that the *vessas* took up agriculture and the *suddas* took up service.

"Each according to their station" means that as they approached [their respective roles], they did so individually in accordance with the rule established by Brahmā, corresponding to the specific station of their own clans.
"Are these made by the Lord?"—thus they say, for it is said that these were indeed created by the Great Brahmā, the Lord (*vasin*).

"Such are these brahmins of great virtue. For whoever gives a gift with a mind of confidence toward them, there is no rebirth for him elsewhere; he goes only to the world of the gods. Having said this, he spoke further:
"Dhātā, Vidhātā, Varuṇa, Kuvera, Soma, Yama, Candimā, Vāyu, and Sūriya—these too, having performed various sacrifices, [bestowed] all desires upon the reciters."
“Five hundred bow-lengths wide was he who was Ajjuna, powerful Bhīmasena;
even he, peerless on earth with a thousand arms, was then consumed by the fire.
In this context, “these too” refers to these divine kings, Dhātā and the rest. “Puthuso” means having performed various kinds of sacrifices.
"Furthermore, having given all desires to the reciting Brahmins, he shows that he has attained these states. "Drawn open" means pulled back.
"Five hundred bows" does not mean five hundred actual bows; rather, he himself draws back a great bow measuring five hundred bows.
"Bhīmasena" means one with a terrifying army. "Thousand-armed" does not refer to his—
Regarding the "thousand arms": this was said because he drew a bow that required the drawing strength of five hundred archers, each possessing a thousand arms.

As for the phrase "he kindled the fire": at that time, that king also satisfied the brahmins with all their desires, kindled the fire—that is, established it—and tended it; for that very reason, he was reborn in the world of the gods.
"Therefore," he said, "the ones called brahmins are the eldest in this world.
Continuing further to praise the brahmins, he spoke this verse:
"He who for a long time has fed the brahmins with food and drink according to his means..."
"With a serene mind, rejoicing, he became a certain god of great wealth.
In this context, "he" (yo) indicates that he was the former King of Bārāṇasī. "According to his power" (yathānubhāvaṃ) means according to his strength;
having renounced everything he possessed, he fed [the monks]. "A certain god" (devaññataro) refers to him as a particular king of the gods of great influence.
Thus he shows that those called brahmins are indeed the foremost recipients of offerings.
Then, bringing forward another reason for this, he spoke this verse:
“He who was able to feed the sacrificial fire—whose seat is great and whose color is pleasing to the gods—with clarified butter;”
“Having performed the sacrifice according to the ritual procedure with choice offerings, he attained the divine state of Mucalinda.

In this context, *mahāsanaṃ* means one who eats much. *Bhojetuṃ* means to satisfy [the gods]. *Yaññatantaṃ* means the ritual procedure of the sacrifice. *Varato* means having sacrificed to the choice fire-god (*aggideva*). *Mucalindajjhagacchī* means that Mucalinda was attained.
It is said that formerly in Benares there was a king named Mucalinda; having summoned the brahmins, he [instructed them on] the path to heaven...
He asked. Then they said to him, "Pay honor to the brahmins and to the deity of the brahmins.
When he asked, "Who is the deity of the brahmins? they replied, "'The Fire-god'—satisfy him with fresh butter and ghee.
He did accordingly. To clarify this matter, he spoke this verse.
Showing another reason as well, he spoke this verse:
“He of great majesty, living for a thousand years, who went forth as one beautiful and sublime;
having abandoned his boundless kingdom along with his army, even King Dvīpa went to heaven.”
Regarding that, "he went forth" means that while ruling for five hundred years, having paid honor to the brahmins, he abandoned his boundless kingdom along with his army and went forth.
"Dudīpa too": this says that the king named Dudīpa, after honoring the brahmins, likewise went to heaven. There is also a reading, "Dujīpo."
Showing other examples as well, he said: "He who,
having conquered the ocean-bound earth, erected a magnificent, beautiful sacrificial pillar made of gold,
and offered the Vessānara sacrifice, became a god of great wealth among the other deities."
“By whose power the Ganges flows with abundant wealth, and the ocean is filled with curd;
that Lomapāda, having served the fire, attained the city of Aṅga with its thousand gates.
In this context, *sāgarantaṃ* means the earth bounded by the ocean. *Ussesi* means [he shone forth] after asking the brahmins about the path to heaven.
When told, “Erect a golden sacrificial post,” he erected it for the purpose of slaughtering animals.
“Vessānaramādahāno” means setting alight the Vessānara fire; there is also a reading, “Vesānariṃ. “Devaññataro” refers to Subhoga;
for it is said that after King [Brahmadatta] offered oblations into the fire, he became a certain powerful deity. “Yassānubhāvena” means, O Subhoga, by whose power the Ganges and the great ocean...
"And by whom was it done? "I do not know. "What will you know? O Brahmin, you only know how to beat people!
For in the past, there was a king of Bārāṇasī named Aṅga Lomapāda who asked the Brahmins about the path to heaven.
When they told him, "Sire, Great King, enter the Himalayas, pay honor to the Brahmins, and tend the sacrificial fire," he—
Taking immeasurable cows and buffaloes, she entered the Himalayas and acted accordingly.
When it was asked, "What should be done with the milk and curds left over after the brahmins have eaten?", she said, "Discard them.
In the place where a small amount of milk was discarded, small rivers were formed; in the place where a large amount was discarded, the Ganges flowed.
That milk, however, where it had become curd and remained settled, became what is known as the ocean.
Thus, having performed such honors and tended the fire according to the ritual prescribed by the brahmins, he reached the city of the Thousand-Eyed One.
Having brought this past event to mind, he spoke this verse:
“Of great psychic power, a glorious and excellent deity, he was the commander-in-chief of Vāsava in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Having destroyed his impurity through the Soma sacrifice, Subhoga became another distinguished god.
In this regard, “having destroyed his impurity through the Soma sacrifice,” O Subhoga, refers to him who is now the highly renowned commander-in-chief of Sakka.
This son of the gods was formerly a king of Bārāṇasī who, having asked the brahmins about the path to heaven, was told by them,
"Having washed away your impurities through the Soma sacrifice, go to the world of the gods.
Having paid great honor to the brahmins and performed the Soma sacrifice according to the procedure they prescribed, he removed his own impurities by means of it and became a certain deity.
He spoke thus in order to clarify the meaning of "he was born.
Furthermore, showing other examples as well, he said:
"He created this world and the next, the Bhāgīrathī, the Himālaya, and the vulture;..."
The glorious and renowned lord of gods, endowed with supernatural power, then kindled the fire:
"Mālāgiri, Himavā, Gijjhakūṭa, Sudassana, Nisabha, and Kuvera—
these and other great mountains were made into funeral mounds by those who perform sacrifices."
"In that regard, O brother Subhoga, even he who was the fire— by whom this world, the other world, the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā, the Himavat mountain, and the Gijjhakūṭa mountain were created—
when he was a young brahmin prior to his rebirth as Mahābrahmā, even then he kindled only fire; having offered oblations into the fire, he became Mahābrahmā."
Having offered [the sacrifice], he performed all of this. This demonstrates that the brahmins possess such great supernormal power (*mahiddhika*).

Regarding the phrase "built by a funeral pyre" (*cityā katā*): it is said that formerly a certain king of Bārāṇasī, having asked the brahmins about the path to heaven and being told, "Perform honor for the brahmins," established a great almsgiving for them. Then, asking, "What is there that is lacking in my gift?"—
When it was said, “Your Majesty, everything is provided, but there are not enough seats for the brahmins,” he had seats constructed by having them piled up with bricks.

At that time, through the supernatural power of the brahmins, the brick-piled altars (*cityā*) grew into the Āsanapīṭhika hills, and from them the Mālāgiri and other mountains arose. Thus they say these were made by the brahmins who performed the sacrifices.
Then he asked him again: “Brother, do you know for what reason this ocean is undrinkable and has become salty water?
“I do not know, Ariṭṭha,” he replied. Then, saying to him, “You only know how to harass a brahmin; listen,” he spoke this verse:
“He who recites the Vedas, endowed with the qualities of the mantras, an ascetic—him they call ‘one devoted to begging.’”
“The ocean, having swallowed the water splashing on its shore, cannot drink it back.
Regarding this, “They call him a seeker of alms” means that people in this world call that brahmin a seeker of alms.
“Splashing the water” means that, it is said, one day while performing a rite to wash away evil, he stood on the shore and took water from the ocean.
He sprinkled it over his own head as it fell upon him. Then, as he continued to act in this way, the ocean grew and swallowed him.
The Great Brahmā, knowing the reason for this, became angry, thinking, "It seems my son has been killed by this one!
He uttered a curse, saying, "May the ocean become undrinkable salt water," and because of that, it became undrinkable. Such, indeed, are these brahmins of great power.
Furthermore, he said:
"Many sites for offerings exist on earth, O Vāsava, belonging to brahmins;
those found in the eastern, western, southern, and northern directions produce the Vedas."
In that context, "of Vāsava" refers to Vāsava, who had previously attained the status of a ruler after giving gifts to brahmins.
"Objects of sacrifice" means that many brahmins, who are fields of merit and the foremost recipients of offerings on earth, exist in abundance.
These, even now existing in the four directions, produce great knowledge for that Vāsava and bring him joy and gladness.
Thus Arittha praised the brahmins, the sacrifice, and the Vedas with fourteen verses.
The false discourse is finished.
Having heard that speech of his, many nāgas who had come to attend upon the Great Being during his illness [thought], "This is indeed the truth..."
Thus they fell into the state of grasping a false conviction, thinking, "He speaks [thus].
The Great Being, while still lying on his sickbed, heard all of this. The nāgas also informed him. Then the Great Being thought: "Ariṭṭha praises the wrong path;
I shall break his argument and make the assembly hold right view. He rose, bathed, and—
Adorned with every ornament, he sat upon the Dharma-seat, caused the entire assembly of nāgas to gather, and summoned Ariṭṭha, saying:
"Ariṭṭha, you have spoken what is untrue, praising the Vedas, sacrifices, and the brahmins.
For the performance of sacrifice according to the brahmins' Vedic prescriptions is considered ignoble and does not lead to heaven; in your doctrine, there is falsehood."
Having said, "Behold!", he began the discourse known as the *Yaññabhedavāda*, saying:

"Indeed, for the wise, the age of strife is a pitfall; it becomes a misfortune for those who have mastered the Vedas, because they fail to discern the nature of a mirage. The qualities of illusion do not surpass wisdom."
“The Vedas do not provide protection for that man who betrays his friends, who destroys living beings;
nor does the fire he has tended protect him, when death—whose nature is hatred—strikes him for his ignoble deeds.
And all mortals, together with their wealth and possessions, are like wood set ablaze and mixed with straw.”
“I am not satisfied with this fire, whose power is insufficient; who would consider that a good meal, knowing it to be but twice-tasted?
Just as milk, subject to transformation, becomes curd and then even butter, so too the fire is subject to transformation: the heat descends upon one who is disciplined in yoga.”
“The fire that has entered into wood, whether dry or even fresh, is not seen;
the fire-god does not arise without being rubbed with the fire-sticks, nor is he born without action.
For if fire were to dwell within from the inside, whether in dry or even fresh wood...”
“May all the forests in the world wither away, and may even dried wood burn!
If a man performing a meritorious act with wood and grass were to produce a blazing fire with smoky crests,
then charcoal-burners, salt-makers, cooks, and even those who cremate bodies would also perform merit.”
“If these people do not perform meritorious deeds— having here kindled the sacrificial fire and studied the Vedic hymns—
and if no one else in the world performs merit by offering food to the smoke-crested, blazing fire—
then how can one who is honored by the world [use] that which has an unpleasant odor and is disliked by many?”
Whatever mortals avoid, that is what one who understands the two flavors should eat as unpraiseworthy.
"Some say even Śikhi among the gods; others, the barbarians, call Water a god.
All these speak falsely; neither Fire nor Water is a god."
“How can one who performs evil deeds, while serving the fire— the Vessānara who works for all people, who is without sense-faculties and without a body of perception—
attain a good rebirth? ‘Brahmā, seeking a livelihood here, is a servant of the fire,’ so it is said.”
“Since you possess all power and are self-mastering, why would you, being uncreated, pay homage to that which is created?
“In the past, for the sake of honor, people scattered what was laughable, unworthy of contemplation, and untrue.
Now that those gains and honors are no longer manifest, they maintain the true Dhamma among living beings.”
“The noble ones attained mastery over the earth through study, the merchants through agriculture, and the laborers through service;
each approached their respective station, and it is said that these were established as masters.
If this statement spoken by the brahmins were indeed true, [then...]”
“A non-Khattiya could never obtain a kingdom; a non-Brāhmaṇa could not study the words of the mantras;
a Vessa alone could perform the work of plowing; and a Sudda could never be freed from the service of others.
Since this statement is untrue, these greedy people speak such falsehoods.
Those of little wisdom place their faith in it, but the wise see it for themselves.
"For the Khattiyas pay tribute to the Vessas; the Brāhmaṇas wander about taking up weapons.
Why does Brahmā not straighten such a world that is so agitated and shattered?"
“If indeed that Brahmā were the Lord of the entire world, the Master of many beings among the progeny, why did he burn the entire world with misfortune? Why did he not make the entire world happy?
“If indeed that Brahmā were the Lord of the entire world, the Master of many beings among the progeny...”
“By means of illusion, falsehood, and intoxication, for what purpose did he rule the world unrighteously?
For if he were the Lord of the entire world, the Brahmā, the Master of many beings, and the Ruler of creatures—
then this Ariṭṭha is indeed unrighteous, since while Dhamma exists, he ordains what is contrary to Dhamma.”
“Worms, moths, snakes, and frogs, as well as maggots and flies—these things, too, are of an ignoble nature, yet among the many Kambojans they are considered otherwise.
In this context, *vedajjhagatānariṭṭhā* means: O Ariṭṭha, these so-called attainments of the Vedas are what is reckoned as defeat for the wise.
A "seizing of the blade" (kaṭaggāha) refers to the victory of fools, like deer; it is called a "seizing of the blade.
"Of the nature of a mirage" (marīcidhamma): for these three Vedas are of the nature of a mirage.

Because they do not investigate this, fools—who do not know what is appropriate and inappropriate—come to their own destruction through the perception of reality, just as deer come to destruction through the perception of water in a mirage. Such is wisdom (paññā).
However, the divisions of deceit do not overcome or deceive a person endowed with wisdom and knowledge.
In the phrase "bhavanti dassa," the letter *da* is merely for the purpose of euphonic junction (*byañjanasandhi*).

For that man who has destroyed what is good, who strikes down prosperity, and who betrays his friends, the Vedas do not serve as a refuge; the meaning is that they are unable to become a firm support. He has been served...
And "fire" means that fire, when fully tended, does not protect or guard a person from the threefold misconduct of body, speech, and mind, nor from a mind possessed of hatred or evil karma.
And "all mortals" means that even if all the wood that exists in the world, along with all wealth and possessions, were gathered together—
If they were to mix it with grass and set it on fire along with their own wealth and possessions,
even while burning all that which has been ignited by them, this fire of yours— possessing incomparable power and peerless heat— would not be satisfied. Thus, O brother,
who is there capable of knowing its taste with two tongues, even one possessing the sense of taste for two flavors, with ghee and other such things?
"Who could provide abundant food and well-being? Who indeed would be able to do so?
But having satisfied this insatiable and expensive one, who indeed will go to the world of the gods? Behold how much this is ill-established!
"Yogayutto" means that by being engaged in the practice of rubbing the fire-sticks together, one obtains the requisite condition and thus the fire descends and is produced.
Thus, you call that which arises through the exertion of another, and is itself insentient, a "god. This too you have spoken as something entirely unreal.
"Fire has entered the man" means fire has entered [him]. "Not being struck by a man with a fire-drill" means it does not arise when not struck by a man holding a fire-stick.
"The Knower of Beings (jātavedas) is not born from action" means that, without the activity of another, it arises solely through its own inherent nature.
"It is not born. "They would wither" means that the forests, being dried up by fire within, would become parched;

they would not remain moist. "Feeding" means while feeding. "Possessing a crest of smoke and blazing" means endowed with a crest of smoke and emitting heat. "Charcoal-makers" (aṅgārika) are those who work with charcoal.
"Salt-makers" (loṇakara) are those who produce salt by boiling salt water. "Cooks" (sūda) are those who prepare meals. "Funeral pyres" (sarīradāha).
"Those who meditate on the funeral pyre": all these people would indeed perform only meritorious deeds (*puñña*).

"The fire of study" means the sacrificial fire of Vedic recitation (*ajjhenaaggi*). "No one at all": whether they be Brahmins who recite mantras or anyone else, no person—even while feeding and satisfying the smoke-crested, blazing fire—fails to produce merit. [This is] honored by the world.
"Being equal" means being honored and revered like you in the world of the gods.
"Whatever it may be" refers to things such as a snake's carcass—repulsive and loathsome—which mortals avoid from afar.

"That is not praised" means that, friend, how and for what reason could one who perceives both tastes consume that which is not praised? "Among the gods" means that some humans [regard] even Śikhin as one among the gods.
“They call it a god. But as for the “barbarians,” those ignorant barbarians call water a “god. Regarding the “unconscious body”:

how will the world, having worshipped the sacrificial fire—which is devoid of sense faculties, a mindless body, insentient, yet performs actions such as cooking—and while committing evil deeds, go to a happy destination? This you have stated quite poorly.

"All-conquering, they say, for the sake of their livelihood": these brahmins, for the sake of their own livelihood, said that Mahābrahmā is "All-conquering" (*sabbābhibhū*), asserting that the entire world was created by him. Furthermore, they also say that Aggika Brahmā is his attendant;
it is said that he too merely offers oblations into the fire. And if he is "all-powerful and masterful" (*sabbānubhāvī ca vasī*): if he is indeed all-powerful and masterful...
And furthermore, for what purpose would he, being himself uncreated, pay homage to one created by himself? This too is poorly stated by you.
The words of the Ariṭṭha brahmins are indeed laughable; they are fit to be laughed at by the wise and are not worthy of serious reflection.
"They scattered" means these brahmins [scattered] such false speech for the sake of their own honor.
"Previously they were spread abroad. "The doctrine of peace maintained by people":

the meaning is that when gain and honor had not yet appeared, they joined together with other people and maintained their own doctrine known as their "view" (laddhi), which was connected with the slaughter of living beings;
thus they composed the so-called *Yajña-sutta*.
"And this is the truth": that which was stated by you, beginning with "The noble [live] by study," would indeed be true. "Not a kshatriya":
if this were so, a non-kshatriya would not obtain a kingdom, and even a non-brahmin would not study the mantra-words.
"These are lies": these are indeed false. "Gluttons" (*odariyā*): those whose livelihood depends on the belly, for the sake of filling the belly.
"Or: *tad-appapaññā* means that their speech is devoid of wisdom (*appaññā*).
But by themselves (*attanāva*), the wise see their speech as 'full of hatred' (*sadosa*). *Tādisaṃ* means of such a kind.
*Saṅkhubhitaṃ* means having become agitated, standing after having broken the boundary established by Brahmā; thus, that Brahmā of yours [stands] shattering the world."
"Why does he not act uprightly? Why, out of malice (*alakkhi*), did he set the whole world ablaze with suffering?
Why indeed did he not make the whole world exclusively happy? O Brahmā, I think you are a thief who destroys the world.

"By deceit" means by trickery. "For what purpose did he act unrighteously?"—by this [question], it is asked for what reason he acted through such unrighteousness as deceit and so forth, in order to bring harm upon the world.

The meaning is "you have joined together. "Ariṭṭha" means O Ariṭṭha; you are unrighteous, O Lord of Beings, you who, despite the tenfold wholesome qualities existing, did not establish the Dhamma but established what is contrary to the Dhamma. "Kīṭā" and so forth are in the accusative case.
"By killing these living beings, such as insects and the rest, a mortal is purified"—this refers to the many ignoble people dwelling in the kingdom of Kamboja.
Those things are false; they are called "Dhammas" though they are actually non-Dhammas. It must be that even those were fashioned by you, O Brahmā.
Now, showing their falsity, he said:
"If indeed he who kills is purified, then even when killed, he would go to a heavenly state."
Those who cry "Bho! might kill others, as would those who have faith in them.
"Neither deer, nor cattle, nor even oxen ever pray for their own slaughter.
Yet, writhing here for the sake of a livelihood, people seize living creatures as victims at sacrifices."
“At the pillar-erecting and the animal-sacrifice, fools lead the face [of the victim] with colorful designs, saying:
‘This pillar of yours will yield desires in the hereafter; it will be eternal in the world beyond.
And if there be gems, conch-shells, pearls, grain, wealth, silver, or gold upon the pillar—”
Even if the gods of the Thirty-Three were to grant all their desires,
and many assemblies possessing the threefold knowledge were to perform sacrifices with dry wood or even fresh wood, they would not cause any non-Brahmin to officiate at a sacrifice.
And from where could there come sacrificial posts made of gems, conch shells, pearls, grain, wealth, silver, or gold?
“When firewood is dry or even fresh, how could there be suffering in the triple heaven where all desires are fulfilled?
‘The crafty, the cruel, and the deluded fools lead others on with various colorful words:
“Take this fire and give me your wealth; then you will be happy in all your desires.”’”
“Having entered the refuge of the fire of ignorance, they lead the face about with various colors;
having shaved off hair and beard as well as the nails, they cause wealth to be spent through rituals.
Like crows finding a solitary owl in secret, many gather together around one who is alone.”
Having eaten their food and practiced deception, these impostors shave their heads and set out on the path of sacrifice.
"Thus indeed is he deceived by the brahmins; being alone, he is surrounded by many.
Plundering him through their various schemes, they carry off his wealth—the seen by means of the unseen."
“Those who have been instructed by kings take away his wealth;
such men, being like thieves and lacking integrity, though they deserve death, are not executed in this world, O Ariṭṭha.
At the sacrifices, people cut off the sacrificial post’s splinter, saying, ‘You are Indra’s right arm.’”
“Even if that were true, Maghava, with his arm cut off, how could Indra, the Lord, conquer the Asuras?
But if that were false and Maghava were whole-bodied, then he would be a slayer and not exempt from blame; he is merely a supreme god.
These Brahmins are like spells of a hollow nature; this is a deception in this world based on what is visible.”
“Mālāgiri, Himavā, and Gijjha, Sudassana, Nisabha, Kuvera—
these and other great mountains were built as funeral mounds by those who perform sacrifices.
Indeed, the bricks were laid out according to their specific requirements, yet these were built as funeral mounds by those who perform sacrifices.”
Mountains do not provide such assistance; other directions remain immovable with their standing rocks.
"Bricks are not stones for a long time; neither iron nor copper is produced there.
While praising this as something else, they say that the *cityā* was built by those performing the sacrifice."
“They say that even a reciter endowed with the qualities of the mantras, an ascetic devoted to sacrifice,
who pours water onto the shore of the ocean— that ocean swallows him up and he cannot drink it.
Even if thousands of rivers flow toward those who have mastered all the Vedas and are endowed with the mantras,”
“Is it not because its water has been corrupted that the immeasurable ocean is undrinkable?

Whatever wells there are here in this world of living beings, dug out by those who dig for wells—even though they contain salt water—the water in them is not undrinkable simply because a brahmin has drunk from them.
Let them not say that water possesses two flavors.”
“Who was the first woman? Whose wife was she? Who first begot human beings?
By that very principle no one is inferior; thus they speak of the analysis of relinquishment.
Even a son of a Caṇḍāla, having mastered the Vedas through his own effort, might speak the mantras, being skilled and wise.”
“Even his head would not split into seven pieces, for these spells were made for his own destruction.
Spoken with words, full of greed, and grasped, they are difficult to release once they have entered the path of poetry.
The minds of fools are settled upon what is uneven; those of little wisdom place their faith in them.”
“In the lion, the tiger, and the leopard, there is no human strength;
their human nature is as distinct as that of cattle, for their births are indeed different.
And even if a king, having conquered the earth, were to live surrounded by obedient vassals...”
He himself shall conquer the host of enemies, and his offspring shall be ever happy.
"The Kshatriya’s counsel and the three Vedas—these are equal in their purpose;
yet without discerning their true meaning, one does not awaken, like one walking upon a hidden path through a flood."
“The Kshatriya mantras and the three Vedas are equal in their meaning;
gain and loss, ill-repute and fame—all these are the four conditions for them.
Just as commoners on this earth perform various deeds for the sake of wealth and grain;”
And likewise today, the Saṅgha of those possessing the threefold knowledge performs manifold works upon the earth.
Those who are equal to the common folk—ever restless and intent upon the strands of sensual pleasure—they perform manifold works upon the earth; they are of little wisdom and crave the two flavors.
In this context, "those who address others as 'bho'" refers to the brahmins. "They would kill those who address them as 'bho'" means they would kill the brahmin himself.
"And those who [believe their word]" means even those who might trust that statement of the brahmins;
they would kill their own attendants and the brahmins as well. But the brahmins, instead of killing the brahmins and their attendants, [would kill] various kinds of animals.
They kill them. Thus, their statement is false. "Some" refers to those who do not exist as supplicants saying, "Do not kill us at the sacrifices; we shall go to heaven.
"They slaughter living beings and animals" means that for the sake of a livelihood, they kill living beings such as deer and animals while they are still writhing.
"They lead them to the mouth" means, in these animal sacrifices performed for the search for sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), to this—[your] mouth.
On the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), all kinds of gems, conchs, pearls, grain, wealth, silver, and gold are accumulated;
they pacify the minds [of the people] with various reasons, saying, "This post of yours will be a cow of plenty (*kāmaduh*) for the sake of the next world, the beyond;
it will bring about the state of eternal existence. The meaning is that by saying this and that, they lead them into a false grasp.

"And if" means: if this jewel and so forth were to be found on a sacrificial post or among the remaining logs, or if it were a cow that milks all desires in the world of the Thirty-three, then the community of those possessing the threefold knowledge (tevijja), having become numerous, would perform sacrifices for the sake of great wealth and the desire for heaven;
they would not cause a non-Brahmin to sacrifice. However, because they desire their own wealth, they also cause others to sacrifice.
Therefore, they should be understood as speakers of what is unreal. As for the question "From where?", [it means]:

from where could this jewel and so forth come, which do not even exist on this sacrificial post or in the remaining wood? And from where could it milk all desires in the triple heaven? In every respect, their speech is entirely unreal.
"Deceitful, cruel, and deluded fools"—O Ariṭṭha, these so-called brahmins are indeed fraudulent and pitiless.
And those fools, having enticed and seduced the world with various means, please their faces [with gifts].

Saying, "Take this fire and sacrifice; give us your wealth, and then, having obtained all desires, you will be happy," they lead that king or royal minister to the place for fire-sacrifice, saying, "Enter this fire-offering as a refuge."
"Having entered the house. "Having shaved off" means: while putting forward various reasons, they shave off the hair and beard as well as the nails.
Because it is said "they cause [him] to overstep," relying on the three Vedas, they say, "This must be given;
this must be done," and thus they cause his wealth to be overstepped—that is, they ruin and destroy it—by means of the Vedas.
"Having eaten the food, having practiced deception"— meaning those deceivers, having performed various kinds of fraudulent acts,
having gathered together and assembled, having praised the sacrifice and deceived him, ate the various choice delicacies belonging to him;
then, having shaved his head, they released him upon the path of the sacrifice— the meaning is that they took him and went outside the sacrificial enclosure.
By means of various yogas, those brahmins, having gathered together in great numbers, plundered that single man through various methods and various applications.

Having made the wealth he saw before his eyes their own, they took it away by describing the unseen world of the gods as a place of acquisition—though that world of the gods had never been seen by him.
Thus instructed by the king, they performed [the rites], saying: "This and this tribute..."
"Seize them!"—thus instructed by the kings, they are like royal officers known as *akāsiyas*.
"Tadassa" means they take and carry away that wealth of his. "Corasamā" refers to base persons who are like thieves who seize by force where it does not exist or who break through walls;
such evil-natured individuals, who deserve execution, are no longer put to death in the world today.
"Bāhārasīti bāhā asi. This is what is meant: "Ariṭṭha, look at this too—the false speech of the brahmins!
It is said that at sacrifices they cut down a large palāsa branch, saying, 'This is Indra’s arm, the sacrificial fee!
If their word were true, then, having had his arm cut off, by what strength of arm could Indra [defeat] the asuras?"
"Jināti" means he conquers. "Samaṅgī" means one who possesses arms; that is, one whose arms are unsevered and who is free from disease. "Hantā" means the slayer of the asuras.
"Paramo" means supreme, endowed with merit and psychic power, and invulnerable to others. "Brāhmaṇā" refers to the brahmins. "Tuccharūpā" means having a hollow nature, fruitless.
"Vañcanā" refers to those things called the mantras of the brahmins; these are, in this world, a visible deception.
"According to the materials used" means: they say that whatever bricks were taken and used by the performers of the sacrifice to construct the *citi* (altar).
"Standing stones" refers to mountains, for they stand immovable, being solid masses of stone rather than being piled up.
Bricks, however, are movable, not solid masses, and not made of stone. "Praising" means: the Brahmins extolling this sacrifice.
"Samantavedā" refers to Brahmins who are perfected in the Vedas. "Vahanti" means that even when people fall into the currents or whirlpools, they carry them away;
having caused them to sink, they bring about their death. Regarding the phrase "na tena byāpannarasūdakā nā," here one *na*-particle has the sense of an inquiry.
By asking, "Are not those rivers possessed of water of corrupted taste? he speaks thus. Why?
For what reason was the great ocean made undrinkable? Is it that Mahābrahmā is unable to make the water in rivers such as the Yamunā undrinkable, yet is able to do so only in the ocean?
"Dvirasaññu māhu" means he became one who perceived two tastes; the sense is that he was born [with that perception].
"Pure puratthā" means formerly, in the past, previously, in the first eon. "Kā kassa bhariyā" means which woman is his wife?
Whose wife could there be? For at that time, even the female gender did not exist; later, through sexual intercourse, those called "mother" and "father" arose.
"Mind produced humans": for at that time, mind alone produced human beings; the meaning is that sentient beings were born mind-made.
"By that law as well"—by that cause, by that very nature, no one was inferior by birth. For indeed...
At that time, there was a distinction between Kṣatriyas and the other classes; therefore, what the Brāhmaṇas say—that "Brāhmaṇas alone are superior by birth, while others are inferior"—is false.

"Even so" means that while the world was thus proceeding, having abandoned the ancient custom, the four divisions beginning with the Kṣatriyas arose according to those whom they themselves subsequently appointed; even so, they call this the "Analysis of Relinquishment."
They explain this distinction by saying that through the relinquishing of kamma performed by themselves, some of those beings were born as khattiyas, while others were born as brahmins and so forth;
therefore, the statement "Brahmins alone are the best" is false. As for the phrase "seven times":
if the Great Brahmā gave the three Vedas only to the brahmins and not to others, such as the caṇḍālas...
"If one were to speak these mantras, one's head would split into seven pieces; yet it does not split.
Therefore, these mantras were composed by these brahmins for their own destruction. By proclaiming their own falsehood, they bring about the destruction of their own virtues.
'Composed by speech' means these so-called mantras were created after being conceived through lying. 'Seized by greed' means they were seized through greed for gain."
"Seized by brahmins": they are difficult to release, like a fish that has swallowed a hook. "Fallen into the path of poetry":
they have entered and followed the verbal path of those brahmins who compose poetry; for having spoken falsehoods according to their own desires, those brahmins bind [others].
"Of fools": for the minds of those fools are settled upon what is uneven, and others [lead them] further astray.
Only those who are free from conceptual proliferation (appañña) have full confidence. "By means of manly strength" means by means of the strength designated as "manly. This is what is meant:
there is no one called a brahmin who possesses that manly strength—reckoned as human virility—which these lions and others possess.

"All these are indeed inferior even to animals. And "the human state is like that of cattle" means that whatever constitutes their human state should be viewed as being like that of cattle. For what reason? Because their birth is not the same;
for those Brahmins, due to their lack of wisdom, are of the same species as cattle, yet they are not equal to them. Indeed, the [nature] of cattle is quite different.
"Another thing for them": by this [phrase], although the brahmins are equal to lions and other animals among the beasts, he does not treat them as such, but treats them as equal to cattle.
"And if he is a king," O Ariṭṭha, means if he is indeed a kshatriya who has conquered the earth by virtue of being granted [the status] by Mahābrahmā.
"Possessing living companions" means being endowed with ministers who live together with him. "Having obedient attendants" means having a retinue that acts according to his own instructions.
If that were the case, it would not be necessary for him to wage war against his assembly to rule; he could defeat the host of enemies all by himself.
If this were so, his subjects would be constantly happy due to the absence of suffering in war, yet this is not the case.
Therefore, their statement is false.

“Khattiya-mantras” refers to the science of kingship (*rāja-sattha*) and the three Vedas; because they proceed according to one’s own command and preference with the thought, “This alone must be done,” they are equal in meaning.

“Without having investigated” means that neither the Kshatriya regarding those Kshatriya-mantras nor the Brahmin regarding the Vedas, having failed to investigate their meaning, learns them merely by way of command; thus, he [is carried away] by that meaning like by a flood of water.
They do not perceive [the truth], just as one does not perceive a hidden path.
They are equal in the sense of being deceived by the meaning [of their own views]. Why is that? Because they say, "Only brahmins are superior;
other castes are inferior. And as for those worldly conditions such as gain and so forth, they are common to all four of those castes.

These are the phenomena (*dhammā*). There is not even a single being who is called "freed" from these. Thus, while the brahmins are themselves entirely unfreed from worldly conditions (*lokadhammā*), they falsely declare, "We are the best.
The *ibbhā* are householders. And the "assemblies of those possessing the three knowledges" (*tevijjasaṅghā*)—the brahmins likewise [engage in] various activities such as plowing and cattle-herding.
They perform their duties. "Constantly zealous" means they are always filled with exertion and filled with desire.
"Therefore, brother, those brahmins who lack wisdom and perceive the taste of meat are far from the Dhamma.
For the ancient qualities of the brahmins are nowadays seen only in dogs.
Thus the Great Being refuted his opponent's argument and established his own.
Having heard his discourse on the Dhamma, the entire assembly of nāgas was filled with joy.
The Great Being had the hunter-brāhmaṇa led out from the nāga abode, and he did not utter even a word of reproach against him. Sāgara-Brahmadatta, too, did not let the appointed day pass by.
He went with a fourfold army to his father’s dwelling place.

The Great Being, thinking, “I shall see my maternal uncle and grandfather,” had the drum beaten and, accompanied by great majesty and splendor, crossed the Yamunā River and set out toward that very hermitage.
His remaining brothers and his parents followed behind him.
At that moment, Sāgarabrahmadatta, not recognizing the Great Being as he approached with a vast retinue,
asked his father:
"Whose are these kettledrums and tabors, conchs, paṇavas, and indimas?"
Proceeding ahead, making the bull among charioteers smile:
“Whose is this youth, girded with a broad band of gold the color of lightning, coming along, radiant with glory?”
“Whose face shines so beautifully, like a flame struck by a torch or like glowing acacia embers?
Who comes here, ablaze with glory?
Whose is this delightful sunshade made of Jambū-river gold, complete with its ribs?”
Who comes to veil the radiance of the sun with his glory?
Whose body, having grasped the supreme yak-tail fan,
is held one above the other upon the heads of those of excellent merit on both sides?
“Whose are these fans with feathered handles, variegated and soft, with shafts of gold and jewels,
moving in both directions? They have the hue of acacia-embers and are fanned from the mouth of a furnace.”
The earrings, beautiful and curling, shine on both sides of her face.
Whose soft, dark locks, fanned by the breeze,
shimmering against the edge of her forehead, look like lightning flashing across the sky?
“Whose are these eyes, so long and wide?
Who shines with such large eyes? Whose is this face with its ūrṇā-hair?
Whose are these teeth, set in rows, pure and like the form of a conch?”
As he speaks, his teeth shine like jasmine buds.
Whose hands and feet, red as lac-dye juice, are so well-nourished?
Who is this one endowed with lips like the *bimba* fruit, who shines by day like the sun?
“In the Himalayas, like a great sal tree in full bloom,
who is this one, draped in white robes, who shines with victory like Indra?
He is strewn with golden knobs and adorned with variegated jeweled handles.”
Who is he that, having entered the assembly, draws his sword slightly?
“Adorned with gold ornaments, well-made and finely sewn—
who is he that takes them off from his feet, having paid homage to the Great Seer?”
Regarding the phrase "those who have set out there": for whom have these musical instruments been set out in front? "Making them laugh" means making this king laugh.

"For whom, with a golden band?"—he asks: for whom does the face shine like a cloud with lightning, by means of the *uṣṇīṣa*-band bound upon the forehead? "A youth with a quiver fastened" means a young man with a fastened quiver.
"Like gold struck by the hammer's mouth" means like gold struck upon the blacksmith's anvil. "Resembling acacia embers" means resembling blazing acacia embers.
"Jambunada" means made of red gold. "Having grasped the handle" means having been grasped by the hand that holds the chowrie.
"The supreme yak-tail fan" means the most excellent yak-tail fan. "Those with hands of feathers" means...
"Peacock-feather-handled. "Variegated" means variegated with the seven precious gems. "With handles of gold and jewels" means handles carved from refined gold (*tapanīya-suvaṇṇa*) and jewels.
"Moving on both sides of the face" means they move on both sides of the mouth.
"Touched by the wind" means struck by the wind. "Glossy ends" means having smooth, lustrous tips. "On the forehead"—to whom do such things belong?
The hair adorns the forehead. "Like lightning risen from the sky" means like lightning that has emerged from the heavens.

"It shines" means it is full, like a golden mirror. "Born from the face" means produced from the mouth. "Resembling *kuppila* flowers" means similar to the *mandārava* flower. "Well-nourished" means well-cared for.
"Like the moon that has attained victory" means like the moon that has achieved triumph. "Studded with golden knobs."
It was strewn with golden knobs. "Variegated with jeweled handles" means variegated with jewels on the shafts.
"Gold-worked" means inlaid with gold. "Variegated" means variegated with the seven gems. "Well-made" means perfectly finished. "Variegated stitching" means multicolored seams.
"Who is this that takes them off from his feet? means who is this person taking such sandals off from his feet?

Thus questioned by his son Sāgara-Brahmadatta, the ascetic, possessing psychic power and having attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā), spoke this verse while explaining: "My dear, these are the sons of King Dhatarattha, your nephews, the Nāgas.
For these Nāgas are the sons born of Samuddajā; they are possessed of psychic power, renowned, and of great majesty."
Even as they were thus conversing, the assembly of nāgas arrived; having paid homage at the feet of the ascetic, they sat down to one side.
Samuddajā too, having paid homage to her father and wept, went back to the nāga abode together with the assembly of nāgas.
Sāgara-Brahmadatta also stayed there for a few days and then returned to Bārāṇasī. Samuddajā passed away right there in the nāga abode.
The Bodhisatta, having guarded his virtue for as long as he lived and performed the Uposatha rites, filled the city of heaven together with his retinue at the end of his life.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, O lay followers, even when no Buddha had arisen,
the ancient wise ones abandoned such worldly prosperity and indeed performed the Uposatha rites," and he then identified the Jātaka by correlating the characters.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the lay devotees were established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the mother and father were the royal families;
the hunter-brāhmaṇa was Devadatta; Somadatta was Ānanda; Ajamukhī was Uppalavaṇṇā;
Sudassana was Sāriputta; Subhoga was Moggallāna; Kāṇāriṭṭha was Sunakkhatta; and Bhūridatta was none other than myself, the Fully Enlightened One.
The sixth *Bhūridattajātaka-vaṇṇanā* is concluded.
[544] 7. The *Candakumārajātaka-vaṇṇanā*:
"You were a king of cruel deeds"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Vulture Peak, concerning Devadatta.
The background story for him has already been related in the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka.

It should be understood according to the method presented there, from the time of his going forth until the death of King Bimbisāra. However, after having him killed, Devadatta approached Ajātasattu and said:
"Great King, your own desire has reached its fulfillment; as for my desire..."
“It will not reach him yet,” he said. “But what, venerable sir, is your intention? “Is it not that I shall become a Buddha by killing the One of Ten Powers?
“What can we do in this matter? “Great King, it is fitting to assemble the archers.
“Very well, venerable sir,” the king replied, and having assembled five hundred archers who could hit a target at a distance, he [spoke].
Then, having selected thirty-one men, he sent them into the presence of the Elder. He addressed their leader, saying:
"Friend, the ascetic Gotama is staying at Vulture Peak; he is walking back and forth at a certain daytime resting place named so-and-so.
Go there, pierce him with a poisoned arrow, bring about his death, and [inform] such-and-such a person..."
Having said, "Come by this path," and having sent him forth, he stationed two archers on that path, saying, "A man will come along the path you are standing upon;
after you have deprived him of life, go by such-and-such a path.
On that same path, he stationed four men, saying, "Two men will come along the path you are standing upon; you..."

“Having deprived them of life, go by such-and-such a path,” he stationed eight men on that path, saying, “Four men will come along the path you are standing upon; having deprived them of life, go by such-and-such a path.
On that path, he stationed sixteen men, [saying], “Eight [men will come] along the path you are standing upon...”
“Men will come; you must deprive them of life and go by such-and-such a path.
But why did he act in this way? It was for the purpose of concealing his own deed.
Then that chief archer, slinging a sword at his left side, fastening a quiver upon his back, and taking up a great bow with horns of rams, [stood] before the Tathāgata.
Having gone into his presence with the thought, "I shall pierce him," he strung his bow, fixed an arrow, drew it back, and was unable to release it.
Unable even to lower the arrow, he became exhausted in appearance as if his ribs were breaking and saliva was trickling from his mouth;
his entire body became rigid, as if it had been subjected to the pressure of a mechanical device.
It became as if he were [in the presence of] death. Trembling with the fear of death, he stood there. Then the Teacher, seeing him, let out a sweet voice and said this:
"Do not be afraid, O man; come here. At that moment, casting aside his weapons, he prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and said:
"A transgression, Venerable Sir, has overcome me—like a fool, like a deluded one, like an unwholesome one."
“Venerable sir, not knowing your virtues, I have come to deprive you of life at the word of the blind fool Devadatta.
Forgive me, bhante. Having thus asked for forgiveness, he sat down to one side.
Then the Teacher, teaching him the Dhamma and proclaiming the Truths, established him in the fruit of stream-entry, saying: “Friend, the path pointed out by Devadatta—”
"Do not proceed by that way; go by another path," he dismissed him. Having dismissed him, he descended from the walkway and sat down at the foot of a certain tree.
Then, as the archer did not return, the other two men thought, "Why is he taking so long? and [set out] by the opposite path.
As they were going along, they saw the One of Ten Powers; having approached and paid homage, they sat down to one side.
The Teacher taught the Dhamma to them as well, proclaimed the Truths, and established them in the fruit of stream-entry.
Then he dismissed them, saying, "Friends, do not follow the path described by Devadatta; go by this path instead. By this same means, [he did so] for the others as well.
When they had arrived and were seated, he established them in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) and dismissed them by means of another path.
Then, the eldest archer, who had arrived first, approached Devadatta and reported: "Venerable sir, Devadatta, I was unable to deprive the Perfectly Enlightened One of life;
that Blessed One possesses great psychic power (*mahiddhika*) and great majesty (*mahānubhāva*). All of them [did likewise].
Thinking, "It is by relying on the Fully Enlightened One that we have obtained our livelihood," they went forth in the presence of the Teacher and attained Arahatship.
This event became well known throughout the Saṅgha of monks. In the Dhamma Hall, the monks initiated a discussion:
"Friends, it is said that Devadatta, out of a mind of enmity toward the Tathāgata, deprived many people of their lives..."
...made an effort to kill him; yet they all obtained their lives by depending on the Teacher.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “For this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Devadatta, with a mind of enmity toward me, relied upon me while I was alone.”
Having said, "Many people indeed made an effort to deprive him of life," he was requested by them to relate a past event.
In the past, this city of Bārāṇasī was named Pupphavatī.
There, a son of King Vasavatti named Ekarāja reigned; his son, Prince Candaka, acted as viceroy. A brahmin named Khaṇḍahāla—
He became the royal chaplain. He instructed the king in both worldly affairs and the Dhamma. The king, thinking him to be "wise," appointed him to the office of judge.
However, having become a taker of bribes, he would accept bribes and declare those who were not owners to be owners, and those who were owners to be non-owners.
Then one day, a man who had lost his lawsuit departed from the court of justice, shouting in protest.
Seeing Prince Canda approaching the royal court, he ran forward, fell at his feet, and wept.
The prince asked, "Good man, why do you weep? He replied, "Master, Khaṇḍahāla is plundering the legal proceedings;
I was bribed by him and defeated. Prince Canda comforted him, saying, "Do not fear."
