Having brought it to a legal decision, he made each owner his own and each ownerless one truly ownerless. The great multitude gave a cry of approval with a loud noise.
Hearing this, the king asked, "What is that sound? "It is said that the wager has been well adjudicated by Prince Candaka;
this is the sound of applause," they replied. Hearing this, the king was pleased. The prince came and [approached] him...
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. Then the king said to him, “Dear son, it seems a certain legal case has been decided by you.
“Yes, Your Majesty,” he replied. “In that case, dear son, from now on you yourself shall establish the judicial process,” and he handed the administration of justice over to the prince.
From that time forth, Khaṇḍahāla’s income was cut off. Consequently, he conceived a grudge against the prince.
Seeking an opportunity and looking for a flaw, he wandered about. Now that king was of dull wit.

One day, having slept during the middle of the night, at the time of dawn, he saw in a dream a city with its gate-towers adorned, surrounded by a wall made of the seven precious gems, possessing a great street of golden sand sixty *yojanas* wide, graced by the Vejayanta Palace rising a thousand *yojanas* high, and endowed with the delights of groves such as Nandana and the beauties of lotus ponds such as the Nandā.
Having seen the realm of the Thirty-three, crowded with hosts of devas, he woke up and, desiring to go there, thought:
"Tomorrow, at the time of my teacher Khaṇḍahāla’s arrival, I will ask him for the path leading to the world of the devas and go to the world of the devas by the path he points out.
Khaṇḍahāla also, having bathed and eaten early in the morning, came to wait upon the king.
Having entered the royal palace, he inquired after the king’s well-being. Then the king, having had a seat provided for him, asked him a question.
To clarify that matter, the Teacher said:
“You are a king of cruel deeds, the sole ruler of Pupphavatī.”
Thus he questioned the deluded Khaṇḍahāla, the chaplain who was a mere nominal brahmin:
“Explain the path to the heavens, for you, O brahmin, are skilled in the Dhamma and Vinaya;
tell how men, having performed meritorious deeds, go from here to a happy destination.”
In this context, *rājāsī* means "there was a king. *Luddakammo* means one whose deeds are cruel and harsh.
*Saggāna maggaṃ* means the path leading to the heavens. *Dhammavinayakusalo* means skilled in the Dhamma of good conduct and in the Vinaya of proper discipline. *Yathā* means:
"Just as people, having performed meritorious deeds, go from here to a happy destination, please explain that path to a happy destination to me"—thus he asked.
However, it is proper to ask this question of either an omniscient Buddha, his disciples, or, in their absence, a Bodhisatta.
But the king questioned Khaṇḍahāla just as a man who has been lost for seven days might ask one who has been lost for only a month for the way. He thought: "This [question] belongs to my enemy..."
“The time has come to show my back; now, having brought Prince Candaka to his death, I shall fulfill my heart’s desire.
Then, addressing the king, he spoke this third verse:
“O King, having given excessive gifts and having caused those who should not be slain to be put to death;”
“Thus do men go to a happy destination after having performed meritorious deeds.

The meaning of this is: “Great King, those who go to heaven give excessive gifts and have those who should not be killed put to death. If you also desire to go to heaven, you too should act in that same way.
Then the king asked for the true meaning of the question:
“But what, then, is that supreme gift? And who in this world are those not to be slain?
Tell us this, and I shall perform sacrifices and give gifts.
He then explained it to him:
“O King, one should sacrifice with sons, with chief queens, and with citizens;
with four bulls of noble breed—O King, one should sacrifice with every kind of quartet.
And while answering the king’s question, having been asked about the path to the world of the gods, he explained the path to hell.
In this context, "by sons" means by one's own beloved sons and beloved daughters.
"By queens" means by beloved wives. "By merchants" means by guild-leaders (*seṭṭhis*). "By bulls" means by all-white royal bulls. "By thoroughbreds" means by auspicious horses.
"By fours" means by all these—elephants and so forth—and others, in groups of four; thus it is by every set of four.

“Your Majesty, a sacrifice must be performed. For those kings who perform a sacrifice by cutting off the heads of these men with a sword, taking the blood from their throats in a golden bowl, and casting it into a pit, go to the world of the gods together with their physical bodies.
Your Majesty, there is only the giving of provisions, clothing, and other necessities to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, the wayfarers, and beggars that takes place.”
Furthermore, he convinced the king that sacrificing a sacrifice with the throat-blood of these sons, daughters, and others after having killed them is what is called "the supreme gift.
Thus, thinking, "If I take Prince Canda alone, they will think it is being done out of a mind of enmity," he included him among the great multitude.
Then, having heard the conversation of those who were speaking thus, all the people of the inner palace...
Terrified, trembling, and with hearts filled with agitation, they all at once let out a great cry. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Hearing that, those in the inner palace—the princes and the chief queens—cried out;
there was a single roar, a sound that rose up like a clamor.”
In that context, the word *tanti* means that upon hearing the sound, "Let the princes and the great seers be slain," there was but a single cry throughout the entire royal residence.
*Bhīma* means terrifying. *Accuggata* means it rose exceedingly high; the entire royal family became like a grove of *sāla* trees struck by the winds at the end of an eon.
The brahmin said to the king: “But, Great King, are you able to perform the sacrifice, or are you not?
“What are you saying, Teacher? Having performed the sacrifice, we shall go to the world of the gods.
“Great King, those who are cowardly and of weak resolve are not capable of performing a sacrifice. Assemble all of you here.”

Thinking, “I shall perform the work at the sacrificial enclosure,” he took a force sufficient for his purpose, departed from the city, and had the sacrificial enclosure leveled and surrounded by a fence.

Why? Because it was the established custom among the ancient brahmins that the sacrificial enclosure should be enclosed with a fence, thinking, “Lest a righteous ascetic or brahmin should come and prevent [the sacrifice].”
[The matter] was set aside. The king, having summoned his men, said:
"Sirs, I shall go to the world of the gods after sacrificing by killing my own sons, daughters, and wives; go, inform them, and bring them all here.
Thus he spoke for the purpose of first bringing his children.
“Go and speak to the princes—Canda, Suriya, Bhaddasena, Sūra, and Vāmagotta—and say:
‘It seems you must be prepared for the sake of the sacrifice.
In that context, “go and speak to the princes” refers to Canda Kumāra and Suriya Kumāra, the two sons of Queen Gotamī.
The sons of the chief queen were Bhaddasena, Sūra, and Vāmagotta; these were their half-brothers.
"Be numerous indeed" means: "Explain it so that you may form a heap in one place.
They first went to Prince Candakumāra and said: "Prince, they say that after killing you..."
“Your father, desiring to go to the world of the gods, has sent us to take you.
“On whose authority did he have me taken? “On the word of Khaṇḍahāla, Your Majesty. “Does he wish to take me alone, or others as well?
“Prince, he wishes to take others too; it is said he intends to perform a sacrifice at every crossroads. He thought:
“He has no enmity toward others; rather, because he thinks, ‘I am not permitted to commit plunder in the court,’ he causes many to be killed out of malice toward me alone.
It is my burden to secure their release so that he may be allowed to see his father.
Then he said to those royal officers, “In that case, carry out the word of my father.”
Having led them there and placed them to one side in the royal courtyard, they summoned the other three as well, brought them into his presence, and announced to the king:
"Your Majesty, your sons have been brought. Upon hearing their words, he said:
"Sirs, now bring my daughters and place them in the very presence of those brothers," and spoke this further verse in order to have the four daughters brought forward.
“Speak also to the maidens, Upasena, Kokila, and Mudita;
and to the maiden Nandā as well—let them be prepared for the sake of the sacrifice.

They replied, “We shall do so,” and going to those girls, they brought them back weeping and lamenting and placed them before their own brothers. Then the king spoke this other verse for the purpose of taking wives for himself:
“May my great mares— Vijayā, Erāvatī, Kesinī, and Sunandā—
be endowed with the most excellent marks and be abundant for the sake of the sacrifice.
In this context, “endowed with the most excellent marks” means that these [mares] should also be told to be possessed of the sixty-four supreme female marks.
Weeping, they brought them back and placed them in the presence of the princes. Then the King, commanding the four guild-leaders to be seized, spoke this other verse:
“Householders, tell Puṇṇamukha, Bhaddiya, and Siṅgāla, And also the householder Vaḍḍha: ‘Be ready, it is said, for the sake of the sacrifice.’”
The king’s men went and brought them as well. While the king’s sons and wives were being seized, no one in the entire city said anything.

However, because the merchant families possessed great influence, when they were seized, the whole city was thrown into agitation and cried out, "We will not allow the king to sacrifice by killing the merchants! and they surrounded the merchants.
Together with his kinsmen, he went to the royal palace. Then those merchants, surrounded by their circle of relatives, paid homage to the king and begged for their lives.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then those householders, having assembled there, surrounded by their wives and children, spoke thus.”
"O god Śikhin, make us all your servants, or else proclaim us to be slaves.
In this context, "make us all your servants" means: bind a topknot upon our heads and make us your personal attendants;
we shall perform the duties of your servants. "Or else proclaim us to be slaves" means: or else, if you do not believe us, [proclaim it].
“Gather all the courtesans together and announce to them in the midst of the crowd that we are your slaves; we shall consent to our slavery to you.

Although they made this request, they were unable to save their lives. The king’s men had the others withdrawn, seized them, and seated them right beside the princes. Then the king, giving orders for the capture of the elephant and the other animals, said:
“Even my elephant Abhayaṅkara, and Nāḷāgiri, and Varuṇadanta, who rises high above [the rest];”
“Bring them quickly, for they will be needed for the sacrifice.
Bring Kesi, the jewel among horses, Surāmukha, Puṇṇaka, and Vinataka;
bring them quickly, for they will be needed for the sacrifice.”
“Bring me even Usabha the leader of the herd, Anoja, Nisabha, and Gavampati;
let them all assemble together, for I shall sacrifice and give gifts.
Prepare everything for the sacrifice when the sun has risen.”
"And give the command to the princes: 'May they enjoy themselves this night.
But when the sun has risen, provide everything for the sacrifice.
Now speak to the princes: 'Today is indeed the final night.'"
"In that regard, let them form groups of four for everything"—meaning not only this much, but let them also form groups of four from all the remaining quadrupeds and flocks of birds, making a heap;
I shall perform a sacrifice consisting of every group of four and give gifts to the begging brahmins.
"Prepare everything"—thus was it said by me, leaving nothing out.
“Prepare them! [The king said: “But when the sun has risen, I shall perform the sacrifice tomorrow morning at dawn.
Prepare everything!”—meaning, “Prepare all the remaining sacrificial requisites as well.
However, the king’s mother and father were still alive. Then his ministers went and informed the mother: “Noble lady,…”
“Your son has killed his wife and children, desiring to perform a sacrifice. She cried out, “What are you saying, dear ones?
and striking her chest with her hand, she came running back weeping and asked, “Is it true that such will be your sacrifice?
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“His mother came from her celestial mansion, weeping, and said to him:
‘It is said, my son, that you will perform a sacrifice with all four of your sons.
In this context, *taṃ taṃ* refers to that very king. *Vimānato* means from her own dwelling place.
The king said:
“All my sons are lost when the moon is being slain;
having offered a sacrifice with my sons, I shall go to a happy destination, to heaven.”
In that context, "all four" refers to the fact that even as Prince Candaka was being slain, they were all surrendered by me for the sake of the sacrifice.
Then his mother said to him:
"Do not believe that, my son; it is said that a good rebirth comes through the sacrifice of a son."
"This path leads to hell; it is not a path to the heavens.
'Give gifts, Koṇḍañña! Non-violence toward all living beings is [the way];
this is the path to a happy rebirth, and not the path by means of a sacrifice of sons.'"
In this context, "to the realms of hell" (*nirayānehi*) means that this is the path to the four states of misery (*apāya*), in the sense that they are devoid of satisfaction (*nirassāda*).

"O Koṇḍañña," he addresses the king by his clan name. "Of those who have been and those who are to be" (*bhūtabhabyānaṃ*) refers to both those who have already come into being and those sentient beings who are yet to be born.
"By the sacrifice of a son" (*puttayaññena*): there is no such thing as a "path to heaven" through a sacrificial offering made by killing one's sons and daughters.
The king said:
“At the word of my teachers, I shall cause both the moon and the sun to be slain;
having performed a sacrifice with sons who are so difficult to give away, I shall go to a happy destination, to heaven.”
"In that regard, 'the word of my teachers' means: 'Mother, this is not my own opinion;
rather, it is the word of my teacher Khaṇḍahāla, who instructed me in proper conduct. This is his instruction. Therefore, I shall have these killed;
by sacrificing with my sons, who are so difficult to give up, I shall go to heaven.'"
His mother, unable to make him accept her words, departed. His father asked about that matter. Explaining the situation, the Teacher said:
“His father also spoke thus to his own legitimate son, who was under his command:
‘It is said, my son, you shall have a sacrifice with four sons.’”
In that context, "Vasavattī" is his name.
The king said:
"All my sons are lost when the moon is being struck."
“Having offered a sacrifice with my sons, I shall go to a happy destination, to heaven,” he said.
Then his father replied to him:
“Do not believe that, my son, that there will indeed be a happy destination through a sacrifice of sons.”
"This path leads to hell; it is not the path to the heavenly realms.
'Give gifts, Koṇḍañña! Non-violence toward all living beings is the path to a happy destination, and not the path of sacrificing one's own son.'"
The king said:
“At the word of my teachers, I shall cause both the moon and the sun to be slain;
having performed a sacrifice with sons who are so difficult to give away, I shall go to a good destination, to heaven.”
Then his father said to him:
“Bestow gifts, Koṇḍañña; non-violence is for the welfare of all beings.
Surrounded by your sons, protect the kingdom and the countryside.”
In that context, "surrounded by his sons" means encircled by his sons. "The kingdom and the province" refers to the entire kingdom of Kāsi and the specific province that constitutes a part of it.
He too was unable to make them accept his word. Then Prince Canda thought:
"The suffering of all these people has arisen because of me alone; having entreated my father, I shall deliver this many people from the suffering of death."
"I shall release them. Speaking thus with his father, he said:
"O King, do not kill us! Give us to Khaṇḍahāla as slaves;
even if bound in fetters, we shall tend the elephants and horses."
“O Lord, do not kill us! Give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla.
Even if we are bound in fetters, let us at least gather elephant fodder.
“O Lord, do not kill us! Give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla!”
“Even if we were bound in chains, we would cast away the horse-dung.
‘O King, do not kill us! Give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla.
Whatever you desire, even if it means being exiled from the kingdom, let that be.’”
“We shall go on alms-round.
In that regard, “even though we are bound with heavy chains” means even if we were bound with great shackles. “Whatever belongs to you” means:
even if you wish to give it to Khaṇḍahāla, give it to us as slaves; we will do it for him.
He said, "A life of servitude. He added, "Even if it means exile from the kingdom—if we have committed some fault, banish us from the realm!
Even if we are exiled from the kingdom, we shall wander for alms like the wretched, carrying begging bowls;
do not kill us, grant us our lives! Thus he lamented.

Hearing his various lamentations, the king, as if his heart were rent asunder, weeping with eyes full of tears, said to release them all: "No one shall succeed in killing my sons; I have no need for the world of the gods. Thus he spoke to liberate them:
"You cause me indeed great sorrow by your lamenting, for you desire life;
release the princes now, let there be enough for me even with this sacrifice of sons."
Having heard the king’s words, they released the entire multitude of living beings, beginning with the princes and ending with the fish.
Meanwhile, Khaṇḍahāla was making arrangements for the work at the sacrificial enclosure. Then a certain man said to him, "Hey, you wicked Khaṇḍahāla!
The king has released his sons; why do you intend to kill your own sons and [drench] their throats with blood?"
“Offer a sacrifice,” he said. [The other] asked, “What indeed has been done by the king? Then, rising up and rushing forward with haste like the fire at the end of an eon, he said:
“I have told you before that this is difficult to do and hard to accomplish.”
“Now that our sacrifice has been prepared, why do you cause this delay?
“All go to a happy destination— those who sacrifice, those who cause others to sacrifice,
and those who rejoice in such a great sacrifice as this.”
In this context, "previously" means that I told you before: "It is not possible for one of such a fearful nature as you to perform a sacrifice;
indeed, the performance of a sacrifice is difficult to do and difficult to accomplish. Thus, you now cause the postponement of the sacrifice that has already been prepared and arranged.
There is also a reading, "vikkhambha," which means "prohibit" or "prevent."
"Great King, why do you act thus? For it is shown that as many as sacrifice, cause others to sacrifice, or rejoice in the sacrifice, all go only to a happy destination.

That foolish king, having taken the words of that man who was under the sway of anger, perceived them as the Dhamma and had his sons seized again. Then Prince Canda, seeking to awaken his father, said:
“Why did people in the past recite blessings for safety to brahmins?
Yet now, O King, you have had us killed for the sake of sacrifice, though there was no such reason.
Previously, when we were still children, you neither struck us nor had us killed.”
“Having passed from childhood into youth, O Father, we were slain though we were innocent.
“Behold us, O Great King—mounted on elephants and horses, clad in armor, whether engaged in battle or prepared for war;
for men such as we do not become heroes merely for the sake of a sacrifice.”
“Whether in border regions in revolt, or in the wilderness, they employ men such as us;
yet, O dear one, we are being slain for no reason, on ground that is not our own.
For even those birds which dwell having built their nests of grass—”
“Even their dear sons—now you, O King, have caused them to be slain.
“Do not believe him; Khaṇḍahāla would not have me killed.
For having had me killed, O King, he will kill her immediately after.”
“They give excellent villages and excellent towns, O Great King, and even wealth to him;
yet even those who receive but a morsel of food from house to house eat among such families.
Even toward such as these, O Great King, they desire to act with malice.”
"For the most part, O King, these brahmins are ungrateful:
'May you not kill us, Your Majesty! Give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla;
even if we are bound in shackles, we shall guard the elephants and horses.'"
“O King, do not kill us; give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla!
Even if we are bound in fetters, let us at least gather elephant fodder.
O King, do not kill us; give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla!”
“Even if we are bound in iron chains, let us cast away the fodder for the horses.
‘O King, do not kill us! Give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla.
Even if we are exiled from the kingdom, let there be those who fulfill your desires.’”
"Let us go on our alms-round.
Therein, "previously, dear father," means: if I am to be killed, then why did our kinsmen previously, at the time of my birth, have the Brahmins recite a blessing for my safety?
At that time, it is said, Khaṇḍahāla himself, having examined my physical marks...
“He said, ‘No obstacle shall come to this prince; after you have passed away, he will rule the kingdom.
Thus his later statement does not accord with his former one; he is a liar.
Therefore, O King, having accepted his word, you had us executed for the sake of a sacrifice—without cause and for no reason at all. Do not kill us, for he is [deceitful] toward me.”
"O King of Men, if you desire to slay the great multitude through enmity alone, observe this well.
"O Great King, it was not so before; even if he desired to slay us, why did he not kill us himself or have us killed by others long ago?
But now we are young, in the prime of our youth, and we are increasing with sons and daughters."
"Why are we, who have done you no harm and are such as we are, being slain?

"Look at us," he said; "look at us four brothers. Look at us as we fight—when our enemies have surrounded the city and we, sons like ourselves, are fighting with them. For kings without sons are without a protector."
They are called "those like me. "Those like me" means that heroes and the powerful such as we are should not be killed for the sake of a sacrifice.
"They incite" means they employ them for the purpose of capturing those enemies.
"Then" means: "Then why, dear father, are we being killed without cause, by no cause, in an improper place, in a place that is not even a proper location? "Do not believe him," O Great King.
"Khaṇḍahāla will not have me killed; do not believe him. 'Even his wealth' means that kings give even the wealth of that brahmin [to others].
'And then they become recipients of the first portions' means that they receive the first water and the first alms-food, and thus they become recipients of the first portions.
'And they wish to deceive even those' means that they wish to deceive such givers of alms in whose families they eat."
Having heard the prince’s lamentation, the king said:
“Indeed, you cause me pain by lamenting, for you desire life;
release the prince now, let there be enough for me with this sacrifice of a son.”
Having spoken this verse, he released him once more. Khaṇḍahāla came and spoke again:
“I told you before that this is difficult to do and hard to accomplish;
why then do you cause a disturbance to our sacrifice that has already been prepared?”
“All go to a happy destination—those who sacrifice, those who cause others to sacrifice, and those who rejoice in such a great sacrifice as this performed by these sacrificers.
Having said this, he made him take it again. Then, for the sake of winning him over, the prince said:
“If indeed, having sacrificed with their sons, people go from here to the world of the gods, then let the brahmin sacrifice first; you may sacrifice later, O King.
If indeed, having sacrificed with their sons, people go from here to the world of the gods...”
“Khaṇḍahāla himself was sacrificing with his own sons.
Knowing this, Khaṇḍahāla, why did you not kill your little sons,
and why did you not kill all your kinsmen and yourself?”
“All those who sacrifice, and those who cause others to sacrifice, and even those who rejoice in such a great sacrifice as this— all go to hell.
For if he who kills were purified by it, and if he who is killed were to go to a heavenly state upon being slain;”
“They might kill one who addresses them as ‘bho’ and those who believe in them.
Regarding that, first of all, let the brahmin Khaṇḍahāla perform the sacrifice with his own sons;
then, after he has sacrificed in this way and departed for the world of the gods, you may sacrifice later on. Your Majesty, for even a meal of delicious flavors—
He spoke thus to show that while one eats after having it examined by others, why does one act without even examining whether the killing of one’s own children and wife leads to the heavenly world?

"Knowing thus" means: knowing that "one goes to the heavenly world by killing sons and daughters," for what reason did he not kill his own sons, his kinsmen, and himself? For if, by killing another, one [goes to] the heavenly world...
"They go [to heaven]; by killing oneself, one will go to the Brahma-world.
Thus, one who understands the merit of sacrifice might kill oneself rather than kill another. But this man, instead of doing that, has me killed.
For this reason also, O Great King, you should know: "He acts in this way because he is unable to carry out a plundering within the judicial process."
Thus did Edisanti offer such a sacrifice of his son.
Even though the prince spoke at such length, he was unable to make his father accept his words; instead, he addressed the assembly standing around the king:
"And how, O householders and wives who desire sons, do they [sacrifice]?"
In the city they do not cry out to the king: "Do not kill your own legitimate son!
How indeed, householders, do wives who desire a son not cry out to the king in the city: "Do not kill your own begotten son"?
“I am one who desires the king’s welfare and seeks the benefit of the entire countryside;
no one has any resentment toward him, nor does any inhabitant of the countryside report anything against me.
In this context, the phrase “those desiring sons” (*puttakāmā*) is said with reference to the wives (*gharaṇīyo*), for householders are indeed those who desire sons (*puttakāmā*).
“They do not reproach” means they do not revile or speak against him. “Born from himself” means born from his own self.
Even when this was said, there was no one at all capable of conversing with the king.
No one thought, “I have been bribed by him,” nor did anyone think, “Out of pride in his power, he has caused such suffering for me. Not a single person [spoke] with me.

"He was not one who would cause resentment. "He does not announce it to the country" means that this countryman does not announce to the King—who desires the welfare of both the King and the country—that "your son is endowed with virtues"; the meaning is that he does not make it known.
Even when this was said, no one said anything at all. Thereupon, Prince Candaka, urging his own wives to go for the sake of making the request, said:
“Go, my wives, and speak to your father and Khaṇḍahāla:
‘Do not kill the princes, who are innocent and resemble lions.
Go, my wives, and speak to your father and Khaṇḍahāla.”
"Do not kill the princes; they are beloved by the whole world.
Having gone there, they pleaded with him, but the king paid them no heed. Then the prince, being left without a protector, lamented:
"What if I were now to be born among the families of chariot-makers..."
"Or if I were born among the Pukkusa outcasts or among the Vessas,
the King would not have had me killed at this sacrifice.
Having said this, he spoke again to dismiss those wives:
“All you women with parted hair, go to the noble Khaṇḍahāla;
fall at his feet, for I see no fault in him.
All you women with parted hair, go to the noble Khaṇḍahāla.”
“Fall at his feet; what offense have we committed against you, venerable sir?”—therein, “I see no offense in myself” means that I, the teacher Khaṇḍahāla, do not perceive any fault in myself.
“What have we done to you, venerable sir? means, noble Khaṇḍahāla, what harm have we done to you? Or rather, it is the fault of Prince Candaka.
“There is [something], say ‘forgive that’.
Then Candakumāra’s younger sister, named Selakumārī, being unable to restrain her grief, fell at her father’s feet and lamented. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Wretched Selā laments, having seen her brother led away.”
“The sacrifice has indeed been postponed for me by my father, who desires heaven,” he said.

Therein, “because it was brought forward” means because its nature was brought forward. “Postponed” means set aside. “Desiring heaven” means desiring heaven after having killed my brothers. “Father, what will you do with heaven after killing these?
she lamented. The king did not heed her words either. Then Candakumāra’s son, named Vasula, [seeing] his father in distress...
Seeing this, he lamented at the feet of the king, thinking, "I shall entreat my grandfather and have my father's life restored.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
"Āvatti and Parivatti, Vasula, in the presence of the king..."
"Do not kill our father; we have reached youth from childhood.
Therein, "we have reached youth from childhood" means: "O King, we are young children, we have not yet reached youth; out of compassion for us as well, do not kill our father.
Hearing his lamentation, the king, as if his heart were breaking, embraced the prince with eyes full of tears and said, "Dear son, take heart; I release your father," and he spoke this verse:
“Vasula, that is your father; speak with your father.
You cause me only sorrow by lamenting thus in the inner apartments.
Release the princes now; let there be enough for me with this sacrifice of sons.”
There, "in the inner palace" means within the king's residence.
Again, Khaṇḍahāla came and said:
"I have told you before that this is difficult to do and hard to accomplish."
“Now that our sacrifice has been prepared, why do you cause this distraction?
“All go to a happy destination— those who sacrifice, those who cause others to sacrifice,
and those who rejoice in such a great sacrifice as this performed by these sacrificers.”
But the king, being blind and foolish, again had his sons seized at the word of Khaṇḍahāla. Then Khaṇḍahāla thought: "This king is of a gentle mind;
he seizes them at one time and releases them at another. He might release my sons again at the word of the children;
I must lead him straight to the place of sacrifice. Then he spoke this verse to him for the purpose of making him go there:
“O Single King, the sacrifice of all treasures has been prepared and arranged for you;
go forth, O Lord, and having gone to heaven, you shall rejoice.

The meaning of this is: “Great King, your sacrifice of all treasures has been prepared and arranged; now is the time for your departure, therefore go forth; having performed the sacrifice and gone to heaven, you shall rejoice.”
Then, at the time of departing for the sacrificial enclosure taking the Bodhisatta with him, his harem women all went out together. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“These seven hundred young women, the wives of Prince Canda, Having disheveled their hair, followed along the road weeping.”
“But others, like deities departing from the Nandana grove out of grief,
went along the road weeping, having disheveled their hair. In this context,
“like deities departing from the Nandana grove” means they went just as deities who have passed away would depart, surrounded by other deities in the Nandana forest.
From here follow their verses of lamentation:
“Clad in fine garments of Kāsī cloth, adorned with earrings, and anointed with aloe and sandalwood paste,
they are led away for the sake of sacrifice to the sole king, like the moon and the sun.”
“Clad in pure Kāsika garments, adorned with earrings and anointed with aloe and sandalwood,
the moon and the sun are led away, causing grief to their mother’s heart.
Clad in pure Kāsika garments, adorned with earrings and anointed with aloe and sandalwood...”
The moon and the sun are led away, causing heart-wrenching grief for the people.
“Those who fed on meat broth, those well-bathed and well-anointed, wearing earrings and smeared with agaru and sandalwood—
these very ones, the moon and the sun, are led away for the sake of sacrifice to the sole monarch.”
“Eating meat broth, bathed and groomed by barbers, adorned with earrings and anointed with aloe and sandalwood paste—
such men are led away, causing heart-rending grief to their mothers.
Eating meat broth, bathed and groomed by barbers, adorned with earrings and anointed with aloe and sandalwood paste— ”
The moon and the sun are led away, causing heartache for the people.
"Those whom they formerly followed on elephants when those elephants were fit to bear the burden—
now both the moon and the sun go on foot."
“Those who formerly followed behind excellent horses on horseback,
now both the moon and the sun must go on foot.
Those who formerly followed behind excellent chariots in chariots...”
“Abandoning the moon and the sun, both now go on foot.
Those who formerly went forth on swift horses adorned with burnished trappings—
abandoning the moon and the sun, both now go on foot.”
In this context: "Wearing fine Kāsī garments" means wearing clean clothes made of Kāsī cloth. "The Moon and the Sun" refers to Prince Canda and Prince Sūriya.
"Well-bathed by bathers" means they were well-anointed with sandalwood powder and thoroughly cleansed by bathers who had performed the preliminary rites.
"Yassu" means "ye assu" (those who would be); "assu" is merely a particle; the sense is "those princes. "Formerly" means prior to this.

"Mounted on the back of the best of elephants" means having reached the position on the back of the finest elephants; the sense is that they were mounted upon the shoulders of decorated, excellent elephants.

"Mounted on the back of the best of horses" means having gone onto the backs of the finest horses. "Mounted on the seat of the best of chariots" means having taken their places in the middle of the most excellent chariots.
"They went forth" means they departed.
While they were thus lamenting, they carried the Bodhisatta out from the city. The entire city was thrown into agitation and began to depart.
When the great multitude had gone out, the gates would not suffice.
Seeing the excessive number of people, the Brahmin thought, "Who knows what will happen? and he caused the city gates to be closed. The great multitude [was unable] to depart.
Not finding anyone, she cried out with a great cry near a park located close to the city gate.
At that sound, the flocks of birds were agitated and flew up into the sky. The great multitude, calling out to this and that bird while lamenting, said:
"If you, O bird, desire flesh, fly before the Puṣpavatī."
“Sacrifice here, O sole king, who is bewildered by your four sons.
If you, O bird, desire meat, fly to the east of Pupphavatī;
sacrifice here, O sole king, who is bewildered by your four daughters.”
“If you, bird, desire meat, fly to the east of Pupphavatī;
there the sole king is sacrificing, having become confused with his four chief queens.
“If you, bird, desire meat, fly to the east of Pupphavatī;”
"Let the sole king sacrifice here, being deluded by four householders.
'If you, O bird, desire meat, fly to the east of Pupphavatī;
let the sole king sacrifice here, being deluded by four elephants.'"
“If you, O bird, desire meat, fly to the east of Pupphavatī;
there a single king is sacrificing, having become bewildered with four horses.
If you, O bird, desire meat, fly to the east of Pupphavatī.”
“Let the sole king sacrifice here,” [she said], “confused by four bulls.
“If you desire my flesh, O bird, fly toward the east of Pupphavatī;
let the sole king sacrifice here, confused by every set of four.”
In this context, "If you desire meat" means: "O bird, if you desire meat, there is a sacrificial enclosure to the east, in front of Pupphavatī;

go there. "Sacrifice here" refers to the fact that a certain king, having become confused by taking the words of Khaṇḍahāla, was performing a sacrifice there with his four sons. The same method applies to the remaining verses as well.

Thus the great multitude, having lamented at that place, went to the dwelling-place of the Bodhisatta. Circumambulating the palace and beholding the inner apartments, the gabled halls, the gardens, and so forth, they lamented with these verses:
“This is his palace, this is the inner apartment so delightful;
yet now, O noble sons, all four have been led away for execution.”
“This is his gabled hall, strewn with golden flowers and garlands;
now these four noble sons have been led away for execution.
This is his pleasure grove, ever-blooming and delightful.”
"Now, noble sons, you four have been led away for execution.
Here is his Asoka grove, ever-blooming and delightful;
now, noble sons, you four have been led away for execution."
“This is his *kaṇikāra* grove, ever-blooming and beautiful at all times;
yet now, these four noble sons have been led away for execution.
This is his *pāṭali* grove, ever-blooming and beautiful at all times.”
"Now, noble sons, you four have been led away for execution.
This mango grove of his is in full bloom, ever-fragrant and delightful;
now, noble sons, you four have been led away for execution."
“Here is his lotus pond, covered with white lotuses;
and here is a ship fashioned of gold, variegated with flowering creepers, most delightful.
Now, these four noble sons have been led away for execution.”
In that context, "Now then" means: "Now these noble sons of ours, headed by Prince Canda, having abandoned such a palace, are being led away for execution.
"Adorned with gold" means inlaid with gold. Lamenting at those various places, they again approached the elephant stables and so forth, and said:
"This is his elephant-treasure, the elephant Erāvaṇa, powerful, tusked, and mighty."
"Now, noble sons, you four have been led away for execution.
'This is his horse-treasure, a one-hoofed horse;
now, noble sons, you four have been led away for execution.'"
“This was his horse-chariot, beautiful with the sound of *sāḷī* grass, variegated with jewels;
where those noble sons shone like gods in the Nandana grove.
But now those four noble sons have been led away for execution.”
“How indeed can the king, utterly bewildered, perform a sacrifice with his four sons— who are as beautiful as the moon and whose limbs are soft as sandalwood?
How indeed can he perform a sacrifice with those who are as beautiful as the moon and whose limbs are soft as sandalwood?”
“The king will perform a sacrifice, deluded by four maidens.
How indeed can the king, deluded, perform a sacrifice with these four queens, who are as beautiful as Sāmā and whose limbs are moist with sandalwood paste?”
“How indeed can the king, utterly deluded, perform a sacrifice with only four householders— though he possesses men as beautiful as the moon and whose limbs are as smooth as sandalwood paste?
It is just as if villages and market towns were empty, and vast forests were devoid of human beings.”
"So shall it be for Pupphavatī, when the moon and sun have been sacrificed.
In this context, *Erāvaṇa* is the name of that elephant. *Ekakhura* means having unsplit hooves.
*Sāḷiyanigghosa* means endowed with a sweet sound like that of mynah birds at the time of walking. *Kathaṃ nāma* means "how indeed? or "by what means?"
By reason of this. "Equal and equal in beauty" means they were like gold in color, equal to one another in their birth, and beautiful in their faultlessness.
"With limbs smeared with red sandalwood" means their bodies were anointed with red sandalwood.
"As the villages and market towns become empty, desolate, and like a great wilderness," so too it was when the sacrifice at Pupphavatī had been offered.
"Among the princes, [the city] will become empty like a wilderness.
Then the great multitude, unable to go outside, wandered within the city itself and lamented. The Bodhisatta was also led to the sacrificial enclosure.
Then his mother, Queen Gotamī by name, cried out: "O gods, grant life to my sons!"
Rolling at the king’s feet and lamenting, she said:
“I shall become mad, ruined, and covered in dust;
if you kill the excellent moon, O King, my life-breaths will cease.”
“I shall become mad, my prosperity destroyed, and covered all over with dust;
if you strike the excellent sun, O King, my very life-breaths will be choked.
In this context, “my prosperity destroyed” means that my wealth has been ruined. “Covered all over with dust” means that, having gone mad, I shall wander about with my body smeared with dust.
Even as she was lamenting thus, having received no word from the king, she embraced the four wives of the prince and, weeping, said:
"How could they not have delighted him? Speaking kindly to one another,"
"The washerwoman, the supervisor, the lotus-pond, and the heavy burden;
they dance among the moon and sun—among them, no equality is found.
In this regard, "Why would we not delight? refers to the reason why these four—the washerwoman and so forth—[speak] to one another.
"Though the dancing girls Piyaṃvadā and Candasūriyakumāra performed before my sons, they did not delight them; rather, they made them weary.
For there exists no other equal to them in the whole of Jambudīpa, whether in dance or in song—this is the meaning.
Thus, having lamented together with her daughters-in-law and seeing no other course to take, she spoke these eight verses while reviling Khaṇḍahāla:
“Let Khaṇḍahāla’s mother take upon herself this grief of my heart,
this grief of my heart that arises because the moon has been led away for execution.
“Let Khaṇḍahāla’s mother take upon herself this grief of my heart.”
The grief in my heart that arose when the sun was led out for execution—
let Khaṇḍahāla’s wife wear this grief of my heart as her ornament.
The grief in my heart that arose when the moon was led out for execution— let Khaṇḍahāla’s wife wear this grief of my heart as her ornament.
“Let Khaṇḍahāla’s wife take upon herself this grief of my heart—
this grief of my heart that arises now that the sun has been led out for execution.
And let not Khaṇḍahāla’s mother see her son nor her husband.”
“He who killed the princes, innocent as lions—
may your mother, Khaṇḍahāla, see neither her sons nor her husband,
you who killed the princes while they were being watched by the whole world.”
“May your wife, Khaṇḍahāla, see neither her sons nor her husband—
she who had you have the princes, who were innocent and like lions,
put to death. “May your wife, Khaṇḍahāla, see neither her sons nor her husband.”
“He who slew the prince, while he was being gazed upon by the whole world.

In this context, “this of mine” means this grief and suffering in my heart. “Let him wear it” means let it enter, let it reach him. “He who slew” means you, who caused him to be killed. “While being gazed upon” means while he was being looked upon and seen by the entire world; the sense is that you murdered him even as he was visible to all.
While at the place of sacrifice, the Bodhisatta spoke thus, entreating his father:
“O King, do not kill us! Give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla;
even bound in chains, we shall guard the elephants and horses.
“O King, do not kill us! Give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla!”
"Even if we are bound in chains, let us cast aside the fodder for the elephants.
'O King, do not kill us; give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla!
Even if we are bound in chains, let us cast aside the fodder for the horses.'"
“O Lord, do not kill us; give us as slaves to Khaṇḍahāla!
Whatever desires you have for us, even if we are banished from the kingdom, we shall live by wandering for alms.”
“Even the poor, desiring sons, pray for divine favors;
yet some, despite their eloquent prayers, do not obtain sons.
They offer blessings, saying: ‘May sons be born to us, and from them, grandsons.’”
"Then why, O King, do you slaughter us for sacrifice when there is no other reason?
People obtain a son through prayers; Father, do not slaughter us!
Do not perform this sacrifice with sons obtained through such hardship."
“They obtain a son through prayers; do not, dear father, cause us grief!
Do not separate us from our mother with sons obtained so piteously.
Therein, they pray for divine [boons]; even poor women who have no sons, being desirous of children, offer many gifts.
They make divine supplications, thinking, "May we obtain a son or a daughter.
"Even having abandoned their longings" means even having cast aside their cravings; that is, even without obtaining them. This is what is meant:
O Great King, for when women do not obtain the cravings that have arisen, the fetus withers and perishes. In that regard, some women, even while making requests for sons...
Some women do not obtain their longings at all; some, even having obtained them, abandon them and do not enjoy them; and some do not obtain them because they cannot fulfill their longings.
But my mother, having obtained the longings that arose, enjoyed them, and without destroying the conceived fetus, obtained a son. Thus, having obtained him, she entreats you: "Do not kill us."
"O Great King, these beings offer blessings (*āsīsikāni*). What [do they say]? 'May sons be born to us.
Then, 'May grandsons be born,' meaning 'may sons be born even to our sons. Then, 'without cause' means that you have caused us to be slain for the sake of sacrifice without any reason.
'By supplication' means by the invocation of deities. 'Obtained by the wretched' means having become like the wretched."
"By us, your sons. "Do not let us be separated from our mother;
do not cause us to live apart from our mother," he said.
Although he spoke thus, receiving no word from his father, he fell at his mother’s feet and, lamenting, said:
“Having raised me with great hardship, Mother, you have grown old because of your son.
I pay homage at your feet; may my father attain the world beyond.
Come now, embrace me; give me leave, Mother, to pay homage at your feet.”
“I am now going abroad for the sake of a sacrifice for the sole monarch.
Come now, embrace me; grant me leave to worship at your feet, mother, as I go abroad, leaving behind grief in your heart.”
“Come now, embrace me; give me leave, mother, to worship at your feet.
I shall now go abroad, causing grief to the hearts of the people.
Therein, *posiya* means having been nourished with many sufferings. *Canda* refers to me, Canda Kumāra, thus—
"Having consoled him, mother, you must now look after my son. May my father attain the world beyond"—by this she means, "May my father obtain a world beyond endowed with wealth.
"Embrace him" means to hug or clasp him. "I go on a journey"—that is, I depart for a final departure, never to return again.
Then his mother, lamenting, spoke these four verses:
“Come now, son of Gotamī, bind a wreath of lotus petals;
let them be interspersed with campaka blossoms—this was your former custom.”
“Now, take this final ointment and anoint yourself with this sandalwood paste,
so that, well-anointed, you may shine within the assembly of kings.
Now, put on these soft garments and wear this final cloth from Kāsī.”
“Though you are well-dressed in these [simple robes], you shine in the assembly of kings.
‘Take hand-ornaments adorned with pearls, gems, and gold;
for it is with those hand-ornaments that you shine in the assembly of kings.’”
In this context, "of lotus petals" refers to a particular ornament called a *padumapattaveṭhana* (lotus-petal wrap); it is with reference to this that he spoke thus.
The meaning is: having lifted your disheveled hair-tuft (*moḷi*) and joined it with the lotus-petal wrap, bind it.
"O son of Gotamī" is an address to Prince Candaka. "Mixed with campaka petals" means mixed with inner campaka petals, possessing both color and fragrance.
“Put on various flower garlands! ‘This is yours’—this, my son, is your ancient nature;
take up that very thing! Thus she laments. “And with those”—the meaning is: “be anointed with those red sandalwood ointments with which you shone in the assembly of kings.
“Kāsika” refers to Kāsī cloth worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. “Take it” means: put it on.
Then his chief queen, named Candā, fell at his feet and, lamenting, said:
“Surely this Raṭṭhapāla is not the lord of the realm, the heir to the kingdom;
for even a great world-ruler does not feel such affection for his own son.”
Having heard that, the king spoke this verse:
“My sons are dear to me, as is my own self, and you are dear as my wives;
yet, longing for heaven, it is for that reason that I shall have you executed.”
The meaning of this is as follows: For what reason do I not feel affection for my children? It is not only Gotamī’s children who are dear;
rather, my own children are dear to me, and likewise you—my daughters-in-law and wives—are dear indeed.
Even so, desiring heaven, that is, longing for heaven, I shall have them executed for that reason; do not be anxious.
"All of you shall go together with me to the world of the gods.
Canda said:
"Kill me first; do not tear at my heart with grief."
“O King, your son Sundaraka is adorned and delicate.
‘Therefore, my lord, kill me; in the next world I shall be with Candaka.
Perform abundant merit, and we both shall wander together in the next world.’”
Therein, "first" means: "O King, kill me before my husband. "Suffering" means:
"Do not pierce my heart with the suffering of Canda’s death. "Adorned" means: "He alone is sufficient and adequate for me"—thus he is adorned.
She indicates: "O Great King, do not have such a son as this killed. "Handayya" means: "Come now! (or "Be so kind!").
"Noble lady," she said while addressing the king: "In the other world with Canda" means I shall be together with Canda in the next world.
"Let us both wander in the other world" means that since we have been killed together by you, let us both wander in the next world experiencing happiness;
do not create an obstacle for our attainment of heaven.
The king said:
“Candā, do not wish for death; you have many brothers-in-law, O large-eyed one.
They will delight you when Gotamī’s son has been sacrificed.”

In this context, "Do not rejoice, Canda" means do not take pleasure in your own death. There is also a reading, "Mā ruddī," which has the same meaning as "do not weep. "Devarā" refers to brothers-in-law.
Following that, the Teacher spoke the half-verse: "When this was said, Canda struck herself with the palms of her hands."
After that, there was her lamentation:
“Enough of life here; I shall drink poison and die.
Surely this king has no friends or ministers who are well-disposed toward him.”
Those who do not say to the king, "Do not kill your own sons"—
surely there are no kinsmen or friends who are well-wishers for this king,
since they do not say to him, "Do not kill your own children."
“O King, these too are my sons, virtuous and wearing armlets;
with them also perform the sacrifice, and then let the sons of Gotamī be released.
Having made me a hundred pits, O Great King, perform the sacrifice by dividing it sevenfold.”
"Do not kill your eldest son, who is innocent and like a lion.
Having made me into a hundred pits, O Great King, offer me as a sacrifice in seven parts;
do not kill your eldest son, who is beloved by the whole world."
In this context, *evaṃ* means "thus," referring to what was said by the foolish and blind sole king.
*Hanti* means that, having said, "What is this you are saying?", he strikes himself with the palms of his hands. *Pissāmi* means "I shall drink.

*Ime tepi*—having taken the remaining children, beginning with Prince Vasula, by the hand and standing at the foot of the king, he spoke thus. *Guṇino* means "possessing strings [of ornaments]," namely, garlands and jewelry.
"Endowed [with these qualities]. Wearing armlets means wearing the ornament of armlets.
'O Great King, Bilasanta, having slain me and divided my body into a hundred parts, perform a sacrifice by cutting it into seven pieces at seven locations.
Thus, having lamented in these verses in the presence of the king, and finding no comfort, she [spoke] only to the Bodhisatta."
Having approached him, she stood there lamenting. Then he said to her:
"Candā, while I was still alive, I gave you many various ornaments such as gems and pearls whenever you spoke well or spoke beautifully on this or that occasion;
but today is your final gift, and I give you the ornaments worn upon my own body—take them."
Explaining the significance of this, the Teacher said:
“Many were the various beautiful ornaments given by you when I spoke well;
pearls, gems, and beryl—this is your final gift.”
Having heard that, Queen Candā also lamented with nine further verses:
“Upon whose aggregates previously garlands of blossoming flowers were spread,
upon those very aggregates now even a sharpened barb shall be spread.”
“Those whose minds previously turned away from the aggregates like garlands of flowers—
now even this well-sharpened barb shall turn away from their aggregates.
Indeed, before long, O princes, this barb shall turn away from your aggregates.”
As long as my heart did not break, my bonds remained firm:
“Clad in fine Kāsī garments, adorned with earrings and anointed with agaru and sandalwood,
go forth for the sake of the sacrifice of the sole king, like the moon and the sun.”
“Wearing clean garments of Kāsī cloth, adorned with earrings and anointed with agaru and sandalwood,
go forth, O Moon and Sun, causing grief to your mother’s heart.
Wearing clean garments of Kāsī cloth, adorned with earrings and anointed with agaru and sandalwood...”
Depart, O Moon and Sun, causing grief to the hearts of the people! Depart, O Moon and Sun,
for the sake of the sacrifice of the sole monarch— [you who were once] fed on meat broth, bathed and well-anointed by your wives, adorned with earrings,
and smeared with agallochum and sandalwood paste!
“Having eaten a meal of meat broth, bathed by barbers, adorned with earrings, and anointed with agallochum and sandalwood,
go forth, O Moon and Sun, leaving heartache for your mother.
Having eaten a meal of meat broth, bathed by barbers, adorned with earrings, and anointed with agallochum and sandalwood...”
"Depart, O Moon and Sun, having caused heart-grief for the people.
In this context, *mālāguṇā* means flower garlands. *Tesajja* means "of these today. *Nettiṃsa* means a sword.
*Vivattissati* means it will fall away. *Aciraṃ vata* means "indeed, before long. *Na phalati* means it does not break. *Tāva daḷhabandhañca* [means] "and with such firm binding."
"Me āsi" means "my heart will become exceedingly firm-bound. "Niyyātha" means "go.
While she was thus lamenting, all the work at the sacrifice-pen was finished. Having led the prince there, they made him sit down with his neck bent forward.
Khaṇḍahāla, having brought forward a golden platter and taken up a sword, [said]: "His neck..."
“I shall cut them off,” she stood there. Seeing her, Queen Candā thought, “I have no other refuge;
by the power of my own truth, I shall bring safety to my husband. Raising her joined palms, she moved through the midst of the assembly and performed an act of truth (*saccakiriyā*).
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“When everything was prepared and the moon had set for the sake of the sacrifice,
the daughter of the King of Pañcāla, with palms joined in reverence, walked around the entire assembly.
‘By that truth through which the foolish Khaṇḍahāla performs evil deeds— ’”
By this utterance of truth, may I be united with my husband.
“Whatever non-human beings are here, and whatever yakkhas, bhūtas, and bhavyas;
may they perform service for me, so that I may be united with my husband.”
“Whatever deities have come here, and whatever spirits, ghosts, and bhūtas;
protect me, who am protectorless and seeking refuge—I entreat you, O Lord, may I not be defeated.
Therein, “when it was prepared” means when all the requisites for the sacrifice had been gathered and made ready. “Samaṅginī” means endowed with [them].

"Sharing one dwelling. "Those who are here" means those who are present here. "Yakkhas, bhūtas, and bhavyas" refers to yakkhas reckoned as deities, bhūtas reckoned as beings who have already grown and are established, and bhavyas reckoned as beings who are currently growing.
"Let them perform service for me" means let them do my work. "Protect me" means guard me. "I entreat you" means I make this request.
"I entreat you: do not strike my husband; may I not be defeated by my husband.

Then Sakka, King of the Devas, hearing her cry of lamentation and learning what had occurred, took a glowing iron mallet, went there, and after terrifying the king, caused them all to be released. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
"Hearing that, the non-human being, having whirled the iron mallet around..."
Inspiring fear in him, he said this to the king:
"Wake up, you wretched king! Do not let me strike you on the crown of your head;
do not kill your eldest son, who is innocent and like a lion."
“Who was seen as a royal gamester?—the wife and children being slaughtered;
and the merchant and householders, who were innocent and desirous of heaven.
Having heard that and having seen this marvel, Khaṇḍahāla and the king [were struck with wonder].
They released all their bonds in a manner that caused no injury.
When they were all set free, those who had gathered there at that time each gave a single clod of earth, saying: "This is the execution of Khaṇḍahāla."
In this context, "amanussa" refers to Sakka, the king of the devas. "Bujjhassu" means you should know or observe. "Rājakali" means a black-spotted king, a wretched king.
"Mā tāhaṃ" means, O evil king, wake up; do not let me strike you on the head.
"Ko te diṭṭho" means where have you seen me before? "Saggakāmā hi"—here, "hi" is merely a particle; "saggakāmā" means those desiring heaven.
"Patthayamānā" means "desiring. "Having heard that," monks, means having heard those words of Sakka.
"'This is a marvel,' [said] the king" means having seen this sight of Sakka, which had not occurred before. "'Just as...
means just as they would release a living being without harming it, even so did they release them. "'They each gave a single clod of earth,' monks" refers to however many...
All those gathered at that sacrificial enclosure raised a great clamor and each struck Khaṇḍahāla with a clod of earth.
"This is his death"—this indeed became the death of Khaṇḍahāla; the meaning is that they brought about the end of his life right there.
Having killed him, the great multitude began to kill the king. The Bodhisatta, having embraced his father...
He did not give permission for him to be executed. The great multitude said, "We shall grant this wicked king his life, but we will not allow him the royal parasol or residence within the city;
having made him a caṇḍāla, we shall cause him to dwell outside the city.

Having spoken thus, they stripped him of his royal robes, made him put on saffron-colored garments, and wrapped his head with a turmeric cloth. Having thus made him a caṇḍāla, they led him to the dwelling place of the caṇḍālas.
He sent him away. But all those who sacrificed this animal slaughter-offering, or caused it to be sacrificed, or even rejoiced in it, were destined for hell alone.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
"All have entered hell, just as they did after committing that evil deed."
"For having committed an evil deed, it is not possible to go from here to a happy destination.

Then that great multitude, having removed the two ill-omened girls and brought together the requisites for consecration right there, anointed Prince Candana. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
"When all had been released, those who were assembled there at that time..."
The assembled royal council consecrated Canda.
When all had been liberated, those who were gathered there at that time—
the assembled royal maidens as well— consecrated Canda.
“When all were liberated, those who had gathered there at that time—
the assembly of deities who had assembled— consecrated the Moon.
“When all were liberated, those who had gathered there at that time— ”
The daughters of the gods gathered together consecrated Canda.
When all were liberated, those who had assembled there at that time,
as well as the assembled royal retinue, raised their garments in celebration.
“When all had been liberated, those royal maidens who were assembled there at that time raised their garments in a gesture of joy.
When all had been liberated, those who were assembled there at that time— ”
The assembled host of devas raised their garments in celebration.
When all had been liberated, those who were gathered there at that time—
the assembled daughters of the devas as well— raised their garments in celebration.
“When all were liberated, many were filled with joy;
they entered the city in celebration, and the proclamation of release from bondage was made known.
In that context, “the king’s retinue” means that the king’s retinue also consecrated him with the three sprinklings. “The king’s daughters” means...

The daughters of the Khattiyas also consecrated him. As for the assembly of gods: Sakka, the king of the gods, took the conch shell Vijayuttara and, together with the assembly of gods, consecrated him. As for the celestial maidens: Sujā also consecrated him together with the daughters of the gods.
They raised their arms, hoisted banners of various colors, and [waved] upper garments.

They threw [garments] into the air and performed the waving of their robes. Both the royal assembly and the other three groups—thus all four groups who performed the consecration—did exactly that. They were delighted; they were filled with joy.
"Joy entered the city" means that when Prince Canda had the parasol raised and entered the city, the drum of joy resounded throughout the city. "What..."
Having said, "Just as our Prince Candaka has been released from bondage, so may all be released from bondage.
Therefore it is said: "The release from bondage was proclaimed.
The Bodhisatta established his duties toward his father; however, he was not permitted to enter the city. Regarding his provisions...

In the time of Khīṇaka, when the Bodhisatta was going out for pleasure excursions and the like, he would approach him and, instead of saluting him with "I salute you," he would simply join his palms and say, "May you live long, Master. When asked, "What do you need?", he would inform him [of his requirements].
Then the king provided him with travel expenses. Having ruled the kingdom righteously, at the end of his lifespan, he departed, filling the world of the gods.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, Devadatta made an effort to have many people killed on my account by relying upon one person," and he then identified the Jātaka.
At that time, Khaṇḍahāla was Devadatta, Queen Gotamī was Mahāmāyā, Queen Candā was Rāhula’s mother, Vasula was Rāhula, and Selā was Uppalavaṇṇā.
Sūra was Kassapa of the Vāma clan; Bhaddasena was Moggallāna; Sūriyakumāra was Sāriputta;
and as for Candarāja, he was none other than myself, the Sammasambuddha.
This concludes the seventh commentary, the Candakumārajātaka-vaṇṇanā.
[545] 8. The Commentary on the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka.
“There was a king of the Videhas”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Laṭṭhivana Grove concerning the taming of Uruvelakassapa and his companions.
For when the Teacher had set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, he [subdued] Uruvelakassapa and the other matted-hair ascetics.
Having subdued [the king], and in order to make his promise to the King of Magadha appear as a lie, he went to the Laṭṭhivana grove surrounded by a thousand former jaṭila ascetics.

At that time, while the King of Magadha had arrived with a retinue of twelve hundred thousand, paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, and sat down, a thought arose among the brahmins and householders in the assembly: "What now could Uruvelakassapa..."
“Is it the Great Ascetic who is practicing the holy life, or is it Uruvelā Kassapa? Then the Blessed One,
knowing with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those twelve myriads, thinking, “I shall make it known that Kassapa has gone forth in my presence,” spoke this verse:
“Having seen what, O dweller of Uruvelā, did you, who are called ‘the emaciated one,’ abandon the fire?
I ask you, Kassapa, about this matter: how was your fire-sacrifice abandoned?
The Elder, having understood the Blessed One’s intention—
“Sacrifices proclaim forms, sounds, tastes, and desirable women;
knowing that this is the stain within the acquisitions (*upadhi*), therefore I took no delight in sacrificing or offering oblations.
Having spoken this verse, for the purpose of manifesting his status as a disciple, he placed his head at the feet of the Tathāgata.
Excepting him, [the others] said, "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my teacher;

I am his disciple," and having spoken thus, they rose into the air seven times to the height of one palm tree, two palm trees, three palm trees, up to the measure of seven palm trees. Having descended and paid homage to the Tathāgata, they sat down to one side.
Seeing that miracle, the great multitude exclaimed, "Oh, how great is the power of the Buddha! Even one whose views were so deeply rooted..."
Thinking, "Even Uruvelakassapa, who imagined himself to be an Arahant, has broken the net of views and been tamed by the Tathāgata," he spoke only of the Teacher’s virtues.
Hearing this, the Teacher said, "It is no wonder that I have now tamed him after attaining omniscience;
for even in the past, when I was still subject to passion, having become the Brahmā named Nārada, I broke his net of views."
"Having split it open, he made it free from its venom," he said, and being requested by that assembly, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Videha, in Mithilā, a king named Aṅgati reigned; he was righteous, a king of Dharma.
He had a daughter named Rucā, who was beautiful, lovely to behold, inspiring, and one whose aspirations had been fulfilled for a hundred thousand eons.
Those of great merit were reborn in the womb of the chief queen. However, his other sixteen thousand women were barren.

That daughter of his was dear and pleasing to him. He sent her daily twenty-five flower-caskets filled with various blossoms and priceless, fine garments, saying, "Let her adorn herself with these," along with hard and soft foods.
There was no limit to his generosity; every half-month he would send a thousand pieces of gold with the message, "Give this as a gift.
He had three ministers named Vijaya, Sunāma, and Alāta.
On the occasion of the Komudī Cātumāsī festival, while the city and the inner palace were decorated like the city of the gods, he—having bathed and anointed himself—[proceeded].
Adorned with every ornament and having finished his evening meal, the King sat upon the great terrace behind the open lion-lattice, surrounded by his circle of ministers.
Seeing the lunar orb ascending the pure expanse of the sky, he asked his ministers, “How delightful indeed is this moonlit night!
With what pleasure might we delight ourselves today? To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“There was a king of the Videhas, a kshatriya named Aṅgati;
he was highly capable, wealthy, and possessed of infinite strength and power.
On the night of the fifteenth day, when the first watch had not yet passed—”
In the fourth month, on the full moon of Kattika, he assembled his ministers:
“The wise Sunāma, endowed with learning, formerly a jester and now discerning;
Vijaya, Senāpati, and Alātaka.”
“The King of Videha questioned them, and they each expressed their preference:
‘Today is the full moon of the fourth month, the Komudi night, when the moonlight has dispelled the darkness;
let us spend this season tonight in the pleasure of the body.’”

In this context, "possessing abundant equipment" means being endowed with many types of equipment, such as elephant-teams and so forth. "Of infinite strength and manliness" means having a body of infinite strength.

"When the future has not arrived" means when the end has not been reached; the meaning is "not yet transcended. "Four months" refers to the night that constitutes the final day of the four months of the rainy season.
"Komudī" means [the full moon] when the kumuda lilies are in bloom. "Having smiled before" means having first smiled.
"To those who were in the habit of speaking afterwards. He questioned him one by one: "He questioned each of those ministers individually.
"Speak to me individually what you prefer" means: "All of you, speak to me individually regarding your own respective inclinations according to your own dispositions.
"On the day of the *komuda* [full moon]" means: today is the *komudī*. "The bright fortnight" (*juṇhā*) refers to the lunar disc which is the support for the bright fortnight.
"It rises up. "That darkness has been struck down" means that all darkness has been dispelled by it.
"The season": "Today, during this night, let us dwell in such a season as this for the sake of bodily pleasure"—thus the king questioned his ministers.
Being thus questioned, they each spoke according to their own inclinations. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
Then the general spoke these words to the king:
“All the troops are joyful and ready; let us arm the army.
O King, lead forth for battle those of infinite strength and prowess.”
“Those who do not come under your sway—we bring them under our own;
this is my own view, Ajita, we overcome the unconquerable.
Having heard Alāta’s words, Sunāma said this:
“O Great King, all your enemies have come under your control.
Your adversaries have laid down their weapons and are now moving toward a place of safety.
Today is a supreme festival; battle does not please me.”
"Let food and drink, and solid refreshments, be quickly brought to you;
O King, delight in sensual pleasures, with dancing, singing, and beautiful music.
Having heard the words of Sunāma, Vijaya spoke thus:
"O Great King, all sensual pleasures are constantly present before you.
These are not difficult to obtain, O Lord, so that you may rejoice in sensual pleasures;
indeed, sensual pleasures are always easily available—this is not my considered view."
“Let us attend upon a recluse or even a brahmin who is deeply learned—
one who can today dispel our doubt regarding the discipline (vinaya), for this sage is a knower of both the meaning and the Dhamma.
Having heard Vijaya’s words, King Aṅgati spoke thus:
‘As Vijaya says, so do I agree:
“Let us attend upon a monk or a brahmin who is very learned,
one who can today dispel our doubt regarding discipline, for he is a knower of the meaning and the Dhamma.”’
“Let us all form this resolution: ‘Whom shall we attend upon, that wise man who today will dispel our doubt regarding the discipline—he, the seer who knows the meaning and the Dhamma?
Having heard the words of Vedeha, Alāta spoke as follows:
“In this Deer Park there is an ascetic, esteemed as wise, a virtuous man of the Kassapa clan, learned, a master of varied discourse, and a leader of a group.
O King, let us attend upon him; he will dispel our doubt.”
“Having heard Alāta’s words, the king commanded his charioteer:
‘We shall go to the deer park; bring the harnessed carriage here.
In this context, *haṭṭha* means joyful and exultant. Regarding *ojināmasa*: whatever is not conquered by us, that we conquer. This is mine.”

"Intention" (*ajjhāsaya*): The king neither rejected nor approved of his words. Seeing that the king neither approved nor rejected the words of Alāta, [Alāta] thought: "This man does not have an intention for war;
I shall win over his mind by praising delight in the strands of sensual pleasure. Having so reflected, he spoke these words beginning with "All [is yours]."
Vijaya spoke thus; however, the king neither welcomed the words of Sunāma nor did he reject them.
Then Vijaya thought, “This king remains silent after hearing the words of both these men. Wise men are indeed eager to hear the Dhamma; I shall praise the hearing of the Dhamma for him.
Having reflected thus, he spoke these words beginning with, “All sensual pleasures... and so forth.

I said: "Established for you" means established for you. "To rejoice" means that when there is a desire to rejoice and delight in your sensual pleasures, these sensual pleasures are indeed not difficult to obtain.
"This is not my heart's desire" means this delighting in your sensual pleasures is not my heart's desire;
my mind does not leap toward this. "Who today" means who [of us] today. "One who knows the meaning and the Dhamma."
One who knows both the meaning of the Pāli and the Dhamma of the Pāli. *Isi*: a seer (*isi*) who has sought out (*esita*) the qualities of a seer.
*Aṅgati mabravīti*: he said, "Come here" (*aṅgati*); he spoke thus. *Mayhampetaṃva ruccatīti*: this very thing is pleasing to me as well. *Sabbeva santā*:
all of you who are present here, apply your minds; reflect upon it. *Alāto etadabravīti*: Alāta said this.
Having heard the king’s words, Alāta thought, "This Ājīvika named Guṇa, who is my own patron, lives in the royal park;
by praising him, I shall make him the king's patron. Having reflected thus, he spoke these words beginning with "For the sake of... and so forth.
In that context, *dhīrasammata* means "regarded as wise" or "esteemed as a scholar. *Kassapagottāyaṃ* means "this one belongs to the Kassapa clan. *Suta* means...
"Learned" means one who is a teacher of a group (*gaṇa*). "He commanded" means he gave orders.
Having heard that speech from the king, the charioteers acted accordingly. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"They prepared his vehicle, Yoked with a trained horse, its fenders of silver."
“With a white, polished, and shining face like the moon,
there were four Sindhava horses yoked to it— white as lilies,
swift as the wind, well-tamed, and adorned with golden garlands.”
"With a white parasol, a white chariot, white horses, and a white fan— Vedeha,
together with his ministers, shines like the moon as he departs.
Many powerful men, bearing maces and swords, followed after him."
The heroes, mounted upon the backs of elephants, [honored] the men, the lords of the best of men.
Having traveled for but a moment, the Kṣatriya Vedeha, having descended from his vehicle together with his ministers, approached on foot to meet the one endowed with virtues.
“Those brahmin women who were gathered there at that time, the king did not remove them when they had come to his land.
In this context, *tassa yānaṃ* means they harnessed the chariot of that king. *Dantaṃ* means made of ivory. *Rūpiyapakkharaṃ* means... [silver-rimmed].
"With silver-plated fenders" means having bright and smooth rims.
"Like the face of a moonlit night" means like the face of a night free from clouds; the sense is that they were like the moon. "There they were" means they existed there.
"Lilies" means those with the color of lilies. "Sindh horses" means those of the Sindhu breed. "With a gallop like the wind" means possessing a speed equal to the wind.
"The white umbrella" means that the umbrella raised upon that chariot was also white. "The white chariot" means that the chariot itself was likewise white.
"Of the white [horse]" means that the horse was also white. "The white fan" means that the fan was also white.
As the King of Videha, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, departs driving in that chariot, he shines like the moon.
"Naravarādhipanti" means the lord of the best of men, the king of kings.
"So muhuttamiva yāyitvā" means that king, having traveled for only a moment, reached the park. "Pattī guṇamupāgamī" means that on foot he approached Guṇa the Ājīvaka.
"Yepi tattha tadā āsuṃ" refers to those who were already there at that time in the park, having gone there earlier and attending upon that Ājīvaka.
They sat down. "He did not remove them" means: "It is our own fault that we arrived later;

do not worry," he said, and thus he did not have those brahmins and commoners—who had arrived at a place where no space had been prepared for the sake of the king—removed by having a proclamation made.
Surrounded by that mixed assembly, the King sat down to one side and exchanged greetings. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then the King, upon a soft cushion, spread with a soft cloth and covered with a soft rug, sat down to one side.”
Having sat down, the king exchanged friendly greetings with him, and then said:
“I hope, venerable sir, that you are getting by, and that the winds are not contrary to you?
I hope your livelihood is not difficult, and that you obtain enough alms to sustain yourself?”
"I hope you are free from illness, and that your sight does not fail you?
Guṇa greeted the Videhan king, who delighted in discipline, saying:
"O Great King, both of these are sufficient for my sustenance."
“O Vedeha, I hope that your border regions are not becoming more powerful;
I hope you are free from illness and fit for action; I hope your mounts are capable of bearing the load;
and I hope there are no diseases afflicting your body.”
Having exchanged greetings, the King then immediately asked about the goal,
the Dhamma, and the method, for that bull among charioteers was a lover of the Dhamma:
“How, Kassapa, should a mortal practice the Dhamma toward his mother and father?”
How should one conduct oneself toward teachers? How should one conduct oneself toward children and wife?
How should one behave toward elders? How toward recluses and brahmins?
And how should one conduct oneself toward the army, and how toward the countryside?
‘Having practiced what Dhamma do mortals go to a happy destination?
And how is it that some who abide in non-Dhamma fall into hell?
In this context, ‘on a soft mattress’ means on a mattress that is soft and pleasant to the touch. ‘On a soft woolen rug’...
"On a pleasant touch, with a mind-clothed seat. "Spread with a soft covering" means it was spread with a soft rug.
"He exchanged greetings" means he engaged in friendly conversation with the Ājīvaka. "Then" means immediately after sitting down;
the sense is that he then spoke words of consolation. In this context, "Is it all well? Is it sustainable? refers to you.
"Venerable sir, it is possible to sustain the body with the necessary requisites.

Regarding 'the non-disorder of the winds' (*vātānam aviyaṅgatā*): is it that the elements in your body are functioning in equilibrium, that there is no disorder of the winds, and that the winds do not afflict you by becoming turbulent here and there?
