The meaning is that they do not trouble you. 'Without difficulty' (*akasira*) means free from suffering. 'Livelihood' (*vutti*) refers to the maintenance of life. 'Free from illness' (*appābādha*) refers to being free from disease that would disrupt one's posture."
"Separated. He asks, "Is your eye? meaning, "I hope your faculties, such as the eye and so forth, are not declining.
"He replied with a greeting" means he answered with a conversation of mutual courtesy. Regarding that, "all this" refers to everything you mentioned, such as the winds moving against the grain;
all of that is exactly so. "Both of these" refers to what you asked: "Are you free from illness? I hope your eye is not failing."
That which was spoken—both of those being likewise so.
"They do not prevail" means they do not overcome or disturb. "Immediately after" means he asked the question immediately after the hospitable reception.
Therein, "the meaning, the Dhamma, and the method" refers to the meaning of the text, the text itself, and the logical reasoning of the cause. He...

For by asking, "How should one live according to the Dhamma? he asks for the Pāḷi, the meaning of the Pāḷi, and the logical reasoning that illustrate the proper conduct toward parents and others; he asks for this matter (attha), the Dhamma, and the method (ñāya).
In that context, "How do some who stand in unrighteousness" means: how do those established in unrighteousness fall into hell and other remaining states of misery?

Among the omniscient Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples of the Buddha, and great Bodhisattvas, the king— failing to question each preceding one regarding the highly significant questions that ought to have been asked—
instead questioned a certain Ājīvaka who was ignorant, naked, stripped of dignity, blind, and foolish.
When he was thus questioned, failing to provide an answer appropriate to the inquiry, he—
like one striking a wandering ox with a staff or like one throwing rubbish into a bowl of rice— asked for the opportunity, saying, "Listen,
Great King," and then set forth his own false doctrine. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
Having heard the words of Vedeha, Kassapa spoke thus:
“Listen to me, O Great King, the truth, the word that is not otherwise:
‘There is no fruit, whether auspicious or evil, for one who lives according to the Dhamma.’”
“Your Majesty, there is no other world; who then has come here from there?
Your Majesty, there are no fathers; where then are mothers, and where are fathers?
There is no such thing as a teacher; who will tame one who is untamed?”
“Beings are equal and alike; there is no honoring of elders.
There is no strength or energy, so how could there be human exertion?
For beings are fixed, just like the *goṭavisa* plant.”
“A mortal obtains what he has acquired; how then can there be fruit of giving there?
There is no fruit of giving, O King, for one who is helpless before the power of the gods.
Giving was ordained by fools and accepted by the wise.”
“The wise give [gifts] at the end, while fools imagine themselves to be wise.

In this context, “come hither” means that there is no such thing as coming here from the world beyond. “There are no gods or ancestors” means that there are no gods, nor grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and so forth;
since these do not exist, where is the mother and where is the father? “Just as Goṭavisa [was]” is as follows:

"Goṭaviso" refers to a tow-rope; just as a tow-rope attached to the back of a boat follows that very boat, he says that these beings likewise follow [their past deeds] with absolute necessity. "Avaso devavīriyo":
thus, in the absence of the fruit of giving, whatever fool gives a gift does so "without mastery" (avasā) and "without effort" (avīriyo), not by his own will or power; [it is] the fruit of giving...
However, it is explained that one gives out of faith in others who are blind fools, based on the perception that [the recipient] exists.
"The gift was established by fools" means it was established and permitted by blind fools with the thought, "A gift should be given.
Fools alone give that gift; the wise receive it.
Having thus described the fruitlessness of giving, he now spoke to describe the fruitlessness of evil:
“There are these seven eternal bodies, indestructible and unshakeable:
fire, earth, water, air, pleasure, and pain.”
And there are these seven bodies, living beings for whom no cutter is found:
"There is neither a slayer nor a cutter, nor is there anyone who is slain;
it is only between the bodies that weapons pass through."
“Even one who, taking up a sharpened blade, cuts off the heads of others—does not cut into their bodies; how then could there be the fruit of evil therein?
All beings wandering through eighty-four great aeons are purified.”
In that future time, even one who is self-restrained is not purified.
Even after practicing much that is auspicious, they are not purified in the future;
and even after committing much evil, that moment does not pass away.
“Purity comes to us gradually over eighty-four eons;
we do not transcend destiny, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore.
In this context, *kāyā* means aggregates (*samūha*). *Avikopino* means they cannot be disturbed. *Jīva* means the life-principle (*jīva*). There is also a reading, *jīvo*.
This is the very same meaning. "These seven bodies" means these seven types of beings. "Even if someone were to kill, he who would kill does not exist.
"They pass beyond" means they move even within the midst of these seven bodies; [those who would harm] are unable to cut them.
"Taking the head" means having seized the heads of others. "With a sharp sword" means he cuts with a whetted blade.
"He does not cut" means that he also does not cut your body; it shows that earth returns to earth alone, water to water and so forth, and that pleasure, pain, and life pass away into space.
"These beings, O Great King, transmigrate even after having turned this earth into a single heap of flesh for so many eons."
They are purified while wandering in *saṃsāra*. Indeed, apart from *saṃsāra*, there is nothing else capable of purifying sentient beings;

all are purified by *saṃsāra* alone. However, when that future time has not yet arrived—that is, when this aforementioned time has not been reached—one who is restrained and whose virtue is perfectly pure does not yet become purified. They "dig up" that which has been described in the manner stated.
"In time. "Gradually we shall attain purity" means that according to our doctrine there is gradual purification; the sense is that for all of us, purification will come about gradually.
Thus, by his own power, that proponent of annihilationism explained his own position in its entirety.
Having heard the words of Kassapa, Alāta spoke as follows:
“As the venerable one says, so it is pleasing to me as well.
‘I too remember my former birth while wandering through existence:
in a previous life, I was named Piṅgala, a hunter and a butcher of cattle.’”
“In Bārāṇasī, while it was prosperous, I committed much evil;
many living beings were killed by me—buffaloes, pigs, and goats.
Having passed away from there, I am born here in this flourishing family of a general.”
"Surely there is no fruit of evil, since I have not gone to hell.

Regarding this, he said "The firebrand": it is said that after he had made an offering of a garland of *anoja* flowers at the cetiya of the Blessed One Kassapa, at the time of his death he was cast into the cycle of existence by another karma according to its power, and while wandering through *saṃsāra*, he [encountered] one...
Due to the outflow of his evil karma, he was reborn in a family of cow-slaughterers and committed much evil.
Then, at the time of his death, that merit-karma—which had remained latent like fire covered by ashes—found its opportunity.
By the power of that merit, he was reborn here and attained such splendor; yet, remembering his past birth, [he recalled] from the immediately preceding one...

Being unable to go further, and supporting his argument with the perception that "I was reborn here after committing the act of slaughtering cows," he spoke these words beginning with, "Just as the Venerable One says.
In this context, *sare saṃsaritattano* means "I remember my own wandering through existence" (*saṃsaritaṃ*). *Senāpatīkule* means "in the family of a general" (*senāpatikulamhi*).
“Now, there was a slave here named Bījaka, a rag-picker;
while observing the Uposatha, he approached Guṇa.
Having heard the words of Kassapa and the speech of Alāta,”
“Sighing repeatedly and hotly, he wept, shedding tears. Regarding this:

*atha ettha* means “then here,” that is, in this city of Mithilā. *Paṭaccarī* means he was poor and destitute. *Guṇasantikam upāgami* should be understood as having approached the presence of Guṇa with the thought, “I will hear some reason [for his state].
Vedeha questioned him: “For what purpose, my good man, do you weep?”
"What have you heard or seen? What feeling makes you feel for me?"—in this context, "What feeling makes you feel for me" means:
"What kind of bodily or mental feeling have you experienced that, weeping thus, you make me feel [sympathy]? Tell me clearly, explain it to me.
Having heard the words of Vedeha, Bījaka spoke as follows:
“I have no painful feeling, O Great King; listen to me.
I too remember my former birth; I myself experienced happiness.
In the city of Sāketa, I was Bhāva the merchant, devoted to virtuous qualities.”
“Appointed by the brahmin women, I was pure and delighted in sharing;
nor do I recall having committed any evil deed myself.
Having passed away from there, O King of Videha, I was born here as the daughter of a wicked woman.”
"Since I was born from the womb of a slave-girl as one so utterly wretched,
even though I am thus miserable, I am resolved upon a life of righteous conduct:
'To whoever desires it, I shall give half my portion of food.'"
“On the fourteenth and the fifteenth day, I always observe the fast;
I do not harm living beings, and I have avoided theft.
Surely all this, though well-practiced, has been in vain.”
"I think this virtue is useless, like a firebrand that flickers.
Surely I am grasping at mere strife, like a gambler without skill;
I grasp at a straw-firebrand like a cheat who has been trained."
“I see no door by which I may go to a happy state;
therefore, O King, I weep, having heard the words spoken by Kassapa.
In this context, “the merchant Bhāva” refers to a merchant of eighty crores of wealth who bore that name. “Delighting in virtues” means one who takes pleasure in virtue.
"Sammatā" means esteemed and praised. "Sucī" means one of pure deeds. "Born here of a wicked woman" means:
"I was born in this city of Mithilā from the womb of a poor, wretched slave-girl.
It is said that in the past, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, while he was searching for a lost ox in the forest, he encountered a monk who had become lost on the way.
When asked about the path, he remained silent; when questioned by him again, he became angry and said, "Ascetic, slaves are indeed talkative;

you ought to be like a slave, for you are far too loquacious. That karma did not yield its fruit then, remaining like fire covered by ashes. At the time of death, another karma presented itself. He [experienced] according to his karma.
While wandering through saṃsāra, by the power of a single wholesome deed, he became a merchant of the aforementioned kind in Sāketa and performed meritorious acts such as giving.
That karma of his remained like a treasure buried in the earth, and having found the opportunity, it will yield its fruit.
As for the evil karma he committed while reviling that bhikkhu, it was as follows:
The ripening of that [kamma] was bestowed upon him in that very existence.
Not knowing this, he spoke thus with the perception: "By the power of another's wholesome kamma, I have been reborn in the womb of a water-carrier slave-girl.
By saying, "Since born, I am very wretched," he indicates that from the time of his birth, he has been exceedingly miserable.
“Established in even conduct” means: I am indeed established in even conduct. “Surely this” means: certainly this.
“I think this virtue, O King, is useless”—I consider that what is called virtue is indeed fruitless. “The firebrand” refers to how this General Alāta says:
“In a previous existence, having committed much kamma consisting of the taking of life, I obtained the position of general.”
"For that reason, I consider my virtue to be useless. "As if at a gambling match" means:
just as an unskilled, untrained dice-player takes a losing position, so indeed do I take it;

having destroyed my own property in a previous existence, I now experience suffering. "Spoken by Kassapa" means: he says this after hearing what was spoken by an Acelaka (naked ascetic) of the Kassapa clan.
Having heard Bījakas words, King Aṅgati said to him:
“There is no door to a happy destination; Bījaka, have doubt regarding destiny.
Whether it be happiness or suffering, it is indeed obtained through destiny.”
"The purification of saṃsāra belongs to all; do not be hasty regarding the future.
'I too was once virtuous, occupied among the brahmins;
while instructing them in their business, I was devoid of joy in the interval.'"
Therein, he spoke thus: having first heard the speech of the other two and afterwards that of Bījaka—having thus grasped a firm wrong view—he spoke these words beginning with, "There is no door.
"O friend Bījaka, look at destiny; look only at destiny! For the duration of eighty-four great aeons is indeed [the measure of time]."
He purifies beings; he spoke thus with the intention that you should not be in too great a hurry. "In the future" means:
do not be hasty with the thought, "I shall go to the world of the gods even before that time has arrived. "Engaged" means:

I was occupied among the brahmins and householders by performing services for them, such as giving gifts and other forms of physical labor. "Legal proceedings" means: in the place of judicial decision.

"Having sat down, while he was still instructing them in royal duties and commerce, [the King said: 'During that interval, I have been devoid of delight'—meaning that for all that time I had been deprived of the delight of the strands of sensual pleasure.
Having spoken thus, he added: "Venerable Kassapa, we were negligent for all this time;
but now we have found a teacher. From this day forward, we shall enjoy only the delights of sensual pleasure; beyond this, [we shall remain] in your presence."
"Even listening to the Dhamma will not be a source of proliferation for us; you stay here, we shall go," he said, taking leave.
"May we see you again, Bhante, if there is to be a meeting," he added.
In this context, "if there is to be a meeting" means: if there is to be a coming together in one place; if not—if there is no fruit of merit—what is the use of seeing you?
“Having said this, the King of Videha returned to his residence,” it is said.

In this context, monks, by “residence” is meant that after the King of Videha had spoken these words, he mounted his chariot and returned to his own quarters, namely the terrace of the Candaka palace.
The king first went into the presence of Guṇa, paid homage to him, and asked his question. However, while returning, he did not pay homage.
He arrived. Because of his own lack of virtue, Guṇa did not even receive a salutation; how much less could he obtain alms or other honors?
The king, having passed that night, assembled his ministers on the following day and said: "Provide me with the objects of sensual pleasure;
from this day forth, I shall experience only the bliss of sensual pleasures. No other duties need be reported to me."
“Let such-and-such and such-and-such perform the judicial duties,” he said, and remained absorbed in sensual pleasure.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Thereafter, at the end of the night, in the assembly hall, [he spoke thus].”
Having assembled his ministers, he spoke these words:
"Let them always provide me with sensual pleasures within my palace;
let them not approach me in matters of private or secret disclosure."
“Vijaya and Sunāma, and the general Alātaka— let these three,
skilled in worldly affairs, sit here for this purpose.
Having said this, Vedeha honored Kāma greatly.
"Nor am I occupied with any purpose among the Brahmin women.
In this context, "in attendance" means in my own place of attendance. "In Candaka, mine" means in the Candaka palace belonging to me.
"Let them provide for me" means let them constantly arrange and present sensual pleasures for me. "In secrets and disclosures" means even in secret matters.
"Even when matters requiring public proclamation have arisen, let no one approach me. 'Attheti' means in the place for deciding legal cases.
'Let them sit' means let them sit together with the other ministers for the purpose of performing the duties to be carried out by me.
Then, after two weeks had passed, the beloved daughter of the King of Videha—
The king’s daughter, named Rucā, spoke to her nurse-mother:
“Adorn me quickly, and let my friends adorn me as well;
tomorrow is the divine fifteenth day, and I am going into the presence of the Lord.”
“They brought her garlands and highly precious sandalwood;
jewels, conchs, pearls, gems, and robes of various colors.
And many women sat around her as she was seated upon a golden throne.”
“They shone, having been adorned, like a woman of radiant beauty.
Therein, “from then” means from the day the king became stuck in the mire of sensual desire. “On the seventeenth night” means on the fourteenth day.
“She spoke to her foster-mother” means that, desiring to go into the presence of her father, she said to her foster-mother. It is said that she...

On every fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, surrounded by five hundred maidens and taking her retinue of attendants, she would descend from her seven-storied *rativaḍḍhana* palace with great splendor and majesty and go to the *candaka* palace to see her father.
Then, seeing her, her father was filled with joy; having arranged for great honors, he sent her away, saying: "My daughter, give alms..."

Having given a thousand [pieces of gold] and saying, "Go," she dismissed him. Upon returning to her own residence, she observed the Uposatha on the following day and gave a great alms-giving to the poor, the destitute, the wayfarers, and the beggars.

It is said that the king had even granted her an entire province; from the revenue of that, she performed all her duties. At that time, however, it was rumored that the king, relying upon the Ājīvika Guṇa—
A great clamor arose throughout the entire city: "He has embraced wrong views! When Rucā’s nurses heard this news, they reported it to the princess:
"Lady, it seems your father, having heard the words of the Ājīvaka, has embraced wrong views;
he has reportedly demolished the alms-halls at the four city gates and [seized] women who belong to others..."
He orders the young girls to be seized by force; he does not administer the kingdom, for it is said he was born merely intoxicated by sensual pleasures.

Hearing those words, she became displeased and thought, “How can my father approach one who has departed from the pure Dhamma, who is shameless and lives naked, to ask him questions? Is it not rather [proper to ask] righteous recluses and brahmins?”
One might approach those who profess the efficacy of karma and ask [about my father], yet apart from me,
there is no one else capable of leading my father away from wrong view and establishing him in right view.
For I recollect fourteen births— seven past and seven future— and therefore, whatever evil karma was committed by me in the past...
Having spoken thus, and showing the fruit of evil karma, I shall liberate my father from wrong view.
However, if I go this very day, then my father will say to me: "My daughter, you used to come every half-month;
why have you come so quickly today? To that, if I were to say: "It seems you [have fallen into] wrong view..."
"Having heard that [the gift] has been taken, I shall say, 'I have come. He will not take it, honoring my word;
therefore, instead of coming today, I shall go on the fourteenth day from now during the dark fortnight, as if knowing nothing at all, just as I did when I previously made the gesture of going.
Then, at the time of my arrival, I shall ask for a thousand pieces for the sake of the ritual offering (*dānavatta*). At that time, my father, realizing that I am possessed by a spirit..."
"He will speak [of it]. Then, by my own power, I shall cause him to abandon his wrong view"—thus she thought.
Therefore, desiring to go into her father's presence on the fourteenth day, she spoke thus.
In that context, "and my friends" means five hundred young women who were her companions, each of whom was unlike the others.
"Let them adorn [him] with various ornaments and with flowers, perfumes, and ointments of various colors.
"Divine" means resembling the divine; it is also called "divine" because it is adorned by a gathering of deities. "They went" means:

"We shall go into the presence of my father, the Lord of Videha, to cause him to fulfill his duty as a donor. "They brought" means: having bathed him with sixteen jars of scented water, for the purpose of adorning him...
They brought her forward. "Parikiriyā" means having surrounded her. "Asobhiṃsu" means that on that day, standing surrounding the hall, they shone exceedingly, like celestial maidens.
"And she, having come into the midst of her friends, adorned with all ornaments..."
Like the moon entering the clouds, she entered with her radiance.
Having approached the Prince of Videha, who delights in discipline, and having paid homage to him,
she sat down to one side upon a seat inlaid with gold.

There he entered: he entered his father’s residence, the Candaka palace. Upon a golden throne inlaid with the seven precious gems—“And having seen that, like the assembly of Apsarases, Rucā standing in the midst of her companions, the King of Videha spoke these words.”
“‘I hope you take delight in the palace, by the inner lotus pond;
I hope they always bring you many kinds of food to eat.
I hope the maidens, having gathered many kinds of garlands, [present them to you].’”
“Each of you is busy with household chores, constantly delighting in play and pleasure.
What is lacking for you? Why do they not bring it quickly?
Make up your mind, Kuḍḍamukhī—even though he is like the moon.”
Therein, "seeing the gathering" means seeing the assembly like the gathering of celestial nymphs (*accharā*).
"The palace" means: "Mother, have you taken pleasure in that palace built by me for you, which is like the Vejayanta Palace and increases one's delight?
"The inner lotus pond" means: "Right within the grounds, I had a lotus pond built for you resembling the Nandā Pond; have you taken pleasure in that pond?"
"Depending on that, you delight in playing in the water. 'Flower-garlands,' mother—do I not send you twenty-five flower-caskets every day?

Do you and all the young girls, having gathered those flowers and woven them into garlands, frequently take pleasure in play and each make separate little houses, saying, 'This one is beautiful; this one is more beautiful'?"
He asks: "Are you making separate flower-houses with effort, as well as flower-chambers, flower-seats, and flower-couches? "Vikala" means deficiency.
"Mano karassu" means "arouse the mind. "Kuḍḍamukhī" refers to one whose face has been refined by a paste of mustard seeds.

He said this to him: "For women, while brightening their facial complexion, first smear their faces with mustard paste in order to extract the pustules that defile them with foul blood; then they use clay paste to equalize the color of the blood;
and then they use sesame paste to brighten the skin. Even among things equal to the moon, there is indeed nothing more difficult to obtain than the moon."
“Even if you have such a desire, tell me; I shall provide it for you.
Having heard the words of Vedeha, Ruci said to her father:
“All this, O Great King, can be obtained from the presence of the Lord.”
“Tomorrow is the divine fifteenth day; let a thousand [pieces] be brought to me.
And as it was given, so shall I give—this gift to all merchants today.
In this context, “to all merchants” means: “I shall give among all those who trade.”
“Having heard Rucā’s words, King Aṅgati spoke thus:
‘Much wealth has been wasted by you, fruitlessly and without result.
You constantly observe the Uposatha and do not eat food or drink.’”
“‘This is certain: it must be eaten; there is no merit for one who does not eat.
Therein, monks, when he said ‘I am going,’ King Aṅgati, even though previously unasked, gave a thousand [pieces of gold], saying, ‘Mother, give alms!
But on that day, although asked, because he was seized by wrong view, he did not give this much:”
He spoke these words beginning with "It has been ruined," and so forth. "It is certain that this must not be eaten" means that by the power of destiny, this will be something you must not eat;
even for those who do eat it and those who do not, there is no merit. For all are purified only after passing through eighty-four great aeons.
“Then Bījak, having heard what was spoken by Kassapa,
sighed repeatedly with hot breath and wept, shedding tears:
‘As long as she has life, let her not be deprived of food!’”
“There is no other world, O Bhaddā; why do you distress yourself in vain?

In this context, regarding the phrase “Bījakopi,” the story of Bījaka—who, having performed meritorious deeds in the past, was reborn in the womb of a slave woman as a result of that—was cited as an illustrative example for her.
“Natthi bhaddeti bhaddeti”: “O Bhaddā,” [said] Guṇācariya.
He spoke thus: “There is no this world; there is no other world; there is no mother; there is no father;
there are no beings of spontaneous birth; there are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have fared rightly and practiced rightly.
For if the other world existed, this world would also exist, yet that very [other world] does not exist. If mothers and fathers exist, then sons and daughters would exist.

If there were such things as merit and demerit, then there would be those who experience their results; yet those very things do not exist. If there were the Dhamma, then there would be righteous recluses and brahmins;
yet those very things do not exist. Why then, giving gifts and guarding your virtue, do you exhaust yourself in vain?
Having heard the words of Vedeha, Rucā, of radiant complexion—
Knowing the sequence of the Dhamma, he said this to his father:
“What was previously only heard has now been seen by me as a witness:
whoever associates with fools, he becomes just like a fool.”
“Indeed, one who is deluded, by resorting to the deluded, goes further into delusion;
it is as if one were to become infatuated with a firebrand or a seed.
In this regard, monks, having heard the words of her father concerning the Dhamma of past and future, Princess Rucā [reflected] on the basis of seven previous births.

Knowing the past phenomena through her father’s previous births and the future phenomena through the future births of sentient beings, and desiring to free her father from wrong view, she said, “I have indeed heard this,” and so forth. In that context, “he attained [the same state]” means:
“I have indeed heard before that whatever person is a companion of fools attains the state of a fool; today, however, I have seen it directly.”
"Deluded": because of one who is deluded regarding the path, even one who is already deluded regarding views falls into further delusion and becomes more deluded.

"By Alāta": O King, by you—who are inferior in birth, clan, lineage, territory, majesty, merit, and wisdom—by the general Alāta, who is utterly base and witless, and by Bījakadāsa, who is like a village boy, [this man] has been rendered shameless.
"It is fitting and appropriate for them to be deluded by relying on the foolish Ājīvaka Guṇa. Why would they not be deluded?
Having thus rebuked both of them, and desiring to release his father from their wrong view, he spoke in praise of him:
"And you, O Lord, are truly wise, steadfast, and skilled in what is beneficial."
How could he have come to resemble fools and adopt such a base view?
"Even if one is purified by the path of saṃsāra, then the going-forth is useless for the sake of virtue;
like a moth flying into a blazing fire, he has fallen into nakedness, deluded by ignorance."
“Those settled previously on the notion that ‘purity comes through saṃsāra’ waste away their karma through ignorance;
having previously grasped the wrong way, like those who have wrongly seized a lotus stalk, they are as difficult to release as fish caught on a hook.
In this context, “one possessed of wisdom” refers to [wisdom] obtained by means of fame, age, merit, visiting sacred fords, dwelling in solitude, wise attention, and discussion.

One who possesses wisdom is "wise" (*sappañño*); for that very reason, one is "steadfast" (*dhīro*). By virtue of steadfastness, one is skilled in discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful, and what is a valid cause and what is not.
"Just as those fools have approached, so why have you, like them, approached this inferior view?"—this means they fall into ruin, even as they are falling;
the sense is "they are falling. This is what is meant: "Dear one, purity comes through *saṃsāra*."
Just as when there is a misconception, a moth, seeing a fire blazing at night and not knowing the suffering caused by it,
falls into it through delusion and undergoes great pain; so too, this "virtue" (guṇa), having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure,
being bewildered by delusion, enters upon a joyless state of nakedness.

"O dear one, 'pure' means established [in purity]. Since no one has ever heard the statement that purity comes through *saṃsāra*, there is no one who was established [in this view] from the very beginning.
Because many people, not knowing that the fruit belongs to well-done and ill-done deeds, deny karma, they likewise deny the fruit of karma.
Thus, their prior grasping at what is wrong—the grasping for defeat—is indeed a false grasp."
The meaning is "it happens. As for the phrase "the fish is difficult to release from the hook":

those fools who, not knowing this, stand having grasped what is harmful through wrong view, are difficult to release from that harm—just as a fish that has swallowed a hook remains difficult to release from that hook.
Bringing forward another illustration as well, she said:
"I shall give you a simile, O Great King, for your benefit;
for by means of a simile, some wise people here understand the meaning."
"Just as a merchant's ship, laden with an immeasurable weight, becomes heavy;
by taking on an excessive burden, it sinks in the ocean.
Even so, a person who accumulates evil, even bit by bit—"
“Having taken up an excessive burden, he sinks into hell.
‘The burden is not yet full, O Lord of the Earth,’ thinks the man of the fire-brand;
yet he accumulates that evil by which he goes to a state of misery.”
“O Lord of the Earth, this happiness which he now receives is the result of merit performed by him in a previous life. Yet, O King,
that merit is being exhausted, for he delights in what is unwholesome.”
Abandoning the straight path, he runs along a wrong path.
Just as when a scale is held steady and the scale-pan is lowered,
it raises the head of the scale once the weight has been removed.
“In the same way, a person who gathers merit little by little,
though he may be intent on sensual pleasures, becomes like a seed-sower who goes to heaven as a servant.
In this context, “in hell” refers to the eightfold great hells, the sixteenfold secondary hells, and the hells of the world-intervals.
“Indeed, dear son, the burden of unwholesome karma for Alāta is not yet full.

‘Of that very same’ means it is the outflow of the merit he performed in the past, by which that General Alāta experiences happiness today. For this, dear son, is certainly not the fruit of the work of a cow-slaughterer.
It is impossible that the ripening of an evil deed should be desirable and pleasing. [Regarding] non-virtues...
"Delighting" means that he now delights in unwholesome action. "The straight path" refers to the path of the ten courses of wholesome action.
"The wrong path" refers to the unwholesome path leading to hell.
"When the scale-pan was set down" means having been placed upon the scale-pan for the purpose of concealing the goods. "He raises it up" means...
He raises it upward. Accumulating even small amounts of merit, a person casts off the burden of evil, lifts up the head of wholesome action, and goes to the world of the gods.

"Saggātimāno" means having great pride regarding heaven—that is, being delighted in wholesome actions which yield pleasant fruits and lead to the attainment of heaven. There is also the reading "saggādhimāno," [meaning] toward heaven...

The meaning is: "having established his authority, his mind is fixed. "Delighting in what is pleasant" means that this slave Bījakadāsa delights only in wholesome states (kusaladhamma), which have a sweet ripening.
When this evil karma of his is exhausted, he will be reborn in the world of the gods as a result of his wholesome karma.

"That he has now entered into this state of servitude is not the result of wholesome karma. One must conclude that there must have been evil committed by him in the past that leads to servitude. Revealing this meaning, he said:
"Since today this sower is a slave, He experiences suffering within himself;
It is the evil he committed in the past That he is now experiencing."
“His evil is exhausted, for he delights in the Vinaya;
having approached Kassapa, do not, O dear one, go upon the wrong path.

Therein, “Do not, O dear one, go upon the wrong path” means: “Dear father, having approached this naked Ājīvika Kassapa, do not indeed go upon the wrong path that leads to hell; do not commit evil,” thus he exhorts his father.
Now, showing the fault in associating with the wicked and the benefit in associating with virtuous friends,
she said: “For whatever person one associates with, O King— whether they be noble or ignoble,
virtuous or immoral— one comes under their very influence.”
“As one makes a friend, as one associates with another, so does one become—
such indeed is the nature of living together.
By associating with one who associates, by coming into contact with one who touches another, [one becomes like them].”
As one who has smeared himself with resin sticks to a bundle of grass, so does one who is defiled smear what is undefiled.
Out of fear of such defilement, the wise person should never have evil friends.
Just as a man might carry a putrid fish on the tip of a blade of kusa grass, [so should he avoid evil company].
Even kuśa grass emits a foul odor when associated with [rotten things];
such is the result of associating with fools. But a man who wraps tagara incense in leaves makes even the leaves fragrant;
such is the result of associating with the wise.
“Therefore, just like one who carries a bowl, having understood his own ripening,
the wise person should not associate with those who are unwholesome, but should associate with those who are wholesome.
The unwholesome lead to hell, while the wholesome cause one to reach a happy destination.”
In this context, "one who exists" means a true person (*sappurisa*); or "one who does not exist" means an untrue person (*asappurisa*).

"An arrow smeared with poison, O Great King, [smears] the bundle"—just as an arrow smeared with *halāhala* poison, when shot into a bundle of arrows, smears that entire bundle of arrows even those not yet smeared with poison, making them all as if smeared with poison;
in the same way, a bad friend, while practicing evil himself, [corrupts] himself...
When one serves another who is touched by evil, and touches that person while remaining untainted by evil oneself, yet makes that person’s intention one’s own, one becomes defiled.
"The stench blows forth" means that even his kusa grass emits a foul odor.
"And the tagara" refers to tagara and other types of fragrant substances. "Thus" means such association with the wise. The wise person...
For by serving oneself, one makes oneself wise.
Therefore, "just as with a leaf-cup" means that since even the leaves wrapped around the *tagara* and other fragrant substances become fragrant themselves, [one should think]:
"By associating with the wise, just as with a leaf-cup of wood-shavings, I too shall become wise. Having understood this thus.

"Knowing the measure of his own ripening"— that is, having understood the extent of his own maturity, his state of wisdom, and his capacity— one should abandon those who are unvirtuous and attend upon the wise.
Regarding the phrases "leading to hell" and "causing one to reach a happy destination," examples should be cited here based on Devadatta and others who were led to hell,
and the Elder Sāriputta and others who were led to a happy destination.
Having thus spoken the Dhamma to her father with these six verses, the princess now spoke, showing the suffering she had experienced in the past:
“I too, having transmigrated through seven births within my own memory,
shall go through seven more in the future once I have passed away from here.”
“In my seventh previous birth, O lord of people,
I was the son of a smith in Rājagaha, in the land of Magadha.
Having come into the company of evil friends, much evil was committed by me.”
“Harassing another’s wife, we wandered like immortals.
That karma lay dormant, like fire covered by ashes;
then, through other karmas, I was born in Vaṃsabhūmi.”
“In Kosambī, in a merchant’s family— prosperous, flourishing, and of great wealth—
I was the only son, O Great King, always honored and revered.
There I cultivated a friend, a companion who delighted in pleasure.”
The wise one, endowed with learning, established me in the goal:
“On the fourteenth and the fifteenth, I observed many nights of fasting;
that deed, though performed, has come to naught, like a treasure placed near water.”
“Then, O King of Videha, having experienced the fruit of those evil deeds committed in Magadha—
which has come upon me in full measure later, like having consumed virulent poison—
I passed away from there and fell for a long time into the Roruva hell.”
“I did not heed my own karma; I do not find happiness in that place.
Having spent many years there, enduring great suffering, I was born as a goat with testicles like inflated bladders, O King.”
In this regard, O Great King, there indeed exist what are called this world and the next world, as well as the fruit of good and evil deeds.
For the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) cannot purify sentient beings; rather, sentient beings are purified by their own karma alone.
Both General Alāta and the slave Bījakā recollect a single birth. Not only do these two remember that birth, but I too—
I remember my own wandering through seven births in the past, and I know that exactly seven births remain to be gone through from here.
That which was my seventh birth in the past—under that birth, I was the son of a smith;
in the city of Rājagaha among the Magadhans, I was the son of a goldsmith.
"Destroying another's wife" means: while destroying another's wife—that is, offending against the excellent goods protected and guarded by others—[the result] "stood" (*aṭṭhā*).

That evil deed committed by me at that time, finding no opportunity [to ripen], remained hidden like fire covered by ashes, ready to yield its fruit whenever an opportunity arose. "In Vaṃsabhūmi" means in the kingdom of Vaṃsa. "An only son"—
I was the only son in a merchant family possessing a wealth of eight hundred million. "Delighting in what is pleasant" means being devoted to wholesome deeds.
"That friend" refers to that companion who established me in skillful work for the sake of prosperity.
"That deed" means that wholesome deed performed by me at that time, which, having found no opportunity then, yields its fruit when the opportunity arises.
Having offered it, it stood like a treasure deposited near water. "Yametaṃ" means:
among the evil karmas within my possession, that which was done by me in Magadha—the act of adultery—its fruit has subsequently come upon me;
this is the meaning. Like what? "Bhutvā duṭṭhavisaṃ yathā," just as if one had eaten food containing poison.
"While I am standing there, that wicked, harsh, and deadly poison agitates me; thus, 'it has come upon me' is the meaning.
"From there" means from the merchant family in Kosambī. "Remembering that" means remembering the suffering experienced in that hell, I do not obtain even a moment of mental ease;
only fear arises within me. "Upon its arrival" means when it has arrived.
In the kingdom named Raṭṭha. "One with arrogant fruit" means one with arrogant seeds.
That goat, moreover, was endowed with great strength. They made him carry [loads] even when mounted upon his back, and they yoked him to carts as well. To illustrate this matter, he said:
"Sons of Sātā were carried by me, both on my back and by means of a chariot."
“The ripening of that karma was for me because of my adultery.
In this context, “Sāta’s sons” refers to the sons of the ministers. “The ripening of that karma,” O King, refers to all of this:
my being cooked in the great Niraya Roruva hell, the tearing out of seeds while I was a goat, and being yoked to carts for carrying loads on my back—all of which is the ripening of that very karma.
"May I not go to another's wife.
Then, having passed away from there, he took rebirth in the womb of a monkey in the forest. On the day he was born, they presented him to the leader of the troop.
He said, "Bring me my son! and seizing him firmly, while the boy cried out, he bit fruits with his teeth.
She plucked it out. To explain that matter, she said:
“Then, O King of Videha, having passed away from there, I was a female monkey in the Great Forest;
I had my tail plucked out by a shameless leader of the troop.”
“This is the result of that karma, of my going to another’s wife.
Regarding this, “I was one whose fruit had been plucked off” means: there, I was one whose fruit had been plucked and torn away by that impudent leader of the herd; such is the meaning.
Then, showing yet other births, she said:
“Then, O Videhan, having passed away from there, I became a draft animal among those used for display.
I was a swift and noble steed, shorn of my tail, and I had long been harnessed to pull the carriage.
This is the result of that karma: my own act of adultery with another’s wife.”
“Then, having passed away from there, O Vedeḥa, I came to a family among the Vajjis.
I was neither woman nor man in that human state so difficult to attain;
this was the result of that karma of mine: my having gone to another’s wife.”
“Then, having passed away from there, O Vedeḥa, I was born in the Nandana grove;
in the abode of the Thirty-three, I was a celestial nymph of lovely form.
Adorned with variegated garments and ornaments, with jeweled earrings fastened upon my ears;”
“Skilled in dance and song, I was a handmaid of Sakka.
Standing there, O Vedehiputta, I remember these births,
as well as seven future ones which I shall undergo after passing away from here.”
“Whatever wholesome deed I performed in Kosambī has reached its full fruition;
having passed away from here, I shall wander among gods and humans.
O Great King, I am of noble birth, always honored and revered.”
“Even from the state of being female I shall not be released; these are the six lower destinies.
But the seventh destiny, O King, is that of a son of the gods with great psychic power;
I shall become a male god, supreme among the host of deities.”
“Even today, in the Nandana grove, they weave garlands made of sandalwood;
there dwells a son of the gods named Java, who accepts my garland.
That divine [time] is like a mere moment, yet here it is sixteen years.”
Day and night that divine being [observes] the hundred autumns of human life.
"Thus deeds follow one through incalculable births—
whether good or evil— for indeed, a deed does not perish."
"In those places of seeing" means in the lands of seeing. "I was a bull" means I was a cow.
"Shorn" means that while I was still a calf, they shorn me, thinking, "He will become so pleasing in this way. Having been shorn and having my seed removed, I became swift and noble.
"I came to a family among the Vajjīs" means that after passing away from the bovine womb, I was reborn in a family of great wealth in the Vajjī country.

[The Blessed One] shows [this]. He said, "Neither woman nor man," referring to the state of being neuter (*napuṃsakatva*). "In the abode of the Thirty-three, I... means "I [was] in the abode of the Thirty-three.

"Standing there, O King of Videha, I remember these births"—it is said that while standing in that world of the gods, she looked about, wondering, "From where did I come when I was coming to such a divine realm? [And so she remembered her birth] in a family of great wealth in the Vajji kingdom.
Having passed away from that state as a neuter being, she saw that she had been reborn there.

Then, looking back and wondering, "By what kamma have I been reborn in such a delightful place?", she perceived the wholesome deeds such as giving performed while she was reborn in the merchant family in Kosambī.
Knowing, "I have been reborn here as the fruit of this," she reflected upon her immediately preceding existence as a neuter being.
Looking back, [she wondered], "From where have we come as we are being reborn? Surveying the realms of sight, she realized the state of having experienced great suffering in the womb of cattle.
Immediately after that, recollecting her birth, she saw the state of having been arrogant while in the womb of monkeys.
Recollecting what followed that, she remembered the state of having been arrogant regarding the seed while in the womb of goats.
Recalling what followed, she remembered her rebirth in the Roruva hell.
As she recalled the suffering she had experienced in that hell and in the animal realm, fear arose within her.
Then, wondering, "By what kamma did I experience such suffering?", she looked back to her sixth birth.

Having seen the wholesome deed performed in the city of Kosambī during that birth, and looking back to the seventh [previous life], she saw the act of adultery committed in the kingdom of Magadha under the influence of an evil companion;
she realized, "By the fruit of this, I experienced that great suffering.
Then, looking forward to see where she would be reborn after passing away from here, she saw that for the duration of her lifespan...
She understood: "Having stayed here, I shall be reborn again as a handmaid to Sakka himself. Observing thus again and again, she thought:
"In my third existence, I shall be reborn as a handmaid to Sakka himself; likewise in the fourth;
but in the fifth, in that very same deva-world, I shall be reborn as the chief queen of the Javana deva-putta."

Having known this, she immediately thereafter looked forward and perceived: "In my sixth existence, having passed away from this Tāvatiṃsa heaven, I shall be reborn in the womb of the chief queen of King Aṅga;
my name shall be ‘Rucā’. Having known this, she then looked forward again, wondering, "Where shall I be reborn after that? and saw:
"In my seventh birth, having passed away from there, I shall [be reborn] in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven."
“I shall be reborn as a son of the gods possessing great psychic power, and I shall be liberated from womanhood”—thus she knew. Therefore she said:
“O King of Videha, while remaining there, I remember seven births;
And seven more yet to come, which I shall undergo after passing away from here. Thus she spoke.
In this context, "arrived by turn" (*pariyāgata*) means arrived according to one's own sequence or rotation. Regarding "seven births" (*satta jaccā*):
including the neuter class in the Vajji country along with the five [classes] in the world of the gods, these are called the "seven births," as this is the sixth.

This shows that these seven births were always honored and revered. Regarding "the sixth birth among the low-born" (*chaṭṭhā nīcā-jātiyo*): however, there are five in the world of the gods, and this is the sixth.
"Six destinies"—she says they will be released from female existence. "And the seventh" refers to immediately after passing away from here.
"Made of a continuous string" means made into a continuous string by way of being on a single stalk and so forth.
"They weave" means that just as they were made of a continuous string, even today my attendants are still weaving garlands in the Nandana Grove. "Whoever receives my garland... [and so on].
"Great King, in my immediately preceding birth, my husband was a son of the gods named Java, who catches the garland as it falls from the tree.
'Sixteen,' Great King—these sixteen years are my age; however, such a duration is but a single moment for the gods.
Therefore, even while I have passed away, they do not know it and continue to weave the garland for me. 'Human'—"
"By human calculation, this is one hundred and fifty years; such is the long life of these devas.
By this reason, know that there is a world beyond and that good and evil kamma exist, O deva.
"They follow" means they follow me just as they have followed before. For kamma does not perish—this refers to [kamma] to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).
In that very same existence, karma to be experienced upon rebirth yields its result in the immediately following life;
however, karma to be experienced in subsequent lives does not perish without having yielded its result. With reference to this, it was said: "Indeed, karma does not perish. [The king said:
"Your Majesty, through the outflow of the karma of adultery, I have experienced great suffering in hell and in the animal realm."

"I have experienced it myself. But if you too, having now accepted this teaching on virtue, should act in such a way, you will experience suffering exactly like what I have experienced; therefore, do not act thus," she said.
Then, teaching him the Dhamma further, she said:
“Any man who wishes to be reborn again and again in birth after birth should avoid another’s wife,
just as one whose feet have been washed avoids the mud.
Any woman who wishes to be reborn again and again in birth after birth [should avoid another’s husband].”
One should honor one's husband, as a handmaid honors her lord.
Whoever desires celestial enjoyments, celestial life-span, glory, and happiness,
should avoid evil deeds and practice the threefold Dhamma.
“Whether by body, speech, or mind, the vigilant and discerning person acts for their own welfare, whether they be a woman or a man.
Whatever illustrious people there are in this world of living beings, possessing all-encompassing wealth;”
“Without doubt, they must have performed pure deeds in the past, for all beings are individually the owners of their own karma.
‘Come now, O Lord, consider this yourself:
from what source, O Ruler of Men, do these nymph-like women come to you—adorned and veiled in nets of gold?’”
In this context, *hotuṃ* means "to become. *Sabbasamantabhogā* means those possessing all kinds of abundant wealth.

*Suciṇṇaṃ* means well-practiced; it refers to wholesome karma that has been performed. *Kammassakāse* means having karma as their own property; they experience the ripening of only the karma they themselves have performed.
For the karma performed by parents does not yield its ripening to sons and daughters, nor does the karma performed by those sons and daughters [yield its ripening to them].
Kamma yields its fruit for one’s mother and father; how then could what is done by others yield fruit for others? *Iṅgha* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation (*codana*).
*Anucintesī* means you should reflect upon this again and again. "These who wait upon you"—referring to these sixteen thousand women who attend to you—where did they originate for you?
Were they obtained while you were lying down and sleeping, or were they acquired through such acts as highway robbery or housebreaking?
"Having committed evil deeds, or having obtained [this state] by means of wholesome karma—this, O King, you should consider for yourself.
Thus she instructed her father. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"In this way, the maiden Rucā satisfied her father Aṅgati."
"She pointed out the path to the bewildered one; she, of excellent vows, proclaimed the Dhamma.
In this context, "Thus indeed," O monks, means that with these such sweet words, Rucākaññā satisfied her father;
she pointed out to him the path of the Sugata as if it were a path to one who was lost, [and taught] the Dhamma of good conduct through various methods.
She spoke. While preaching the Dhamma, Subbatā Sundaravatī recounted even her own past births.
Thus, having taught the Dhamma to her father from the forenoon until the end of the night, she said: "O King, do not accept the words of the naked man of wrong view;
rather, [accept that] 'this world exists, the other world exists, and there is the fruit of well-done and ill-done deeds.'"
"Accept the words of a virtuous friend like me as I speak; do not leap across a ford where there is no footing," he said.
Even so, she was unable to free her father from his wrong view. For he was merely pleased upon hearing her sweet words;
indeed, parents cherish the words of their beloved children, but they do not [easily abandon] that wrong view.
She caused him to relinquish it. In the city, too, a great clamor arose: "It is said that Princess Rucā, having taught the Dhamma to her father, has caused him to abandon his wrong view.
The great multitude rejoiced, thinking, "The wise princess, having today liberated her father from wrong view, will bring about the welfare of the city's inhabitants.
Being unable to awaken her father, she did not yet relinquish her effort.
Thinking, "By whatever means possible I shall ensure my father's safety," he placed his palms together in reverence upon his head, paid homage to the ten directions, and said:
"In this world there are those who uphold the world—righteous recluses and brahmins, world-protecting deities, and Great Brahmās.
May they come here and, by their own power, [turn] my father away from wrong view..."

"Let them release him! Even though he lacks these virtues, by my own virtue, my conduct, and my truth, may they come here, cause him to abandon this wrong view, and bring safety to the entire world," he resolved, and then paid homage.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was the Great Brahmā named Nārada. And indeed, it is the nature of Bodhisattas that through their cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*),...
Out of compassion and by virtue of his greatness, he surveys the world from time to time in order to see beings who have practiced rightly and those who have practiced wrongly.
On that day, while surveying the world, he saw the king’s daughter paying homage to the deities who sustain the world for the sake of freeing her father from wrong view,
and [he thought], "Except for me, no one else can [free] this king from his wrong vision..."
"There is no one capable of making [him] relinquish [the horse]. Today, it is fitting for me to return after having ensured the welfare of the king’s daughter and the king along with his retinue.
In what guise, then, shall I go? Having thus reflected, he thought:
"Among people, those who have gone forth are beloved, respected, and their words are authoritative; therefore, I shall go in the guise of one who has gone forth."
Having made a firm resolve, he fashioned a charming human form with a golden complexion;
he bound a beautiful circle of matted hair and inserted a golden needle within it. He put on a red cloth beneath and a red bark-garment over it as an upper robe.
Placing a silver antelope skin, inlaid with golden stars, over one shoulder, he fastened it with a pearl-ornamented clasp.
Taking a golden alms-bowl and placing upon his shoulder a golden staff bent at three points,
and carrying a coral water-pot with a pearl handle, he came through the air shining like the moon in the firmament in this guise of an ascetic;
having entered the great terrace of the decorated Candaka Palace, he stood in the air before the king.
To illuminate that meaning, the Teacher said:
“Then Nārada came from the Brahma-world to the human race;
looking down upon Jambudīpa, he saw King Aṅgati.”
“Then, from the palace, to the east of Vedeha’s city, seeing that [the seer] had not yet arrived, Rucā paid homage to the seer.
Therein, *addā* means: while still standing in the Brahma-world, looking down upon Jambudīpa, she saw the wrong view that Guṇājīvaka had adopted.
He saw King Aṅgati; therefore, the meaning is "he has come from there. From there he established himself:
from that place, that Brahmā, appearing to set foot where there was no ground, established himself in the air before the king as he sat surrounded by his assembly of ministers.
"Arrived" means having come. "Seer": because he had come in the guise of a seer, the Teacher called him "seer."

He said: "Bow down. Thinking, "Out of favor toward me, out of compassion for my father, one king of the gods must have come," she—elated and overjoyed like a golden plantain tree bent by the wind—bowed down to the Brahmā Nārada.

The king, too, upon seeing him, was overcome by the majesty of his brahmin power; unable to remain steady in his seat, he descended from it, stood upon the ground, and asked where he had come from and what his name and lineage were. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:
Then, descending from his seat with a troubled mind,
the king, questioning Nārada, spoke these words: “From where have you come,
O one of divine appearance, illuminating all directions like the moon?”
“Being asked, tell me your name and clan; how do people in the world of men know you?

Therein, *byathitamānaso* means one whose mind is terrified. Thinking, “From where [does he come]?”—wondering, “Could this perhaps be a master of spells (*vijjādhara*)?”—he asked thus without even bowing.
Then he [the other], thinking, “This king imagines that there is no world beyond; I shall first explain the world beyond to him,” spoke this verse:
“I am indeed coming now from the world of the gods, illuminating all directions like the moon.
Being asked, I declare my name and clan to you: they know me as Nārada by name and Kassapa by clan.
In this passage, “from the world of the gods” means from the celestial realm. “Nārada by name and Kassapa by clan” means they know me as Nārada by name and as Kassapa by clan.
Then the king, thinking, "I shall ask him about the next world later; for now, I will ask the reason for his attainment of psychic power," spoke this verse:
"Such a wondrous form as yours, that you travel and stand in the air— I ask you, Nārada, about this matter: by what quality is this psychic power of yours attained?"
In that regard, "of whatever kind" means: whatever your shape is, and that you go and stand in the sky—this is a marvelous thing.
Nārada said:
"Truth, Dhamma, self-control, and generosity—these qualities have been inherent in me from of old."
“Because those very qualities were well-cultivated, I have gone to the delightful realm of my desire.
In this context, *sacca* (truth) is truthful speech free from lying. *Dhamma* refers both to the threefold conduct of wholesome behavior and to the practice of the kasiṇas and jhānas.
*Dama* is the taming of the sense faculties. *Cāga* is the relinquishing of defilements as well as the relinquishing of things worthy of being given.

“*Ca* means ‘these. *Mamete guṇā* means ‘these qualities of mine,’ indicating they are endowed with and accompanied by qualities. *Pakatā purāṇā* indicates that they were performed by me in previous existences.
‘*Teheva dhammehi susevitēhī*’ indicates that all those qualities were well-cultivated and practiced.
*Manojavo* is obtained through the power of supernormal success (*iddhi*). ‘*Yena kāmaṃ gato’smi*’ means to whichever divine realm...”
And there was a desire to go to both the human realm and the celestial realm; thus, the meaning is, "I have gone by means of that.
Even while he was speaking thus, because the king had embraced wrong view and did not believe in the next world, he said, "Is there indeed a ripening of merit? and spoke this verse:
"You describe the accomplishment of merit as something marvelous, if indeed it is as you say through these [deeds]."
“I ask you this matter, Nārada; being asked, please explain it well to me.
In that regard, by declaring the accomplishment of merit—that is, the fact that merits yield their fruit—you are declaring something wonderful.
Nārada said:
“Ask me, O King, whatever this matter of yours may be that you harbor as a doubt, O protector of the earth;
I shall bring you to freedom from doubt by means of methods, principles, and reasons.
In this context, *tavesa attho* means “this matter of yours is indeed what ought to be asked. *Yaṃ saṃsayam* refers to whatever [doubt] regarding any particular thing.
If you have doubt regarding a matter, ask me about it. I shall lead you to a state free from doubt. "By methods" (*nayehi*) means by means of reasons;

"by principles" (*ñāyehi*) means by means of knowledge; and "by causes" (*hetūhi*) means by means of conditions—not merely by verbal assertion, but by delimiting [the truth] through knowledge and by stating the reasons consisting of the conditions that give rise to those phenomena.
"And I shall make that free from doubt"—this is the meaning.
The King said:
"I ask you this matter, Nārada; being questioned by me, Nārada, do not speak falsely."
“Are there gods? Are there ancestors? Is there a world beyond, which people speak of?
In this context, “which people speak of” means that he asks whether all that which people say—namely, “there are gods, there are ancestors, there is a world beyond”—is indeed so.
Nārada replied:
“There truly exist gods and ancestors; there exists the other world which people speak of.
But men who are greedy for sensual pleasures and utterly deluded do not know the other world, being possessed by ignorance.

In this regard, “There truly exist gods” means, O Great King, that both gods and ancestors exist, and that which people call the next world also truly exists. “They do not know” means that people who are greedy for sensual pleasures and bewildered by delusion do not perceive or understand the next world.
Having heard this, the king spoke thus in jest:
"If you believe it exists, Nārada, that there is a dwelling place in the world beyond for those who have died,
then give me five hundred right here, and I will give you a thousand in the world beyond."
In that context, "dwelling" means a place of residence. "Five hundred" means five hundred kahāpaṇas.
Then the Great Being, censuring him right in the midst of the assembly, said:
"We would indeed give five hundred to you, sir, if we could know one who is virtuous and generous."
Who would lend a thousandfold in the next world to that greedy man dwelling in hell? Even here,
the wise do not lend money to one who is unrighteous in character, of evil conduct, lazy,
and cruel in his deeds, for there is no repayment from such a person.
“Once people have recognized a person as capable, industrious, virtuous, and generous, they themselves invite him to share their wealth, saying:
‘Having done the work, bring it back to us again. In that context, “If we should know you” means:
if we were to recognize you as one who is virtuous and generous toward righteous recluses and brahmins...
"Having understood that 'at this time, such is the purpose for this name,' we would know him as one who performs his respective duties and is generous.
Then we would give you five hundred [coins] for your prosperity;
yet you, being cruel and violent, having adopted wrong views, destroyed the hall of giving, and committed adultery with another's wife—you, fallen from here, will be reborn in hell.
Who, having gone there, would demand of that hunter dwelling and suffering in hell, "Give me a thousand"?
"Tathāvidhamhā" means that for such persons as these, there is no returning of a debt once given.
"Dakkhanti" means those skilled in producing wealth. "Puna māharesī" means: having performed your own work and produced wealth, [bring it] again.
“Bring what belongs to us; do not live here without performing service,” she said, thus inviting him personally with wealth.

Thus, being restrained by her, the king remained speechless. The great multitude, becoming joyful and delighted, raised a single clamor throughout the entire city, saying, “Even today, a god of great power will cause the king to abandon his wrong view!”
Through the power of the Great Being, there was then no one in Mithilā, which extended for seven yojanas, who did not hear his teaching of the Dhamma.
Then the Great Being thought: “This king has grasped a very firm wrong view;
I shall terrify him with the fear of hell, cause him to relinquish that wrong view, and then comfort him with the prospect of the world of the devas. Having thus reflected, he—
“Great King, if you do not relinquish this view, you will go to hell, where there is endless suffering,” he said,
and then began a discourse on hell:
“When you have passed away from here, O King, you shall see there a place being torn apart by flocks of crows.”
“Who would urge you on toward the next world, while you dwell in hell being devoured by flocks of crows, vultures, and hawks—your limbs mangled and blood flowing?
In this context, “by flocks of crows” means by flocks of crows with iron beaks. “Being torn apart” means you will see yourself being dragged there into that hell. “That” refers to you, sir.
Having described that Kākola hell, he said, "Even if you are not reborn there, you will be reborn in the Lokantara hell," and then spoke this verse to show that hell:
"Blinding darkness is there, where neither moon nor sun shines; the hell is ever tumultuous and terrible in form.
There, neither night nor day is discerned; who, seeking wealth, would wander in such a place?"
In this context, O Great King, "blind darkness" refers to that which obstructs the arising of visual consciousness in the Lokantara hell where those with wrong view are reborn;
it is the blinding gloom there. "Ever tumultuous" means that hell is constantly filled with dense darkness.
"Of terrible form" means its nature is fearsome. "That is neither night nor day" refers to what here is called night and day.
It is not perceived there at all. Who is it that wanders about? Who is it that will wander about clearing away the debris?

Having described that Lokantara hell in detail, [the Teacher] spoke this verse, showing: "Great King, if you do not abandon wrong view, you will experience not only this, but other suffering as well":
"Sabala and Sāma, two dogs, with fully grown bodies, strong and large..."
“They devour with iron teeth those who have been expelled from here and have reached the other world.
In this context, “expelled from here” means deceased from this human world. The same method applies to the hells that follow as well.
Therefore, all those hellish places, together with the devices of the hell-wardens, are to be understood according to the manner explained below.
Having expanded upon this, the unexplained words of each of those verses should be commented upon:
"Who would urge one who dwells in hell, being devoured by greedy beasts and fierce wild animals,
with limbs severed and blood flowing, to [commit evil] in the next world?"
In this context, "by the fierce" means by the cruel. "By the wild" means by the wicked. "By the wretched deer" means by those animals that bring about misfortune;
the meaning is "by dogs that bring about suffering. "With very sharp spears and lances, their enemies strike and pierce them;
in the terrible Kāḷūpakāḷa hell, they [suffer] for having performed evil deeds in the past."
Therein, "they strike and pierce" means that having cast them down upon the blazing iron earth, they strike and pierce them, making their entire bodies perforated here and there.

"Kāḷūpakāḷā" refers to hell-wardens of such names. "In hell" means in that very hell designated as Kāḷūpakāḷa, by virtue of those [wardens] themselves. "One who has committed evil deeds" refers to one who acts through wrong view.
“Who would urge on in the next world the doer of evil deeds—
him who is being slain as he goes to hell, with his belly ripped open by the belly and the anus, his limbs severed and blood flowing?”

In this context, *tatra* means "there," referring to that venerable one being thus slain in hell. *Vajantaṃ* means running here and there. *Kucchismiṃ* means being struck and pierced in both the belly and the flanks—this is the meaning.
"Swords, spears, javelins, and slings, various weapons rain down there from the gods;
they fall like blazing embers, and stones rain down upon the one engaged in cruel deeds."
In that context, "flaming like glowing coals" means that specific weapons resembling blazing coals fall. "Lightning bolts" refers to flaming thunderbolts.

"It rains upon their cruel deeds" means that just as lightning falls when it rains from the sky, even so a rain of flaming stones, rising up from the air with a crackling sound, falls upon those who commit cruel deeds.
“The heat and the wind in hell are unbearable; not even for a moment can any happiness be found there.
Who would urge that one—who is afflicted by running hither and thither and covered in filth—to go to the world beyond?
In this context, *ittarampi* means even for a short time. *Vidhāvantam* means running in various directions.
“Even one who runs about, yoked to chariots, blazing with fire, treading upon the earth, and being thoroughly urged on by goads—what person would urge such a one in the world beyond?
In this context, “yoked to chariots” means yoked in turn to those chariots made of glowing iron. “Treading” means walking. “Thoroughly urged on” means being well-prodded.
“Who would urge one toward the next world who is climbing that mountain, which is bristling with spikes, terrifying, ablaze, and fearsome,
with its limbs severed and blood flowing? In this context,
“climbing that [mountain]” means climbing that blazing iron mountain, which is heaped with blazing spikes, unable to endure the blows of blazing weapons.
“Who would urge one who is climbing up that mountain-like heap of glowing embers, terrifying and blazing,
with limbs thoroughly burnt, miserable and weeping, into the world beyond? In this context,
"sudaḍḍhagattaṃ" means "with a body thoroughly burnt."
“High as mountain peaks, the trees are thick with thorns;
they are made of iron, sharp, and drink the blood of men.
In this context, “thick with thorns” means covered with blazing thorns. The phrase “made of iron” is stated to show the nature of those thorns by which they are covered.
“Women and men who have gone to another’s wife climb that tree, being prodded with swords in hand by those who carry out the commands of Yama.

In this context, “they climb that” means they climb such a *simbali* tree. “By those who carry out the commands of Yama” means by the guardians of hell (*nirayapāla*) who act according to Yama’s word.
“Ascending that hell, the *simbali* tree smeared with blood,
his body ablaze and scorched, he is afflicted by intense agony.
He breathes out hot air repeatedly, a sinner for his past deeds.”
“On the evil path, with body scorched, who would beg you for that wealth?

Herein, *vidaḍḍhakāyaṃ* means with a body that has been tormented. *Vitacaṃ* means with the skin and flesh pierced through and through, like a *koviḷāra* flower or a *kiṃsuka* flower because of their being cut.
“The trees are high, like mounds of clouds, covered with sword-leaves;”
“With sharp blades made of iron, which drink the blood of men.
Therein, “strewn with sword-leaves” means covered with leaves made of swords.
“As he climbs that tree of sword-leaves, being cut by sharp swords;”
“Who would urge one whose limbs are severed and from whom blood is flowing toward the next world?
Therein, “climbing upon him” means climbing upon that being who, unable to endure the blows of the weapons of the hell-guardians, has climbed up.
“Just as he has emerged from there, those trees are covered with sword-leaves.”
"Who would beg for that wealth from one who has fallen into the Vetaraṇī?
In this context, "sampatitaṃ" means fallen.
"The river Vetaraṇī is difficult to cross, filled with caustic water, hot, and harsh."
“Covered with iron lotuses, it flows with sharp leaves.
In this context, *khara* means harsh. *Ayo-pokkharasañchannā* means covered with iron lotus petals that have sharp edges. *Pattehi* means by those petals that river flows, being sharp.
“Therein, with its limbs severed, floating and smeared with blood;”
"In the Vetaraṇī, which offers no support—who would beg you for that wealth?
Therein, "in the Vetaraṇī" means in the waters of the Vetaraṇī river.
Having heard this account of the Great Being’s descent into hell, the king, his heart filled with agitation, sought refuge in the Great Being alone and said:
“I am pierced as if a tree being cut down; my consciousness is bewildered and I know not which direction to take.
I am terrified and filled with remorse, for great is my fear upon hearing these words spoken by you.
“Like one who has entered the midst of water when the world is ablaze, like an island in a great ocean’s flood;”
"Like a lamp in the darkness, you are our refuge, O Lord.
Teach me the goal and the Dhamma, O Lord; for in the past, I have committed transgressions.
Explain to me, Nārada, the path of purity, so that I may not fall into hell."
In this context, "I am tormented by fear" means I am tormented by the fear of the evil I have committed.
"And great is my fear" means that a great fear of hell has arisen for me. "As an island in a flood" means as an island amidst a flood. This is what is meant:
just as in a time of conflagration, those whose boats have been wrecked find no foothold in the middle of the water, falling instead into a vast oceanic flood.
"O Lord, as a lamp is for those in darkness and as a light, may you be our refuge.
'In the past, I have committed an offense'—this means that my past action was entirely an offense, a failure; having bypassed what is wholesome, I have done only what is unwholesome."
Then, in order to explain the Path of Purification, the Great Being spoke, citing ancient kings as examples for those who have entered the right practice:
"Just as Dhatarattha, Vessāmitta, Aṭṭhaka, Yāmataggi, Usindara,
and King Sivi were attendants of recluses and brahmins."
“Both these and other kings who have gone to the heavenly realm did so by avoiding unrighteousness;
therefore, O lord of the earth, practice righteousness.
Let those with food in their hands proclaim this throughout your city.”
“Who is hungry? Who is thirsty? Who is naked? Who shall put on this garland and ointment, these garments of various colors?
And who brings an umbrella and soft, beautiful sandals upon the path?”
“Thus, both evening and morning, let them proclaim in your city:
‘Do not employ an aged man, nor an ox or horse, as you did before;
and you should grant exemptions from taxes for those who perform labor service.’”

In this regard, "these too" means: just as these six kings—Dhataraṭṭha, Vessāmitta, Aṭṭhaka, Yāmataggi, Usindara, and Sivī—and others, having practiced the Dhamma, went to the heavenly realm, so too you should avoid unrighteousness and practice the Dhamma.
"Who is hungry? [the king asked]. "O Great King, in your palace and throughout the city, there were those with food in their hands."
Let men cry out with the desire to give to them: "Who is hungry? Who is thirsty?
Let them cry out: "Who desires garlands? Who desires ointments? Whoever desires whatever among various colored garments, who, being naked, shall put it on? And let them cry out:
"Who brings an umbrella for the road?"—meaning, who will hold an umbrella over [him] on the road? And "sandals" means footwear.
And who would desire soft and beautiful things?

As for those who support you—an official among your attendants or another who previously rendered assistance—who, at the time of old age, is no longer able to perform work as he could in former times;
and even those cattle, horses, and so forth, due to their old age, are unable to perform work.
He was not able [to employ them]; he did not appoint even one among them to their former tasks.
For in their state of old age, they were no longer capable of performing those works. Regarding the term "parihāra" (support): here, "parihāra" refers to a retinue. This is what is meant:
as for whoever, while he was strong, had previously rendered assistance through his service, to him—upon the arrival of the time of decrepitude—the former retinue [was restored] as before.
"You should give it. For base persons (asappurisa) show honor to those who have helped them only when they are still able to be of service;
but when those people are no longer capable, they pay them no heed. Noble persons (sappurisa), however, continue to show such respect even when those people are no longer capable.
Therefore, you too should act in this way."
Thus, having discoursed with the king on the subject of giving and the subject of virtue, the Great Being now spoke,
teaching the Dhamma by means of the simile of the chariot that milks all desires, for this king would be pleased when his own person was praised through the metaphor of a chariot.
“The body is known as your chariot, with the mind as its swift charioteer;
non-violence is its axle-pin, and sharing is its covering.
Restraint of the feet is its rim, and restraint of the hands is its fender.”
Restraining the body within bounds, restraining speech and not making noise;
with limbs made even by truthful speech, well-restrained from slander;
with speech free from harshness and frivolity, he is established in the virtue of measured talk.
“With faith as its well-prepared foundation, with hands folded in reverence like a roof-beam,
free from pride and overeating, and bound by the restraint of virtue;
unangry and not given to violence, with the white parasol of the Dhamma.”
Great learning is the handle, a steady mind the shaft,
Knowledge of the right time the core of the heartwood, Confidence the shaft,
modest conduct the cord, And freedom from arrogance the light yoke.
“The unwavering mind is the rug; serving the elders is the broom for dust;
mindfulness is the goad of the wise man, and steadfastness and application are the reins.
The tamed mind leads him along the path, drawn by those steeds with well-tamed teeth.”
Desire and greed are the wrong path; self-restraint is the straight path.

O King, when a vehicle is racing along, wisdom is the goad, and the self alone is the charioteer. Regarding forms, sounds, tastes, and smells—when the vehicle is speeding, wisdom is the goad, and the self alone is the charioteer.
“If, by means of this vehicle, one’s conduct is even and one’s fortitude firm, O King, it will yield all desires; such a person shall never fall into hell.
In that regard, “known as a chariot,” O Great King, let your body be known as the chariot. “With the mind as the charioteer” means by that which is designated as the mind...
He is endowed with a skillful mind as his charioteer. "Light" means he is free from sloth and torpor, thus being very light.
