"Endowed with an axle made of non-violence" means he is possessed of an axle that is well-finished and made of the nature of non-violence.

"A covering consisting of sharing" means he is endowed with a covering made of the sharing of gifts. "With a rim consisting of restraint of the feet" means [endowed] with a rim made of the restraint of the feet.
He is endowed with a felly. "Possessed of a hand-restraint-felly" means he is endowed with a felly consisting of the restraint of the hands.
"Filled within with belly-restraint-oil" means his interior is filled with the oil consisting of measured eating, which is termed belly-restraint.
There is also a reading: "Let the hub be anointed. "Silent through speech-restraint" means he is not chattering due to restraint of speech.
"Saccavākyasamattaṅgo" means one whose limbs are complete through truthful speech; one whose chariot-limbs are unbroken.

"Apesuññasusaññato" means well-restrained and uplifted by the absence of slanderous speech. "Girāsakhilanelaṅgo" means one whose limbs are faultless due to smooth speech—that is, gentle words—and whose chariot-limbs are polished.
"Mitabhāṇisilesito" means well-connected by the bond known as measured speech.

“Possessed of the beautiful adornment of faith and non-greed” means being endowed with the beautiful ornament consisting of the faith that believes in the results of karma, and that which consists of non-greed.

“Possessed of the lovely conduct of respectful salutation” means being endowed with the lovely conduct consisting of both the nature of being free from wind (serenity) and the performance of joining the palms in reverence toward those possessed of virtue.
“Free from stubbornness and devoid of arrogance” means [being endowed] with the state of being free from stubbornness, which is characterized by friendliness and a spirit of mutual greeting.
"Anataiso" means "slightly bent. "Sīlasaṃvarabandhano" means endowed with the binding rope consisting of the restraint of the five precepts, the sense-faculties, and so forth, which are unbroken.
"Akkodhanamanugghātī" means endowed with the quality of non-agitation known as the state of being free from anger. "Dhammapaṇḍarachattako" means...
He is endowed with the white parasol known as the ten wholesome states (*dasakusaladhamma*).
He is endowed with the canopy, which is the state of being possessed of great learning based on the support of the [true] meaning (*attha*).

He is endowed with the upper bedspread or royal throne, which is the mental adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of a mind that has attained a well-established one-pointedness through its immovability by the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).

“Kālaññutācittasāra” means one who possesses the essence of skillfulness through a mind that acts having understood the proper time—known as *kālaññutā* (knowledge of the right occasion)—thinking: “This is the time for giving; this is the time for guarding virtue. This is what is meant:
just as, O Great King, the various materials of a chariot, beginning with its axle-pin, are pure and made of essential substance...

It should be desired; for in this way that chariot becomes capable of enduring the journey. Likewise, may your own "chariot of the body," having recognized its time [of passing], be endowed with a purified mind and the essence of wholesome deeds such as giving.

"Possessing the triple staff of fearlessness" means being endowed with the triple staff known as the state of confidence even when speaking in the midst of an assembly. "Possessing the cord of humble conduct" means...
It is endowed with a supple yoke-rope, which is characterized by the application of instruction.

For horses draw a chariot easily when it is bound with a supple yoke-rope; likewise, the meaning is that your chariot of the body, being bound by the application of the wise ones' instructions, may proceed with ease.
It is "light with a yoke that is not too proud," meaning it is endowed with a light yoke characterized by the absence of excessive pride.

"Alīnacittasaṇṭhāro" means: just as a chariot is beautified by a magnificent seat-cover made of ivory, so too may the chariot of your body have a seat-cover of a mind that is not dejected or contracted due to generosity and other virtues. "Vuddhisevī rajohato" means:
just as a chariot traveling over uneven ground covered with dust does not shine, whereas [one traveling] on level ground...

Just as one traveling by way of the stainless path shines forth, so too may your chariot of the body, having entered upon the straight path that is level through the cultivation of wisdom, be freed from dust.
"The goad of mindfulness for the wise man": let the goad of mindfulness be firmly established in that chariot of your body, O wise one.
And "fortitude and application as the reins" refers to those characterized by uninterrupted energy.
May fortitude and the application known as the state of being intent upon practicing what is beneficial be the firm reins fastened to that chariot of the body for you.

Just as a chariot goes astray when yoked with horses of uneven teeth, but follows only the straight path when joined with well-trained horses of even teeth—so too does the mind lead one along the path. Thus it is said: "The mind leads the tamed [body] along the path; by means of well-tamed bearers."
Just as a well-trained horse follows [the rider’s will], so too the mind, when tamed and free from vice, abandons the wrong path and takes to the straight path.
Therefore, let your well-tamed mind, endowed with right conduct, perform the duty of a thoroughbred steed for the chariot of your body.
"Desire and greed" (icchālobho): desire for things not yet attained and greed for those already attained—this is what is called the "wrong path."

A crooked, uneven path leads only to the states of misery (*apāya*). However, the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃyama*) that proceeds by way of the ten courses of wholesome action or the eightfold path is called the "straight path. May this be the path for the chariot of your body.

For your chariot of the body, which runs about having grasped the signs (*nimitta*) in these desirable objects such as forms and other qualities of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), [this straight path is necessary].
Let wisdom be the goad for striking the horses of the royal chariot that has entered upon a wrong path;
for it will restrain you from going astray and lead you onto the straight path of good conduct.
In this regard, "the self alone is the charioteer" means that in this chariot of your body, there is no other so-called charioteer than your own self.
"Let him be the charioteer. If, O Great King, one possesses such a vehicle as this, then by that vehicle [one travels].
'Firm is his even conduct and fortitude' means that for whom even conduct and fortitude are firm and stable, he [travels] by that vehicle;
because, O King, this chariot grants all desires, it bestows every wish exactly as intended."
"You shall never go to hell; hold this as a certainty: you will not go to hell by means of such a vehicle.
This is the meaning. Thus, Great King, that which you said to me—"Tell me, Nārada, the path of purity, so that I may not fall into hell"—that has been explained to you by me in many ways.
Having thus taught him the Dhamma, caused him to abandon wrong view, and established him in virtue, he gave this exhortation:
"From now on, having abandoned evil friends, approach virtuous friends; be constantly heedful.
Then, praising the virtues of the princess, and giving advice to the royal assembly and the king’s women, he departed with great majesty from among them.
While passing by, he went straight to the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that I have tamed Uruvela Kassapa by breaking his net of views; I did so even in the past. Then, identifying the Jātaka, he spoke these verses:
"Alāta was Devadatta, and Sunāma was Bhaddaji;"
Vijaya was Sāriputta, and Bījaka was Moggallāna.
Sunakkhatta, the son of a Licchavi, was the naked ascetic Guṇa;
and she who won over the king was Rucā, who became Ānanda.
“King Uruvelakassapa then held an evil view;
the Bodhisatta was Mahābrahmā—thus you should remember this Jātaka.
The commentary on the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka, the eighth.
[546] 9. The Exposition of the Vidhura Jātaka:
The Section on the Four Uposatha Days.
"Pale, emaciated, and weak"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning his own perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī).
He related it. For one day, the monks in the Hall of Truth raised this discussion:
"Friends, the Teacher is of great wisdom, of broad wisdom, of deep wisdom, of swift wisdom, of smiling wisdom, of sharp wisdom, of penetrative wisdom;
he is the crusher of the doctrines of others. By the power of his own wisdom, [he has answered] the subtle questions contrived by the wise khattiyas and others."
“Having broken them, having tamed them, and having rendered them harmless, he established them in the three refuges and in the precepts, and set them upon the path leading to the Deathless.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not surprising that the Tathāgata...”
Having attained supreme perfect enlightenment and having shattered the doctrines of others, he would subdue the kṣatriyas and the rest.
For even while seeking the knowledge of enlightenment in a previous existence, the Tathāgata was wise and a crusher of the doctrines of others.
Thus, in a time of distress, upon the peak of Mount Kāla, which rose sixty yojanas high, [he subdued] the general of the yakkhas named Puṇṇaka.
"Having tamed his own mind by the power of his own wisdom and rendered it free from wickedness, he gave up his own life while establishing others in the five precepts," he said;
and being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Kuru, in the city of Indapatta, a king named Dhanañjaya Koravya reigned. [There lived] the wise Vidhura.
A minister named [Nāma] was his instructor in matters of welfare and the Dhamma. He was sweet-spoken and a great preacher of the Dhamma;
like elephants enticed by the sound of a lute played upon an elephant’s trunk, he captivated the kings throughout the whole of Jambudīpa with his sweet preaching of the Dhamma.
Not allowing them to return to their respective kingdoms, he taught the Dhamma to the great multitude with the grace of a Buddha, on a grand scale.
Yasa lived in that city. At that time, in Bārāṇasī as well,
four wealthy brahmin householders who were his lay companions, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures in their old age,
entered the Himalayas, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, and attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).
Having thus been reborn and lived there for a long time subsisting on forest roots and fruits, they set out on a journey to seek salt and sour condiments.
Upon reaching the city of Kālacampā in the kingdom of Aṅga, they stayed in the royal park and entered the city for alms on the following day.
There, four householder friends, becoming inspired by their deportment, [invited them].

Having paid homage to them, they took their alms-bowls, seated each one in his own residence, served them with excellent food, and having obtained their promise, they had them dwell right there in the park. Those four ascetics ate regularly at the houses of the four householders;
then, for the sake of their midday rest, one ascetic would go to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
One went to the abode of the *nāgas*, one to the abode of the *supaṇṇas*, and one went to King Koravya’s Migājina park.
Among them, he who went to the world of the gods and spent the day there, having observed the glory of Sakka, praised that very thing to his own attendant.
He who went to the abode of the *nāgas* and spent the day there [praised] the prosperity of the *nāga* king.

Having observed it, he praises that very thing to his own attendant. He who goes to the abode of the Supaṇṇas and spends the day there, having observed the splendor of the Supaṇṇa king, praises that very thing to his own attendant.
He who goes to the garden of King Dhanañjaya Koravya and spends the day there, [praises] that of King Dhanañjaya Koravya...
Having observed her glorious beauty, he praised that very same woman to his attendant.
Those four people, aspiring for that very same state, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms;
at the end of their lives, one was reborn as a Sakka, one was reborn as a Naga king with his wife and children in the Naga realm, and one...
In the abode of the Supaṇṇas, he was reborn as a king of the Supaṇṇas in the *simbalī* celestial mansion.

Another was reborn from the womb of the chief queen of King Dhanañjaya Koravya. Those three ascetics, having passed away without falling away from their meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), were reborn in the Brahma-world.
As the Prince Koravya grew up, upon the passing of his father, he was established in the kingdom and ruled according to the Dhamma.
He ruled the kingdom with impartiality. However, he was addicted to gambling.
Abiding by the advice of the wise Vidhura, he gave alms, guarded his virtue, and observed the Uposatha fast.
One day, having undertaken the Uposatha vows, thinking, "I shall cultivate seclusion," he went to a garden and stayed in a delightful place.

Having sat down, he practiced the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). Sakka, having likewise undertaken the observance day (*uposa-tha*), thinking, "In the world of the gods there are hindrances," came to that very same park in the human world; having sat down in a pleasant spot, he practiced the duty of a recluse.
The Naga King Varuṇa, too, having undertaken the observance day, thinking, "In the Naga realm there are hindrances," came to that very place.
Having sat down in a pleasant place, he practiced the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).

The king of the *supaṇṇas*, having likewise undertaken the *upoṣadha* observance, thinking, "There is an obstacle in the *supaṇṇa* abode," came to that very spot, sat down in a pleasant place, and practiced the duty of a recluse.
Then those four persons, departing from their respective places in the evening, [went] to the bank of the Maṅgala lotus pond.
Having come together and looked at one another, they became harmonious and joyful through the influence of their former affection;
establishing a mind of loving-kindness toward each other, they exchanged sweet greetings.
Among them, Sakka sat upon a slab of auspicious stone, while the others also sat down, each taking his appropriate seat. Then Sakka said to them: "We..."
"Are you not all four like kings? But among us, whose virtue is the greatest?
Then Varuṇa, the Nāga king, said to him, "In terms of virtue, my virtue is greater than that of you three. "What is the reason for this?
"This Supaṇṇa king is an enemy to us both born and unborn; yet I [maintain] such [virtue] toward him."
"Even upon seeing an enemy who would bring about the destruction of my life, I do not give way to anger; for this reason, my virtue is great.
Having said this, he spoke the first verse in the Catuposa-tha Jātaka of the Dasaka Nipāta:
"He who does not give way to anger toward one who should be angered, that noble person never becomes angry."
“Even when provoked, he does not manifest anger; him indeed they call a *śramaṇa* in the world.

In this context, “he” refers to anyone among the kṣatriyas and other classes. “Toward one who should be provoked” means that toward a person who is fit to be angered, he does not give way to anger, like the ascetic Khantīvādin.
“Never” means that at no time whatsoever does he become angry. “Even when provoked” means: if, however...
That good person becomes angry, yet even when angry, he does not manifest that anger, like the ascetic Cūḷabodhi.
"Him indeed they call a man," O Great Kings; because of his having stilled evil, the wise in the world call that man a "recluse" (samaṇa).
"But these virtues exist in me; therefore, my virtue alone is great."
Having heard this, the Supaṇṇa king said, "This nāga is my foremost food;
yet, even upon seeing such a foremost food, I endure hunger and do not commit evil for the sake of food. Therefore, my virtue alone is great," and he spoke this verse:

“He who has a small stomach and endures hunger, who is self-controlled, an ascetic, moderate in food and drink, and does not commit evil for the sake of food—him indeed they call a *samaṇa* in the world.

In this context, “self-controlled” (*danta*) means endowed with the restraint of the sense faculties. “Ascetic” (*tapassī*) means one who relies upon austerity. “For the sake of food” (*āhārahetu*) means...
"Even when oppressed by extreme hunger, one who does not commit evil or base deeds—like the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma—does not do so.
As for me, I do not commit evil today for the sake of food; therefore, my virtue alone is great.

Then Sakka, the King of the Devas, said, "I have abandoned the various forms of happiness found in the celestial realms and come to the human world for the sake of guarding my virtue; therefore, my virtue alone is great," and he spoke this verse:
“Having abandoned all play and delight, he does not speak anything false in the world;
abstaining from the grounds for adornment and from sexual intercourse—him indeed they call a *samaṇa* in the world.
Herein, “play” (*khiḍḍā*) refers to physical and verbal play. “Delight” (*rati*) refers to delight in the divine strands of sensual pleasure. “Anything” (*kiñci*) means even the slightest thing.
"Adornments" refers to two types of adornment: adornment of the flesh and adornment of the skin.
Therein, edible food is called "adornment of the flesh," while garlands, perfumes, and so forth are called "adornment of the skin.

The unwholesome state of mind by which these are maintained is the basis for that [adornment]. One who abstains from that, and who is also refrained from sexual intercourse—him indeed they call a recluse.
"Today, O celestial nymphs," he said, "having abandoned the world and come here, I practice the duty of a recluse;
therefore, my virtue alone is great. Thus Sakka praised his own virtue.
Hearing this, King Dhanañjaya thought, "Today, I possess a vast retinue, complete with sixteen thousand dancing girls..."
"Having abandoned the inner palace, I practice the duty of a recluse in the park; therefore, my virtue alone is great. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"He who, having fully understood, renounces all possessions and the nature of greed;
who is self-controlled, steadfast in mind, free from 'mine-ness,' and without craving—him indeed they call a recluse in the world."
In this context, "possessions" (*pariggaha*) refers to sensual objects of various kinds. "States of greed" (*lobhadhamma*) refers to the craving that arises toward them.

"Having fully understood" (*pariññāya*) means having fully understood by means of these three types of full understanding: full understanding as knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*), full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*), and full understanding as abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*).

Among these, the knowledge of the aggregates and so forth as having the intrinsic nature of suffering and so on is full understanding as knowledge; the investigation of their defects after having reflected upon them is full understanding as investigation.

Thorough comprehension by investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*) is the seeing of faults in those [objects]. Thorough comprehension by abandoning (*pahānapariññā*) is the drawing away of desire and lust once those faults have been seen.

One who, having understood through these three types of thorough comprehension, relinquishes sense-desires as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sense-desires as defilements (*kilesakāma*), casts them off and goes on.

"Tamed" (*danta*) means free from turbulence. "Stable in nature" (*ṭhitatta*) means having a nature established by the absence of wrong thoughts. "Selfless" (*amama*) means free from the craving that conceives "I" and "mine."
“Free from anxiety” means being devoid of desire and lust for children, wife, and so forth. “They call such a person a ‘recluse’ (samaṇa).
Thus, all of them, praising their own respective virtue as supreme, asked Dhanañjaya:
“But, Great King, is there anyone in your presence who is wise enough to dispel this doubt of ours?”
“Yes, Great Kings, I have a counselor who teaches us matters of profit and Dhamma—one of great wisdom, peerless in his burden-bearing, and known as Vidhura Paṇḍita.
He will dispel this doubt of ours; let us go into his presence.
Then they all agreed, saying, “Very well. Thereupon, they all departed from the pleasure grove, went to the Dhamma Hall, and [prepared] their seats.
Having adorned the Bodhisatta and seated him in the midst of the excellent couch, they paid him their respects and sat down to one side.
Saying, "O Wise One, a doubt has arisen in us; please dispel it for us," they spoke this verse:
"We ask the Maker of wonders, possessed of peerless wisdom; a dispute has arisen among our discourses."
“Cut off today your doubts and hesitations; let us all cross over this doubt today.
In this context, “one who acts” (*kattāraṃ*) means one who performs what is appropriate to be done. The analysis (*viggaha*) is: “there is a dispute (*atthi jāto*)”;

that is, one dispute regarding virtue (*sīla-viggaha*), a quarrel concerning virtue, has arisen. “Cut off today” (*chindajja*) means [cut off] our doubt and those hesitations as if [cutting] Mount Sineru with a thunderbolt.
“Strike! Cut it today! “Let us cross over! Let us cross over!
Having heard their words, the wise man said, “Great kings, by means of your own virtue, I shall determine whether your dispute was well-spoken or ill-spoken,” and he spoke this verse:
“Those who are wise and see the true goal speak appropriately on that matter at the right time.”
"How indeed might wise leaders lead to the meaning those words that have not yet been spoken? In this context, "seers of the meaning" (*atthadassā*) means those capable of seeing the meaning.
Therein, "at the time" refers to when that dispute has been reported and it is the appropriate time for application;
those wise ones, explaining that matter, speak with systematic reflection (*yoniso*). "Wise ones who would lead to the meaning" means those who are skillful.
Even those who are experts, how could they lead to the meaning and investigate discourses that have not been spoken?
"O lords of men"—this he addresses to kings. Therefore, please tell me this first:
"How indeed does the Naga king speak, and what does the Garuda, the son of Vinatā, say?"
"But what does the King of the Gandhabbas say, and how does the supreme king of the Kurus act?
Therein, "the King of the Gandhabbas" refers to Sakka.
Then they spoke this verse to him:
“The Naga king speaks of patience; the Venerable Venateyya, the Garuḷa, of fewness of food;
the Gandhabba king, of the abandoning of delight; and the best of kings among the Kurus, of nothingness.
The meaning of this is as follows: O wise one, first of all, the Naga king speaks of the patience of endurance, which consists in being unperturbed even toward persons who are prone to provoke anger.
The Garuḍa praised the non-committing of evil for the sake of food, characterized by a meager diet;
Sakka praised the complete relinquishing of delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure; and the King of Kuru praised the state of being free from obstacles.
Then, having heard their words, the Great Being spoke this verse:
“All these are well-spoken; herein there is nothing ill-spoken.
And he upon whom these are firmly established, like spokes well-fixed in a hub—him, being endowed with these four qualities, they truly call a ‘recluse’ in the world.”
In this context, "these" refers to these four types of virtues which, like spokes well-settled upon the hub of a chariot wheel, are firmly established in that person;
the wise call such a person, endowed with all these four qualities, a "recluse" (samaṇa) in the world.
Thus the Great Being made the virtue of each of the four equal. Hearing this, the four kings were delighted and, offering praise, spoke this verse:
“You are indeed the best, you are unsurpassed; you are a guardian of the Dhamma, a knower of the Dhamma, one of excellent wisdom.
Having grasped the question with wisdom, the wise one has severed his doubts;
he has cut through uncertainty and hesitations, just as Cunda cuts an elephant’s tusk with a saw.”
"In this regard, you are unsurpassed" means that you are without superior; there is indeed no one higher than you.
"Guardian of the Dhamma" means both a protector of the Dhamma and one who knows the Dhamma. "Knower of the Dhamma" means one for whom the Dhamma is manifest. "Sumedha" means one of beautiful wisdom;
by means of his own wisdom, having thoroughly grasped our question, he [perceived]: "This is the reason here."
"Having known it as it truly is. "Cut them off"—O Wise One, cut away our doubts.
And while cutting them thus, fulfilling our entreaty that "today you shall cut away hesitation and doubts," you have indeed cut away hesitation and doubts.
Just as Cunda cuts ivory with a saw. (The phrase) "as a tooth-worker [cuts] with a saw" means...
"He would cut an elephant's tusk"—the meaning is "he would cut it in this manner.
Thus, all four kings were satisfied in their minds by his explanation of the question.
Then Sakka honored him with a divine *dukūla* cloth, Garuḷa with a golden garland, Varuṇa the Naga king with a jewel, and King Dhanañjaya...
He honored him with a thousand cows and other offerings. For this very reason, he said:
“O Wise One, I give you this stainless, priceless cloth, blue-lotus-hued and the color of smoke, out of devotion to the Dhamma, for I am satisfied by your answer to the question.”
“O wise one, I give this golden garland— blossoming with a hundred petals, possessing filaments, and adorned with a thousand jewels— to you in honor of the Dhamma,
satisfied by your answer to my question. This priceless, radiant,
and beautiful gem, which adorns my neck, is fastened there as my jewel-ornament.”
“Satisfied by your answer to my question, O wise one, I give this to you as an offering of Dhamma:
a thousand cows and a bull, a noble elephant, and ten chariots yoked with thoroughbred horses.
Satisfied by your answer to my question, I give you sixteen excellent villages.”
Thus Sakka and the others, having honored the Great Being, returned to their own places.
The Chapter on the Four Uposatha Days is finished.
The Chapter on the Longing.
Among them, the wife of the Naga king was named Vimalādevī. Not seeing the jewel adorning his neck, she asked, "Your Majesty, where is that gem of yours?

"My dear," he replied, "having heard the discourse on the Dhamma from Vidhura the wise, the son of the Brahmin Canda, my heart was filled with faith, and I honored him with that gem. It is not I alone who did so..."
Sakka honored him with divine silk garments; the King of the Supaṇṇas with a golden garland; and King Dhanañjaya with a thousand cows, horses, and other gifts.
“He is a preacher of the Dhamma, O Queen,” [the others replied]. “Good lady, what are you saying? On the surface of Jambudīpa, it is as if a Buddha has appeared!
For throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, one hundred kings have been captivated by his sweet discourse on the Dhamma.”
"Like intoxicated elephants captivated by the sound of a lute played upon the neck of an elephant, they do not wish to go to their respective kingdoms;
such is that sweet preacher of the Dhamma. Thus he praised his virtue.

Having heard this account of Vidhura Paṇḍita’s virtues, she became desirous of hearing his discourse on the Dhamma and thought: "If I were to say, 'Sire, [let me hear] his discourse on the Dhamma...'"
“If they wish to hear it, bring her here,” he said, “but she will not bring herself. What if I were to feign illness, declaring, ‘A longing has arisen in my heart’?
She did so; having entered the inner chamber and given instructions to her attendants, she lay down upon the royal couch.
When the time for his visit arrived, the Nāga king, not seeing her, asked, “Where is Vimalā?”

Having questioned his attendants and being told, "She is ill, Your Majesty," he rose from his seat, went to her side, and sitting at the head of her bed, while massaging her body, he spoke this first verse:
"You are pale, emaciated, and weak; such was not your complexion or form before."
"O Vimalā, being questioned, tell me: what is the nature of your bodily pain?
In this context, "pale" (*paṇḍu*) means having the color of a withered leaf. "Emaciated" (*kisiyā*) means thin. "Weak" (*dubbalā*) means lacking strength.
"Your complexion and form are not as they were before": your form, which is designated as complexion, was previously not like this; it was faultless and blameless.
Now, having turned over, it has become something unpleasant in nature. "Vimalā" addresses it.
Then, explaining it to him, she spoke this second verse:
"O Lord of Men, among humans, Dhamma is called the longing (*dohaḷa*) of mothers."
"O elephant-like Nāga, you who have brought the Dhamma, I long for the heart of Vidhura.
In this context, *dhamma* means intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). *Mātīnam* means of women. *Janinda* means lord of the people of the Nāgas.
"O elephant-like Nāga, you who have brought the Dhamma, I long for the heart of Vidhura": O best of Nāgas, by means of the Dhamma, by what is right, and by action free from violence...
"I desire the heart of Vidhura, which has been brought here; for me, life exists only if I obtain it, but if I do not obtain it, my death shall be right here.
It was with reference to his wisdom that he spoke thus.
Having heard this, the Nāga king spoke the third verse:
“You long for the moon, or perhaps the sun, or even the wind;
for the sight of Vidhura is indeed difficult to obtain—who here would honor Vidhura?
In this context, “the sight of Vidhura is indeed difficult to obtain” means that the very sight of Vidhura, who is of incomparable burden, is difficult to find.
"For throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, kings move about having established righteous protection, defense, and security;
no one even obtains a sight of him, so who here could bring him?
Having heard his words, she thought, "If I do not obtain him, my death shall be right here," and turning away, she presented her back.
Covering her face with a *sāḷaka* leaf, she lay down. The Nāga king, displeased, entered the inner chamber and sat upon the bed;

perceiving that Vimalā was having the heart-flesh of the wise Vidhura brought to her, he thought, "If Vimalā does not obtain the heart of the wise man, she will have no life. How indeed can his heart-flesh..."

"I shall obtain her," he thought. Then his daughter, a Naga maiden named Irandhatī, adorned with every ornament and approaching her father’s presence with great majesty and splendor, bowed to him and stood to one side.
Seeing the change in his faculties, she asked, "Father, you appear exceedingly distressed; what indeed is the cause?"
Questioning him, she spoke this verse:
"Why indeed, dear father, do you brood? Your face is like a lotus fallen from your hand;
why are you so dejected in appearance, O Lord? Do not grieve, O scorcher of your enemies!"

In that context, *pajjhāyasi* means you thought about it again and again. *Hatthagataṃ* means your face has become like a lotus flower crushed by the hand. *Issarā* means the mistress of the Naga palace-mansion measuring five hundred yojanas;
*sāmī* means the owner. Having heard his daughter’s words, the Naga king, explaining the matter, said:
“For your mother is Irandhatī; Vidhura’s heart is being tormented.”
“Indeed, it is difficult to see one who is separated from us; who here will honor Vidhura?
In this context, *dhaniyati* means she yearns for or desires him.

Then the Nāga king, sending her away while saying, “Mother, there is no one capable of bringing Vidhura back to me; give up your life for your mother’s sake, and seek a husband who is capable of bringing Vidhura back,” spoke this half-verse:
“Go forth in search of food for him who will honor Vidhura here.
In this context, *cara* means “wander about.
Thus, out of his own delight in defilements, he spoke words unsuitable for his daughter. To clarify this meaning, the Teacher said:
“Having heard her father’s words, she went out at night and acted with lustful intent.
In this context, monks, that Nāga maiden, having heard her father’s speech,
comforted her father, went to her mother’s presence, comforted her as well, and then, having gone to her own bedchamber, adorned herself with all her ornaments...
Having adorned herself, she put on a single garment dyed with safflower, draped one shoulder over her shoulder, and during that very night, having divided the waters,
she departed from the Nāga realm and went to the mountain named Kāḷapabbata— an ointment-mountain (añjanagiri) sixty yojanas high and solid as one mass—
situated on the shore of the ocean in the Himālaya region; there she practiced *avassuti*, which means she practiced the "flowing away" of defilements, namely, the seeking of food.
Gathering whatever flowers were endowed with color and fragrance that grew in the Himalayas,
she adorned the entire mountain as if it were a jeweled casket; then, having spread a carpet of flowers upon its summit,
she danced in a charming manner and, singing a sweet song, spoke the seventh stanza:
“Who among the gandhabbas, rakkhasas, and nāgas? Who among the kimpurisas and humans?
Which wise one, who grants all desires, will become my husband for a long time?
In this context, “who among the gandhabbas, rakkhasas, and nāgas” means which one—whether a gandhabba, a rakkhasa, or a nāga—and “which wise one” [means which one].
"Who among these Gandhabbas and others is wise enough to grant all desires?
He who shall fulfill the heart's longing of my mother—who craves the flesh of Vidhura’s heart—will become my husband for a long time.
At that moment, Vessavaṇa the Great King’s nephew, the yakkha general named Puṇṇaka, [who was] three gavutas in height...
Mounting his mind-made steed and traveling toward the assembly of yakkhas over the summit of Mount Kāḷapabbata, he heard that sound of singing.
Because it was the song of a woman he had experienced in a previous existence, the sound of her singing pierced through his skin and other layers until it struck right against his very marrow.
With his heart bound to her, he turned back and [remained] upon the back of the steed.
Remaining seated, he comforted her with the eighth verse, saying: “Bhaddā, by means of my own wisdom, I am capable of winning Vidhura’s heart through righteousness and fairness; do not worry.
“‘I shall be your consolation, your husband, O lady of unblinking eyes; I shall be your supporter.’”
“For my wisdom is such as this; you shall be my comfort and my wife.
Therein, “O you with blameless eyes” means one whose eyes are not to be censured. “Such as this” means capable of extracting the heart-flesh of Vidhura.
Then Irandhatī said to him, “In that case, come, let us go to my father’s presence,” and she led him away. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
“Iranda-tī spoke to Puṇṇaka with a mind following the former path:
‘Come, let us go into the presence of my father; he himself will explain this matter to you.
In that context, ‘with a mind following the former path’ means [a mind] directed toward him who was her husband in a previous existence.”
"Follow me. "Come, let us go," said that general of the *yakkhas*, O monks;
having spoken thus, thinking, "I shall mount her upon the back of this horse and carry her away," he descended from the mountain peak and extended his hand to take hold of her.
She, however, did not allow him to grasp her own hand, but instead took hold of the hand he had extended himself, saying, "My lord, I—"
“O helpless one, my father is the Naga king named Varuṇa, and my mother is the queen named Vimalā. Come, let us go to my father’s presence;
he will explain this matter to you exactly as our auspicious rites ought to be performed.
Having spoken thus, she took the yakkha and went to her father’s presence. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Adorned, well-clothed, garlanded, and anointed with sandalwood paste,
she took the yakkha by the hand and approached her father.
In this context, “she approached her father” means she went into the presence of her own father, the king of the city.
The yakkha Puṇṇaka, having returned, went into the presence of the Nāga king and, entreating Irandhatī, said:
"O best of Nāgas, listen to my words; act in a manner worthy of your merit.
I long for Irandhatī; do you unite me with her."
“A hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred chariots drawn by mules,
a hundred covered wagons filled to the brim with all kinds of jewels—
O Nāga, accept these and give me your daughter, Andhatī.”
In this context, "suṅkiyanti" means: accept and take the bride-price (suṅka) or wealth according to the custom of your own family lineage.
"Samaṅgiṃ karohi" means: make me one who is united with her. "Valabhiyo" refers to merchandise-carts.
"Nānāratnassa kevalā" means entirely full of various kinds of jewels.
Then the Naga king said to him:
"Until I have taken leave of my kinsmen, friends,
and beloved people, an action performed without taking leave will lead to regret later."
In that regard, the phrase "I invite my kinsmen" means: "O General of the Yakṣas, I shall give you my daughter; I will not refuse her.
However, wait a little while until I have informed my kinsmen as well. The phrase "lest he regret it later" means that women, wherever they go, may find pleasure or may not find pleasure;
and at the time when they do not find pleasure, their kinsmen and others [think]: "We..."
"An act performed without having consulted together is of such a nature," [they thought], and thus they made no effort;
in this way, that act later brought about regret.
Having said this, he went to his wife's dwelling and conversed with her. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
Then that Naga Varuṇa, having entered his residence and addressed his wife, spoke these words:
“This is that Yakkha Puṇṇaka, who asks me for Irandhatī.”
“With much gain of wealth, we shall give her who is dear to me to him.
Therein, “having entered” means that Varuṇa, having left Puṇṇaka right there, rose up himself and entered that dwelling where his wife was lying.
“Dear to me” means my own dear daughter; to him, with much...
"Demati asked: 'Is she to be obtained by the acquisition of wealth?
Vimalā replied:
'Neither by wealth nor by riches can we obtain Irandhatī.'"

"But if the heart of the wise man is inclined, and he should bring [the girl] here having obtained her according to the Dhamma, then by this wealth the maiden may be won; we do not seek any other wealth beyond this.
In this context, "our Irandhatī" means our daughter Irandhatī. "By this wealth" means by this cause for satisfaction.
Having consulted with her, he then consulted again with Puṇṇaka. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then that Nāga Varuṇa, having emerged from his dwelling and consulted with Puṇṇaka, spoke these words.”
“Neither by wealth nor by riches can we obtain Irandhatī; but if you, O wise one,
having obtained her here according to the Dhamma, give her to our heart,
then by that wealth alone may the maiden be won— no other wealth do we seek beyond this.”
In that context, "having addressed Puṇṇaka" means having called out to Puṇṇaka.
Puṇṇaka said:
"Those whom some in the world call wise, others again call fools."
"Tell me, O Nāga, as they dispute here, whom do you call wise?
Therein, regarding the phrase "whom some call wise," it is said that he, having heard "the heart of the wise man," thought:
"What one some call wise, others speak of as foolish. Although it has been declared to me by Irandhati that [you are] Vidhura..."
"Nevertheless, I shall ask so that I may know it as it truly is. Therefore he spoke thus.
The Naga King said:
"If you have heard of the builder named Vidhura, belonging to King Koravya Dhanañjaya;"
"Bring that wise man who has obtained her by righteous means; let Irandhatī be your footmaid.
In this context, "obtained by righteous means" (*dhammaladdhā*) means having acquired her through the Dhamma.
"Footmaid" (*padacarā*) means a female attendant. Having heard this, Puṇṇaka, filled with joy, commanded his attendant to bring the horse. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having heard these words of Varuṇa, the yakkha rose up, supremely delighted;
standing right there, he commanded a man: ‘Bring a well-bred horse, harnessed and ready, right here!

In this context, “commanded a man” means he gave orders to his own attendant. “Well-bred horse” (*ājañña*) refers to a thoroughbred steed that knows what is appropriate and inappropriate. “Harnessed” (*yutta*) means prepared for service.
“Earrings made of gold, bits of glass and brass, and a breastplate of refined gold from the Jambu River.
Therein, “earrings made of gold” was said while describing that very horse. For that horse was mind-made.
The ears were made of gold, the hooves of glass; the meaning is that its hooves were made of red gems.
It was a breast-plate of ripe Jambunada gold—that is, of mature, red-golden Jambunada.
That man brought the Sindhu horse right then and there. Puṇṇaka mounted it and [proceeded] through the air to Vessavaṇa’s...
Having gone into his presence and praised the Nāga-abode, he reported that occurrence. To explain the meaning of this, it was said:
“Mounting a vehicle drawn by divine horses, Puṇṇaka—adorned and with hair and beard trimmed—set forth through the sky by way of the air.”
“Thus Puṇṇaka, greedy with sensual lust and desiring to win the Naga maiden Irandhati,
went to that glorious lord of spirits, Vessavaṇa Kuvera, and spoke thus:
‘In the mansion named Bhogavatī, your dwelling is called Hiraññavatī.’”
When the city made of gold was constructed, it was completed for the serpent Maṇḍalaka.
"The watchtowers and the battlements were made of ruby and cat's-eye gem;
the palaces there were made of stone and covered with gold and jewels."
“The *ambā*, *tilaka*, and *jambu* trees, the *sattapaṇṇa*, *mucalinda*, and *ketaka*;
the *piyaṅgu*, *uddālaka*, and *sahā*, the *uparibhaddaka*, and *sinduvāraka*.
The *campeyyaka*, *nāgamallikā*, *bhaginīmālā*, and then the *mettha koliya*.”
These trees, having been transformed, beautify the serpent’s abode.
Here are many date-palm trees made of stone, with golden flowers that bloom eternally;
there dwells the powerful Naga king Varuṇa, who is spontaneously born.
His wife was a young maiden, Vimalā, her body like a polished rod of gold;
she was dark-complexioned, youthful, tall, with breasts like *pucimanda* fruits, and beautiful to behold.
With skin as lovely as lac-dye, she was like a *kaṇikāra* tree in full bloom in a windless place.
“Like lightning flashing from clouds in the sky, the celestial nymphs of the Tāvatiṃsa realm have emerged.
‘That pregnant woman, filled with wonder, yearns for the heart of Vidhura;
I shall give him that, O Lord, and through him they will give Irandhatī to me.’”

In that context, "the vehicle carrying the divine draft-animals" (*devavāhavahaṃ yānaṃ*): it is called a "draft-animal" (*vāha*) because it must be driven; it carries a draft-animal known as a "divine" one, thus it is "carrying the divine draft-animals.
It is a "vehicle" (*yāna*) because one goes by means of it. "With hair and beard trimmed" (*kappitakesamassū*) means having the hair and beard well-arranged for the sake of adornment.
However, there is no such thing as the act of grooming hair and beard among the gods; this was stated by the storyteller [Vicitrakathika]. "They desire to win" (*jigīsanti*).
*Patthayanto*: longing for. *Vessavaṇa*: the sovereign king of the royal capital Visāṇā. *Kuvera*: one who bears this name. *Bhogavatī nāmā*:
having acquired the name "Possessor of Wealth" due to her abundance of riches. *Mandire*: a palace; the meaning is "dwelling. *Vāsā hiraññavatī*:
it is called *vāsā* because it is the dwelling place (*vasanaṭṭhāna*) of the Nāga king, and it is called *hiraññavatī* because of its golden rampart (*suvaṇṇapākāra*).
Because it is surrounded [by a moat], it is called "Hiraññavatī" (Possessing Gold). "In the city that was built" means the city was constructed. "Made of gold" means made of refined gold (*suvaṇṇa*).
"Of one who possesses a circle" means of one endowed with a circle of prosperity (*bhoga-maṇḍala*). "Completed" means finished through the completion of its construction.
"Turrets on the necks of elephants" refers to watchtowers (*aṭṭālaka*) shaped like elephant necks, made of red gems and *masāragalla*. "Palaces here" means...
Here, in this Nāga abode, there are palaces. "Made of stone" means made of jewels.

"With golden jewels" means with jewels known as gold; the meaning is that they are covered with golden bricks. *Saha* means mango trees (*sahakāra*). *Uparibhaddaka* refers to trees of the *uddālaka* species.
*Campesyyakā nāgamallikā* means campaka trees, nāga jasmine, and mallikā jasmine. Then there is the *bhaginīmālā*.
"Mettha Koliyā" refers both to the garland of sisters and, furthermore, to the trees called *koliya* that are here in this Nāga abode.
"These trees are intertwined" means these flowering and fruit-bearing trees are intertwined with one another, being pressed closely together in a dense thicket.
"There are date palms here" means there are *khajjuri* trees here. "Made of stone" means made of sapphire (*indanīla-maṇi*).
"Ever-blooming with golden flowers" means they are perpetually in bloom with golden blossoms.
"Wherein dwells the spontaneously born one" refers to the place where a spontaneously born (*opapātika*) Naga king resides in his Naga abode.

"With bodies like streaked gold" means their forms are as beautiful as a heap of refined gold. "Tall and dark like young creepers" means that, due to their graceful charm, they stand tall like the sprouts of dark vines swaying in a gentle breeze.
"Pucimanda-thaṇī" means having nipples shaped like the fruit of the nimba tree.

"Lākhā-rasa-ratta-succhavī" refers to the skin of the palms and soles of the feet being as beautifully red as lac-dye. "Tidivokacara" means those who roam in the realm of the Thirty-three (the Tāvatiṃsa heaven).
"Vijju-vabbha-ghana" means like flashes of lightning issuing from between the clouds and rain-clouds. "Taṃ tesaṃ demī" means "I give that heart of his to them. Thus...
"Know this. With "Lord," he addresses his uncle.
Thus, being unable to depart without Vessavaṇa’s permission, he spoke these verses in order to obtain it.
However, Vessavaṇa did not hear his words. For what reason? Because it was the half of the celestial mansion belonging to two devaputtas.
"He is deciding. Knowing that his words had not been heard, Puṇṇaka stood before the son of the gods, Jinakadevaputta.
Vessavaṇa, having adjudicated the wager and having caused the defeated party to rise, said to the other, "Go, you may dwell in your own mansion.
At the very moment Puṇṇako was told, "Go," [he thought], "By my maternal uncle..."
“Know that I have sent this message,” saying this, Puṇṇaka made several sons of the gods his witnesses;
then, having caused the Sindhu horse to be brought in the manner described above, he mounted it and departed. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“He addressed the glorious lord of beings, Vessavaṇa Kuvera: Puṇṇaka, the master of spirits, [spoke thus].”
Right there, the virtuous men spoke to the man: "Bring a well-bred horse harnessed right here!
Its ears are made of gold, its hooves of silver, its breastplate of refined gold from the Jambu river."
“Puṇṇaka, having mounted a horse-drawn carriage,
adorned and with hair and beard trimmed, departed through the air into the sky.
Therein, *āmantayitvā* means “having addressed.”
As he was traveling through the air, he thought: "The wise Vidhura has a great retinue; it is not possible to capture him.
However, Dhanañjaya Koravya is a gambler; having defeated him at dice, I shall take Vidhura.
Moreover, there are many jewels in his house; he will not play for a stake of little value, so [I must bring] a precious jewel."

"It is fitting to take it; the king will not accept any other jewel. In the vicinity of Rājagaha, within the Vepulla Mountain, there is a wheel-turning monarch’s paribhoga-maṇiratana of great power. Let us take that, entice the king with it, and we shall win.
He did exactly so. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Thus he arrived at the most delightful Rājagaha, the city of King Aṅga, difficult to assail;
it abounded in food and drink, like Masakkasāra, the city of Vāsava.
It resounded with the cries of flocks of peacocks and herons, filled with the calls of birds, and frequented by hosts of winged creatures.”
The beautiful mountain peak resounded with the cries of various birds and was strewn with flowers like the Himavat mountain.
Puṇṇaka ascended Mount Vepulla, a mass of rock frequented by kimpurisas;
searching for that sublime jewel, he saw it there in the midst of the mountain peak.
In that context, "of King Aṅga" means that at that time the kingdom of Magadha belonged to King Aṅga himself; therefore it is said, "the city of King Aṅga.
"Hard to withstand" (*durāyuta*) means difficult for enemies to attack. "Like Masakkasāra belongs to Vāsava":
because it was built on the summit of Mount Sineru, which is known as Masakkasāra, it received the name "Masakkasāra."
Like the palace of Vāsava. "Resounding with the cries of birds" means it was filled with the clamor of other winged creatures and made resonant with their calls.
"Made to cry out by various birds" means it was made to resound by various kinds of birds as if they were singing with sweet voices;
the meaning is that it was filled with song. "With a beautiful courtyard" means having a lovely courtyard and a pleasing ground. "Like the Himalaya mountain."
"Like the Himavanta mountain. "He ascended Mount Vepulla," monks—Puṇṇaka thus ascended that Mount Vepulla.
"In the midst of the mountain peak"—he saw that jewel within the mountain peak.
"Having seen the radiant jewel, of noble birth, captivating, a sublime gem of jewels..."
Shining with glory, the glorious one illuminated [the sky] like lightning in the atmosphere.
He took up that precious beryl, named Manohara, which was of great power;
mounting his noble steed, he of mind-made form departed through the air into the sky.
In this context, "captivating" means capable of bringing about the wealth desired by the mind. "Radiant" means shining brightly.
"With glory" means with a multitude of surrounding jewels. "It illuminates" means that jewel shines like lightning in the sky.
"He took it" means he seized that jewel. Now, as for that jewel, it was called Kumbhira.
A *yakkha* surrounded by a thousand *kumbhaṇḍas* guarded it.
But he, having become angry with him, fled in terror at the mere glance [of Puṇṇaka], and reaching the Cakkavāḷa mountain, stood there trembling and looking about.
Thus, having made him flee, Puṇṇaka took the jewel-treasure. "Manohara" means that it brings whatever wealth one has thought of in the mind.
"Sakkoti" means he who has thus acquired that name.
Thus, taking her with him, he traveled through the air and reached that city. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"He arrived at the city of Indapattha, and having descended, he approached the assembly hall of the Kurus."
When one hundred and one kings had assembled together, a *yakkha*, remaining unshaken, challenged them:
“Who here excels as the best among kings? Whom shall we conquer with the prize of wealth?
Which unsurpassed and most excellent jewel shall we win? Or who, indeed, might defeat us with the prize of wealth?”

"Having descended there, he approached the assembly hall of the Kurus," monks, means that Puṇṇaka, having dismounted from the back of his horse and left the horse invisible, approached the assembly hall of the Kurus in the guise of a young brahmin.
"A hundred and one"—meaning a hundred and one kings—challenged him with dice, speaking such words as "Who will play? while remaining undaunted. "Ko nīdha" means "Who here [will play]?"
Who indeed in this assembly of kings—among the kings—is it that surpasses the king?
"He surpasses the best treasure belonging to us," he dares to say, "I am the victor. "Whom shall we surpass?
means, whom among us might we conquer? "By supreme wealth" means by the most excellent riches. And while conquering, whom as the unsurpassed one?
“We shall conquer the King, the unsurpassed, the most excellent jewel, the Victor. Who indeed could defeat us? Or rather, “What king indeed could defeat us with such superior wealth?
Thus, with these four lines, he challenges the King of Kaurava himself.
Then the King, thinking, “Never before have I seen anyone speak with such courage; who might this be? asked him, speaking this verse:
“In what kingdom is your birthplace? This speech of yours is not like that of a Kuru.
You are not afraid of our appearance; tell me your name and your kinsmen.
In this context, “not like that of a Kuru” means that your speech is not like that of one who dwells in the kingdom of the Kurus.
Hearing this, the other thought, "This king is asking for my name, and my name is Puṇṇaka.
If I say, 'I am Puṇṇaka,' he will despise me, thinking, 'He is a slave; that is why he speaks thus out of insolence.
Therefore, I shall tell him my name from my immediately preceding existence. Having reflected thus, he spoke this verse:
“I am a young brahmin named Kaccāyana, O King; they call me by this name which is not deficient.
My kinsmen and relatives are in Aṅga, and I have arrived here by means of a wheel.
In this context, “anūnanāmo” means “not deficient in name. By this, he speaks while concealing his own full name, Puṇṇaka.
“They call me thus” means they call out to and summon me. “In the Aṅgas” means they dwell in the city of Kālacampā in the kingdom of Aṅga.
“By dice, O Lord,” [he says]—O Lord, I have arrived here for the purpose of playing with dice.
Then the king, asking, “Young man, you have been defeated by dice; what will you give? What do you possess? spoke this verse:
“What jewels does this young man have that a dice-player, defeating him, might take away?
The king has many jewels; how can you, being so poor, invite him?
The meaning of this is: “How many jewels does your honor, the young man, possess, which a dice-player, defeating him, might take away?”
Saying, “Bring it,” he would have brought it. But in the king’s palace there were many jewels;
so they said to the kings, “Since you are so wealthy, how is it that you, being poor, are playing with dice?
Then Puṇṇaka spoke this verse:
“This jewel of mine is named Manohara, a magnificent and captivating gem;
and this thoroughbred horse that torments his enemies—having won these, let the dice-player take them.

However, in the manuscript copies of the text, it is written: “A ruby (lohitaṅka) jewel exists for me. But since that jewel was actually a beryl (veḷuriya), therefore this [version] alone is consistent.
In this context, having pointed out the horse and saying, "A gambler might take both of these from me—the thoroughbred and the jewel," he spoke thus.
Having heard that, the king recited this verse:
"O young man, what will one jewel do? And what will one thoroughbred do?"
"The king has many precious gems, and not a few thoroughbred horses swift as the wind.
The Chapter on the Longing is finished.
The Chapter on the Gem.
Having heard the king’s words, he said, “Great King, what are you saying?
One horse is worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and one jewel is worth a hundred thousand. For not all horses are alike;
first, behold his speed! Having spoken thus, he mounted the horse and sent it along the top of the wall for seven yojanas.
The city appeared as if it were surrounded by horses striking neck against neck.
Then, in due course, neither the horse nor the spirit was seen; only a red cloth tied around the belly remained visible.
Having dismounted from the horse, he said, "Great King, you have seen the speed of the horse. When [the King] replied, "Yes, I have seen it," he said, "Now look again!"
Having said, "Great King," he sent the horse into the city, into the park, onto the surface of the water in the lotus pond;
it leaped forth even as its hooves were still touching the ground. Then, after making it walk upon lotus leaves, he clapped his hand and extended his arm;
the horse came and settled upon the palm of his hand. Thereupon [the king thought], "O Lord of Men, such a horse-treasure is indeed fit for you!"
Having said this, when it was replied, "It is fitting," he said, "Great King, let the horse-treasure stand aside for now;
behold rather the great majesty of the jewel-treasure. Proclaiming its power, he said:
"And this jewel-treasure of mine, behold it, O Best of Bipeds!"
"Herein are the forms of women and the forms of men;
here too are the forms of deer and the forms of birds;
see the king of serpents and the garuḍas fashioned upon this gem."

In that context, regarding the phrase "of women": for within this jewel, many forms of women, forms of men, various kinds of herds of beasts and flocks of birds, and military divisions and so forth are perceived. Showing these, he spoke thus.
"Fashioned" means: behold such a marvel fashioned within this gem.
“Look at another thing as well,” he said, and spoke these verses:
“The elephant division, the chariot division, The cavalry and the armored infantry—
Behold this fourfold army fashioned within the jewel.”
“Elephant-riders stationed in the ranks, chariot-fighters, and foot-soldiers—behold the elite forces arrayed, fashioned within the gem.
In this context, *balaggāni* means the very forces themselves. *Viyūḷhāni* means they stand in the form of military arrays (*byūha*).
“Behold the city fashioned upon a jewel— endowed with lofty towers,
many walls and arched gateways, and beautiful grounds at its crossroads.
See also the pillars, the moats, the ditches, and the bolts.”
"And on the watchtowers and at the gates, behold what is fashioned upon the jewel.
In this context, "city" (*pura*) means a town. "Endowed with a rampart" (*uddhāpasampanna*) means possessed of a defensive wall and moat.

"With many walls and arches" (*bahupākāratoraṇa*) means endowed with high walls, arches, and city gates. "Crossroads" (*siṅghāṭaka*) refers to junctions of three or four streets. "Beautiful grounds" (*subhūmiyo*)...
There were various delightful grounds within the precincts of the city. *Esikā* refers to the pillar-standards erected at the city gates.
*Palikhā* means a crossbar; this is also the reading for the word itself. *Aggaḷāni* refers to the door-panels of the city gates. *Dvāre ca* means the gate-towers as well.
"Behold the many flocks of various birds upon the paths of the archways."
“Swans, cranes, and peacocks, ruddy geese and cuckoos,
many variegated kuṇālaka birds, crested shrikes, and pheasants—
see how this place is strewn with flocks of various birds, fashioned upon the jewel.”
Therein, "at the gate-towers" means at the tops of the gate-towers in this city. *Kuṇālaka* refers to the black cuckoo. *Citrā* refers to the variegated-winged cuckoo.
"Behold the city with its well-built ramparts, wonderful and hair-raising;
beautiful, with banners raised aloft, and strewn with golden sand."
“Behold the leaf-huts, partitioned and measured out in their divisions;
the dwellings and residences, the junctions, the enclosures, and the roads.
Therein, “well-fortified” means surrounded by a golden wall. “Leaf-huts” refers to market-stalls filled with various goods.
“Dwellings” (*nivesana*) and “residences” (*nivesa*) refer both to houses and the sites where houses stand.
“Junctions and crossroads” (*sandhi-byūha*) refers to house junctions and unpaved streets. “Roads” (*pathaddhi*) refers to paved streets.
“And taverns and drinking dens, slaughterhouses, and rice-gruel houses;”
See a courtesan and female entertainers fashioned within the gem.
See garland-makers, dyers, perfumers, and cloth-merchants;
see goldsmiths and jewelers fashioned within the gem.
“In the cooks and the stewards, in the actors, dancers, and singers,
in the hand-clappers, the gong-beaters, and in the jewel— behold what is fashioned there. In this context,
“in the drinkers” refers to those at the drinking grounds who are adorned with necklaces and earrings suited to themselves.
When the drunkards have prepared themselves and are seated; *āḷārika* means a maker of pastries; *sūda* means a cook;
*pāṇissara* means one who sings by clapping hands; *kumbhathūnika* means a player of the *daddari* drum shaped like a jar.
“Behold the kettledrums and the small drums, the conchs, the *paṇava* and *indima* drums!”
And see all the percussion instruments fashioned upon the jewel.
See the rhythmic clapping, the lute, the dancing, the singing, and the well-played music;
see the resounding chorus of cymbals and drums fashioned upon the jewel.
“Herein, acrobats and boxers, illusionists and Sobhiyas, corpse-revivers and wrestlers—behold them fashioned within the jewel.
Therein, *sammatālañca* means both the gong made of acacia wood and so forth, and the bronze cymbal (*kaṃsatāla*). *Tūriyatāḷitasaṅghuṭṭhaṃ* means...
Resounding with the beating of various musical instruments. *Muṭṭhika* refers to prize-fighters.
*Sobhiya* refers to women who adorn the city and men of handsome appearance. *Vetālika* refers to those who raise up corpses. *Jalla* refers to barbers who trim the facial hair.
"And there, assemblies proceed, crowded with men and women."
“On couches above couches, on the ground—behold what is fashioned upon the gem!
Therein, “on couches above couches” means on couches fastened atop other couches. “On the ground” refers to delightful grounds for the festival.
“Behold the Mallas at the festival, brandishing their arms twofold!”
“Behold the figures fashioned upon the jewel, both those already defeated and those being defeated.
Therein, “in the arena” means in the wrestling ring. “Defeated” means standing after having been struck down and conquered. “Being defeated” means those who have been vanquished.
“Behold, at the foot of the mountains, the many multitudes of various wild beasts.”
Lions, tigers, and boars, bears, hyenas, and leopards;
"Palāsādas, gavajas, buffaloes, rohit deer, ruru deer;
eneyya deer, boars, herds of nīkas and wild pigs."
“Many variegated *kadalī* deer, wildcats, hares, and thorny animals—behold, O Maṇi, how this place is strewn with various herds of beasts, all fashioned [therein].
In this context, *palāsādā* refers to rhinoceroses (*khaggamiga*). There is also a reading, *palatā*. *Gavajā* refers to gayals (*gavaya*). *Varāhā* refers to a certain species of deer.
Likewise, there were herds of cattle and wild boars. "Many variegated" means deer of various kinds. "Cats" refers to wild cats of the forest.
"Hares and thorny plants" refers to hares and thorny shrubs. "The rivers have well-established banks, strewn with golden sand."
“Clear waters flow there, frequented by schools of fish.
‘Crocodiles and sea-monsters dwell there,
as do dolphins, turtles, pāṭhīna fish, pāvusa fish, balaja fish, and muñca-rohitā fish.’”

In that context, "rivers" (*najjā*) refers to streams. "Strewn with golden sand" means having surfaces covered with golden sand. "Crocodiles" (*kumbhīla*) refers to such aquatic creatures that roam within the rivers;
"see them too in the gem. "See in the gem the construction of rivers whose banks are made of beryl, crowded with flocks of various birds and filled with various groves of trees."
In that regard, "making sounds like striking beryl stones" means that such sounds are produced by those [women] in the river.
"Behold the lotus ponds, well-apportioned in the four directions;
crowded with flocks of various birds and frequented by many kinds of aquatic creatures."
“Behold this earth, encircled by the ocean as its earrings, endowed with all waters on every side, and adorned with rows of forests, fashioned out of jewels.
In this context, “frequented by large fish” means inhabited by great sea-monsters. “With rows of forests” means with ranges of forests; or rather, this very reading [“vanarājehi”] is the correct one.
“Behold, Videha, the Puratō in front, and the Goyāniya behind;
behold the Kurus and Jambudīpa fashioned upon this gem.
Behold the moon and the sun illuminating the four quarters.”
Behold what is fashioned upon the jewel as it encircles Sineru:
"Behold Sineru and the Himavat, the ocean and the surface of the earth,
and the four Great Kings— all fashioned upon the jewel."
“In groves and forest thickets, on plateaus and rocky crags,
in delightful places teeming with *kimpurisa* spirits— behold what is fashioned upon the jewel.
[Therein are] the Phārusaka, Cittalata, Missaka, and Nandana groves.”
And see the Vejayanta palace fashioned within the gem.
See Sudhamma and the Tāvatiṃsa assembly hall, and the blossoming Pāricchattaka tree;
see Erāvaṇa, the king of nāgas, fashioned within the gem.
“Behold these celestial maidens, rising like lightning from the sky;
see them wandering in the Nandana grove, fashioned within this jewel.
Behold these celestial maidens, who entice the sons of the gods.”
“Behold the sons of the gods sporting, fashioned upon the jewel.
In this context, *videha* refers to the continent of Pubbavideha; *goyānīya* refers to the continent of Aparagoyāna;
and *kuru* refers both to Uttarakuru and to Jambudīpa in the south. *Anupariyanta* means these two, the moon and the sun, as they revolve around Sineru.
*Pāṭiyeti*: like on a back-slab (*piṭṭhipāsāṇa*) that has been spread out and set down.
“In a palace of more than a thousand [pillars], strewn with beryl fruit, and blazing in color—behold what is fashioned upon the gem.”
“In the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, in Yāma, and also in Tusita and Nimmāna;
in Paranimmitavasavatti, behold the one fashioned upon the jewel.
Behold there the lotus ponds, with their clear and pure water.”
“Covered with mandārava flowers and with lotuses and water-lilies.
Therein, “more than a thousand” means more than a thousand palaces in the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
“Therein, ten rows are white, ten blue and delightful;”
Six were tawny, fifteen were turmeric-colored, and fourteen were yellow.
Therein, twenty were made of gold and twenty of silver;
thirty more appeared with the luster of indragopaka insects.
“Ten there were Kāḷiyas, six Mañjeṭṭhās,
and twenty-five mixed with Bandhuka flowers, variegated with blue lotuses.
Thus, endowed with every limb, radiant and luminous— ”
"Behold, O Great King, the price of this jewel, O Best of Bipeds!
In that passage, "ten white lines here" means there are ten white streaks on this cluster of jewels.
"Sixteen brown" means six and fifteen, totaling twenty-one brown streaks. "Turmeric-colored" means fourteen streaks of the color of turmeric.
"Thirty" means thirty streaks with the color of the *indagopaka* insect. "Ten and six" means sixteen dark streaks.
"Twenty-five" means twenty-five brilliant streaks of the color of *mañjeṭṭha*. "Mixed with *bandhuka* flowers" means look at these mixed and variegated streaks of dark and *mañjeṭṭha* colors;
for here the dark streaks are mixed with *bandhujīvaka* flowers, and the *mañjeṭṭha* streaks [are mixed with others].
It was variegated with blue lotuses. *Odhisuṅkaṃ* means a portion of the tax.
He says, "Whoever defeats me at dice, let him look upon this portion of the tax. In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, there is also the reading:
"Let there be the tax, O Great King. Its meaning is: "O Best of Bipeds, behold this such-like mass of jewels; this very thing, O Great King," [is the tax].
"Let there be a wager: 'Whoever defeats me at dice, this [treasure] shall belong to him.
The Chapter on the Jewel-Necklace is finished.
The Chapter on the Dice.
Having spoken thus, Puṇṇaka said, "Great King, as for me, having been defeated at dice, I shall give this jewel-treasure; but what will you give?
"My dear," he replied, "with the exception of my own body, the queen, and the white parasol, let all else that belongs to me be the stake.
"In that case, Your Majesty, do not delay; I have come from afar, so let us go quickly to the gambling hall."

“Have it prepared! the king commanded his ministers. They quickly prepared the gaming hall, spread out the king’s choice carpet, arranged seats for the other kings, and having prepared a fitting seat for Puṇṇaka as well, they announced the time to the king.
Then Puṇṇaka addressed the king with a verse:
“O King, come and approach the stake; you do not possess such a jewel-treasure as this.
We shall win by righteousness and without violence; and if we have won, pay us quickly! The meaning of this is:
Great King, the work at the gambling hall has been completed and brought to an end; such a jewel-treasure as this [is yours].
"It is yours; do not make excuses. Come, cast the die and approach the place of play.
While we play, may we win according to the rules; let our victory be by fair means alone, not through violence.
But if you should be defeated, then pay us back quickly; do not make excuses—you must give the won wealth," this is what was said.
Then the king said to him, "Young man, do not fear me, thinking 'he is the king'; victory and defeat shall be determined by righteousness alone, not by force.
Hearing this, Puṇṇaka, declaring that they should know the matter of victory and defeat to be decided by righteousness alone, spoke this verse while making those kings his witnesses:
“Let the Pañcālas, the Sūrasenas, the Macchas, the Maddas, together with the Kekakas, behold this battle fought by one who is not deceitful;
let them see that we do nothing in their assembly.
Therein, “the Pañcālas” refers specifically to the kings of the Pañcālas because they are eminent, renowned, and well-known. “The Macchas”...
"And you too, dear King Macchara. "Madda" refers to the King of Madda. "Together with the Kekakas" means together with the King of the Kekakas, who resides in the country named Kekaka;

and you too. Alternatively, by placing the word "saha" (together with) after the term "Kekakebhi," and making the word "paccuggata" (welcoming) an adjective qualifying "Sūrasena," [the compound] becomes "Pañcāla-paccuggata-Sūrasena."
The meaning here should be understood as follows: "The fish, the frogs, and the peacocks, along with the other kings. "Let them see us" means:
"let these kings see this honest dice-game of ours. Regarding the phrase "they do nothing in the assembly," here *no* is a mere particle;
they do not fail to appoint some witness in the assembly.
“They do so among both kṣatriyas and brahmins; therefore, if any groundless matter arises, you will not be permitted to say, ‘We have not heard it, we have not seen it. Be heedful!
Thus the general of the yakkhas made the kings his witnesses. Then the king, surrounded by one hundred kings and taking Puṇṇaka with him, [departed].
He entered the gambling hall. Everyone sat down in suitable seats, and they placed golden dice upon silver boards.
Puṇṇaka, in great haste, said: "Great King, as for the 'advantages' (āya) on the dice, there are twenty-four, beginning with Mālika, Sāvaṭṭa, Bahula, Santibhadra, and so forth;
from among these, please choose whichever advantage you prefer. The king said, "Very well," and chose the Bahula.
He took his turn. Puṇṇaka took his turn. Then the king said to him, "In that case, young man, cast the dice first.
When he replied, "Great King, it is not yet my turn; you should cast them first," the king consented, saying, "Very well.
Now, in his third previous existence, there had been a protective deity who was his mother; by her power—
The king was playing at dice. She stood not far from him. Recalling the daughter of the gods, the king sang this gambling song and spoke these verses:
“All rivers have a winding course; all forests consist of wood.”
"All women commit evil when they obtain a husband.
"Then let my mother see me, O Mother; let victory be seen for me.
Have compassion for me, O Mother; may she grant me great victory."
“O deity, protect me today, O goddess! See that no one may perceive me.
You are compassionate and a firm support; look upon my blessings to guard me.
[I see] a noose made of Jambū-river gold, four-cornered and eight finger-breadths wide.”
“You shine in the midst of the assembly, O Lord who grants all desires!
‘O deity, grant me victory; see how I am one who has no share [of merit].
A person who is compassionate toward his mother always beholds auspicious things.’”
“Eight is said to be *mālika*; six is considered *sāvaṭṭa*;
four is to be known as *bahula*, along with *dvibindu*, *santi*, and *bhadra*.
These twenty-four *āyās* were proclaimed by the Lord of Sages.”
Having thus sung the song of dice, the king turned the dice over in his hand and threw them into the air.
By the supernatural power of Puṇṇaka, the dice were destined to fall for the king’s defeat.

Recognizing that the dice were falling for his own defeat due to his extreme skill in the art of gambling, the king gathered them while they were still in the air, caught them, and threw them back into the air once more.
Knowing that he was losing for a second time as well, the king took the dice in exactly the same way. Then Puṇṇaka thought:
"This king, while playing dice with a yakkha such as myself, gathers up the dice as they fall;
what could be the reason for this? Observing him, he recognized the power of the deity who protected him.
Opening his eyes, he looked at her as if enraged. Terrified and trembling, she fled until she reached the summit of the Cakkavāḷa mountain;

standing there, she looked back and remained still. The king threw the dice for a third time, and although he knew he was losing, he was unable to reach out his hand and seize them due to Puṇṇaka’s supernatural power. To the king—

They fell into defeat. Then, knowing that he had been defeated, Puṇṇaka clapped his hands and, with a great sound, let out a lion’s roar three times, crying, "I have won! That sound pervaded the whole of Jambudīpa.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Intoxicated by the pride of their skill, they entered—King [Dhananjaya] of the Kurus and the yakkha Puṇṇaka as well.
King Kali took up the dice, while the yakkha named Puṇṇaka took up the leather bag.
There, both of them gathered together for the game of dice in the presence of the kings and in the midst of their friends.”
“Ajeṣi the yakkha [defeated] the best of men; there a tumultuous clamor arose.
In that context, “they entered” means they entered the gambling hall. “He chose” means the king, while choosing among twenty-four throws, took the losing throw (*kali*).
“He took the stake” means the yakkha named Puṇṇaka took the winning throw (*jaya*).
"Those two having come together there in the game" means that those two, having met there in the gambling match, played the game together.

"Of the king" means that then, in the presence of those one hundred and one kings and among his remaining friends, that *yakkha* defeated the king, the best of men-heroes. "A tumultuous roar arose there" refers to that circle of gamblers.
“A great clamor arose: ‘Know that the king has been defeated! Victory is mine! Victory is mine!
The defeated king was displeased. Then Puṇṇaka, comforting him, spoke this verse:
‘Victory and defeat, O Great King, belong to one of those who engage in combat.’”
“O Lord, you have lived [your life] with supreme wealth;
having been defeated by me, quickly restore it!”—in this regard, *āyūhati* means that when two people are striving, the result belongs to only one of them; therefore, do not think, “I am defeated.
*Jīnosi* means you have lost. *Varaddhanena* means by means of supreme wealth. *Khippamavākarohī* means “quickly restore [it].”
"Quickly give me victory and wealth!
Then the king, saying to him, "Take it, dear one," spoke this verse:
"Elephants, cattle, horses, jewels, and earrings, and whatever treasure I possess upon the earth;"
“Take, Kaccāna, a boon of wealth; having taken it, go wherever you wish.
Puṇṇaka said:
“Elephants, cattle, horses, jewels, and earrings, and whatever treasure you have upon the earth—”
“Their chief was named Vidhura, the maker; he has been won by me, and he shall be mine.

Regarding this, “He has been won by me, and he shall be mine”: for I have won the supreme jewel in your kingdom, and that Vidhura is the best of all jewels; therefore, O King, he is said to be won by me—give him to me!
The king said:
“He is my own self, my refuge, and my destination; he is my island, my shelter, and my final resort.
He is not to be weighed against my wealth, for he is the one who made me equal even to his own life.
In this context, “He is my own self” means he is my very self; and by me [thinking], “Setting aside myself, I shall give the rest,” [he was given].
It has been said; therefore, do not accept that [view]. Not only is it the self, but furthermore, he is my refuge, my destination, my island, my shelter, and my ultimate resort.
"He is not to be weighed against my wealth" means he is not to be compared with the sevenfold treasure.
Puṇṇaka said:
"Long has been the dispute between you and me; let us go to him and ask him as we wish.
Let him alone explain this matter to us; let there be an end to the debate between the two of us."

In that context, "let him explain this matter" means: "let him himself reveal this matter: 'Is that your self, or is it not? "Let the discussion be between us both" means: let whatever he says be the discussion between us both; let that be the authority—this is the meaning. The King said:
"Truly you speak the truth, and there is no rashness on your part, young man."
"Let us go to him and ask; by that we both shall be satisfied.
Therein, "O young man, do not speak rashly" means you do not speak a forceful or impulsive word against me.
Having said this, the king, taking the hundred and one kings along with Puṇṇaka, went with a joyful mind in haste to the Dhamma Hall.
He arrived. The wise man also descended from his seat, paid homage to the king, and stood to one side.

Then Puṇṇaka addressed the Great Being, saying: "Wise man, the fame that 'you do not speak a lie even for the sake of your life because you are established in the Dhamma' has spread throughout the whole world;
today, however, I shall know whether you are truly established in the Dhamma. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Is it true that the gods appointed for the Kurus a minister named Vidhura who stands firm in the Dhamma?
Are you a servant of the king, or are you his kinsman? By what means did you come to be known as ‘Vidhura’ in the world?
In this context, “Is it true that the gods appointed for the Kurus a minister named Vidhura who stands firm in the Dhamma? refers to the Kurus.
“In the kingdom, there was a minister named Vidhura who stood firm in the Dhamma and would not speak a falsehood even for the sake of his life.
Thus do the gods proclaim, declare, and explain; as they thus proclaim, do those gods speak the truth, or are they merely speakers of what is false?
Regarding the phrase “Vidhura was known in the world”—what is this designation “Vidhura”? It is that which belongs to you [as such].
