“In the world, there is reckoning and designation; what was that [designation] for you? Explain it:
were you of a lower birth than the king’s slave, or were you equal, or even superior to him as a kinsman? First tell me this: were you the king’s slave, or were you his kinsman?
Then the Great Being thought, “He asks me this; however, I must say to him, ‘As the king’s kinsman... [and so forth].
Thinking, "I can convince him that I am neither superior nor even of any account to the king;
nevertheless, in this world there is no refuge equal to truth, so it is right to speak only the truth," he spoke two verses to show:
"Young man, I am neither the king’s kinsman, nor his superior, but rather one of his four slaves."
“Some become slaves by birthright, some become slaves purchased with wealth;
some even enter into slavery of their own accord, and some become slaves driven by fear.
These are the four kinds of slaves among men; indeed, by my very birth, I too am a slave.”
“Whether there be existence for the king or non-existence for the king, I am the slave of the lord, even having gone to the next world.
O young man, let him give me to you according to the Dhamma.
In this context, “born-slaves” refers to those born from the womb of a female slave. “Some themselves also go as slaves” refers to whoever [are such].
Those who are of the nature of attendants—all of them, having themselves entered into the state of servitude, are called slaves.

"Driven away by fear" means that even those who, driven from their own dwelling place by fear of kings or fear of thieves, have become fugitives and gone to another territory, are still indeed called slaves.
"For surely, young man, I too am born from a womb"—in this one respect alone, I too [am included] among the four wombs of slaves.

"On one side, I am a slave born from the womb of a slave. Whether there be prosperity or lack of prosperity for the king—whether the king’s fortune increases or diminishes—it is not possible for me to speak a falsehood.
'Even further,' means that even if I were to go far away, I would still be the king's slave.
'He might give' means that if the king were to divide my winnings and give them to you, he would give them according to what is right and by his own nature."
Having heard that, Puṇṇaka, delighted and joyful, clapped his hands again and spoke this verse:
“This is my second victory today, for when asked, the questioner has indeed revealed the answer.
Alas, this best of kings is truly unrighteous, for he does not acknowledge my well-spoken words!”
In this context, "this best of kings" refers to this king who is indeed of unrighteous form.
"Well-spoken" means it was well-delivered and well-judged by the wise Vidhura. "Why do you not grant it to me?"—he says this now, asking: "Why do you not grant this to me, the wise Vidhura?
For what purpose do you not teach it?"
Hearing this, the king became displeased and, thinking, "Without looking at one like me who bestows honor,
he now looks instead at this mere boy he has seen," he grew angry with the Great Being and said, "Boy, if that man were my slave,
take him and go! Having spoken thus, he uttered this verse:
“If he were to answer our question thus: ‘I am your slave, and not your kinsman;
take, Kaccāna, a boon of wealth and go wherever you wish,’ then [you would have succeeded].
In this context, “If he were to answer our question thus” means: if he were to answer our question, “I am your slave, and not... [kinsman]...”
"And I am your kinsman"—thus he spoke here within this circle of the assembly. "Now, why do you remain?
This is the best of all riches in the entire world; take it! And having taken it, go wherever you wish.
The Chapter on the Shoulder-Joint is finished.
The Questions on the Householder’s Life.
Having spoken thus, the king thought: “Once the wise man has been taken away, the young brahmin will go wherever he pleases;
from the moment he departs, sweet discourses on the Dhamma will become difficult for me to obtain. What if I were now—”
“Having established him in his own place and having seated him upon the decorated Dhamma-throne, I shall ask him the question regarding household life.
Then the king said to him: “O wise one, in your absence, sweet Dhamma-talk will be difficult for me to obtain;
therefore, having seated him upon the decorated Dhamma-throne and established him in his own place, [ask] me the question regarding household life.”
"Please speak. Having consented with "Very well," he sat upon the decorated Dharma-seat and, being questioned by the king, answered the question. This is the question:
"O Vidhura, for a householder living in his own home..."
“What would his peaceful livelihood be? How indeed would there be his gathering [of provisions]?
How would he be free from affliction? And how, as a youth who speaks the truth, would he not grieve when passing from this world to the next?”
In that regard, how might there be a secure livelihood? How might there be a secure and fearless livelihood for a householder living in the household life?
How indeed would he have the fourfold means of integration known as the *saṅgahavatthu*?
"Harmlessness" (*abyābajjha*) means freedom from suffering. And "one who speaks the truth"—how indeed [would this apply] to the young man?
"One should be a speaker of truth. "Having passed away" means having gone to the other world.
Having heard that, the wise man explained the king's question. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"There, one who possesses understanding, fortitude, intelligence, and insight into what is beneficial..."
Having analyzed all phenomena, Vidhura spoke thus:
"One should not have a wife held in common with others, nor eat delicious food alone;
one should not pursue worldly philosophy, for that does not increase wisdom."
“Virtuous, perfected in conduct, heedful and discerning;
humble in behavior, free from arrogance, gentle, sociable, and mild.
A gatherer of friends, sharing with others, and possessed of order.”
One should always satisfy the ascetics and brahmins with food and drink.
One should be a lover of the Dhamma, a retainer of what has been heard, and an inquirer;
one should respectfully attend upon those who are virtuous and learned.
“For a householder living in his own home,
his livelihood may be secure in this way, and thus there may be his support.
In this way, too, he would be free from harm, being a youth who speaks the truth.”
“From this world to the next world, thus having passed away, he does not grieve.
In that context, “him there,” O monks, means: him—the king—there in the Dhamma assembly; one who has reached the destination by means of the course of knowledge;
one who is steadfast through unflagging energy; one who possesses intelligence through vast and abundant wisdom; and one who perceives the subtle and refined meaning.

Through knowledge, he was one who saw the goal; having delimited and understood all phenomena by means of wisdom—which is defined as the knowledge of discernment—the wise Vidhura spoke these words beginning with, "She is not a common wife.
In this context, one who commits adultery with the wives of others is called a "common wife" (sādhāraṇadāra); such a person he should not be. "He shall not eat delicious food alone."
One should not eat delicious, choice food alone without giving some to others. Regarding the "Lokāyatika" (materialist):
one should not frequent the Lokāyatika doctrine, which is based on what is unbeneficial, does not provide the path to heaven, is not conducive to liberation, and consists of frivolous debate.
"This does not increase wisdom": for this Lokāyatika teaching does not lead to the growth of wisdom. "Virtuous": with unbroken [precepts]...
Endowed with the five moral precepts (*pañcasīla*). "Perfect in conduct" (*vattasampanno*) means endowed with either the conduct of a householder or the conduct of a king.

"Diligent" (*appamatto*) means diligent regarding wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). "Humble in behavior" (*nivātavuttī*) means one who does not act with excessive pride, but behaves modestly and accepts instruction and admonition.
"Free from stubbornness" (*atthaddho*) means devoid of the stubbornness of stinginess. "Gentle" (*surato*) means endowed with amiability (*soracca*). "Kindly disposed" (*sakhilo*)...
He is one whose speech is pleasant. "Gentle" means he is not harsh in body, speech, or mind.
"A gatherer of friends" means he is one who gathers virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitta*). He is a gatherer by whatever means—such as giving and so forth—that a person desires to be gathered.
"One who shares" refers to sharing with righteous recluses and brahmins, as well as with the poor, the destitute, mendicants, beggars, and so forth.

One who shares [in abundance]. Regarding "one who knows the proper method": it means being endowed with the knowledge of the proper method for all tasks, such as thinking, "It is appropriate to plow at this time; it is appropriate to sow at this time.
"He would satisfy" means that by filling and giving away whatever vessels he has taken, he would satisfy them.
"One who desires the Dhamma" means one who desires and aspires to both the traditional lineage-Dhamma and the Dhamma of good conduct.
"Sutādhāro" means one who serves as a receptacle for what has been heard.
"Paripucchako" means one whose habit is to approach righteous recluses and brahmins and inquire with such words as, "Venerable sir, what is wholesome? and so forth. "Sakkaccaṃ" means with reverence.
"Evaṃ nu assa saṅgaho" means that his gathering [of people] would indeed be accomplished in this manner. "Saccavādī" refers to one who has practiced in just this way.
"He may indeed be called one who speaks the truth.

Thus the Great Being, having explained the question on the household life to the king, descended from his cross-legged seat and paid homage to the king. The king, having rendered him great honor, returned to his own residence surrounded by one hundred and one kings.
The Questions on the Household Life are concluded.
In the Chapter on Characteristics, the Great Being turned back. Then Puṇṇaka said to him:
"Come now, let us go; he has been given to me by my master."
"Follow this purpose of mine; this is the eternal Dhamma.
In this context, *dinno* means "given"; here *no* is merely a particle. The sense is: "You have been given to me by the Lord (*Issara*). As for the word *sanantano*:
by following this purpose of mine, you indeed follow the purpose of your own master. And as for this...
“Carrying out the master’s business—this is the eternal law, the very nature of the ancient wise ones.
The wise Vidhura said:
“I know you, young man; I have been given to you by my lord.”
"And let us keep you in our home for three days, so that we may now instruct our son.
In this context, "I am yours" means "I know that I have been obtained by you," and one who is obtained is not obtained in any other way.
"I am given to you by my lord" means "I have been given to you by my lord, the King. And "for three days," O young man—
"I have been of great benefit to you; I spoke only the truth without looking to please the king, and for that reason I have been won by you.
You should recognize my great virtue. Let us dwell in our own home for three days;
therefore, please consent to whatever time it takes for us to settle matters regarding our children and wife."
Having heard this, Puṇṇaka thought, “The wise man speaks truly; he is very helpful to me. When it is said, ‘Sit for seven days or even half a month,’ it must certainly be consented to.
Having reflected thus, he spoke this verse: “Let it be so for me; let us dwell together for three days. Perform today the duties of the household;
instruct your sons and wife today, so that you may be happy after passing away.”
In this regard, "that which belongs to me" means: may all that you say regarding me be so. "O Lord, from today onward, may you instruct us for three days.
"And after you have passed away" means: may he instruct us in such a way that, after you have gone, your sons and wife may live happily.
Having spoken thus, Puṇṇaka entered his residence together with the Great Being. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Saying ‘Very well,’ the Yakkha, full of desire, departed with Vidhura;
that best of nobles entered the inner palace, which was frequented by noble elephants and fine horses.”

In this context, "one who has abundant desires" means one who possesses great wealth. "Traversed by elephants and noble steeds" means it was fully supplied with and frequented by both elephants and thoroughbred horses.
"The noblest of the noble" refers to the *yakkha* Puṇṇaka, the most excellent among those who are noble in conduct; he entered the wise man’s inner palace.

Furthermore, for the Great Being, there were three palaces intended for the three seasons. One was named Koñca, another Mayūra, and the third Piyaketa. It is with reference to these that this verse was spoken:
“He approached Koñca, Mayūra, and Piya-keta, that most delightful palace there;
it was abundant in food and drink, like Masakkasāra to Vāsava.
Regarding this, “there, there” means: among those three palaces, he approached whichever one was his own residence at that time—that most delightful palace—taking Puṇṇaka with him.
Having approached him, they prepared the bedchamber and the great terrace on the seventh floor of the decorated palace;

having spread out the royal couch and provided every kind of food, drink, and service, they presented five hundred women like celestial nymphs, saying, "Let these be your attendants at your feet; dwell here without longing for anything else."
Having handed him over, he went to his own dwelling place.
When he had departed, those women took up various musical instruments and began dancing and other performances as an offering to Puṇṇaka. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“There they dance and sing, calling out ‘Excellent! Excellent!’”
“Like celestial nymphs among the gods, women fully adorned.
Therein, they call out, “Choose the best from the best,” as they perform dance and song and summon him.
“Having provided the Yakkha with beautiful women, Dhammapāla [provided him] with food and drink.”
Reflecting upon that very purpose, he then approached his wife.

In this context, *pamadāhi* means being provided with both women and food and drink. *Dhammapālo* means a protector and guardian of the Dhamma. *Atthatthamevā* means the very purpose that constitutes the goal. *Bhariyāyā* refers to his eldest wife.
“Him, who was anointed with the fragrance and essence of sandalwood, resembling refined gold, Jāmbunada gold, and precious gems;”
He spoke to his wife: "Come, my lady, listen! Summon your sons, O tawny-eyed one!
Therein, "spoke to his wife" means he addressed his eldest wife. "Summon" means call out.
Having heard her husband's words, she who was not disobedient spoke to her daughter-in-law, the tawny-nailed and fair-eyed one:
“‘Address my sons, who wear beautiful garments, O lady, they who resemble blue lotus flowers.
In this context, *anujjā* is her name. Regarding the words “the daughter-in-law with copper-colored nails and beautiful eyes”:
having heard his speech, she, with a tearful face and weeping, thought, “It is not proper for me to go myself to summon my sons; I shall send the daughter-in-law. To her—
Having gone to his dwelling place, he spoke to his daughter-in-law Sunettā, who had copper-colored nails:
"O wearer of armor" (*vammadharānī*)—meaning, O wearer of armor, O brave one; or alternatively, here "armor" (*vamma*) is intended to mean ornaments, so the meaning is "O bearer of ornaments.
He addresses her by that name. "My sons" refers to both my sons and daughters. "O you who are as dark as the *indīvara* flower"—with this he addresses her.

Having accepted this with the words, “Very well,” she descended from the palace and, after wandering about, she gathered together all his well-wishing people, sons, and daughters, saying, “Your father wishes to give you his final exhortation;
this, they say, is his last sight of you. But Prince Dhammapāla, upon hearing those words, began to weep, surrounded by his group of younger brothers.
He went into the presence of his father. Upon seeing him, the wise man was unable to maintain his composure;
with eyes filled with tears, he embraced him, kissed him on the head, and for a moment laid his eldest son upon his heart.
Having drawn him close to his own heart, he emerged from the inner chamber and sat cross-legged in the center of the great hall before his thousand sons.
He gave him this advice. To clarify that matter, the Teacher said:
“When they had arrived, Dhammapāla, without wavering, kissed his sons on the head;
then, having addressed them, he spoke these words: ‘I have been given here by the king to this young man.’”
“Therefore, being devoted to my own happiness, I shall take [the people] and go wherever I wish.
And since I have come here to instruct you, how could I depart without protecting you?
If the King of the Kuru kingdom, the leader of the people who dwell there, should ask you what he desires so much—”
"What do you recognize as ancient, what did your father do of old?
'All of you should sit down together with me; who here is a person of lower status than the king?
Paying him homage with joined palms, speak thus: "Do not say this, O King, for this is not the way of Dhamma. "
"O King, how could one of low birth be seated on the same seat as the Tiger King?
In this context, "Dhammapāla" refers to the Great Being. "I am given" means that I have been bestowed by the king after he had divided his winnings.
"From today onwards, for three days, I shall be happy and obedient to him" means that starting from this day, for a period of three days, I shall be content with this happiness of my own.
I am happy for myself; however, beyond that, I have become subject to the will of that young man. For on the fourth day from now, he will certainly take me and go wherever he wishes.
I have come to instruct you, asking: "How could he go without providing protection for you?
"Janasaṃdhā" means the binding of friends through friendship with one's circle of friends.
He is a maker of connections. "In the past, what ancient cause do you remember?
means: he instructs. Thus, being questioned by the king, you should say: "Our father gave us this and that advice. "Be concise" means:
if, at the time I am giving you the advice, the king says to you, "Come now, you..."
“Sit on the same seat as me; for in this royal court, who else is a person more intimate to the king than you?
He would then have you sit upon his own seat. Then, having joined your palms in reverence, you should say to that king:
“Sire, do not speak thus. For this is not our ancestral custom. One of low birth [cannot sit] with a tiger-king or a maned lion.”
“O King, how could a jackal be the equal seat of a lion? Just as a jackal is not the equal seat of a lion, so too are we to you.

Upon hearing these words, his sons and daughters, kinsmen and friends, and his slaves, laborers, and servants—all of them unable to maintain their composure—let out a great cry. The Great Being reassured them.
The Section on Characteristics is finished.
The Section on Living with Kings:
Then the wise man, having approached his sons, daughters, and kinsmen, and seeing them standing silent, said, "Sirs, do not..."
He thought: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; fame indeed ends in misfortune.
Nevertheless, I shall tell you the means for attaining fame, known as 'Royal Residence'; listen with one-pointed minds. Thus, with the grace of a Buddha, he began the discourse on "Royal Residence.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
Then Vidhura, his mind free from attachment and his thoughts composed, spoke thus to his sons, ministers, kinsmen, and dear friends:
“Come, noble sirs, enter the royal residence and sit down; listen to me.”
"Just as a person who has entered a royal court attains glory.
In this context, "suhadajjana" means "among those of good heart. "Ethayyo" is "come, sir. He addresses his sons with an expression of affection.
"Rājavasatiṃ" means "listen to the service of a king as it is being described by me. "Yathā" means "by which reason" [one enters] the royal court.
The meaning is: "Listen to the reason why a person who has reached the presence [of the king], one who moves about in the vicinity of a king, attains and receives glory:
'Indeed, one who has reached the royal court does not receive glory if he is unknown;
nor if he is not a hero, nor if he is dull-witted, nor if he is ever heedless.'"
“When one attains virtue, wisdom, and purity, then one trusts me, and does not conceal secrets from me.
In this context, “unknown” means one whose virtues are not manifest and whose deeds and reputation are not known. “Not a coward” means not being of a timid or fearful nature.
"When he knows his virtue" means when the king comes to know the virtue, wisdom, and purity of that servant;
when he recognizes his excellence in conduct, the power of his knowledge, and his state of cleanliness.
"Then he trusts in him" means then the king places his trust in him and does not conceal or hide his own secrets from him.
“As a balance-beam held up straight, well-balanced and properly maintained,
so one who, when questioned, does not waver, may dwell in the king’s service.
As a balance-beam held up straight, well-balanced and properly maintained...”
“Overcoming all [obstacles], he shall dwell in the king’s service.

In this context, “just as the scale” means: just as this aforementioned scale neither sinks nor rises, even so a royal servant, when requested and commanded by the king regarding some task, saying, “Do this,” does not act according to the influence of desire and the other [unwholesome] courses.
He should not waver; in all duties he should remain balanced like a well-balanced scale.
"He would dwell in the king's service" means that such a servant might live in the royal household and attend upon the king;
the meaning is that by attending in this manner, he would obtain glory. "Overcoming all" means performing all the king’s duties.
Whether by day or by night, when summoned for royal affairs, a wise man should not waver;
such a person may dwell in the king’s service.
Whether by day or by night, when summoned for royal affairs, a wise man...
Overcoming all [obstacles], he dwells in the king’s service.
Even on that well-prepared path, so well-laid out for the king, he should not go when told to do so; he dwells in the king’s service.
In that regard, "he should not waver" means he should perform those duties without wavering. And as for "he who":
even if told, "Go by this path," he should not go by that royal highway which is well-prepared, well-laid out, and well-adorned.
"I shall never eat like the king, nor ever enjoy sensual pleasures."
One should always walk behind [the king] and live under the king’s authority.
One should not wear clothing like the king’s, nor garlands, nor ointments;
one should not adopt the king’s manner of dress or his deportment.
“He might adopt another deportment; he would live under the king’s authority.
In this context, “not like the king” means that he should not enjoy sensual pleasures in the same manner as the king enjoys them; for the king becomes angry with one such as that.
“In all respects” means that among all the strands of sensual pleasure, such as forms and so forth, he should follow after the king, being indeed inferior to him.
The meaning is "he should serve. "He should act otherwise" means he should adopt a different manner of conduct from that of the king's own appearance and demeanor.
"The king plays with his ministers, surrounded by his wives;
but a wise minister should not harbor improper feelings toward the king's wives."
“Unagitated and not fickle, prudent and with restrained faculties, endowed with a resolute intention of mind—he may dwell in the king’s service.
In this context, *bhāva* means intention by way of trust. *Acapala* means one whose nature is not frivolous. *Nipaka* means one whose knowledge is fully matured.
"With restrained faculties" means one whose six sense-faculties are covered; he would not look at the limbs or members of a king, nor at his harem.
"Endowed with mental resolve" means being possessed of a mind that is steady and well-established.
"He should not sport with his wives, nor should he consult with them in secret."
He should not seize the wealth from his treasury; he should live under the king's authority.
He should not prize sleep excessively, nor drink liquor for intoxication;
he should not hunt deer in the forest; he should live under the king's authority.
“He who thinks, ‘I am highly esteemed,’ should not mount a throne, a couch, a chair, a boat, or a chariot;
such a person may dwell in the royal residence.
Being discerning, he should keep neither too far from the king nor too close.”
Even if one were to stand directly before him, visible to his master,
a king is truly neither a friend nor does he engage in intimacy;
kings become angry quickly, like an eye struck by a thorn.
“A wise and intelligent man, considering himself not honored,
should not speak harshly to a king when in his assembly.
In this context, “he should not speak” means that he should neither play nor converse in private with the wives of that king.
"The king's treasury is his wealth": one should not take wealth by stealing from the king's treasury. "Not for intoxication":
dear ones, a royal servant should not drink liquor for the sake of intoxication. "He should not kill the deer in his preserve": he should not kill the deer that have been granted safety by the king.
"A couch" means a fine seat. "'I am authorized'": thinking "I do this because I am authorized," one should not act [in such a way].
He would climb up. "He would stand before him" means he would stand in front of that king in a place where small or large conversations are being heard.
"Appearing in the sight of his master" means that whatever royal servant stands in a place where his master can see him.
"By a speck" means just as an eye irritated by a speck of rice or the like fallen into it abandons its natural state; so too...
"He becomes angry" means they become angry in this way; one should not place trust in them. "Thinking himself honored" means thinking, "I am honored by the king.
"One should not speak harshly to him" means one should not speak in such a manner that he would become angry.
"Having gained access, one may gain further access, but one should never place trust in kings."
Like a fire, he should remain self-restrained while living in the king’s service.
A nobleman may seize a son or a brother,
[taking them away] from villages or towns, from kingdoms or provinces.
"One should remain silent and equanimous; one should not speak cleverly or wickedly.
In this context, "one who has gained entrance should gain entrance" means that one who has gained entrance without opposition should not enter without having opposed [the request];
rather, one should enter only after having opposed it, so that one may gain entrance once again—this is the meaning. "Self-controlled" means heedful.
"Having sacrificed. "To his own brother" means to his existing brother.

"He favors him" refers to when he speaks with his servants, saying, "We shall give this to him [as the heir] of such-and-such a village or such-and-such a town. "He should not speak of him as clever or wicked" means that at that time, he should not speak of either his virtues or his faults.
“To those who serve as elephant-riders, chariot-warriors, or foot-soldiers,
the king increases their wages according to their performance of duty;
he does not bypass them, for he dwells in the king’s service.”
“One who is firm-waisted like a bow and as supple as a bamboo may tremble,
yet he would not live contrary to the Dhamma while dwelling in the king’s service.
One whose waist is as thin as a bow and whose tongue is as long as a fish— ”
“One who is modest, prudent, and brave—let him dwell in the king’s service.
In this context, “he should not go between them” means he should not go between their gains; he should not create an obstacle.
“Like a bamboo shoot” means that just as a bamboo shoot rising from a thicket shakes when struck by the wind, so too [should one behave] toward the king.
At the time for speaking, one should speak. "Like a bow, not pot-bellied" means that just as a bow is not large-bellied, so too one should not be large-bellied.
"Tongueless" means that just as a fish does not speak because it lacks a tongue, so too a servant should be "tongueless" by virtue of being slow to speak.
"One who eats little" means one who knows the proper measure in food.
“One should not engage excessively with a woman, seeing the exhaustion of one’s vital energy;
through coughing, asthma, consumption, and weakness, one whose wisdom is wasted comes to ruin.
One should not speak at excessive length, nor should one remain silent all the time.”
One should utter speech that is unscattered and measured, at the appropriate time.
Free from anger, non-violent, truthful, gentle, and free from slander—one should not speak idle chatter; such a person may dwell in the king’s service.
“He should support his mother and father, honor the elders of the family, be gentle and friendly in speech—he may dwell in the king’s service.
In this context, “not excessively” means he should not go [to the king] again and again on account of the defilements. “To the destruction of his vitality”—going in such a manner...
For a person indeed undergoes and reaches the exhaustion of his vitality; seeing this, one should not become excessively [heedless].

"They tear" refers to bodily distress. "Weakness" refers to a state of frailty. A person whose wisdom is exhausted—due to repeatedly delighting in the defilements—undergoes these conditions such as coughing and the like.
"Not beyond measure" means, dear ones, that which exceeds the proper limit in the presence of kings.
One should not speak. "When the time has come" means when the time for one's own speech has arrived. "Without conflict" means not causing conflict with another.
"Frivolous talk" means useless speech. "Speech" means words.
"Disciplined, skilled in arts, tamed, self-controlled, restrained, and gentle..."
Diligent, pure, and skillful, he may dwell in the king’s service.
Humble in conduct toward the elders, respectful and reverent,
gentle and pleasant to live with— he may dwell in the king’s service.
“One should avoid from afar people who are intent on socializing;
one should look only to one’s own husband, and not to another king.
In this context, *vinīta* means endowed with proper conduct. *Sippavā* means possessed of the craft that should be learned within one’s own family.
*Daṇḍoti*: one who is harmless toward the six sense-doors. *Katattoti*: one who has accomplished what was to be done. *Niyatoti*:

one whose nature is unshakable, not relying on fame and the like. *Mudūti*: one who is free from excessive pride. *Appamattoti*: one who is devoid of negligence regarding duties that ought to be performed.

*Dakkhoti*: one who is skillful in attendance. *Nivātavuttīti*: one who lives in humility. *Sukhasaṃvāsoti*: one whose character is such that it is pleasant to live with. *Sahitun ti*... [to endure]...
"Sent" means sent by foreign kings to one's own king for the purpose of guarding secrets, or for the purpose of making hidden matters public.
For even when conversing with such a person, one should speak only in the presence of the king.
"She should look only toward her husband" means she should look only at her own master. "And not belonging to another king" means she should not become the property of another king.
“One should respectfully attend upon ascetics and brahmins who are virtuous and learned;
such a person may dwell in the king’s service. One should respectfully attend upon ascetics and brahmins who are virtuous and learned.”
One should provide service with care; such a person may dwell in the king’s residence.
One should satisfy with food and drink both ascetics and brahmins who are virtuous and learned; such a person may dwell in the king’s residence.
“Toward recluses and brahmins as well—those who are virtuous and learned—one should attend upon them with wisdom, desiring one’s own growth.
In this context, “one should attend upon them respectfully” means one should approach them again and again with reverence. “One should dwell near them” means...
While observing the Uposatha residence, one should follow [the precepts]. "Should satisfy" means one should satisfy them with gifts according to their needs.
"Having approached" means having gone near. "Wise" (paññā) means the wise ones; or it means those whose wisdom is unattached, or those whose wisdom does not cling—this is the sense.
"One should not let slip what was previously given: gifts to recluses and brahmins."
He should not obstruct anything at the time of giving to merchants.
Wise, endowed with intelligence, skilled in the methods of procedure,
knowing the right time and knowing the proper occasion— he should dwell in the king’s residence.
“One who is industrious in their own sphere of action, heedful and discerning, with well-ordered tasks—that one may dwell in the king’s service.
In this context, “given before” refers to the customary obligation of giving that has been prepared in advance. “To recluses or brahmins” means to either recluses or brahmins.
"Or: *vaṇibbaka* means that when a beggar has arrived at the time of giving, one should not turn them away with anything.
*Paññavā* means endowed with the wisdom of investigation. *Buddhisampanno* means endowed with unimpaired intelligence.

*Vidhānavidhikovido* means skilled in the various methods of organizing the distribution of servants, laborers, employees, and so forth. *Kālaññū* means [knowing], 'This is the time to give a gift...'"
One should know: "This is the time to guard one's virtue; this is the time to perform the Uposatha ceremony.

One who knows the proper occasion (samayaññū) should know: "This is the season for plowing; this is the season for sowing; this is the season for trade; this is the season for attending upon [the teacher].
Regarding "in the spheres of activity" (kammadheyyesu): it refers to the tasks that ought to be performed by oneself.
“Frequenting threshing floors, sal groves, cattle pens, and fields,
one should have grain measured out in moderation and have it cooked in the house in moderation. Likewise,
one should not associate with a son or a brother who is not established in virtuous conduct.”
"Those fools are indeed bodiless, for they are just like the departed spirits;
one should offer them clothing and alms while they remain seated.
"Regarding slaves, laborers, and servants who are well-established in moral conduct..."
"One who is skillful and endowed with diligence should establish authority.
In this context, "livestock" and "field" refer to a herd of cattle and a place for crops respectively. "One who goes" means one who is habituated to going.

"Measured" means having measured it and known it to be "this much," one should have it stored in granaries. "In the house" means that even in the house, one should have food cooked only after counting the dependents and measuring the amount.
“Unsettled in the precepts” means that one should not appoint such an immoral person of improper conduct to any position of authority.

For it is said, “Indeed, they are fools who lack a limb; for among men, a brother is called a ‘limb’ (aṅga),” thus elder and younger brothers are called “limbs” by virtue of being like limbs; yet these [others] are immoral, and therefore they are not like limbs.
They are not [fit]. Just as hungry ghosts (*peta*) discarded in a charnel ground are dead, so too are they. Therefore, such persons should not be placed in positions of authority.
For they ruin the household; and for one whose household is ruined and who is impoverished, residence at court is not possible.
"Of those sitting" means of the sons and brothers who have come and sat down to receive the funeral meal for the deceased.
He would grant him only food and clothing, providing just enough for his sustenance.
"Endowed with enterprise" means possessed of the energy of exertion. "Virtuous, not greedy, and protective of the king;
beneficial to him both openly and in private—he may dwell in the royal residence."
“Knowing the king’s desire and understanding the king’s mind,
he should live in the royal residence with conduct free from thorns.
He should clothe him, bathe him, and wash his feet while the king lies with his head downward.”
"Even when struck, one should not become angry; such a person may dwell in the king's service.
In this context, "not greedy" means free from covetousness. "Stable in mind" means established in the mind; the meaning is that one is under the control of the king’s mind.
"Of straightforward conduct" means one whose behavior is not perverse. "With head bowed" means that even while washing his feet, he should do so with his head lowered, facing downwards.
The meaning is that one should not look up at the face of a king.
[It is better] to raise one's joined palms like a water-pot and circumambulate even a beggar’s bowl;
how much more so the giver of all desires, the supreme wise one?
“He who gives a bed, clothing, a vehicle, a dwelling, or a house,
rains down enjoyments upon living beings like the rain-god Pajjunna.
Such a person lives as a recluse even while residing in a royal palace.”
“He gratifies the king; he receives honor from his master.

Regarding this, the phrase “making an añjali toward a water-pot and circumambulating a bird” means that a man, desiring prosperity, would see a pot filled with water and make an añjali gesture toward it, and would also circumambulate a bird in a clockwise direction.
When one offers salutation with joined palms or performs a circumambulation, they are unable to give anything at all.
"Kimeva" means: why indeed would one not pay homage to that wise king who is the giver of all desires? For it is the king alone who should be honored and propitiated.
"Pajjunno-riva" means like a cloud. "Esayyo rājavasati" means this noble one (ayyo) who dwells here with me.
This has been told: it is called "The Royal Court," an instruction for those who serve kings.
"As" means that by means of this conduct in the royal court, a man pleases the king and receives honor from the kings;
such is this [instruction]. Thus, the peerless Vidhura Paṇḍita, with the grace of a Buddha, spoke on the royal court.
The Chapter on the King’s Residence is finished.
The Intermediate Repetition Series:
Thus, as he was instructing his sons, wife, kinsmen, friends, companions, and others, three days passed for him. On the [third] day...

Having understood that [the time] was complete, he bathed early in the morning, ate various kinds of exquisite food, and thinking, "I shall go with the young brahmin after taking leave of the king," he went to the royal palace surrounded by his circle of kinsmen.
Having paid homage to the king, he stood to one side and spoke words appropriate to the occasion. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
Having thus instructed his circle of kinsmen, the discerning one,
surrounded by his well-wishers, approached the king.
Having bowed his head at the king’s feet and circumambulated him three times, he spoke.
Vidhura, raising his hands in reverent salutation, said to the king:
“This young man is leading me away, wishing to act according to his own judgment.
O subduer of enemies, I shall speak for the sake of my kinsmen; listen to that.”
“Look after my son and whatever wealth I have in the house,
so that when I have passed away, my circle of kinsmen shall not suffer loss.
Just as one who stumbles upon the ground stands firm again upon that very ground;”
"Truly, this is my lapse; I see this as a transgression.
In that context, "with those of good heart" means with kinsmen, friends, and others who are well-disposed.

"And whatever they think," and "whatever else has been given to me by you and by other kings—an immeasurable amount of wealth in the house—all of that you alone shall oversee. *Pecca* (having passed away)..."
"At a later time. "To stumble" means to slip. "Evetan" means "this is so.
For just as a man who has stumbled on the ground stands up right there, so too, having stumbled among you, I stand firm among you alone. "I see this":
when I was asked by the young brahmin, "Why do you not become a king?", I did not look toward you, but rather regarded the truth.
“If one says, ‘I am a slave,’ that is a transgression; I see this as my transgression, but there is no other fault in me.
Forgive me for this transgression, and having taken this to heart, do not wrong my sons and wife hereafter.

Having heard this, the king spoke a verse, demonstrating: “O wise man, your departure does not please me; rather, it pleases me to have the young brahmin summoned by some means, executed, and covered with a palm-leaf mat.”
“It occurs to me that it is not possible to go; having struck and slain Kātiyāna right here, it pleases me that you remain right here—do not go, O lady of supreme and vast wisdom.
Therein, “having struck” means: “Having beaten and killed him right here in the royal palace, I shall conceal [the body].”
Having heard this, the Great Being said, “Your Majesty, such is your inclination, but it is unbecoming of you,” and spoke thus:
“Do not set your mind upon ignoble things; be devoted to what is meaningful and to the Dhamma.
Woe to that unwholesome and ignoble deed, having done which one must later go to hell!”
“‘It is not the nature of things that this must be done again; for the Noble One is the master over his servant, O Lord of Men.
To kill, to burn, or even to strike—there is no anger in me, and I am departing.
Therein, ‘do not set your mind upon unrighteous things’ means: do not direct your heart toward unrighteousness, toward harmful matters, or toward what is improper.”
"Do not resolve thus" is the meaning. "Afterwards" means that even having performed such an action, one does not become free from old age and death;
rather, one would subsequently be reborn in hell alone. "Woe to that action! means that such an action should be censured and should come to pass as such.
"Neither this" means "not this. "Master" (ayiroti) means husband. "To kill" means to perform these acts, beginning with killing.
"The master has authority over his servant; he is entitled to do all these things. I have not the slightest anger toward the young man.
From the moment you gave him away, it was right for you to restrain your mind. I shall depart, O Lord of Men," he said.
Having spoken thus, the Great Being paid homage to the king, and [took leave] of the king’s harem, his sons and wives, and the royal assembly.
Having exhorted them, when they were unable to remain in their natural state and were uttering loud cries of lamentation, the Great Being departed from the royal palace.
All the inhabitants of the city, having deliberated, "The wise man is said to be going with the youth;
come, let us see him," saw him right there in the royal courtyard. Then the Great Being, comforting them, said: "You..."
"Do not grieve; all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, the body is transient, and fame ends in misfortune.
Nevertheless, you must remain heedful in meritorious deeds such as giving. Having given this exhortation to them and sent them back, he set out toward his own home.
At that moment, Prince Dhammapāla, surrounded by a host of brothers, went out to meet his father.
Thinking, "I shall do so," he set out and appeared before his father at the very gate of the residence.
Upon seeing him, the Great Being was unable to maintain his composure; he embraced him, laid him down upon his breast, and entered the house.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Embracing his eldest son and removing the anguish from his heart,
he entered the great palace with eyes full of tears. Now,
in his house there were a thousand sons, a thousand daughters, a thousand wives, and seven hundred maidservants of the seven complexions.

And there were those who remained; with them, along with all the rest—the female and male slaves, laborers, kinsmen, friends, and companions—the entire residence became as densely packed as a grove of *sāla* trees struck down by the winds at the end of an eon. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Like *sāla* trees fallen together, crushed by the wind;”
His sons and wives were in Vidhura’s house.
A thousand women as wives and seven hundred female slaves raised their arms and wailed in Vidhura’s house.
“Eunuchs and princes, merchants and brahmins,
raised their arms and wailed at Vidhura’s residence.
Elephant-riders, cavalrymen, charioteers, and infantrymen— ”
They raised their arms and wailed in the house of Vidhura:
“The people of the countryside have gathered, and the merchants have gathered;
they raise their arms and wail in the house of Vidhura.”
“This thousand wives and seven hundred female slaves—
why do you abandon us as we flee with arms outstretched? Why do you leave behind the male servants, the princes, the merchants, and the brahmins?”
“With arms outstretched they cry out: ‘Why will you abandon us?
‘The elephant-riders, the cavalrymen, the chariot-fighters, and the foot-soldiers—with arms outstretched they cry out: Why will you abandon us?’”
“The people of the countryside have gathered, and the townspeople have gathered;
stretching out their arms, they cry out: ‘Why will you abandon us?
Therein, “they lie” means that having fallen like those whose feet have been cut off upon the great floor, they lie rolling and tossing about. A thousand women...
"‘Wives’ means a thousand wives, women themselves. ‘Why will you abandon us?’—they lamented thus, asking by what cause you would leave us.
The Great Being, having comforted that great multitude and performed all the remaining duties at home, [dismissed] both his own people and those from outside."
Having exhorted him and explained everything that ought to be explained, he went into the presence of Puṇṇaka and announced that his own task was finished.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having performed the duties in the household, And having instructed his own people...”
Having arranged for his affairs of state, instructed his ministers, servants, children, wife,
and kinsmen regarding the household wealth, the hidden treasures, and the debts owed, Puṇṇaka spoke thus to Mitta: “Having settled my business, and having explained the wealth in the house,
as well as the hoards and the loans given, [I depart].”
“You have stayed for three days in my house; the duties to be performed in my home have been carried out.
My sons and wife have been instructed by me as well. Now, Kaccāna, do as you see fit.
In this context, “having arranged the work” means: “It is proper to act in this way,” referring to what is appropriate to be done in the household.
"Having made an agreement regarding the work; 'a treasure' means wealth deposited and set aside; 'the giving of a debt' means wealth bound by way of a loan.
'According to your wish'—he says this, meaning, 'Now we shall act in accordance with your inclination.
Puṇṇaka said:
“If indeed, Kaccāna, your sons, wives, and dependents have been instructed by you, then give me the horse now with all haste; for this journey ahead is long.
Grasp the tail of this noble steed without any fear.”
“This is the last time you shall behold the world of the living.

Therein, the word *kattā* is the yakkha, filled with joy, addressing the Great Being. For the phrase *dīgho hi addhāpi* means that even the path to be traveled is long. “*Achambhito vā*” (or without fear) was said by him because, wishing to go from right there without descending to the lower palace, he spoke thus.
Then the Great Being said to him:
“Why indeed should I fear anything, when for me there is no evil deed—whether by body, speech, or mind—by which I might go to a miserable rebirth?
In this regard, “Why indeed should I fear anything? was said by the Great Being because he had been told, “Take it without trembling.”
Thus the Great Being, having let out a lion’s roar, remained fearless and undaunted like a maned lion; resolving,
"Let this garment not be released against my will," he made the perfection of resolve his precursor,
fastened it firmly, brushed aside the horse's tail, and grasping the tail firmly with both hands, he pressed down upon the horse with his two feet.
Having wound [the horse’s tail] around his thighs, he said, “Young man, I have seized the tail; go as you please.
At that moment, Puṇṇaka gave a signal to the mind-made steed. Taking the wise man with him, it leapt into the air.
Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
“Thus the king of horses, carrying Vidhura, departed through the sky across the firmament;
without clinging to branches or crags, he quickly reached Kālāgiri.
Therein, “without clinging to branches or crags”: it is said that Puṇṇaka thought, “Without having gone far, in this region of the Himālaya...”
“Having struck down and killed [them] among the trees and mountains, and having taken their heart-flesh and discarded the carcasses in the mountain clefts, we shall go back to the Nāga realm.
Without avoiding the trees and mountains, he drove his horse right through the midst of them.
By the power of the Great Being, both from the trees and from the mountains, [the flesh fell] from both sides of the body...
They retreated for the distance of a jewel’s measure into the mountain passes. He, wondering whether he was dead or not, turned around and looked into the face of the Great Being;

seeing it as serene as a golden mirror, he thought, "He does not die in this way," and again sent [the elephant] to strike at the trees and mountains throughout the entire region of the Himālaya three times. Even while striking thus...
In the same way, the trees and mountains retreated even further away. But the Great Being’s body became exhausted.
Then Puṇṇaka, overcome with anger, thinking, "He does not die; now I shall reduce him to powder with a mass of wind," launched the seventh mass of wind.
Through the power of the Bodhisatta, the mass of wind split into two.

He gave the Bodhisatta an opportunity. Then he had him struck by the Veramba winds; yet even those Veramba winds, making a sound like a hundred thousand thunderclaps, gave the Bodhisatta an opportunity.
Seeing that there was no obstacle for him, Puṇṇaka took him and went to Mount Kāḷa. Thus it is said:
“Thus the king of horses, carrying Vidhura, departed through the sky in the air;
unattached to branches or crags, he quickly reached Mount Kāḷagiri.
Therein, “unattached” means not clinging and not being obstructed; carrying the wise Vidhura, he arrived at the summit of the Black Mountain.
Thus, when Puṇṇaka had departed taking the Great Being with him, the wise man’s wife, children, and others went to Puṇṇaka’s dwelling place;
not seeing the Great Being there, they fell down like those whose feet have been severed and, rolling back and forth, lamented with a great cry.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“A thousand wives and seven hundred female slaves raised their arms and wailed,
crying: ‘A yakkha in the guise of a brahmin is taking Vidhura away!’”
“Orohas and princes, merchants and brahmins,
raising their arms, cried out: ‘A yakkha in the guise of a brahmin is taking Vidhura away!’”
“Elephant-riders, chariot-warriors, cavalrymen, and foot-soldiers,
raising their arms, cried out: ‘A yakkha in the guise of a brahmin is taking Vidhura away!’”
“The people of the countryside gathered together, and the townspeople also assembled;
raising their arms, they cried out: ‘A yakkha in the guise of a brahmin is going away, taking Vidhura with him!’”
“A thousand wives and seven hundred female slaves raised their arms and wailed, ‘Where has that wise man gone?
So too did the eunuchs, the princes, the merchants, and the brahmins.”
Raising their arms, they cried out, "Where has that wise man gone?
The elephant riders, the cavalrymen, the charioteers, and the infantry—
raising their arms, they cried out, "Where has that wise man gone?"
The people of the countryside gathered together, and the townspeople also assembled;
raising their arms, they wailed, "Where has that wise man gone?
Having thus wailed and wept together with all the inhabitants of the city, they [approached] the palace gate.
They arrived. Hearing the great sound of lamentation, the king opened the window-lattice and asked, "Why are you lamenting?
Then they said to him, "Your Majesty, it is said that this young man was not a brahmin;
rather, a *yakkha* came in the guise of a brahmin and took the wise man away. Without him, we have no life. If..."

“Thus he will not return from here for seven days; having gathered firewood with hundreds and thousands of carts, we shall all enter [the fire] after kindling the flames. Proclaiming this matter, they spoke this verse:
“If that wise man does not return within seven nights,”
“We shall all enter the fire; there is no purpose for us in life.
Even at the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One’s final passing away (parinibbāna), there were none who said, “We shall die by entering the fire.
“Oh, how well spoken by the citizens to the Great Being! When the king heard their words, he said, “Do not worry, you all.”

"Do not grieve, do not lament; the sweet-spoken wise man, having enticed the young brahmin with a discourse on the Dhamma and made him fall at his own feet, will return before long, making all the inhabitants of the city laugh with tears in their eyes.
Thus he spoke this verse while offering consolation.
“Wise, proficient, discerning, and far-sighted;
having quickly liberated yourself, do not fear—he will come.

In this context, “proficient” means endowed with the wisdom of discrimination through analytical skill. “Discerning” means [discerning] what is beneficial and what is not, and what is the cause and what is not the cause.

"Vibhāvetvā" means having analyzed; "dassetvā" means having shown; he is capable of explaining. "Vicakkhaṇo" means endowed with the wisdom that considers the causes appropriate to the occasion at that very moment.
"Mā bhāyittha" means "do not fear"; he reassures them, saying, "He will release you and return quickly.
The citizens also, gaining confidence by thinking, "The wise man has surely gone after speaking to the king," departed for their own homes.
The Intermediate Repetition Section is finished.
In the Chapter on the Virtues of Good Men, Puṇṇaka, having placed the Great Being upon the summit of Mount Kāḷāgiri, said: "As long as he lives, there will be prosperity for me."

“There is no [other way]; having killed this man, taken his heart-flesh, gone to the Nāga realm, and given it to Vimalā, I shall take Irandhatī and go to the world of the gods,” he thought. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having gone there and reflecting, he thought: ‘The volitions of beings are diverse and manifold.’”
“Of this [being] there is nothing whatsoever belonging to me by way of life; having slain him, I shall bring his heart.
Therein, “he” refers to that Puṇṇaka. Therein, “having gone” means having gone and standing upon the summit of Mount Kāḷagiri.
“Volitions arise high and low” means that volitions arising moment by moment arise both as high and as low. This is the occasion.
"However, it is possible that even the volition to give him my own life might arise in me. But the meaning is that he made this firm resolve:
"There is not even the slightest need for me here in the Naga realm with his life;
rather, having killed him right here, I shall bring his heart."
Then he thought again, "What if I were not to kill him with my own hand, but instead bring about the end of his life by showing him a terrifying form?
Having conjured up the form of a fearsome yakṣa, he approached, threatening the Great Being;
having struck him down and placed him between his fangs, he acted as if he wished to devour him, yet the Great Being did not experience even a single hair standing on end.
Then, having approached in the form of a lion and a great rutting elephant, he seemed as if he wished to pierce him with his fangs and tusks.
Nevertheless, when [the Bodhisatta] remained unafraid, [Māra] manifested a great serpent-form the size of a single-droṇa boat;
panting and hissing, making the sound "susū," it came and coiled itself around the entire body of the Great Being.
He stood there having formed a hood over his head, yet not even the slightest bit of fear arose within him.
Then, thinking, "I will place him on the mountain peak, cast him down, and reduce him to powder," he unleashed a great wind. But that wind was unable to move him even by the breadth of a hair.
Then, leaving him right there on the mountain peak, [he approached] like an elephant approaching a date-palm tree.
He shook the mountain back and forth, yet he was unable to move it even a hair’s breadth from its place.

Then, thinking, "I shall kill him by splitting his heart with the terror of my roar," he entered into the interior of the mountain and let out a great roar, making the earth and the sky resound with a single clamor; thus, not even a trace of fear remained in him.
He was not. For the Great Being knew: "Even if he comes in the guise of a yakkha, a lion, an elephant, or a king of serpents;
even if he raises a great wind and rain, causes mountains to tremble, or enters into the heart of a mountain and lets out a roar—he is still just the young brahmin, and no other.
Then Puṇṇaka thought: "I cannot kill him by external means."

"I am able; I shall kill him with my own hands. Then the yakkha, having placed the Great Being on the summit of the mountain, went to the foot of the mountain and entered it as if threading a yellow string through a cluster of jewels.
Terrifying and roaring, he emerged from within the mountain, seized the Great Being firmly by the feet, turned him over, and held him upside down.
Having done so, he released it into the unsupported sky. Thus it is said:
“Having gone there, he entered into the midst of the mountains with a corrupted mind;
in that unprotected region of the world, he held [the rock] upside down, desiring to kill.”
Regarding the phrase "having gone there from there": Puṇṇaka, having gone from the mountain peak to the foot of the mountain, stood there in the midst of the mountain;
then, entering within it, he carried [the elephant] beneath him while standing on the mountain peak, over an open stretch of ground.
He did not carry it from the very beginning, but rather, having hurled it there, for a distance of about fifteen yojanas.

While he was falling, standing upon the mountain peak, [the Elder] reached out his hand, caught him by the feet as he fell headlong, and lifted him up still headfirst while looking into his face. Knowing that he was not dead, he threw him a second time;
when he had fallen for about thirty yojanas, he lifted him up in the same manner and, looking again into his face, saw that he was indeed still alive.
Seeing this, he thought, "If he does not die after falling sixty yojanas now, I shall seize him by the feet, dash him against the mountain peak, and kill him.
Then, having hurled him for a third time and when he had fallen sixty yojanas, he reached out his hand, seized him by the feet, and lifted him up. Thereupon, the Great Being thought: "This..."
He threw me first to a distance of fifteen yojanas, the second time thirty yojanas, and the third time sixty yojanas;
now he will not throw me again, but as soon as he lifts me up, he will strike me on the mountain peak and kill me.
Therefore, before he has lifted me up and dashed me against the mountain peak, I shall remain hanging with my head downward.
"I shall ask the cause of his death. Having thought thus, he did so without fear or trepidation.
Therefore it is said: "Kātiyāna held on," meaning that after being thrown three times, he held on.
"Hanging there in the precipice of hell, in great terror, hair-raising and difficult to traverse..."
Thus spoke the best of doers among the Kurus, who was himself non-existent though appearing existent, to the yakkha named Puṇṇaka:
“You are one who makes room for the noble while having the form of a non-noble; you are unrestrained yet have the appearance of being restrained.
You perform cruel deeds that bring great harm, and there is no skill whatsoever in your disposition.”
“Since you wish to throw me down from this precipice, what need have you for my death?
Your appearance today is like that of a non-human being; tell me, who are you, a deity?
In this context, “he hanging” refers to that best of the Kurus, the son of Kuntī, as he hung there on the third occasion. “The noble opening” (ariyāvakāsa) means...
In form, you wander about having become like a noble one with the appearance of a deity. "Unrestrained" means unrestrained in body and so forth, being immoral.

"Exceedingly harmful" means that which has transgressed what is beneficial, or that which is excessively harmful. "And in your state of being" means that there is not even the slightest bit of wholesome virtue in your mind.
"Today your appearance is like that of a non-human" means that today this condition of yours is indeed like that of a non-human.
“Which deity are you? [He asked: “Among the *yakkhas*, what kind of *yakkha* are you by name?
Puṇṇaka said:
“If you have heard of the *yakkha* named Puṇṇaka, he is indeed the companion of King Kuvera.”
“The serpent named Varuṇa is the upholder of the earth, tall, pure, and endowed with beauty and strength.
‘I desire his younger sister, that Naga maiden named Irandhatī;
for the sake of that slender-waisted beloved, O wise one, I have plotted your death.’”
In this context, *sajīvo* means a living minister. *Brahā* means one endowed with height and girth, resembling a cast golden image.
*Vaṇṇabalūpapanno* means possessed of bodily complexion and physical strength. *Tassānujaṃ* means a daughter born after him (his younger sister).
*Patārayiṃ* means I set my mind upon her; the meaning is that I formed a resolution [to marry her].

Having heard this, the Great Being thought, "This world perishes through wrong graspings; what purpose is there in my death for one who merely longs for the Naga maiden? I shall learn the truth of the matter.
Reflecting thus, he spoke this verse: "Do not, O Yakkha, be deluded; many in the world have been ruined by wrong graspings.
What need have you for that slender-waisted beloved? As for my death, listen to everything first."
Having heard that, Puṇṇaka spoke, explaining it to him:
"I am a kinsman seeking a daughter for the majestic Mahoraga;
when I requested her, my father-in-law said, 'As they have considered me well-favored.'"

“Give us your daughter, who has beautiful ears, beautiful eyes, a lovely smile, and limbs anointed with sandalwood paste—if you have given her heart to a wise man, having obtained her by righteous means, do not withhold her here.
It is for this wealth, O maiden, that she may be won; we seek no other wealth beyond this.”
“Thus I am not deluded; listen, Katta! Nor is there anything in my grasp that is wrongly understood.
With hearts won over by the Dhamma, the Nāgas give you their Nāga maiden Irandhati.
Therefore, though I am intent on your destruction, such is my purpose that your death serves my own end.”
"Having cast him right here into hell and having struck his heart, I shall bring him back.
In this context, "desiring a daughter" means: "I desire and long for a daughter; I wander about for the sake of a daughter.

"I am one who is supported by kinsmen" means: "Therefore, I am indeed one whose maintenance is provided by his kinsmen. "Him" refers to that Naga maiden. "While he was entreating" means: while he was making a request.
*Maṃ*: Because they counsel me thus (*yathā manti yasmā maṃ*). *Aññiṃsu*: they knew. *Sukāmanītaṃ*: he is well led by desire, thus "well-led-by-desire" (*sukāmanīta*);
[the text refers to] that one who is well-led-by-desire. Therefore the father-in-law said, "We would indeed give [her] to you," and so forth.
Therein, *dajjemu*: we would give. *Sutanaṃ*: one with a beautiful body. *Idha māharesī*: you should bring her here from this Nāga-abode, having obtained her in accordance with the Dhamma.
Having heard those words, the Great Being thought: "Vimalā has no need for my heart;
however, when Varuṇa, the Nāga king, hears my discourse on the Dhamma, worships me with his jewel, and returns there, he will surely praise my status as a preacher of the Dhamma.
Consequently, Vimalā’s longing for my Dhamma discourse will arise, and by Varuṇa..."
"Having grasped it wrongly, Puṇṇaka will have been commanded; thus, by his own wrong grasp, he has brought me to such suffering as this to kill me.
What will my wisdom—my capacity for thinking on the spot and considering the circumstances—avail when they are killing me?
Come now, I shall persuade him. Having thought thus, he said: "Young man,..."
"I know what is called the 'Duty of a Good Man. As long as I do not die, have me seated upon the mountain peak and let me hear this 'Duty of a Good Man'; afterwards, you may do whatever you wish.
Having thus spoken and extolled the duty of a good man, he uttered a verse while hanging head-downwards, seeking to preserve his own life:
“O Kāṭiyāna, lift me up quickly if you have any concern for my heart;
whatever noble qualities there are in a virtuous man, all of them I shall reveal to you today.
Hearing this, Puṇṇaka thought, “This must be a teaching never before spoken by a wise man to gods or humans.”
Thinking, "I shall quickly lift him up and hear the Dhamma of the virtuous man," Puṇṇaka lifted the Great Being and set him down upon the mountain peak.
Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
"He, Puṇṇaka, having quickly established Kattuseṭṭha, the best of men, upon the mountain peak..."
Having observed him seated under the Assattha tree, he questioned the Maker of Unrivalled Wisdom:
“You have been drawn up from the abyss; today my heart has a task for you.
Whatever qualities there are of a virtuous person, reveal them all to me this very day.”

In that context, *assatthamāsīnaṃ* means sitting after having regained one’s breath. *Samekkhiyānaṃ* means having seen. *Sādhunarassa dhammā* means the excellent qualities of a man; the meaning is "beautiful qualities.
Having heard this, the Great Being said:
“If you have need of my heart, I shall be uprooted from this precipice.”
“Whatever qualities there are of a virtuous person, all of those I shall reveal today.
In that context, *tyasmī* means “I am by you.
Then the Great Being said, “My body is defiled; let me bathe first. The yakkha replied, “Very well,” and [prepared] bathing water.
Having brought these, at the time of bathing, he gave divine garments, perfumes, garlands, and so forth to the Great Being;

and when he had been adorned and prepared, he offered divine food. Then, after the Great Being had finished his meal, he had the summit of Mount Kāḷāgiri decorated, had a seat prepared, and sat upon the decorated Dharma-seat. Displaying the grace of a Buddha, as he taught the Dhamma for the welfare of virtuous men, he spoke this verse:
“Follow those who have gone before you, young man, and avoid a hand that is wet;
never be treacherous toward your friends, and do not fall under the power of unchaste women.
In this context, “avoid a hand that is wet” means: do not burn, do not scorch a hand that is wet or moist.
Unable to understand the four duties of a good person that had been spoken in brief, the yakkha asked for a detailed explanation and spoke this verse:
“How indeed does one follow what has gone before? How does he burn his moist hand?
Who is the unchaste woman, and who is the betrayer of friends? Being questioned, tell me the meaning of this.”
The Great Being also said to him:
“One who would invite even a stranger whom he has never seen before to a seat—
the wise call such a person ‘one who follows the traveler,’ for he acts for that person’s own benefit.”
“One should not harbor even a thought of evil toward that person in whose house one might stay for a single night and obtain food and drink.
Betraying a friend burns the betrayer, who has harmed one with hands that were once innocent.
One should not harbor even a thought of evil toward him under whose tree’s shade one might sit or lie down.”
One should not break its branch, for he who betrays a friend is evil.
Even if a man were to give this entire earth, filled with wealth, to a woman approved by him, once he has gained an opportunity, he might despise her as well;
one should not fall under the power of such unfaithful women.
“Thus indeed does one follow what has gone before,
and likewise one burns the moist hand again;
she is an unchaste woman, and he is a betrayer of friends.”
“Be thus righteous; abandon what is unrighteous.
In this context, “not well-acquainted” means one who has never before stayed together for even a single day or two.

“Whoever [invites] even with a seat” means whoever would invite such a person even with the mere offering of a seat, let alone with food, drink, and so forth. “Of that very person” refers to that benefactor.
A person surely accomplishes their purpose. "One who follows the traveler" means one who follows a person who has already traveled by virtue of having acted first.
For those who act first are called "travelers," while those who act later are called "followers"—thus the wise speak.
This, O King of Devas, is the first duty of a good man. "Not betraying living beings" means holding back from betraying even one's own hand that is about to eat.
For he is indeed called a betrayer of friends. Thus, this second duty of a good man is not setting fire to another's hand.
"Not his" means one should not break off his branch or leaf. Why? Because a betrayer of friends is evil.
Thus, even toward an insentient tree that has provided shade, one who commits an injury against it is called a betrayer of friends.
"How much more so, then, when one has become a human being? Thus, this third quality of a good person is non-betrayal toward friends.
"Dajjitthiyā" means one should give to a woman. "Sammatāya" means she who is highly esteemed [by her husband], thinking: "I alone am dear to her, no other; she desires only me.
"Laddhā khaṇaṃ" means having obtained an opportunity, having found a chance for transgression. "Asatīnaṃ" means...
"Of women who are possessed of unrighteous qualities. Thus, the non-performance of evil by relying on a woman—this is the fourth duty of a good man.
"May you be righteous in this, O King of the Gods; may you be endowed with these four duties of a good man.
In this way, the Great Being spoke of the four duties of a good man to the yakṣa with the grace of a Buddha.
The Section on the Virtues of Good Men is finished.
The Section on Kāḷāgiri:
While listening to those teachings, Puṇṇaka observed, "In all four respects, this wise man values his own life alone..."
"He requests this: 'This man indeed showed me honor when we were previously unacquainted;
I lived in his residence for three days experiencing great glory. While I was committing this evil deed, I did so by means of a woman, yet in every respect, I alone am the betrayer of friends.
If I offend a wise person, I shall not abide in the conduct of a good man.'"
"I shall indeed continue to live [here]; therefore, what need have I for the young girl Nāgā?
Let me take her there with haste, making the inhabitants of the city of Indapatta shed tears, and cause her to enter the Dhamma Hall," he thought, and spoke this verse:
"For three days I dwelt in your house, served with food and drink."
"You were my friend; I release you. Go home as you wish, O one of supreme wisdom.
Let even the wealth of the Naga clan perish; let there be enough for me with a Naga maiden alone.
By your own well-spoken words, you have today been released by me from the death penalty."

In that context, "I am present" means I have been placed there by you. "I shall answer that question" means I shall resolve it for you. "Categorically" means without reservation. "For the sake of death" means from death. "Wisdom" means one possessed of wisdom.
Then the Great Being, saying, "Young man, do not send me to your own house; lead me instead to the abode of the Naga," spoke this verse:
"Come now, O Yakkha, lead me also to your father-in-law; let him attend to my welfare."
"And may we see the palace of the lord of the nāgas, never seen before by the nāga.
In this context, *handā* is a particle used for emphasis or exhortation. "Sasuraṃ te atthaṃ mayi carassū" means: "Deal with the wealth belonging to your father-in-law through me;
do not destroy it. "Nāgādhipatiṃ vimānaṃ" means: "I too [shall see] the lord of the nāgas and the palace."
And he might see a celestial mansion such as he had never seen before.
Having heard this, Puṇṇaka said:
"That which would be for a man's harm, the wise one ought not to look upon."
"Then for what reason, O one of supreme wisdom, do you wish to go to Amittagāma?
Therein, "Amittagāma" means the dwelling place of an enemy; the meaning is "an encounter with an enemy.
Then the Great Being said to him:
“Truly, I understand this as well: that one lacking wisdom does not deserve to see [the truth];
yet there is no evil deed whatsoever committed by me, therefore I have no fear regarding the arrival of death.
In this context, *maraṇāgamāya* means for the arrival of death.
"Furthermore, O King of Devas, such a harsh yakkha as he was has been softened by me through a discourse on the Dhamma;
yet even now you say to me, 'I have had enough of the Naga maiden; go to your own home. Softening the Naga king is my task;
do not send me there. Having heard those words of his, Puṇṇaka accepted them, saying "Very well," and with a joyful heart, he said:
“Come, Kaccāyana, let us go to that place of incomparable splendor which you shall behold with me—
the place where the Naga dwells amidst song and dance, like King Vessavaṇa in Naḷiniṃ,
where the Naga maidens sport in groups, playing day and night.”
Abundant with garlands and covered with many flowers, it shines like lightning in the sky.
"Supplied with food and drink, with dances, songs, and instrumental music;
filled with adorned maidens, it is resplendent with garments and ornaments."
In this context, *handa ca* is merely a particle. *Ṭhānaṃ* means the dwelling place of the Nāga king.
*Naḷiññaṃ* refers to the royal capital named Naḷinī. *Caritaṃ gaṇena* means it was frequented by a multitude of Nāga maidens.
*Nikīḷitaṃ* means it was constantly played upon and enjoyed by the Nāga maidens both day and night.
Having spoken thus, Puṇṇaka placed the Great Being upon the back of the horse and led him there. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Puṇṇaka seated that best of doers among the Kurus behind him on the seat;
taking with him that doer of matchless wisdom, he brought him to the palace of the city’s king.”
“Having reached that place of incomparable power, the Creator stood behind Puṇṇaka;
observing their harmony, the Nāga King spoke first to his son-in-law.
Therein, monks, “that Puṇṇaka” refers to him who, having thus described the abode of the Nāgas, [sent] his wise thoroughbred horse.
Having mounted [the horse], he led him to the abode of the Nāgas. "The place" refers to the dwelling-place of the Nāga king.
Regarding the words "behind Puṇṇaka": it is said that this thought occurred to Puṇṇaka: "If the Nāga king, upon seeing the wise man, becomes gentle-minded, that is well;
but if not, then while he has not yet seen him, I shall mount the steed and take him away. Then...
He placed him behind. Therefore it is said: "behind Puṇṇaka. "Looking for harmony" means looking for concord.
There is also the reading "sāmaṃ apekkhī," which means that, having seen his own son-in-law, he addressed him first of all by himself.
The Naga King said:
"Since you have come from the world of the dead, searching for the heart of the wise man—
have you arrived here having succeeded, bringing with you the doer of matchless wisdom?"
Therein, "Have you come here with your wish fulfilled? means: "Have you come here with your desire accomplished and realized?
Puṇṇaka said:
"This very one has arrived whom you desired; Dhammapāla, who was obtained by me in accordance with the Dhamma."
“Behold him speaking in your presence; indeed, meeting with the virtuous is blissful.
In this context, *yaṃ tvam icchasi* means “that which you desire. There is also the reading *yaṃ tu micchasi*.
*Sammukhā bhāsamānaṃ* means that very Dhammapāla, honored by the world, is now speaking the Dhamma with a sweet voice right before your eyes.
"Behold! For indeed, meeting with virtuous men in one place is a source of happiness.
The Chapter on Kāḷāgiri is finished.
Then the Naga king, seeing the Great Being, spoke this verse:
“Having seen what was never seen before, the mortal, terrified by the fear of death, is struck with awe and does not pay homage;
this is not like those who possess wisdom. In this context, “byamhito” means frightened.
This is what is meant: O wise one, you [should not act thus] toward the abode of the Nāgas, which has never been seen before.
Seeing this, and being distressed and terrified by the fear of death, he thought, "The reason why he did not salute me is not something that would occur to those possessed of wisdom.
Thus, instead of saying to the Naga king who expected a salutation in return, "You are not to be saluted by me," the Great Being,
through his own possession of knowledge and skillful means, said, "I salute you because you have reached the state of one deserving of execution."
Speaking thus, he recited these two verses:
“I am not terrified, O Naga, nor am I overcome by fear of death.
One who is not himself subject to execution should not bow down, nor should one bow down to one who is subject to execution.”
“How could one bow down to us, or even cause us to be bowed to?
For that deed which a man might wish to kill [us] does not take effect.
The meaning of this is: O King of Nagas, it is not because I have seen a naga-abode never seen before that I am afraid, nor am I driven by the fear of death.

For one such as I, there is indeed no fear of death; however, one who is condemned to death is not permitted to pay homage, nor is it permitted for one who is not condemned to cause a condemned person to pay homage.
For how could a man who intends to kill someone pay him homage, or how could he have himself paid homage by that person? Indeed, such an action is not appropriate for him. And you—
"He has surely commanded this man to have me killed; how then can I pay homage to him?
Hearing this, the Naga king spoke two verses in praise of the Great Being:
"It is even so as you say; you speak the truth, O wise one."
"One who is not to be executed should not bow down, nor should one bow down to one who is to be executed.
How could one bow down? One should indeed cause [the other] to bow down.
For the deed that a man intends to do against another does not come to pass."
Now the Great Being, exchanging greetings with the Naga king, said:
"Is this of yours eternal or non-eternal—this psychic power, radiance, strength, heroism, and rebirth?
O King of Nagas, I ask you about this matter: how was this celestial mansion obtained by you?"
“Was this obtained by overreaching, born of transformation, made by yourself, or given by the gods?
