O King of Nagas, tell me the truth of this matter—how exactly was this celestial mansion (vimāna) obtained by you?
In that context, *tava-y-idam* means “this glory of yours,” or “this celestial mansion which, though impermanent, appears as if permanent. “Do not…” [the rest follows].
With the words, “He committed evil depending on you, Yasa,” he begs for his own life. Regarding “supernormal power” (*iddhi*):

I ask you, O King of Nāgas, about this matter—how did you obtain all this: the supernormal power of a nāga, the radiance of a nāga, physical strength, mental vigor, rebirth in the nāga realm, and this celestial mansion (*vimāna*) of yours? How was all this acquired by you? It was obtained through merit.
"Has this celestial mansion been obtained by you through chance, without cause; or is it produced by the transformation of the seasons;
or was it made by your own hands; or was it given to you by the gods? Tell me the truth regarding how this was obtained by you."
Having heard that, the Naga king said:
"This was not obtained by chance, nor born of transformation; it was not made by myself, nor given by the gods.
By my own blameless deeds, by merits, this celestial mansion (vimāna) has been obtained by me."
In that regard, "by those who are not evil" means by those who are faultless.
Then the Great Being said:
"What is your vow? What is your holy life? Of what well-practiced deed is this the result?"
“Supernatural power, radiance, strength, heroism, and rebirth—this, O Naga, is your great celestial mansion.

Therein, “What was your vow? means: O King of Nagas, what was your vow in a previous existence? What was your dwelling in the holy life? And of what kind of well-performed conduct is this result, namely supernatural power and the rest?
Having heard that, the King of Nagas said:
“Both my wife and I, in the world of men, were faithful patrons of giving.
My home was then like a public well, where recluses and brahmins were satisfied.
Garlands, perfumes, ointments, lamps, bedding, and dwellings—”
“Clothing, bedding, food, and drink—we gave these gifts there with due respect.
That was my vow, that indeed was my holy life (brahmacariya); this is the result of that well-practiced conduct:
psychic power, radiance, strength, heroism, rebirth, and this great celestial mansion (mahāvimāna) of mine, O wise one.”

"There, in the human world," means in the city of Kālacampā in the province of Aṅga. "That very thing which was given by me with reverence" refers to that very undertaking of my duties and holy life (*brahmacariya*);
"this result, beginning with supernatural power (*iddhi*), is the ripening of that very well-performed conduct.
Thus spoke the Great Being.
“If you have obtained this celestial mansion in this way, you surely recognize that it is the arising of the fruit of meritorious deeds.
Therefore, practice the Dhamma with heedfulness, so that you may not lose this celestial mansion again.
In this context, “you recognize” means: if you have obtained it through the power of your giving, then, such being the case, you indeed recognize [the source].
And [he spoke of] the fruit, which is rebirth produced by the fruit of merit. Therefore, he said: "Because this has been obtained by you through merits, therefore.
Furthermore, "Do not neglect," meaning: practice the Dhamma so that you may continue to dwell in this abode of the Nāgas.
Having heard that, the Nāga king said:
“There are no ascetics or brahmins here, O charioteer, to whom we might give food and drink.
Being asked, tell me this matter: how it is that we shall not dwell again in this celestial mansion.
The Great Being replied:
“For here you have been born with enjoyments, sons, wives, and dependents;
toward them, always remain free from malice in both word and deed.
Thus, O Naga, maintain this freedom from malice through both word and deed.”
"Having remained here in this celestial mansion for the duration of your lifespan, you shall go from here upward to the world of the gods.

In that context, "bhogī" means possessors of wealth; "nāgā" is the meaning. Regarding "tesu": toward those children, wives, and so forth who possess wealth, may you always remain undefiled in both speech and action.
"Anupālaya": thus, toward children and others, as well as toward all other beings, [maintain] that which is known as a mind of loving-kindness (*mettacitta*).
“Guard against ill-will. “Upward from here” means that having passed away from this Nāga realm, he will go to the higher world of the devas;
for a mind of loving-kindness is a merit greater than giving.
Then, having heard the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma, the Nāga king thought, “It is not possible for a wise man to engage in external elaboration.”
"Having shown Vimalā what is well-spoken and having satisfied her longing,
it would be right to send a wise man to make King Dhanañjaya laugh," she thought, and spoke this verse:
"Certainly that best of kings must grieve, for whom you, his dear friend, are without him."
"Even one brought to suffering, by meeting with you, may find happiness as if he were healthy.
Therein, *sajīvō* means the minister Sajīva. *Samecca* means having come together with you. *Āturōpi* means even though he is severely ill.
Having heard that, the Great Being, offering praise to the Naga king, spoke the following verse:
“Truly, O Naga, you speak the Dhamma of the virtuous, the unsurpassed state of well-practiced meaning.
For in such calamities as these, the distinction between those like me and others becomes evident.
In this context, *addhā santaṃ* means that you speak with certainty the Dhamma of the peaceful and wise. *Atthapadaṃ* refers to a portion of what is beneficial.
“In such circumstances” means: in calamities of this kind, when such a danger has arisen, the distinction of wise people like me becomes apparent.
Having heard that, the Naga king was exceedingly pleased and, questioning him further, spoke this verse:
“Tell us, was it won by you for nothing? Did you defeat us at dice with those very dice?”
"She said to him, 'It was obtained righteously,' but how did it come into his hand?
In this context, "Tell us" (*akkhāhi no*) means "explain to us. "She said to him" (*tāyamāha*) means "she said to him.

"Was it obtained for nothing? (*mudhā nu laddho*) means: "Was it indeed obtained for nothing, without any basis at all, or did he win it in gambling? Thus she said to him; this Puṇṇaka [said], "Righteously..."
“I have found a wise man,” he says. “How indeed did you come into his hand? means: how did you fall into his grasp?
The Great Being said:
“The king who was the master there, him this man defeated at dice.”
"So the King, having been defeated, gave him to me; I have obtained him through righteousness, not by force.
Therein, "he who is my lord" means he who is my master. "He gave him to this one" means he gave him to Puṇṇaka.
Having heard that, the Nāga king was pleased. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Delighted and uplifted, having heard the well-spoken words of the Wise One,
Mahoraga took the one of peerless wisdom by the hand and then went into the presence of his wife.
‘O you who are stainless and pale, for whom food is no longer pleasing;’”
"And my splendor is not like this; this is the dispeller of darkness.
'He for whose sake you have come with longing in your heart—this maker of light has arrived.
Listen to his words, for a sight such as this is difficult to obtain again.'"
In that context, *pāvekkhi* means "entered. *Yena* means, O Bhaddā Vimale, for what reason you are pale and do not find pleasure in food.

*Na ca me tādiso vaṇṇo*: neither on the surface of the earth nor in the world of the devas does anyone else possess such a complexion as this one’s radiant quality of virtue has spread. "This one is the dispeller of darkness."
"He who, depending upon whom your longing arose—he is indeed this very one who dispels the darkness of the entire world.
To see him again is truly difficult to obtain," she said.
Vimalā, having seen him, offered him hospitality. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having seen him, the one of stainless and vast wisdom, she raised her ten fingers in an añjali gesture;
with a joyful disposition and a heart full of rapture, she spoke thus to the best of the Kurus.
Therein, “with a joyful disposition” means with a delighted mind. “With a heart full of rapture” means having given rise to gladness.
From here follow the verses of exchange between Vimalā and the Great Being:
“Having seen what was never seen before, a mortal, though standing in fear of death, did not bow down in awe;
this is not as it is for those possessed of wisdom.”
“O Naga, I am neither terrified, nor am I overcome by fear of death;
nor would one who is condemned to death pay homage, nor would I pay homage to one who is condemned to death.
How then could I pay homage? Indeed, how could I cause another to pay homage?”
Whatever deed a man might wish to kill, that action does not follow him.
"It is even so as you say; you speak the truth, O wise one.
One who is not to be executed should not bow down, nor should one bow down to one who is to be executed."
“How could one bow down to us, or even cause us to be bowed to?
The very action that a man might wish to kill with does not come to pass.
Is this power, radiance, strength, vigor, and rebirth of yours eternal, or is it non-eternal?”
“I ask you this matter, O Naga maiden: how was this celestial mansion obtained by you?
Was it obtained by chance, or born of transformation, or was it made by yourself, or given by the gods?
Tell me this matter, O Naga maiden: exactly how was this celestial mansion obtained by you?”
“This celestial mansion was not obtained by me through overreaching, nor born of transformation, nor produced by my own talk, nor given by the gods;
it was obtained by me through my own blameless deeds, through merits.
What was your vow, and what was your holy life? Of what well-practiced deed is this the result?”
Supernormal power, radiance, strength, heroism, rebirth, and this great celestial mansion of yours, O Nāgī—these are yours.
But as for me and my husband, we were both masters of faith and givers of alms;
our home was like a well of water, and we satisfied the ascetics and brahmins.
“Garlands, perfumes, and ointments, lamps, beds, and dwellings;
clothing, refreshments, food, and drink—we gave these gifts there with due respect.
This was my vow, this was my holy life; this is the fruit of that well-practiced conduct.”
“Supernatural power, radiance, strength, heroism, and rebirth— this great celestial mansion is mine, O wise one.
Since you have obtained this mansion as a result of merit and understand that such rebirth is the fruit of meritorious deeds,
therefore practice the Dhamma with heedfulness, so that you may not remain deficient in this mansion again.”
“There are no recluses or brahmins here, O charioteer, to whom we might give food and drink.
Answer this question for me when asked: how shall we not dwell again in such a celestial mansion?
For there are wealthy ones born here, as well as sons, wives, and dependents.”
“Among them, you must always remain undefiled in both word and deed.
Thus, O Nāgī, maintain this freedom from malice through word and deed;
having remained here in this celestial mansion for the duration of your lifespan, you shall go henceforth to the world of the gods.”
“Truly that best of kings must grieve, for whom you, his dear friend, are now apart from him.
Even a man brought to suffering would find happiness by being reunited with you, even if he were already healthy.
Truly, O Nāgī, you speak the Dhamma of the virtuous—the unsurpassed, pure, and well-practiced word of truth.”
For in such calamities, the distinction between those like us becomes evident:
“Tell us, was she won by you for nothing? Did you win her from us at dice?
“She was won righteously,” he replied. “How then did she come into your hand?”
“The king who was the lord there, him this man defeated at dice with the Ajjuka nuts.
Having been defeated, that king gave me [this]; I have obtained it righteously, not by force.
The meaning of these verses is to be understood in the same manner as explained below.
Having heard the words of the Great Being, Vimalā was even more delighted; she took the Great Being and bathed him with jars of a thousand kinds of scented water.
While he was being bathed, she gave the Great Being celestial garments, divine perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
When he had been adorned and prepared, she fed him celestial food. After the Great Being had finished his meal, she prepared a decorated seat and a decorated Dharma-seat.
Having sat down, he taught the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
"Just as the Naga Varuṇa asked a question of the Wise One, even so did the Naga maiden ask a question of the Wise One."
“Just as the wise one, when questioned, satisfied the Naga Varuṇa,
so too did the wise one, when questioned,
satisfy the Naga maiden. Having perceived that both of them— the great serpent and the Naga maiden— were pleased, the wise one [proceeded].”
Fearless, undaunted, and without bristling hair, he spoke thus to Varuṇa, the Nāga king:
“Do not obstruct me, O Nāga; I am one who has come for this purpose.
Use my heart and my flesh as you require; I myself shall do whatever you wish.”
In this context, *achambhī* means unshakable; *alomahaṭṭho* means one whose body hair does not stand on end due to fear.

*Iccabravī* means he spoke thus by way of investigation. *Mā rodhayī* means "do not be afraid, thinking 'I am committing an act of treachery against a friend,'" or "do not worry, thinking 'How indeed shall I kill him now?
*Nāga* is an address to Varuṇa. *Āyāhamasmi* means "I am one who brings wealth."

Or this is the reading: "I myself shall do it. If you are unable to kill me because of [the thought], "I have just heard the Dhamma from his presence," then I myself shall act according to your own desire.
The Naga king said:
“Wisdom indeed is the heart of the wise; we are well-pleased with your wisdom.
Let Anūnanāma receive a wife today; let him reach Kururaṭṭha this very day.
In this passage, *te tyamha* means “we [are] yours,” that is, we are well-pleased with your wisdom. *Anūnanāmo* means one whose name is complete, namely Puṇṇaka.
"Yakkha general! May he receive a wife today; may he receive a wife today. I give him my daughter, Irandhatī.
Let him go to Kururaṭṭha this very day—let Puṇṇaka conduct him there.
Having spoken thus, Varuṇa the Nāga king gave Irandhatī to Puṇṇaka. Having obtained her, his heart filled with joy, he conversed with the Great Being. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Puṇṇaka, having obtained Irandhatī, the Nāga maiden, was joyful and elated;
with a heart full of joy and a serene countenance, he spoke thus to the best of the Kurus, the supreme doer:
‘You have made me possessed of a wife; and I, Vidhūra, shall perform your service.’”
"And I give you this jewel-treasure; I shall send you to Kurura this very day. In this context, "jewel-treasure" means:
"O wise one, I am well-pleased with your virtues and am worthy to perform a service befitting you;
therefore, I give you this jewel-treasure used by a wheel-turning monarch, and I shall send you to Indapattha this very day."
Then the Great Being, offering praise to him, spoke the following verse:
“May this friendship of yours with your beloved wife be invincible, Kaccāna!
Rejoicing, joyful, glad, and delighted, give me the jewel and lead me to Nandipatta.”

In this context, "ajeyyamesā" means: "Let this [woman] be invincible in her dear companionship with your wife. With the words "Ānandi vitto," etc., he expresses his state of being possessed of joy. "Nayindapatthaṃ" means: "Lead to Indapattha.
Having heard that, Puṇṇaka did accordingly. Therefore it is said:
"Then Puṇṇaka seated him, the best of doers for the Kurus, upon a seat in front."
Taking the builder of incomparable wisdom, he brought him to the city of Indapatta.
"Just as the mind of a man might travel,
even more swiftly than that did Puṇṇaka bring Kattuseṭṭha of the Kurus to the city of Indapatta."
“The city of Etindapattha is visible, and the delightful mango groves appear in all their parts;
I am reunited with my wife, while you have returned to your own home.
In this regard, although that which is called “mind” does not actually go anywhere, it nevertheless grasps an object at a distance.
"He is said to have 'gone' (gata); therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: the movement of that mind-made steed was even swifter than the mind's grasping of its object.
"Etindapatta" means he spoke thus while showing him [the destination] even as he remained seated upon the horse's back.
"Sakaṃ niketaṃ" means he said, "You have arrived at your own dwelling."
On that day, at the time of dawn, the king saw a dream. Such was the dream:

at the gate of the king’s residence stood a great tree, whose trunk was the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*), whose branches were made of virtue (*sīlamaya*), whose fruit was the five products of the cow (*pañcagorasa*), and which was covered by well-adorned elephants, cattle, and horses.
A great multitude of people stood there, having paid him honor, with palms joined in reverence, offering him worship.
Then a certain dark man, harsh, dressed in red garments, wearing red flowers on his ears, and holding weapons in his hands, arrived;

while the great multitude was still lamenting, he cut that tree down at its roots, dragged it away, took it with him, and having brought it back again, placed it in its original position and departed. As the King was reflecting upon that dream:

“No one else was like the great tree; no one else was like the man who, while the multitude was still lamenting, cut it down with its roots, took it away, and departed—just as the young brahmin took the wise man and went away.
Again, just as that man returned, placed it back in its original spot, and left, so too did that young brahmin bring the wise man back and [place him] in the Dhamma assembly.”
“Having stationed him at the gate, he will depart; certainly today we shall see the wise man,” he resolved with great joy.
He had the entire city decorated, prepared the Dhamma hall, and arranged the Dhamma throne within the exquisitely adorned Jewel Pavilion.
Surrounded by a retinue of one hundred kings, ministers, city-dwellers, and country-folk, he said: “Today, you...”
"See the wise man; do not grieve," he said, comforting the great multitude.
Then, awaiting the arrival of the wise man, he sat down in the Dhamma Hall, as did the ministers and others.
At that moment, Puṇṇaka, having brought down the wise man and placed him right in the midst of the assembly at the door of the Dhamma Hall, took Irandhatī and departed for the city of the gods.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Puṇṇaka did not set down the best of craftsmen among the Kurus in the midst of the Dhamma assembly;
instead, mounting his noble steed, he of extraordinary beauty departed through the air into the sky.”
“Seeing him, the king was exceedingly pleased; rising up, he embraced him with both arms and, remaining unshaken in the midst of the Dhamma assembly, seated him on the foremost seat.
Regarding this, “of extraordinary beauty” means of non-deficient beauty, of supreme beauty. “Remaining unshaken,” monks, that king [honored] the wise man...
Having embraced him in the midst of the great multitude, without wavering and without shrinking back, the King took him by the hand, turned him toward himself,
and had him sit upon the decorated Dhamma-throne. Then the King,
having exchanged greetings with him and engaging in sweet conversation, spoke this verse:
“You are our trainer, like a charioteer guiding a harnessed chariot; they rejoice at the sight of you.
Being asked, tell me this matter: how did the liberation of the young man come about?
In that passage, “harnessed” (*naddha*) means: just as a charioteer guides a harnessed chariot, so do you [guide us] for our sake.
A guide in deeds of benefit through his method. These inhabitants of the Kurū kingdom rejoice upon seeing him;
they rejoice at the sight of you. Regarding "of the young brahmin": from what cause did your release come about from the presence of that young brahmin?
Or rather, by what reason did the release of that young brahmin who was setting you free occur? This is the meaning.
The Great Being said:
"O Lord of Men, that youth who addresses you as 'Sir' is not a human being, O best of heroic men.
If he is heard of by you, he is the yakkha named Puṇṇaka, the companion-in-arms of King Kuvera."
“There was a nāga named Varuṇa, the Earth-Sustainer, tall, pure,
and endowed with beauty and strength. Desiring his younger sister, that daughter of the nāgas named Irandhatī,
for the sake of that beloved woman with the slender waist, he plotted my death.”
“Thus I am united with my wife, and I have been granted permission and obtained the jewel.
In this regard, O Lord of Men, when you address him as “young man” (*māṇava*), he is one who dwells in the Nāga-abode of Bhūmindhara.
She is the Nāga maiden whom he desired, even at the cost of his own death.
She directed her mind [toward him], and that Naga maiden was named Irandhatī.
"For the sake of my beloved," O Great King, means that the Naga king, having gained faith by answering four questions on the Uposatha day, honored me with a jewel and returned to the Naga realm.
When Queen Vimalā did not see that jewel and asked, "Sire, where is the jewel?", he [the Naga king] told her of my status as a preacher of the Dhamma.
He praised it. She, desiring to hear my discourse on the Dhamma, conceived a longing in her heart for me.
However, the Naga king, having misunderstood the situation, said to his daughter Irandhatī: "Mother, you have a longing for the heart-flesh of Vidhura;
seek out a husband capable of bringing that heart-flesh. While she was searching, [she came upon] Vessavaṇa...
Having seen the yakkha named Puṇṇaka, his nephew, and knowing that his heart was bound to him, he led him to his father.
Then his father said to him, "If you are able to bring the heart-flesh of the wise Vidhura, you shall obtain Irandhatī.
Puṇṇaka, having brought from Mount Vepulla the wish-fulfilling gem (*maṇiratana*) used by a universal monarch, [arrived] together with you.
Having played at dice and defeated me, he won [me]. I, having had him dwell for three days in my own residence, paid him great honor.

He, too, having caused me to be seized by the horse’s tail and having struck me against trees and mountains in the Himalayas, being unable to kill me, entered the seventh whirlwind, the mouth of the Verambha wind, and proceeded by stages.

Although he was unable to kill me even after placing me on the summit of Mount Kāḷāgiri, which rises sixty yojanas high, and assuming various forms such as a lion and so forth, he questioned me about the cause of my own death when I asked him. Then I spoke to him concerning the virtuous conduct of good men.
Having heard that, his mind became clear and confident, and he desired to bring me here.
Then, taking him with me, I went to the abode of the nāgas and taught the Dhamma to the king of the nāgas and to Vimalā.
Thereupon, the nāga king, Vimalā, and the entire assembly of nāgas gained faith. When it was time for me to dwell there for six days, the nāga king gave Irandhatī to Puṇṇaka.
Having received her, he became full of confidence and offered me a jewel-treasure.
Having paid homage, the Nāga king was commanded; he mounted the mind-made steed, sat himself on the middle seat, had Irandhatī sit on the rear seat, and had me sit on the front seat.
Having come here and descended into the midst of the assembly, he took Irandhatī and returned to his own city. Thus, Great King, did Puṇṇaka treat her.
"For the sake of his beloved wife, he even attempted to cause my death. Yet, by relying on me, he has been reunited with his wife;

and having heard my discourse on the Dhamma, the Naga king, being filled with faith, granted my permission and obtained from Puṇṇaka this wish-fulfilling gem that provides all desires, as well as the enjoyment of a universal monarch. Take it!"
"Your Majesty," he said, and gave the king that jewel, the king's treasure.
Then, at dawn, desiring to tell the citizens of the dream he had seen himself, the king said, "Sirs, citizens, listen today to the dream seen by me," and spoke thus:
"A tree has grown well at my gate, with the aggregate of wisdom as its trunk and the branches made of virtue."
Established in both wealth and the Dhamma, wise, possessing cattle and fruit,
covered with elephants, cows, and horses— this man, having cut off his army amidst the resounding music of dance,
song, and instruments, has come back to our settlement; pay him honor for this tree.
“Whoever possess wealth through my favor, let them all display it today;
having prepared excellent offerings, pay honor to this tree.
Whoever are bound in fetters within my kingdom, let them all be released from their bonds.”
"Just as this one is released from bondage, so may these be released from bondage.
Let them plow this month with upturned plows; let the brahmins eat meat and rice;
let those who do not drink liquor drink the broth of cats, with their bowls full and overflowing."
“Let them constantly call upon the Great Path and establish fierce protection throughout the kingdom, so that they may not harm one another; perform this honoring of the tree.
In this context, “branches made of virtue” means the branches of this tree consist of virtue (*sīla*). “In meaning and in Dhamma” refers to prosperity and the Dhamma.
And by its very nature: "standing firm," that tree made of wisdom is firmly established. "Yielding cow-fruit" means it has the five kinds of milk products as its fruit.
"Covered with elephants, cows, and horses" means it is covered with decorated elephants, cows, and horses.
"Resounding with dance, song, and music" means that while the great multitude is performing worship for that tree, it is made to resound with these dances and so forth.

"A man has come and taken away the army after cutting it down"—one dark-skinned man arrived, cut down that tree, drove away the army that stood surrounding it, and having seized it, departed. Then that tree came back and stood right at the door of our residence.
This wise one, who resembles that tree, has come to our vicinity. Now, all of you [should follow] the tree's...
"Pay him honor; extend great hospitality toward him. 'By way of my requisites' means:
O ministers, let all those who have become joyful in heart through the fame and wealth obtained by depending on me now display their own riches.
'Tibbāni' means thick, vast, or great. 'Upāyanāni' means presents or offerings."
"Whatever there may be" means including even the birds and wild animals bound for the sake of sport.
"Let them be released" means let them go free. "Let them plow with their noses raised for this month" means:
having lifted the plows and set them aside for this month, let all the people in the city sound the drums and hold a great festival. "Let them eat" means let them consume [the crops].

"Amajjapāti": here, the syllable *a-* is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*); the meaning is: "Let those who drink liquor, the destroyers of themselves, sit down in their respective drinking places and drink.
"Puṇṇāhi thālāhi" means "with full bowls. "Palissutāhi" means "overflowing" because they are so full that they are dripping.
"Mahāpathaṃ nicca samavhayantu" means "let them constantly fill the great highway," that is, the royal road adorned within the city.
The meaning is: "Let the courtesans, standing there, constantly summon people who are driven by defilements through the power of those very defilements.

*Tibbaṃ* means "intense" or "firm. *Yathā* means: "Just as, because of the well-arranged protection, they might remain free from strife and, while paying honor to this tree, would not harm one another—thus let them arrange the protection," is the meaning.
When the king had spoken thus:
“Eunuchs and princes, courtesans and brahmins,
brought much food and drink for the wise man.”
“Elephant-riders, chariot-warriors, cavalrymen,
and foot-soldiers brought much food and drink to the wise man.
People from the countryside gathered, and merchants also gathered.”
They brought much food and drink for the wise one, saying:
"The multitude has confidence upon seeing that the wise one has arrived;
now that the wise one has come, let there be a waving of garments."

In that regard, "they brought [the gifts]" means: having been thus commanded by the king, they prepared a great festival, released all beings from their bonds, and having arranged various kinds of offerings for all these women of the harem and others, they sent food and drink along with them to the wise man.
"When the wise man arrived" means: when the wise man had come, upon seeing him, the multitude became full of faith.
The festival reached its conclusion within a month. Then, as if accomplishing the work of a Buddha, the Great Being taught the Dhamma to the great multitude and instructed the king;
having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, he remained for the duration of his lifespan and, at the end of his life, was destined for heaven.
Beginning with the king, all the city-dwellers likewise stood by the advice of the wise man.
Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, they filled the city of heaven at the end of their lives.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, the Tathāgata was endowed with wisdom and skilled in means," and he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the wise man’s parents were the royal families."
“His eldest wife was Rāhula’s mother; his eldest son was Rāhula; Vimalā was Uppalavaṇṇā; Varuṇa the Nāga King was Sāriputta;
Supaṇṇa the King of Birds was Moggallāna; Sakka was Anuruddha; Dhanañjaya the Koraṇya King was Ānanda; Puṇṇaka was Channa;
the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly; and as for the wise Vidhura, he was none other than myself, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
The ninth: The Exposition of the Vidhura Jātaka.
10. The Exposition of the Vessantara Jātaka:
The Exposition of the Ten Boons.
"Phussatī of excellent complexion"— this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at the Nigrodha Monastery near Kapilavatthu,
concerning the rain of lotuses. For when the Teacher, having set the supreme Wheel of Dhamma in motion,
had gradually proceeded to Rājagaha and spent the winter there, he was accompanied by twenty thousand arahants whose taints were destroyed, with the Elder Udāyī acting as his guide along the way.
On his first journey, he went to Kapilavatthu. At that time, the Sakyans, thinking, "We shall see our own foremost kinsman," assembled together;

while searching for a suitable dwelling place for the Blessed One, they observed that "the Nigrodha Sakka’s monastery is delightful," and having prepared all the arrangements there, they set out with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in their hands.
To welcome him, they first sent out young city boys and girls, all adorned with every kind of ornament, followed by the princes and princesses.

In their midst, having personally honored the Teacher with perfumes, flowers, powders, and other offerings, they took the Blessed One and proceeded to the Nigrodha Monastery. There, the Blessed One was surrounded by twenty thousand arahants whose taints were destroyed.
He sat down upon the excellent Buddha-throne that had been prepared. At that time, the Sākyans were of a proud nature and stiff with arrogance.

Thinking, "This Prince Siddhattha is younger than we; he is our junior, our nephew, our son, and our grandson," they said to the very young princes and princesses, "You should pay homage to the Blessed One; we [shall pay homage] to you."
"We shall sit behind them.
While they were thus sitting without having paid homage, the Blessed One, observing their disposition, thought: "My kinsmen do not pay homage to me;
well then, I shall now cause them to pay homage. He then entered the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge, and emerging from that, he—
Rising into the air, as if scattering the dust from his feet upon their heads, he performed a miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree similar to the Twin Miracle at the root of the Yaṃaka tree.

King Suddhodana, seeing that marvel, said: "Venerable sir, on the day you were born, when you were brought for Kāḷadevala to pay homage, your feet turned around and stood upon the head of the brahmin."
Having seen [you], I bowed at your feet; this was my first salutation.

Again, on the auspicious day of the Vappa festival, having seen that you were seated upon the couch of glory under the shade of a rose-apple tree and that the shadow of the rose-apple tree did not shift from you, I bowed at your feet;
this was my second salutation. Now, having seen this unprecedented miracle as well—

“I bow at your feet; this is my third salutation. When the king had thus paid homage, there was not even a single member of the Sākiya clan who was able to remain standing without bowing; indeed, they all paid homage.
Having thus caused his kinsmen to pay homage, the Blessed One descended from the sky and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared. Once he was seated...
And when the Blessed One had attained the crest-lock stage, there was a gathering of kinsmen; they all sat down with one-pointed minds.
Then a great cloud arose and rained a shower of lotuses; the copper-colored water went rumbling below.
Those who wished to get wet were drenched, but not even a single drop fell upon the body of him who did not wish to be wetted. That—
Seeing this, they were all struck with a sense of wonder and amazement. “Oh, how wonderful! Oh, how marvelous!
Oh, how great is the power of the Buddhas, that such a rain of lotuses fell during the gathering of their kinsmen! Thus the monks began a discussion.
Hearing this, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, at the gathering of my kinsmen—”
"Only a great cloud will rain down raindrops," he said; and being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while the Great King Sivi was ruling his kingdom in the city of Jetuttara in the realm of Sivi, he obtained a son named Sañjaya.
When the prince had reached maturity, the king brought him the royal maiden named Phussatī, the daughter of the King of Madda.
Having handed over the kingdom, he made Phussatī his chief queen. This was her past connection:
ninety-one aeons ago, a Teacher named Vipassī arose in the world.
While he was dwelling in the Khema Deer Park near the city of Bandhumatī, a certain king [offered] to King Bandhuma a priceless sandalwood heart along with a hundred-thousand [pieces of gold].
He sent a golden garland. Now the king had two daughters;
wishing to give that gift to them, he gave the choice sandalwood to the elder and the golden garland to the younger.
Both of them, thinking, "We shall not wear this upon our own bodies, but shall instead honor the Teacher," addressed the king.
They said, "Father, we shall honor the One of Ten Powers with sandalwood essence and a golden garland. Upon hearing this, the king accepted it, saying, "Very well.
The eldest daughter had fine sandalwood powder prepared, filled a golden casket, and had it brought to her.
The youngest sister, however, had a golden garland and a breast-plate garland fashioned, and [placed them] in a golden casket.

She had [the powder] taken. Both of them went to the Migadāya Monastery; the elder sister, having honored the golden-colored body of the One of Ten Powers with sandalwood powder, scattered the remaining powder inside the Gandhakuṭī and made this aspiration:
"Venerable Sir, may I become the mother of a Buddha such as you in the future. The younger sister likewise [honored] the golden-colored [body] of the Tathāgata...

Having honored the body with a breast-cloth made of golden garlands, she made this aspiration: "Venerable Sir, until I attain Arahatship, may this ornament not depart from my body. The Teacher also offered words of thanksgiving for them.
Both of them, having lived out their full lifespan, were reborn in the world of the devas. Of those two, the elder sister [descended] from the world of the devas...
Migrating from the human world to the celestial world, at the conclusion of ninety-one *kappas*, during the time of our own Buddha’s appearance, she became the Buddha’s mother named Queen Mahāmāyā.

Her younger sister likewise migrated in the same manner and was born during the time of the Great Sage Kassapa as the daughter of King Kiki. She [was adorned] with a breast-covering garland that appeared as if it were fashioned by a master artist.
Because she was born from an adorned breast, she became a maiden named Uracchadā.
At the age of sixteen, having heard the Teacher’s expression of gratitude after a meal (*bhattānumodana*), she established herself in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*).

Later, on the very day her father attained the fruit of stream-entry while listening to that same expression of gratitude after a meal, she reached Arahantship, went forth, and attained final Nibbāna. King Kiki also had seven other daughters.
They obtained [the status of female stream-enterers]. Their names were:
“The ascetic (samaṇī), the one protected by the ascetics (samaṇaguttā), the nun (bhikkhunī), the giver of alms (bhikkhadāyikā);
Dhammā and Sudhammā, and Saṅghadāsī as the seventh.”
In this present arising of a Buddha, they are as follows: “Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā, Paṭācārā and Gotamī;
Dhammadinnā, Mahāmāyā, and Visākhā as the seventh.”
Among them, she named Phussatī, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving,
was born with a body that seemed as if sprinkled with the essence of red sandalwood due to the fruit of her offering of sandalwood powder to the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipassī;
thus, as a maiden named Phussatī, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and later, among the Sakkas...

She was reborn as the chief queen of the king of the gods. After she had lived there for the full span of her life and the five portents had appeared, Sakka, the king of the gods, knowing that her lifespan was exhausted, took her with great splendor and went to the Nandana grove.
There, while she sat upon a decorated couch, he himself sat by the side of the couch.
Having sat down, he said this: “Bhadde Phussati, I grant you ten boons; take them.
Speaking thus, he recited the first verse in this *Mahāvessantarajātaka*, which is adorned with a thousand verses:
“O Phussati of radiant and excellent complexion, choose ten boons as you wish.”
"O lady with beautiful limbs, who are dear to my heart!"—in this way, this teaching on the Dhamma by Mahā-Vessantara is said to have been established in the world of the devas.
Therein, "Phussati" is an address using her name. "Varavaṇṇābhe" means endowed with excellent complexion and radiance.
"Tenfold" means of ten kinds. "Of the earth" (*pathabyā*)—having taken it as referring to the earth that is to be grasped—he says, "Choose," meaning "take.
"With a beautiful forepart" means endowed with a beautiful forepart, which is a noble mark (*varalakkhaṇa*).
"Whatever is dear to your mind"—whatever is dear to your mind, take each of those with ten portions; thus he speaks.
Not realizing her own subjectivity to death, she became heedless and spoke the second verse:
“O King of Devas, homage be to you! What evil have I committed?
You have driven me from this delightful place, like the wind from a tree.”
In this context, *namo* means *atthu*: "Homage be to you. "What evil? she asks, meaning: "What evil have I committed in your presence? *Dharaṇīruha* means a tree.
Then, knowing her state of negligence, Sakka spoke two verses:
"Indeed, no evil has been done by you, nor are you unloved by me;..."
“Your merit has been exhausted, which is why I speak thus to you:
‘Death is near for you; there will be separation from what you hold dear.
Accept these from me as I grant you ten boons.’”
In that context, "by which I say to you" means "by which I speak thus to you. "Separation from you" means your parting from us. "To one who bestows" means to one who gives.
Having heard Sakka’s words and having ascertained with certainty her own death, she spoke while choosing a boon:
"If a boon is granted to me, O Sakka, Lord of all beings,"
“O Blessed One, may I dwell there in the residence of King Śibi.
There, O Vanquisher of Cities, I would see her named Phussatī— blue-eyed, with blue eyebrows and blue pupils, like a doe.”
“May she obtain a son who is a giver of boons, devoted to making requests,
free from stinginess, honored by rival kings, renowned, and illustrious.
While she carries the fetus, may her waist not be prominent.”
May my belly not protrude, but be smooth like a drawn bow.
May my breasts not sag, nor may grey hairs appear, O Vāsava.
May dust not soil my body, and may I release even one condemned to death.
Resounding with the cries of peacocks and herons, filled with throngs of excellent women,
crowded with hunchbacks, female slaves, and dwarfs, and praised by bards and panegyrists;
noisy with the clamor of variegated throats, and stimulating with liquor and meat.
“O Venerable One, may I be the beloved chief queen of King Sivi there.
In this context, “of King Sivi” means that she, looking over the entire surface of Jambudīpa, saw a residence of King Sivi that was suitable for herself;
longing for the position of chief queen there, she spoke thus. “Just as a doe” refers to one who is one year old.
For the young doe has blue eyes; therefore he spoke thus. "There they see" means there too they would see her by this very name.

"May I obtain" (*labheyyaṃ*) means may I receive. "O Giver of Boons" (*varadaṃ*) refers to one who gives whatever excellent things are requested—whether it be a decorated head, a pair of eyes, the flesh and blood of the heart, a white parasol, a son, or a wife.
"Womb" (*kucchi*) is stated as "the middle limb" (*majjhimaaṅga*) according to its actual form.
He shows [this]. "Well-drawn" means: just as a bow well-drawn by a skilled archer is even—neither too high in the middle nor too low, but balanced like a scale—may my belly be of such a form.
"May they not hang down" means: having fallen, they should not be pendulous. "O Vāsava, may there be no grey hairs"—Vāsava is the best of gods.
"May there be no grey hairs upon my head; may they not appear. (The reading "palitāni siroruhā" [grey hairs on the head] is also found.
"And even one deserving of death"—meaning I would be capable of releasing by my own power a thief who has committed a crime against the king and has reached the point of execution.
By this, he demonstrates his state of sovereignty. "In the description of the Magadhan meal," etc., refers to the manner of praising [the food] at times such as the mealtime.
In such a royal residence of King Sivi, where the charioteers and the Magadhan heralds announced the time;
where the door-panels, variegated with the seven precious gems, resounded with a delightful noise like the sound of fivefold musical instruments, proclaiming, "The red gates are now whitened";
and where the people were being awakened by wine and meat with cries of, "Drink! Eat!"—in such a place as this.
He took these ten boons, saying, "May she become his chief queen.
Therein, the first boon was the status of chief queen for King Sivi; the second was having blue eyes; the third was having blue eyebrows;
the fourth was the name Phussatī; the fifth was the obtaining of a son; the sixth was having an unprotuberant belly.
"Longevity is the seventh, the state of being free from grey hair is the eighth, the state of having delicate skin is the ninth, and the power to release those condemned to death is the tenth boon.
Sakka said:
"These ten boons have been granted by me to you, O lady beautiful in every limb;"
“In the realm of King Sivi, you shall obtain all those boons.

Then Sakka, the king of the gods, granted ten boons to Phussati. Having given them, he said, “May all these be fulfilled for you, O blessed Phussati,” and offered his approval. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having spoken thus, Maghavā, the king of the gods, the lord of the Sujā, [bestowed the boons].”
"Having granted a boon to Phussatī, Vāsava expressed his appreciation.
In this context, "expressed his appreciation" means that after granting the boons in this manner—saying, "You shall obtain all those boons"—he was delighted and became joyful in mind.
The Discourse on the Ten Boons is concluded.
The Description of Himavanta:
Thus, having been taken up by that noble one, she passed away from there and was reborn in the womb of the chief queen of King Madda.
And as she was being born, she was born with a body as if strewn with sandalwood powder. Therefore, on the day of her naming, she was given the name "Phussatī."
They gave her a name. As she grew up with a great retinue, at the age of sixteen, she possessed the most excellent beauty.
Then King Sivi brought her for his son, Prince Sañjaya;
having raised the royal parasol over him and made her the senior among sixteen thousand women, he established her in the position of chief queen. Thus it is said:
“Then, having passed away from there, Phussatī was reborn at Chattiya;
in the city of Jetuttara, she met with Sañjaya.
She became dear and pleasing to Sañjaya. Then Sakka, reflecting upon her, [considered] among the boons granted by me to Phussatī—
Seeing that nine excellent boons had been fulfilled, he thought, "But one boon regarding a son has not yet been granted; I shall cause even that to be fulfilled.
At that time, the Great Being was dwelling in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and his lifespan had come to an end.
Knowing this, Sakka went to him and said, "Venerable sir, it is fitting for you to go to the human world; there—"
"It is fitting for me to take rebirth in the womb of the chief queen of King Sivi.
Having said this, and having obtained the promise of sixty thousand other sons of the gods who were subject to death, he returned to his own place.
The Great Being, passing away from there, was conceived therein; and the remaining sons of the gods [were conceived] among the sixty thousand ministers.
They were reborn in their respective homes. When the Great Being had entered her womb, Phussatī became pregnant with longing;

she had six alms-halls constructed at six locations—namely, at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the gate of the royal palace—and desiring to give great gifts, she began to distribute six hundred thousand coins every day.
When the king heard of her pregnancy longing, he summoned the brahmins skilled in omens and questioned them.
The fortune-tellers said, "Great King, a being devoted to giving has been conceived in the queen’s womb; she will never reach satiety with giving.
Hearing this, the king was delighted in heart; he had six halls for almsgiving constructed and established the aforementioned kind of giving.
From the time of the Bodhisatta’s conception, there was no longer any limit to the king’s income.
Through the power of his merit, the kings of the entire Jambudīpa sent him tribute.
The queen, carrying her child with a large retinue, when the ten months were complete, desired to see the city and informed the king. The king—
Having adorned the city like a city of the gods and having placed the queen upon an excellent chariot, he caused her to circumambulate the city.
When she reached the middle of the street of the Vessas, the winds of karma stirred.
Then the ministers informed the king. Upon hearing this, he had a birth-chamber constructed right there in the street of the Vessas and had her take up residence there.
There she gave birth to my son. Therefore it was said:
"Having carried me for ten months, Performing a circumambulation of the city, In the middle of the merchants' street, Phussatī brought me forth."
As soon as the Mahāsatta emerged from his mother’s womb, he became free from impurity; opening his eyes, he came forth.
Immediately upon emerging, he extended his hand toward his mother and said, “Mother, I wish to give alms; do you have any wealth?
Then his mother replied, “My son, give alms according to your own inclination,” and placed a purse containing a thousand coins into his outstretched hand.
For in the *Ummagga Jātaka*, in this present birth, and in his final existence—thus in three places—the Great Being spoke with his mother immediately upon being born.
On the day of his naming, because he was born in the street of the Vessas, they gave him the name "Vessantara.
Therefore it is said:
“Neither my name is derived from my mother’s side, nor is it born of my father’s side;
I was born on Vessavīthi, therefore I am called Vessantara.
On the very day of his birth, a female elephant roaming through the sky brought a completely white elephant calf, which was considered auspicious.
Having brought him back and placed him in the auspicious elephant-stable, he departed.
Because he had arisen on account of the Great Being as his condition (*paccaya*), they gave him the name "Paccaya. On that very day, sixty thousand boys were born in the houses of the ministers.
The king, avoiding such faults as being too tall for the Great Being, [selected] sixty-four *alambathani* cows with sweet milk.
He appointed nurses for himself, and for each of the sixty thousand boys born with him, he appointed one nurse.
Thus, surrounded by a great retinue of sixty thousand boys, he grew up.
Then the king had a princely ornament made for him worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. When he was four or five years old, he [put on] that...
Having removed it and given it to the nurses, he did not accept it even when they offered it back to him. They reported this to the king.
Upon hearing it, the king said, "Let what was given by my son remain as a *brahmadeyya* (a royal gift to a Brahmin)," and he had another set made.
The prince gave that away as well. Thus, even during his childhood, he gave ornaments to the nurses nine times.
But at the age of eight, while seated upon his royal couch within the excellent palace, he thought: "I give only external gifts;
this does not satisfy me. I desire to give internal gifts. If anyone were to ask for my head, I would cut off my head and give it to him.
Even if someone were to ask for my heart, I would break open my chest and [give] the heart."
Having extracted it, I would give it. If he should ask for my eyes, I would pluck out my eyes and give them.
If he should ask for the flesh of my body, I would cut the flesh from my entire body and give it.
Even if someone should ask me for my blood, I would take the blood and give it. Or if someone should say, "Be my slave," I would offer myself to him.

“Having made him a slave, I shall give him [to you]. As he was thus reflecting on his own nature, this great earth—four hundred and twenty-four thousand yojanas in thickness—trembled, roaring like a noble, rutting elephant.
Sineru, the king of mountains, bent down like a well-tended bamboo sprout and stood facing the city of Jetuttara. With the sound of the earth, the gods roared and sent down a brief rain.
It rained, untimely lightning flashed, and the ocean was stirred. Sakka, king of the gods, clapped his hands, and Mahābrahmā gave his approval.
From the surface of the earth up to the Brahma-world, there was a single great uproar.
And this has also been said:
“When I was a young boy, eight years from birth,
while sitting in the palace, I thought of giving a gift.
‘I would give my heart, my eye, my flesh, and even my blood.’”
“Having announced that I would give my body, if anyone were to ask me for it—
while I was contemplating its true nature, which is unshakable and immovable— the earth, with Mount Sineru and its forest garlands as its ornament, trembled there.”
The Bodhisatta reached mastery in all the arts at the very age of sixteen.

Then his father, desiring to give him the kingdom, consulted with his mother; he brought from the royal house of Madda a princess named Maddī, the daughter of his maternal uncle, and having made her the chief consort over sixteen thousand women, he consecrated the Great Being in the kingship.
From the time the Mahāsatta was established in his kingdom, he bestowed a great almsgiving, distributing six hundred thousand [pieces of gold] every day.
Later on, Queen Maddi gave birth to a son. They received him with a golden net, and therefore they gave him the name Jālī Kumāra.
When he was able to walk on foot, she gave birth to a daughter.
They received him with a black antelope skin, and so they gave her the name "Kaṇhājinā.
Six times a month, the Great Being, mounted upon the back of a magnificent, adorned state elephant, surveyed the six halls of almsgiving.
At that time, there was a drought in the kingdom of Kāliṅga; the crops failed, and a great fear of hunger arose among the people.
Unable to survive, people committed acts of theft. Oppressed by famine, the country folk gathered in the royal courtyard and reproached the king.
Upon hearing this, when the king asked, "What is it, sirs? they reported the matter to him.
The king said, "Very well, sirs; I shall cause the rain-god to send rain," and having dismissed them, he undertook the observance of the Uposatha while maintaining his moral precepts.

Even Vāsava was unable to make the god rain. He assembled the citizens and asked, "Though I have observed the seven-day Uposatha fast while maintaining my moral precepts, I have still been unable to make the god rain; what indeed should be done?
[The people replied,] "If you, O Lord, are unable to make the god rain, this son of King Sañjaya from the city of Jetuttara..."
There was one named Vessantara who delighted in giving. It is said that he possessed a magnificent all-white elephant, and wherever it went, the rain fell.
“It is fitting to send brahmins to request that elephant; please give the command,” [the king] said.
Having agreed, saying “Very well,” he assembled the brahmins and selected eight among them who were endowed with excellent qualities.
Having investigated their needs and provided them with travel expenses, he sent them forth, saying, "Go, and having requested the elephant Vessantara from him, bring it back.
The brahmins traveled by stages to the city of Jetuttara;
there they ate at the alms-hall, covered their bodies with dust and dirt, and on the full-moon day approached the king for the elephant.
Desiring to beg, they went to the eastern gate at the time when the king was coming to the head of the almsgiving procession.

The king also, thinking, “I shall look upon the head of the almsgiving,” rose early in the morning, bathed, ate various kinds of exquisite food, adorned himself, and, mounted upon the back of a magnificent, decorated state elephant, proceeded to the eastern gate.
The brahmins, finding no space there, went to the southern gate and stood on a high place.

Having stood at the eastern gate of the king’s alms-hall and watched it, they extended their hands as he was approaching from the southern gate and cried out three times, “Victory to you, O Lord Vessantara!
When the Great Being saw those brahmins, he directed the elephant toward the place where they were standing;
seated upon the elephant’s neck, he spoke the first verse:
“With their armpits, nails, and body hair grown long, with teeth stained by dirt and veins showing,
why do these brahmins, raising their right arms, beg from me? The brahmins replied:
“O King, increaser of the realm of the Sivis, we ask for a treasure:
grant us the noble elephant, the tusker with tusks like plow-poles, who is capable of being mounted.
In this context, “capable of being mounted” means fit for riding.
Having heard this, the Great Being thought, “I am desirous of giving the gift of my own internal body, beginning with my head;
yet these people ask me only for external things. I shall fulfill their wish. Having reflected thus, while seated upon the back of his noble elephant, he spoke the third verse:
“I give and do not waver, whatever the brahmins ask of me.”
“A tusker elephant in rut, a tamer, a mount for riding, the best of elephants.
Having thus identified him, the king,
his mind overflowing with generosity, descended from the back of the elephant and said:
“The giver of gifts to the brahmins, the increaser of the kingdom of the Sivis.
In this context, *opavayha* means a royal vehicle. *Cāgādhimāno* refers to the king whose mind was preeminent in generosity.
“He gave gifts to the brahmins”: having circumambulated the elephant three times to the right in order to look at its unadorned parts...
Seeing no spot that was not adorned, he took a golden water-pot filled with fragrant water mixed with flowers and said,
"Come this way. Grasping the trunk of the elephant— which resembled a decorated silver chain— and placing it in their hands,
he poured out the water and gave the adorned elephant to the brahmins.
The ornamentation on its four feet is worth four hundred thousand; the ornamentation on both sides is worth two hundred thousand;
the blanket on its belly below is worth one hundred thousand;
on its back are three nets—the net of pearls, the net of jewels, and the net of gold—worth three hundred thousand; and the ornamentation on both ears is worth two hundred thousand.
The blanket spread upon his back was worth a hundred thousand; the ornament for his forehead was worth a hundred thousand; the three crest-ornaments were worth three hundred thousand;
the ornament for his ears and head was worth two hundred thousand; the ornament for his two tusks was worth two hundred thousand;
the svastika ornament on his trunk was worth a hundred thousand; and the ornament for his tail was worth a hundred thousand.
The ladder for ascending was worth one hundred thousand; the food bowl was worth one hundred thousand;
and setting aside priceless goods, the ornaments worn on the body were worth twenty-two hundred thousand. Thus, that much wealth amounts to two million four hundred thousand.
Furthermore, there was a gem in the sunshade-handle, a crest-jewel, a gem in the pearl necklace, a gem in the hook, and a gem on the elephant’s neck.
The pearl used for the head-wrap, the gem on the elephant’s forehead, and the gems on its temples—these six were priceless;
and since the elephant itself was also priceless, there were seven priceless items including the elephant. He gave all of these to the brahmins.
Likewise, he gave five hundred families who were attendants of the elephant, together with the elephant-herders and the elephant-guards. Along with that gift...
In the very manner described below, earthquakes and other portents occurred. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then there was that which was terrifying, then there was that which caused the hair to stand on end;
when the noble elephant was given away, the earth trembled all over.”
“At that time there was terror, at that time there was hair-raising horror;
when the noble elephant was given away, the city was then thrown into agitation.
The town was completely overwhelmed, and a vast, great clamor arose.”
“When the elephant-nāga was given away, increasing the kingdom of the Sivi people.
Therein, *tadāsī* means “at that time it was. *Hatthināge* means “in the nāga known as the elephant. *Khubhittha nagaraṃ tadā* means “at that time the city of Jetuttara was shaken.
It is said that the brahmins, having obtained the elephant at the southern gate, sat upon its back and were surrounded by a great multitude.
They went through the middle of the city. When the great multitude saw them, they said, "O brahmins, you have mounted our elephant;
where did you obtain this elephant? The brahmins, repelling the crowd with gestures of their hands and other such means, saying, "The Great King Vessantara gave us the elephant;
who are you?", proceeded through the middle of the city and out by the northern gate.
They departed. The citizens, enraged by the turning of the deities, gathered at the palace gate and raised a great outcry.
Thus it was said: “The city was thrown into total confusion, and a vast, loud clamor arose.”
When the elephant Nāga was given away, increasing the realm of the Sivis,
a tumultuous, terrifying, and great noise arose there;
when the elephant Nāga was given away, the city was then thrown into agitation.

“Then there arose a sound, tumultuous, terrifying, and great, when the noble elephant was given away, he who increased the kingdom of the Sivi people. In this context, *ghosa* means the sound of lamentation;
it is *vipula* because it has spread far and wide, and *mahā* because it has risen high. “Increasing the kingdom of the Sivi people” means causing the prosperity of the Sivi realm.
Then the city-dwellers, their minds agitated by his giving, reported it to the king. Thus it is said:
“The Uggas and the princes, the Vessikas and the Brahmins;
The elephant-riders, the cavalrymen, the chariot-fighters, and the foot-soldiers.”
“The entire town and the Sivis gathered together;
seeing the elephant being led away, they informed the king:
‘O Lord, your son Vessantara is destroying your kingdom.’”
"How might you give us the elephant, honored by the kingdom?
'How might you give us the tusker, with tusks like plow-poles, broad-backed, knowing the field in all battles, all-white, the supreme among elephants? "
“Covered with a pale-white blanket, a crusher of enemies,
a rutting elephant with its trunk like a fly-whisk, white and resembling Mount Kelāsa;
accompanied by a white parasol, a footstool, a palanquin, and a hand-drum.”
“O King, he gave the elephant, the foremost vehicle that carries royalty, to the brahmins.
In this context, *uggā* means those who are eminent and renowned. *Nigama* refers to the people of the towns, the householders.
“O King, your kingdom is being destroyed”—that is, O King, your kingdom is being ruined. “Why would you give us the elephant?”—by what reason would you give the elephant to us?
One should give it to the brahmins dwelling in the Kāliṅga country, who are esteemed for their auspiciousness.

"An expert in all battles" means one capable of knowing the strategic positions and terrain of all battles. "With tusked [elephants]" means equipped with beautiful tusks. "With a yak-tail fan" means together with a yak-tail fan.
"With a coverlet" means together with a rug. "With a goad" means together with a driver's whip. "With a hand-guard" means together with a hand-protector.
"Along with the five hundred families of elephant attendants, as well as the elephant trainers and elephant keepers, it is 'with the elephants' (sahatthipaṃ).
Having spoken thus, they further said:
"Whoever should give food and drink, and clothing and lodgings..."
“This indeed is a fitting gift; this indeed is worthy of Brahmins.
“This is your ancestral king, the increaser of the realm of the Sivis;
how is it that Vessantara, your son, gives away the elephant, Sañjaya?”
“If you do not carry out these words of the Sivi people, I think the Sivi will seize you along with your son.

In this context, *vaṃsarāja* means a great king descended through a lineage. *Bhājeti* means he gives. *Sivī hatthe karissare* means that the inhabitants of the kingdom of Sivi will take him, together with his son, into their own hands.
Hearing this, the king, perceiving that they wished to have Vessantara killed, said:
"Let the countryside perish, and let even the kingdom be destroyed;
yet I will not, at the word of the Sivi people, [punish] the prince who is without fault."
“I would banish him from my own kingdom, for he is my own biological son.
‘Let the countryside perish, and let even the realm be destroyed;
yet I will not, at the word of the Sivi people, exile the prince who has done no wrong.’”
"I would banish my own son from my kingdom, for he is my biological offspring.
Yet I could not betray him, for he possesses the virtue of a noble one;
otherwise, I would incur ill repute and generate much demerit."
“How shall we have Vessantara’s son executed by the sword?

Therein, *māsī* means “let it not be,” that is, “let it not happen. *Ariyasīlavato* means one endowed with noble virtue and noble perfection of conduct. *Ghātayāmase* means “we shall have him executed.
Having heard this, the Śivis said:
"Do not strike him with staff or sword, for he is not worthy of imprisonment;
rather, banish him from the kingdom, and let him dwell on a crooked mountain.

In this context, "Do not strike him with staff or sword" means: O King, you must not have him killed by either staff or sword. "For he is not worthy of imprisonment" means that he is certainly not even fit for confinement.
The king said:
"If this is the desire of the Sivis, we shall not reject that desire;
let him dwell here for this night and enjoy sensual pleasures."
“Then, at the end of the night, as the sun was rising, let them, having become united as Śivis, banish him from the kingdom.
In this context, by saying “let him dwell,” he is giving advice to his son and wife, saying: “Let him dwell; give him the opportunity for even a single night.”
They accepted the king’s command, saying, “Let him stay for just one night.
Then the king, having dismissed them, sent for Kattāra and dispatched him to his son’s presence to deliver a message.
He consented, saying, “Very well,” went to Vessantara’s residence, and reported the matter to him. To illustrate this point, the Teacher said:
“Arise, Katta! Go quickly and speak to Vessantara:
‘The Sivis, O King, are angry with you, as are the assembled townspeople.
The nobles, the princes, the merchants, and the brahmins—’”
Elephant-riders and those who serve in the ranks, charioteers and foot-soldiers,
as well as the entire town and the Sivis gathered together:
"At the end of this night, toward the rising of the sun, we shall go."
“Having become united as Śivis, they banish him from the kingdom. He,
acting with haste as he was sent by King Śibi,
had ornaments fastened upon his hands, was well-clothed, and adorned with sandalwood paste.
“Having bathed his head in water and adorned himself with jeweled earrings,
he approached the delightful city, the residence of Vessantara.
There he saw the prince enjoying himself in his own city.”
Surrounded by his ministers, like Vāsava among the Thirty-three gods, he went there in haste and said to the maker, Vessantara:
"I shall cause you suffering; do not be angry with me, O bull among charioteers."
Having paid homage and weeping, Kattā said to the king:
"I am your servant, O Great King, the provider of all flavors of sensual pleasure.
I shall experience suffering for you; let them comfort me there."
“O King, the Śivis are enraged, as are the assembled townspeople:
the Ugras, the princes, the Vaiśyas, and the Brāhmaṇas;
the elephant-riders, the cavalry, the chariot-warriors, and the infantry.”
“The entire town and the Sivis have gathered together:
‘At the end of this night, at the rising of the sun,
having become united as Sivis, they will banish him from the kingdom.’”
Therein, "the prince" refers to the king who, while his parents were still living, was designated as such;
"rejoicing" means sitting down having attained a state of gladness while speaking in praise of the alms he had given himself;
"surrounded by ministers" means being encircled by the sixty thousand ministers born together with him, beneath a raised white parasol.
"Seated upon the royal throne. "I shall inform you"—that is, I shall speak. Regarding the phrase "may they comfort me," the intention is:
"O King, since I am exhausted by the inability to speak when reporting this painful news, may your feet comfort me;
speak with confidence. Thus he said.
The Great Being said:
“With what am I angry, that my fawns are so? I see no misdeed of mine.
Tell me this, O hunter: why do they drive me away?”
In that context, "in what" means for what reason. "Explain" means speak in detail.
The author said:
"The Uggas, the princes, the Vesiyans, and the Brahmins..."
“Elephant-riders, those who serve in the army, chariot-warriors, and foot-soldiers—because of the gift of an elephant, they become resentful; therefore, they cause him to be expelled.
In this context, “they become resentful” means they grow angry.
Having heard this, the Great Being was filled with joy and said:
"I would give my heart and my eyes; what need have I for external wealth—be it gold or silver, pearls, beryl, or gems?"
“Seeing a supplicant arrive, I would give my right arm away without wavering; my mind delights in giving.
Let all the Śivis wish to banish me or even kill me.”
"I shall not desist from giving; let them cut me into seven pieces as they wish.
In this context, "when the beggars have come" means when the beggars have arrived and he has seen that beggar. "I shall not desist from giving" means "I shall not cease from giving.
Having heard that, Kattā, neither because it was given by the king nor because it was given by the citizens, spoke another message according to his own judgment:
“Thus the Sivis and the assembled townspeople said:
‘Toward Mount Arañjara on the banks of the Kontimārā River—
let him of noble conduct go by the path where those who have gone forth travel.’”
In that context, "by the Kontimārā" means by the bank of the river named Kontimārā.

"Facing Girimārañjara" means facing toward the mountain named Ārañjara. "By which [path]"—the Sivi people spoke thus: "By whichever path kings who have been exiled from their kingdom travel, by that same path let Subba Vessantara also go. It is said that he spoke this while possessed by a deity.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta thought: "Excellent! I shall go by the same path as those who committed the offense.
Indeed, the citizens do not banish me for any other fault; they banish me because I gave [the lotus] to the elephant.
Even so, I shall give the Great Gift of Seven Hundred; let the citizens grant me the opportunity to give this gift for one day tomorrow."
Having said, "I will go on the third day after giving the gift," he spoke thus:
"I shall go by that same path by which the violators go;
forgive me for this night and day while I am giving the gift."
Having heard this, Kattā said, “Very well, Your Majesty, I shall inform the citizens,” and then he departed.
The Great Being, having dismissed him, summoned Mahāsenagutta and said, “Dear son, tomorrow I shall give the great gift known as the ‘Seven Hundreds’:
seven hundred elephants, seven hundred horses, seven hundred chariots, and seven hundred women.”
"Prepare seven hundred cows, seven hundred male slaves, and seven hundred female slaves;
and set out all that is fit to be given, including various kinds of food and drink, even down to liquor," he said.
Having thus arranged the great gift of the "Seven Hundreds" and dispatched his ministers, he went alone to Maddi’s dwelling place and sat upon the back of his state couch.
Having sat down, he engaged in conversation with her. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“He addressed the king, saying: ‘Maddī, who is beautiful in every limb, whatever wealth and grain have been given to you by me still exist.’”
“Gold or silver, many pearls and beryl gems—all that you should bury as a hoard, as well as the wealth inherited from your father.
In this context, “you should bury” means you should set it aside as a treasure-store. “Inherited from your father” means that which has come down from the paternal line.
“Maddī, the princess, beautiful in all her limbs, said to him:
‘Where, O Lord, shall I deposit it? Tell me that when you are asked.

In this context, “she said to him” means: she thought, “My husband Vessantara has never before told me, ‘Deposit wealth,’ yet now he says so; where indeed should it be deposited? I shall ask him. Having thus reflected, she spoke to him.
Vessantara said:
“O Maddi, you should give gifts to those who are virtuous, according to their worth;
for there is no support for all living beings greater than giving.”

In this regard, "you should give," O Bhaddā, means that Maddī, instead of burying it as a following treasure in storehouses and such, you should give it to those possessed of virtue. For there is no support higher than giving; indeed, there is nothing superior to giving.
She accepted his words, saying, "Very well. Then, instructing her further, he said:
"Maddī, show compassion toward your children, and toward your mother-in-law and father-in-law."
"Whoever considers you a husband should serve you with diligence.
If you do not consider me your husband, then because we shall dwell apart, seek another husband; do not suffer distress without me."
In this context, "you should show compassion" means you should exercise loving-kindness (*mettā*).
And as for "whosoever might consider himself your husband": O Bhaddā, whosoever, upon my departure, might think, "I shall be your husband," you should attend to him with due care.
"By reason of my absence from you" means: if, because of my being away from you, someone [should say], "I shall be your husband."
She should not think of him; rather, she should seek another husband for herself.
"Do not be distressed without me" means: having been separated from me, do not become emaciated, do not suffer.
Then Maddī, thinking, "What kind of words is he speaking to me? said, "Why, O King?"
"Why did you speak such an improper word? he asked. The Great Being replied, "My lady, because I gave [the elephant] away, the Śivis are angry and are banishing me from the kingdom.
Tomorrow I shall give the great gift of seven hundred [elephants], and on the third day I will depart from the city.
Having said this, he spoke further:
“I am indeed going to the forest, which is filled with fierce wild beasts;
my life is in jeopardy, being all alone in the great wilderness.

In this context, “in jeopardy” (saṃsaya) means: “Since I am living alone in the forest, delicate as I am, and have many enemies, how can there be life for me? I shall certainly die”—it was with this intention that he spoke thus.
To him spoke the princess Maddī, beautiful in all her limbs:
"O groundless one, why do you speak thus? Indeed, you speak an evil word.
This is not the Dhamma, O Great King, that you should go alone."
“I too shall go with you, O Kṣatriya, wherever you go.
Death together with you, or life without you—
of these two, death is better than to live without you.”
“Having kindled a fire and concentrated it into a single flame,
death therein would be better for me than life without you.
Just as a female elephant follows a wild forest tusker,” so [I follow you].
“Even in mountain fastnesses, on level ground, and on uneven terrain—thus I shall follow you, taking your sons behind me.
I will be easy for you to support; I shall not be difficult for you to support.”
In that context, "abhūme" means: "Indeed, you would be speaking what is untrue to me.
"Nesa dhammo" means: this is not his nature; this is not the reason. "Tadeva" means: that very death which exists together with you is better.
"Tattha" means: in that single-net-like funeral pyre of wood. "Jessantaṃ" means: wandering about.
Having spoken thus, she again described the region of the Himalayas as if she had seen it before,
saying: "Beholding these two youths, gentle and sweet-spoken,
sitting in the forest thicket, you will not remember the kingdom."
“Beholding these youths, so charming and sweet-spoken,
playing in the forest thickets, you will not remember the kingdom.
Beholding these youths, so charming and sweet-spoken...”
"In this delightful hermitage, you will not think of the kingdom.
Seeing these two boys, so charming and sweet-spoken,
playing in the lovely hermitage, you will not think of the kingdom."
“Seeing these youths, wearing garlands and adorned with ornaments,
in this delightful hermitage, you will not remember the kingdom.
Seeing these youths, wearing garlands and adorned with ornaments...”
“Playing in delightful hermitages, you will not remember the kingdom.
When you see the young princes, wearing garlands,
dancing in the lovely hermitage, you will not remember the kingdom.”
“When you see young princes wearing garlands dancing and sporting in the delightful hermitage, you will not remember the kingdom.
When you see the elephant Mātanga, a sixty-year-old tusker...”
Wandering alone in the forest, you will not remember the kingdom.
When you see Mātanga, the sixty-year-old elephant,
roaming about at evening and at dawn, you will not remember the kingdom.
“When the sixty-year-old elephant, the lord of the herd, trumpets before the troop of she-elephants,
you will no longer remember the pleasures of the kingdom upon hearing him cry out.”
“When you see the giver of desires flourishing with a forest on both sides,
you will no longer remember the kingdom in that forest teeming with wild beasts.
Having seen a deer in the evening, come to you wearing a garland of five flowers,” [he said].
And while the *kimpurisa* spirits dance, you will not think of the kingdom.
When you hear the roar of the flowing river and the singing of the *kimpurisa* spirits, you will not think of the kingdom.
“When you hear the cry of the owl dwelling within the mountain caves as it hoots, you will not remember your kingdom.
When you hear the roar of the lion, the tiger, the leopard, and the wild ox...”
In the forest you will hear the cries of wild beasts, and you will not remember the kingdom.
When you see the peacock dancing, surrounded by peahens, with his tail-feathers spread out and standing at the top of the tree, you will not remember the kingdom.
“When you see the peacock, the egg-born bird with variegated wings,
dancing surrounded by peahens, you will not remember your passion.
When you see the blue-necked, crested one, surrounded by peahens...”
"You shall see a peacock dancing, and you will not remember the kingdom.
When you see the trees in bloom during the winter,
exhaling their fragrant scent, you will not remember the kingdom."
“When, in the month of winter, you see the Medani forest green and covered with *indagopaka* insects, you will not remember the rainy season.
When, in winter, you see the trees of the earth in full bloom...”
When the *kuṭaja*, the *bimbajāla*, and the flowering thickets of *loddha* are wafting their fragrance, you will not remember the cord.
When, in the month of winter, you see the forest in full bloom—
"And when the flowers have fallen away, you will not remember the string.
Therein, "mañjuka" means sweet-voiced. "Of the herd of kareṇus" means of the troop of elephants.

"Of the herd" means walking while moving in front of the elephant herd. "On both sides" means on both flanks. "In the forest-clearings" means in the thickets of the forest. "Desiring pleasure" (kāmadā) means...
"It shall grant me all desires. Regarding the river named Sindhuyā: "of the hooting owl while it is hooting" means of the bird-owl while it is making its sound.
"Of the wild beasts" means of the predatory animals; for at the time of evening, that sound of theirs will be like the sound of fivefold musical instruments.
Therefore he says: "Upon hearing their sound, you will not remember the kingdom," [and] "bari-hīnaṃ" [means...]
“Covered with clusters of blossoms” means covered by bunches of flowers. “Seated upon the mountain peak” means constantly seated on the summit of the mountain.
There is also a reading, “mattakāsinaṃ,” which means sitting while intoxicated by the madness of sensual desire. “Bimbajāla” refers to a tree with red sprouts.
