“Opupphāni” means hanging flowers and fallen flowers.
Thus Maddī, like a dweller of the Himalayas, praised the Himalayas with these many verses.
The description of the Himalayas is finished.
Now begins the description of the section on giving.
Queen Phussatī, thinking, "A harsh message has been sent to my son; what indeed is he doing?
I will go and find out," went there under a disguise and stood at the door of the bedchamber. Hearing their conversation, she lamented piteously.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having heard the lamentation of her son and daughter-in-law,
the illustrious princess wailed piteously:
‘Better for me were poison swallowed, or that I should have leapt from a precipice;’”
“I am being bound with a rope; why do they exile my son Vessantara, who is innocent?
He is a reciter of the Vedas, a lord of givers, devoted to charity, and free from stinginess.”
Why do they cause the son Vessantara— who is honored by rival kings, renowned, illustrious, and blameless— to go forth into homelessness?
[He who is] a person supporting his mother and father, one who honors the elders of the family...
Why do they cause the blameless son Vessantara to go forth?
"For the benefit of the king, for the benefit of the queen, for the benefit of kinsmen and friends,
for the benefit of the entire kingdom— why [do they exile] the son Vessantara?"
“They ordain those who are innocent.
In this context, “the king’s daughter” refers to Phussatī, the daughter of King Madda. “I would throw myself down” means I would cast myself from a precipice.
“I would die bound with a rope” means I would die by tying a rope around my neck. “Why?”—because even though it is the deathless [state], they act thus.
"For what reason are they banishing my innocent son from the kingdom?
He is a student who has mastered the three Vedas and attained perfection in various arts and crafts.
Having thus lamented piteously, she comforted her son and daughter-in-law, went into the presence of the king, and said:
“Like honeycombs plundered by crows, like mangoes fallen to the ground—
such will your kingdom become, as they banish those who have done no wrong.
Like a swan whose wings are clipped, stranded in a waterless marsh.”
“Abandoned by your ministers, you stand alone, O King, deprived of all.
‘I say this to you, Great King: let not your welfare pass you by;
do not, because of the words of the Sivis, banish one who is innocent.’”
In this context, "scattered" means like honey from which the flies have fled. "Fallen like mangoes on the ground" means like ripe mango fruits fallen upon the earth.
Thus he indicates: "When my sons have gone forth, your kingdom will become common property for all.
"With his bowl drained" means like one whose bowl has leaked out. "Abandoned by his ministers" means abandoned by those born together with my son.
"Having been abandoned by sixty thousand ministers. "You will suffer" means you will become weary.
"By the word of the Sivis" means by the word of the Sivis [saying], "Do not ordain my innocent son.
Having heard that, the king said:
“I shall pay homage to the Dhamma, the banner of the discipline of the Sivi people;
I am sending forth my own son, for he is dearer to me than life itself.
The meaning of this is: O Bhaddā, I, while disciplining and sending forth Prince Vessantara, the banner of the Sivi people—
"I am honoring the ancient royal tradition of the kings of the Śibi kingdom;
therefore, even though he is dearer to me than my own life, I shall nevertheless ordain him.
Hearing this, she spoke while lamenting:
“For him whose banners of old were like blooming *kaṇikāra* flowers,
which followed him as he went— today alone he shall depart.
For him whose banners of old were like groves of *kaṇikāra* trees...”
They follow him as he goes, yet he himself will depart this very day.
He for whom the ranks of old were like blooming *kaṇikāra* flowers—
they follow him as he goes, yet he himself will depart this very day.
“Whose armies, like groves of *kaṇikāra* trees, once used to follow him as he went—
today he will depart all alone. Those horses, with the hue of *indagopaka* insects,
from Gandhāra, with the color of pale woolen blankets;”
They follow him as he goes along, yet today he will go all alone.
"He who formerly traveled by elephant, by palanquin, and by chariot—
how does King Vessantara go on foot today?"
“How will he, whose body is anointed with sandalwood,
who is awakened by dance and song, cast away his razor, antelope skin, axe, and carrying-pole?
Why will they not bring him saffron robes and antelope skins?”
“Why are the rags not fastened as he enters the great forest?
How indeed do these people who have renounced the world from royalty wear their rags?
How will Maddī put on the rag-robe made of grass?”
“Wearing garments of Kāsi silk, and those of linen and cotton, and wearing robes of grass— how will Maddī manage?
Having been carried about in palanquins, and in litters and chariots...”
“Why is she today walking along the road on foot,
her limbs unanointed? She whose hands have soft palms and whose feet are so tender—
why is she today walking along the road on foot, her limbs unanointed?”
“She whose feet are soft and tender, whose soles are delicate,
who used to go about oppressed by her golden sandals—
how is it that today, with her limbs unadorned, she travels the road on foot?”
“She who used to walk at the head of thousands of women,
adorned with garlands— why is she today going alone to the forest,
her limbs trembling? She who formerly, upon hearing a mere jackal’s cry, would tremble again and again.”
She, timid and lacking confidence, goes to the forest today.
Having heard the owl of the Inda clan hooting as it rains,
she trembles with fear like a wave agitated by Varuṇa.
“Today she goes to the forest, timid and lacking her companions.
Like a bird whose young have been killed, seeing its nest empty,
I shall brood for a long time in sorrow, having come to this empty city.”
“Like a bird whose chicks have been killed, seeing her empty nest,
I shall become thin and pale, not seeing my beloved children.
Like a bird whose chicks have been killed, seeing her empty nest...”
I shall run here and there, not seeing my beloved children.
Like a female osprey whose chicks have been killed, seeing her nest empty,
I shall brood with long-lasting sorrow upon reaching this empty city.
“Like a kurarī bird whose chicks have been killed, seeing her nest empty,
I shall become emaciated and pale, not seeing my dear children.
Like a kurarī bird whose chicks have been killed, seeing her nest empty...”
“I shall run hither and thither, not seeing my dear children.
Surely, like a female ruddy goose in a pond that has gone dry,
I shall brood for a long time in sorrow, having come to this empty city.”
“Surely, like a ruddy goose in a pond that has run dry,
I shall become thin and pale, not seeing my beloved sons.
Surely, like a ruddy goose in a pond that has run dry...”
“I shall run hither and thither, not seeing my beloved sons.
“As I lament thus, the king has banished his innocent son from the kingdom to the forest; I think I shall lose my life.”
In this context, "like *kaṇikāra* flowers" means they are like fully blossomed *kaṇikāra* trees because they are adorned with golden ornaments and golden garments.
"Following him as he goes" means they follow Vessantara as he proceeds for the sake of excursions to parks and groves.
"He alone today" means that today he will go all by himself. "Armies" refers to the elephant corps and so forth. "Gandhāra blankets" refers to [blankets] from Gandhāra.

Red woolen blankets (*rattakambala*) produced in the kingdom of Gandhāra, worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold, which had been worn by the army—[the phrase] "he will carry" means he will carry them on his shoulder.
"Entering" refers to one who is entering. "Why are the bark garments not tied? means:
why do those who know how to tie them not tie the bark garments? "Kings who have gone forth" means: those who, having been kings, have gone forth. "Of linen and *koṭumbara* cloth."
Garments produced in the kingdom of Khoma and the kingdom of Koṭumbara.
"Sā kathaññū, sā kathañjā" means she knows how to speak. "Anujjhaṅgī" means one whose limbs are not censurable.
"Pīḷamānāva gacchati" means she walks as if she were trembling again and again. In the phrases beginning with "yāssu itthisahassānaṃ," *assu* is a particle; *yā* means "who."
The meaning is as follows. There is also a reading: “yā sā. *Sivāyā* means “by the female jackal. *Pure* means “formerly,” while she was living in the city.

*Indasagottassa* means “of one of the Kosiya clan. *Vāruṇīvā* means like a female servant of a *yakṣa* who has been possessed by a deity. *Dukkhenā* means “with suffering,” that is, with the suffering of grief caused by separation from her son.
*Āgammi maṃ puraṃ* means “having come to this dwelling of my son” after my sons had departed. *Piye putte* refers to Vessantara and [his brother].
And he spoke with reference to Maddī. "Hatachāpā" means those whose young ones have been killed. Regarding "he banished her to the forest from the kingdom":
if one interprets this as "if he banished her from the kingdom," then upon hearing the sound of the queen’s lamentation, all of Sañjaya’s daughters-in-law gathered together and wailed aloud.
Hearing the sound of their wailing, they likewise wailed in the Great Being’s own residence. Thus, in both royal households...
Some, unable to remain in their own state, fell like *sāla* trees crushed by the force of the wind;
rolling about, they lamented. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Hearing her wailing, all the many women in the inner apartments…”
Raising their arms and wailing, the gathered women of the Śibi clan cried out:
“Like a hall shattered and crushed by a whirlwind,
sons and wives lie prostrate in the dwelling of Vessantara.”
“Eunuchs and princes, courtesans and brahmins,
raised their arms and wailed at the residence of Vessantara.
Elephant riders, cavalrymen, charioteers, and foot soldiers [did the same].”
They raised their arms and wailed at the residence of Vessantara.
Then, when the night had passed away and the sun was rising,
King Vessantara approached to give his gift.
“Give garments to those who desire garments, and give strong liquor to the drunkards;
bestow food properly upon those who seek food.
Do not cause any hardship for the mendicants who have come here.”
"Satisfy them with food and drink; let them go, having been honored.
Then a tumultuous, terrifying, and great noise arose there:
"They are carrying him out by means of alms-giving, yet you did not give alms again."
“Exhausted as if intoxicated, those seeking alms fall down as the Great King, the prosperer of the Sivi realm, goes forth. ‘Alas!
They are cutting down the tree, the great tree bearing various fruits!’”
"Just as they banish Vessantara from the kingdom, though he is innocent:
'Alas, they have cut down the tree that grants all desires!
Just as they banish Vessantara from the kingdom, though he is innocent.'"
“Alas, they have struck down the tree that brings forth the essence of all desires!
For they are banishing Vessantara from the kingdom, though he is innocent.
Those who are old, those who are young, and those of middle age—”
They raised their arms and wailed as the Great King,
the prosperer of the kingdom of the Śivis, was departing.
"The excessive hunters, the chief rain-makers, and the king’s women [followed him]."
Lifting up their arms, they wailed as the Great King was departing,
he who increased the prosperity of the Śivi kingdom.
Even the women there who were present in that city cried out.
As the Great King, the prosperer of the Śivi realm, was departing, the brahmins, the ascetics, and other mendicants raised their arms and cried out: "Alas! This is surely unrighteousness!"
"Just as King Vessantara, while performing sacrifice in his own city,
was exiled from the kingdom at the word of the Sivi people,
even after giving away seven hundred elephants adorned with every ornament."
“Mounted upon the elephant Suvaṇṇakaccha, who is adorned with golden trappings and garments,
and led by village chiefs holding spears and goads in their hands—
this King Vessantara is being banished from the kingdom.”
“Having given away seven thoroughbred Sindhu horses, swift of pace and noble by birth, adorned with every ornament,
and mounted by village chiefs bearing quivers and bows.”
This King Vessantara is being banished from the kingdom.
Having given away seven hundred chariots— equipped with armor, their banners raised high,
adorned with leopards and tigers, and decorated with every ornament.
“Mounted by the village chiefs, clad in armor and holding bows in their hands—
this King Vessantara is being driven out from the kingdom.
Having given away seven hundred women, each standing upon a chariot,”
They were girt with leather thongs and adorned with gold.
Clad in yellow ornaments and yellow garments, decorated with yellow jewelry,
with broad hips and smiling faces, they were well-proportioned with slender waists.
This King Vessantara is being banished from the kingdom.
Having given away seven hundred cows, all of them with bronze milking vessels—
this King Vessantara is being banished from the kingdom.
“Having given away seven hundred female slaves and seven hundred male slaves,
this King Vessantara is being banished from the kingdom.
Having given away elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as women adorned with ornaments...”
This King Vessantara was banished from his kingdom.
At that time, there was a terror, at that time there was a hair-raising dread;
when the great gift was bestowed, the earth trembled all over.
“Then there was that which was terrifying, then there was that which caused the hair to stand on end:
that the king, with palms joined in reverence, was banished from the kingdom.
Therein, monks, having heard the sound of Phussatī’s lamentation, all the women of Sañjaya—
The women of King Sivi gathered together and wailed and lamented.
Hearing the sound of those women wailing at Vessantara’s residence, the women in Vessantara’s own residence likewise wailed;
thus, in both royal households, some were unable to maintain their composure and were like sal trees shattered by the force of the wind.

Falling down and rolling about, they lamented. Then, when the night had passed, O monks, at the end of that night when the sun had risen, the attendants announced to the king: "The gift has been prepared.
Thereupon, King Vessantara, having bathed early in the morning and adorned himself with all his ornaments, ate a meal of delicious food.
Surrounded by a great multitude of people, he approached the head of the assembly to give a great gift consisting of seven hundred items.
Having gone there, he spoke thus while commanding his sixty thousand ministers: "Give!

Although he knew that "the gift of liquor is indeed fruitless," nevertheless, when those addicted to wine reached the head of the assembly at Vessantara’s distribution of gifts, [he said: "In the gift-assembly of Vessantara..."
He had it given [to them], thinking: "May they not be allowed to say, 'We did not obtain liquor. Regarding "beggars":
he said, "Do not harass even a single person among the beggars. Regarding "honored": he says, "Having been honored by me, act in such a way that they depart praising me."
Thus, he gave seven hundred elephants adorned with golden ornaments, bearing golden banners and covered with nets of gold;

likewise, seven hundred horses of the same kind; seven hundred chariots draped with lion skins and other furs, variegated with various gems and bearing golden banners; and [men] possessing supreme beauty, adorned with every ornament.
He gave a great gift consisting of seven hundred items: seven hundred women, such as daughters of the khattiya class; seven hundred well-trained and well-disciplined male slaves;
likewise, seven hundred female slaves; seven hundred cows that had recently calved and were yielding milk from their udders, with excellent bulls as their leaders;
and immeasurable quantities of food and drink. While he was thus bestowing this gift,
The kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and others residing in the city of Jetuttara lamented, saying:
"Sire, the inhabitants of the kingdom of Sivi are ordaining Vessantara because he 'gives gifts'; yet you, in turn, are giving only gifts! Therefore it was said:
"Then there arose here a sound, tumultuous, terrifying, and great;"
“They take it away by means of giving; you, however, have not given any more.

But the recipients of the gift, having received the alms, fell down like those whose feet have been cut off, thinking: “Now, it seems, King Vessantara will enter the forest, leaving us without a protector; from now on, to whom shall we go?”
As they turned and rolled about, they lamented with a great cry. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Like those intoxicated or exhausted, the mendicants fell down as the Great Kings, the enhancers of the Śivi realm, were departing.”
In that context, *te sumattā* means "those [who were] intoxicated"; *su-* is merely a particle, and the sense is "those mendicants.
*Mattā kilantāvā* means "having become as if intoxicated and as if exhausted. *Sampatanti* means they fall to the ground after rolling over.
*Acchecchuṃ vata* means "they cut them off"; *vata* is merely a particle. *Yathā* means "by which cause. *Atiyakkhā* refers to those skilled in the science of spirits (*bhūtavijjā*).
*Ikkaṇikā* refers to fortune-tellers. *Vassavarā* are those who remove seeds [from the fields], namely the guards of the royal harem. *Vacanatthena* means by way of the cause of speech.
*Saṃhā raṭṭhā nirajjatī* means he goes out from his own kingdom. *Gāmaṇīyehi* means by elephant trainers.
*Ājānīyeva* means those of noble birth. *Gāmaṇīyehi* means by horse trainers. *Illiyācāpadhāribhī* means by those carrying the *illiyā* (a type of bow) and the *cāpa* (bow). And *illiyā*...
And they were carrying bows. Furthermore, "on lamps" means on those surrounded by leopard skins and tiger skins.

"Each one standing on a chariot" means, it is said, that he placed each of the women-treasures upon a chariot and gave them away, having surrounded each with eight female attendants of various complexions.
“Nikkharajjūhi” means with golden thread necklaces. “Āḷārapamhā” means those with broad eyes and cheeks.
“Hasulā” refers to speech preceded by smiles. “Susaññā” means those with beautiful hips. “Tanumajjhā” means those whose waist-regions are as slender as the palm of a hand.
At that time, however, the deities announced throughout the surface of Jambudīpa to the kings: “King Vessantara is giving a great gift.”
Therefore, those khattiyas, having arrived through the power of the deities, took them and departed.
Regarding the phrase *kaṃsupadhāraṇā*: here, *kaṃsa* is a name for silver; the meaning is that she gave [the milk] together with a silver vessel for containing the milk.
Regarding *padinnamhi*: while it was being given. Regarding *sampakampatha*: you trembled due to the splendor of the gift. Regarding *yaṃ pañjalikato*: because of one who stood with palms joined.

When King Vessantara, having given the great gift, raised his hands in *añjali* and, while paying homage to his own generosity, stood with palms joined, saying, “May this be a condition for my attainment of omniscience,” even then it was truly terrifying;
the meaning is that at that moment the earth shook. “It departs” means that having done this, it indeed goes out.
The meaning is that no one prevented him.
Moreover, it was only while he was actually giving the gift that evening that [the result] occurred.
Having returned to his own residence, he thought, "I will pay homage to my mother and father and depart tomorrow," and went by means of a decorated chariot to the place where his parents lived.
Queen Maddī also, thinking, "I too shall go with my lord and obtain permission from my parents," went along with him.
The Great Being paid homage to his father and spoke of his intention to depart. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
"He addressed the king, the excellent Sañjaya, who was righteous in Dhamma."
“You have obstructed me, O King; I shall go to Mount Vaṅka.
For whatever beings there have been, O Great King, and those who will be—unless they are satisfied with sensual pleasures, they go to the realm of Yama.”
“Alas! I shall perish for my own sake, sacrificing my own former prosperity;
because of the words of the Śivis, I have been driven out from this kingdom.
I shall experience that calamity in the forest, which is teeming with fierce beasts.”
"I perform meritorious deeds while being served by those who possess the Khaggavisāṇa-sutta;
you, however, sink into the mire.
In this context, "the best among the righteous" means the most excellent among righteous kings. "You have obstructed me" means you have expelled me from the kingdom.

“Beings” (*bhūtā*) means those who have passed away. “Will be” (*bhavissare*) refers to those who will exist in the future and those currently born in the present. “The instrument of Yama” (*yamasādhana*) is the place where the commands of King Yama are carried out.
“I myself oppressed my own people” (*svāhaṃ sake abhissasiṃ*): I, that very person, oppressed the inhabitants of my own city.
What was I doing? “Sacrificing in my own city” (*yajamāno sake pure*). In the canonical text (*pāḷi*), however, it is written as “so ahaṃ. “Without a king” (*nirajjhaṃ*).
“I have departed. I shall undergo that misfortune (*agha*)—the suffering which must be endured by one dwelling in the forest.
By “in the mire,” he says: “But you, however, are sinking in the mire of sensual pleasures.
Thus, having conversed with his father through these four verses, the Great Being went to his mother, paid homage to her, and spoke as follows, seeking permission for his renunciation:
“Give me leave, mother; renunciation is what I desire.
Having performed my own consecration while sacrificing in my own city, I have been driven out from this kingdom because of the words of the Śivis.”
“I shall endure that hardship in the forest teeming with fierce beasts,
frequented by tigers and leopards, while I perform meritorious deeds;
you, however, are sinking in the mire.”
Having heard this, Phussatī said:
“I grant you permission, my son; may your going-forth be successful!
And here is the noble Maddī, well-proportioned and slender-waisted.”
“Let him live together with his sons;

what will he do in the forest?”—therein, “let it succeed” means let him be successful through meditative absorption (*jhāna*). “Let him live” (*acchatu*) means let him remain right here; thus he speaks.
Vessantara replied:
“I cannot venture to take even a slave-girl to the forest against her will;
if she wishes, let her follow; if she does not wish, let her stay.
In this context, “against her will” means: “Mother, what are you saying? I would not dare to take even a slave-girl if she were unwilling.”
Then, having heard his son’s words, the king set about asking for the daughter-in-law. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then the great king set about asking for the daughter-in-law:
‘Let her not wear dust and dirt, though her conduct is as pure as sandalwood.’”
“Do not wear these garments; wear instead a garment of kusa grass.
Dwelling in the forest is painful; do not go to Lakkhaṇa.
Regarding this, “he proceeded,” O monks, means that having heard his son’s words, the king proceeded to ask for his daughter-in-law.
“Candanasamācāra” means one whose body is smeared with red sandalwood. “Mā hi tvaṃ lakkhaṇe gamī” means:
do not go to the forest, you who are endowed with auspicious marks.
Maddī, the princess, beautiful in all her limbs, said this to him:
“I would not desire that happiness which is without Vessantara.
Therein, *taṃ abravi* means he spoke to his father-in-law.
“The Great King, the prosperer of the kingdom of the Sivis, spoke to him:”
"Come now, Maddi, listen to those things that are difficult to endure in the forest:
'There are many insects, moths, mosquitoes, and honey-bees;
they too would bite you there, and that would be even more painful for you.'"
“Look, there is a place free from distress, frequented by rivers;
there are snakes called pythons, non-venomous and very powerful.
They [will spare] a human or even a deer, even if it has come close to them.”
Having surrounded them with their possessions, they bring others under their own control.
There are also others, dark-haired ascetics, who are like the "accha" deer of evil dhamma;
a man has never been seen by them who, having climbed a tree, is released.
“Battering their horns and striking with sharp points,
wild buffaloes roam here, heading toward the Sotumbara River.
Having seen herds of deer and cattle wandering in the forest,”
“Like a cow greedy for her calf, how will you fare, Maddi?
Seeing the fierce monkeys fallen upon the difficult paths,
O Maddi, who knows no field of their own, great terror will come upon you.”
“You who, having heard the cry of the *sivā* bird, were once so terrified;
now that you have reached Vaṅka, how will you fare, Mādhavī?
When the time of midday has arrived and the birds are sitting still...”
“The vast forest rustles as it were; why do you wish to go there?
Regarding that, “he spoke to her” means he spoke to that daughter-in-law. “See others being tormented” means look at others who are being tormented by things that produce fear.
“Frequented by rivers” means in a place near to rivers, the meaning being: dwelling on the banks of rivers.
*Avisāti nibbisā*: "They have lost their taste. *Api māsannan* means "even though it has come near," that is, it has come near to the touch of one's own body;
this is the meaning. *Aghammigā* means "deer that cause misfortune," that is, deer that bring suffering; this is the meaning. *Nadiṃ sotumbaraṃ pati* means "on the bank of the river named Sotumbarā.
*Yūthānaṃ* means "of the herds"; or rather, this very reading [yūthāni] is the text. *Dhenuva vacchagiddhāvā* means "like a cow longing for her calf. Regarding you...
"How will you manage, like a cow greedy for her calf, not seeing her young?"—here the syllable *va* is merely a particle.
"Sampatite" means "while it was falling. "Ghore" means "terrible" or "frightful," and "virūpe" means "deformed. "Plavaṅgame" means "monkey.
"Akhettaññāya" is due to being unskilled in the terrain of the forest. "Bhavissate" means "it will be. "Sivāya sutvāna" means "having heard the sound of a female jackal."
Having heard it, for a moment he trembled again and again—“trembles” means he was terrified. “It seems to sound” means it will be as if it is crying out, as if it is making a noise.
Maddī, the princess, beautiful in every limb, said to him:
“As for those things you have described to me as fearsome in the forest...”
"I shall overcome them all as I go along, O bull among charioteers.
Kāsa grass, kuśa grass, poṭakila, usīra, muñja, and pabbaja—I shall push them aside with my chest; vanish, you ill-guided ones!"
“Indeed, by many kinds of conduct, a maiden finds a husband:
by the restraint of her belly, by the binding of her calves,
by service to the fire, and by swimming in water.”
"O bull among charioteers, one must endure what is piercing and bitter in this world even while going along.
Even if it has not yet been reached, there may be the need to eat what is left over;
for he who, having seized her by the hand, drags her against her will."
“Piercing is bitter in this world, O Bull among Charioteers,
as you depart. Seizing us by the hair, throwing us up, and trampling us upon the ground—
having done these things, he departs, leaving behind much suffering that is not small.”
"O Bull among Charioteers, piercing words are bitter in this world even for one who is departing.
Those with white skin, who are envious of piercing words and pride themselves on their beauty,
drag one along against one's will, just as crows drag down an owl."
“Piercing and bitter is [the world] in this life, O Bull among Charioteers,
as you depart. Even though I dwell in a prosperous kinsman’s house,
shining like molten bronze, I receive neither kind words nor favor from my brothers or even my female friends.”
“Piercing is bitter in this world, O bull among charioteers, as you depart.
A river is naked when it is waterless; a kingdom is naked when it is without a king;
and even a woman is naked who is a widow, even if she has ten brothers.”
“Piercing is bitter in this world, O bull among charioteers, as you go forth.
“The banner is the sign of the chariot; smoke is the sign of the fire;
the king is the sign of the kingdom; the husband is the sign of the woman.”
“O Bull among Charioteers, one who acts with hostility toward the world will surely suffer bitter consequences.
But those women who are renowned for being kind to the poor and generous to the wealthy—
the gods indeed praise them, for they perform what is difficult to do.”
“I shall follow my husband, always clothed in saffron robes;
though the earth were filled with wealth, it would be a bitter ordeal for a woman like me.
Even if it were the entire world, bounded by the ocean and possessing vast riches—”
“Filled with various jewels, there is nothing that lacks Vessantara.
“How indeed can their hearts be so devoted to pleasure?
Alas, these women who desire their own happiness while their husband is suffering!”
“When the Great King, the prosperer of the Śivi realm, goes forth, I shall follow him, for he is the giver of all my desires.
Therein, “he spoke to him,” monks, means that Maddī, having heard the king’s words, spoke to that king. They will overcome [it].
"I shall endure; I shall patiently accept. *Poṭakila* means *poṭakila* grass.
"I shall push aside" means that having split it in two, I will go before Vessantara. "By the restraint of the belly" means by fasting and by enduring hunger. And "by the cow's jaw" (*gohanuveṭhana*):
considering that women with broad hips and sloping flanks obtain their husbands, [he thought] he would cover his hip-bone with the cow's jaw.
Having had it fortified and having covered the openings with a covering, the young woman obtains a husband. "Bitter" means unpleasant.
"I shall surely go" means I will certainly go.
"It is not even fit for her, though she has not yet arrived" means that even the leftovers of that widow are indeed unsuitable for her to eat. He who...
Later, one of low birth seizes that widow by the hand and drags her away even though she does not wish it.

"Seizing by the hair, tossing up, and striking upon the ground"—having committed these acts of contempt, they pass by, seizing the hair with their hands and feet, tossing her up, and throwing her down upon the ground.
And "having given" refers to such [treatment] toward a woman who has no protector.
Having given much and not a little suffering, the man of another family departs; free from apprehension, he stands looking on.
"With white skin" means with the complexion of the skin produced by bathing powder. "Men who desire to pierce and win" refers to men who wish to penetrate and captivate.
"Having given" means having given even a very small amount of wealth. "Thinking themselves fortunate" means imagining, "We are beautiful."
They dragged that widow, who was without a husband and against her will, like crows dragging a crow, saying, "She is but a female owl.
She lived in such a kinsman's family, shining with the luster of golden vessels.
Yet she did not receive even a word of welcome, such as, "This woman is without a husband; from now on, she has become our responsibility for life," and so forth.
Even from her brothers or her female friends who speak words against her, she never receives excessive speech or words of reproach.
"Paññāṇa" means the cause for making oneself known.
"O King, that woman who is endowed with fame, even if her husband is poor... [refers to] a woman who is poor [yet renowned].
When she encounters suffering, being herself poor, she too suffers;
when he becomes wealthy, she becomes wealthy along with him and attains happiness—it is such a woman that the gods truly praise. *Abhijjantī* means "she is coveted.
For even if the entire earth does not break apart for a woman, she alone becomes the mistress of that whole earth; nevertheless...
The meaning is that piercing is indeed extremely harsh. "Women are truly rough" means women are indeed very rough.
"The Great King spoke thus to Maddī, who was beautiful in all her limbs:
'These young sons of yours—both Jālī and Kaṇhājinā;'"
“Leave the two signs behind and go; we shall nourish them for you.
Therein, “both Jālī and Kaṇhājinā” means both Jālī and Kaṇhājinā. “Leaving them behind” means: “Having left these two behind, go.
To him, the princess Maddī, beautiful in all her limbs, spoke:
“O King, my sons Jālī and Kaṇhājinā are both dear to me;
they will delight us there in the forest, even though we are grieving for our lives.
In this context, “tyamhaṃ” means “those children, of ours, there in the forest”; “jīvasokinaṃ” means they will delight the hearts of those whose sorrow has not yet departed.
The Great King, the prosperer of the Śivi realm, said to him:
“Having eaten rice porridge with pure meat as a condiment,
how will these children live when they eat only the fruits of trees?”
“Having eaten from golden bowls weighing a hundred *pala*s,
adorned with a hundred royal lines, how will these children eat from the leaves of trees?
And having worn garments of Kāsi silk, as well as those of linen and cotton— ”
Wearing garments of grass, how will these children manage?
Carried about on litters, in palanquins, and in chariots;
now running about on foot—how will these children manage?
“Having slept in gabled houses, with doors closed against the wind,
how will these children sleep at the foot of trees?
Having slept on couches covered with woolen rugs and embroidered cloth,”
“Lying on a bed of grass, how will the children endure?
Having smeared themselves with perfumes, agallochum, and sandalwood,
how will the children endure while bearing the dust and grime?”
“With their limbs fanned by yak-tail whisks and feeling comfortable, how will the children fare when touched by gadflies and mosquitoes?
In this context, *palasate kaṃse* means in a golden bowl made of a *palasata* measure of gold. *Gonake cittasanthateti* refers to a variegated rug spread upon a large back [of a couch].
And there were black antelope skins and variegated rugs. "With yak-tail whisks and peacock-feather fans" means their limbs were fanned with both yak-tail whisks and peacock-feather fans.
Thus, even as they were conversing, the night passed away and the sun rose.

Having brought a decorated chariot yoked with four Sindhava horses, they stationed it at the palace gate. Maddī, too, having paid homage to her mother-in-law and father-in-law, [and to] the other women...
Having taken leave and taking her two sons, Maddī, who was beautiful in all her limbs, went ahead of Vessantara and stood upon the chariot.
To explain this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then the princess Maddī, beautiful in every limb, spoke to him.”
“O King, do not lament, and do not be despondent;
for as we shall become, so shall these children become.
Having said this, Maddī, beautiful in every limb, departed.
“Lakkhaṇā, taking her sons, sought the path to safety.
In this context, “by the path to safety” means by the road to be traveled by King Sivi. “Sought” means she went there; the sense is that, having descended from the palace, she mounted the chariot.
Then King Vessantara, the kshatriya, having given his gift...
Having paid homage to his father and mother, and having circumambulated them clockwise,
he quickly mounted the chariot drawn by four horses,
took his wife and children, and set out for Mount Vaṅka.

In this context, "there" (*tatra*) means, monks, at the time when she had mounted the chariot and was standing there. "Having given" (*datvā*) means having given alms yesterday. "And having circumambulated her" (*katvā ca naṃ padakkhiṇaṃ*) means having performed a circumambulation.
"Her" (*naṃ*) is a mere particle. "Then King Vessantara said: 'O you by whom many people are [protected], we shall depart after bidding you farewell; may our kinsmen be free from illness.'"

The meaning of this is as follows: "Monks, from there King Vessantara, having sent the chariot to the place where many people were standing with the thought, 'We shall see King Vessantara,' addressed the great multitude, saying:
'I bid you farewell, let us go; may our kinsmen be well. In that context, *taṃ* is merely a particle. Monks, from there Vessantara...
The king said to his kinsmen, “Having taken leave of you, we shall depart; may you be happy and free from suffering.
Thus the Great Being, having addressed the great multitude, exhorted them, saying, “Be diligent; perform meritorious deeds such as giving,” and then he departed.
As the Bodhisatta was leaving, his mother said, “My son is a master of giving; let him give...”
Saying, "Let there be [chariots]," he dispatched carts filled with the seven precious gems on both sides, along with ornaments.
He too, having removed the very ornaments he was wearing on his own body and given them to the beggars who had arrived eighteen times, gave away everything that remained.
Having departed from the city, he desired to turn back and look upon it once more. Then, for him—
Dependent upon his thought, at a spot the size of a chariot, the great earth split open and, spinning like a potter’s wheel, turned the chariot toward the city.
He looked toward the dwelling place of his parents; for that reason, there was an earthquake. Thus it is said:
“Having departed from the city, when he turned back and looked,
even then the earth, with Sineru as its forest-diadem,
trembled. Then, having looked himself, he spoke this verse in order to have Maddi look as well:
“Come now, Madhī, look upon this: it appears like a form of delight;
it is the dwelling of the most excellent Śiva, my ancestral abode.
In that context, “look upon” means “behold.”

Then the Great Being, having caused his sixty thousand ministers born with him and the rest of the people to turn back, drove the chariot forward and said to Maddī, “My dear lady, if any supplicants come from behind, you must take note.
She sat watching. Meanwhile, four brahmins who were unable to reach the Great Almsgiving of seven hundred items arrived at the city.
Having arrived, they asked, "Where is King Vessantara? When told, "He has gone after giving gifts," they asked, "Did he take anything with him?
Upon hearing, "He went by chariot," they pursued him, thinking, "We shall beg for his horses.
Then Maddī, seeing them approaching, announced, "Sire, beggars are coming! The Great Being brought the chariot to a halt.
They approached him and asked for the horses. The Great Being gave them the horses. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“The brahmins followed after him and asked him for the horses;
being asked, he bestowed the four steeds upon the four.”
But when the horses had been given, the chariot-pole remained suspended in the air.
Then, as soon as the brahmins had departed, four sons of gods arrived in the guise of roe deer, took up the chariot-pole, and went on their way.
The Great Being, knowing them to be sons of gods, spoke this verse:
“Come now, my lady, listen: it appears like a form of mind;
they carry me along with the color of deer-skins.
Therein, “they carry me” means that well-trained horses carry me as it were.
Then, as he was going along in this manner, another brahmin approached and asked for his chariot.
The Great Being, having helped his wife and children down, gave him the chariot. But once the chariot had been given away, the sons of the gods vanished.
To make known that the chariot had been given, the Teacher said:
“Then a fifth person arrived there and asked for that chariot;
he gave it to him when asked, yet his mind was not disturbed.
Then King Vessantara, having dismissed his own people...”
“He comforted the Brahmin who sought wealth, along with his horse and chariot.
Regarding this, “then there” means then, in that forest. “And his mind was not overcome” means his mind was not dejected. “He comforted” means he reassured him and gave him back [the chariot].
From that time on, however, they all became mere foot-soldiers. Then the Great Being said to Maddī:
“Maddī, you take Kāḷa; he is the youngest and light.
I shall take Jāli, for he is my elder brother and heavy.
Having spoken thus, both the Khattiyas departed, each taking one of the two boys upon their laps. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“The king, taking the prince, and the princess, taking the girl,
departed together in mutual joy, speaking kindly to one another.
The commentary on the section on giving is finished.
Commentary on the Chapter on Entering the Forest:
Seeing people coming from the opposite direction, they asked, "Where is Vaṅkapabbata? The people replied, "It is far away. Thus it was said:
"If any men come along the path, on the way back;..."
"We ask you about the path: 'Where is Vaṅkata Mountain?
Having seen us there, they lamented piteously;
they informed us of our suffering, saying, 'Vaṅkata Mountain is far away.'"
Seeing trees bearing various fruits on both sides of the road, the children cried out.
Through the power of the Great Being, the fruit-bearing trees bent down until they came within reach of his hands.
Then, having gathered ripe fruits from them, he gave them to the children. Seeing this, Maddī expressed her wonder. Thus it is said:
“If children see fruit-bearing trees in the forest,
those children cry out for the sake of those fruits.
Seeing the children weeping, the vast trees rise up.”
Bowing down of their own accord, they approached the children.
Having seen this marvel, this wonder that makes the hair stand on end, Maddī, beautiful in all her limbs, uttered a cry of "Well done! (Sādhukāra).
“Truly a marvel in the world, a wonder that makes the hair stand on end:
by the majesty of Vessantara, the trees have bent down of their own accord!
From the city of Jetuttara, five yojanas away, was a mountain named Suvaṇṇagiritāla; from there, [came] those known as the Kontimāras.
The river was five *yojanas* away; beyond that was a mountain named Añjana-giri, five *yojanas* away; beyond that was a Brahmin village named Dunniviṭṭha, five *yojanas* away;
and beyond that was the city of Mātula, ten *yojanas* away. Thus, the distance from the city of Jetuttara to that road was thirty *yojanas*.
The deities shortened that path for them, so that they reached the city of Mātula in a single day.
They reached [their destination]. Therefore it was said:
“Out of compassion for the children, the yakkhas shortened the road;
on the very day they set out, they arrived at Cetaraṭṭha.”
Setting out from the city of Jetuttara at the time for the morning meal, they arrived at Mātula in the kingdom of Ceta at the time of evening. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having traveled a long distance, they arrived at Ceta, A prosperous and flourishing country, abundant in meat and rice-soup.”
At that time, sixty thousand kṣatriyas were residing in the city of Mātula. Without entering the city, the Great Being sat in a hall right at the city gate.
Then Maddī, having wiped the dust from the Bodhisatta’s feet and massaged them, thought, “I shall let him know that Vessantara has arrived,” and so she emerged from the hall and [approached] him.
He stood at the gate of the hall within the range of vision. The women entering and leaving the city, seeing him, surrounded him.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“The people surrounded Cetiya, having seen him endowed with the auspicious marks.”
“O, how delicate the noble lady is! She runs about on foot.
Having been carried about in palanquins, in litters, and in chariots—today Maddī runs about on foot in the forest.”
In this context, "arrived with her characteristic marks" means that Maddī, endowed with all auspicious marks, had arrived.
"She wanders about" means that, being so delicate, she travels about on foot. "Having wandered" means having traveled through the city of Jetuttara. "In a palanquin" means in a golden palanquin.
When the great multitude saw Maddī, Vessantara, and his two sons arriving as if without a protector, they went [to meet them].
He informed the kings. Sixty thousand kings came into his presence weeping and lamenting.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Seeing him, the leaders of the Cetis approached him while weeping.”
“Is it well with you, O King? Is it free from ailment, O King?
Is your father healthy, and is all well with the Śivis?
“What is your strength, O Great King? What indeed is your circle of chariots?”
"Anassaka the Arathaka, having come from a long distance, was harassed by the Kaccāyans; he has now arrived in this region.
Therein, "having seen" means having seen from afar. "The chiefs of the Cetis" means the kings of the Cetis. "They approached" means they drew near.
“Welfare” (*kusalanti*) means health. “Freedom from affliction” (*anāmayanti*) means the state of being free from suffering. “Where is your strength? (*ko te balanti*) asks: where is your army?

“The circle of chariots” (*rathamaṇḍalanti*) asks: where is that chariot by which you arrived? “Without horses” (*anassako*) means devoid of horses. “Without chariots” (*arathako*) means without vehicles.
“Having come a long way” (*dīghamaddhānamāgato*) means having traveled a long distance. “Overpowered” (*pakato*) means overcome.
Then, explaining the reason for his arrival, the Great Being said to them:
"All is well with me, truly, and all is well and free from ailment;
my father is healthy, and the Sivi people are likewise free from ailment."
“I would indeed give an elephant, with tusks like chariot poles, of great stature,
knowing the field of all battles, entirely white, the best of elephants;
covered with a pale blanket, in rut, and a crusher of enemies.”
I gave to the brahmins a palanquin that was equipped with ivory fans, white like Mount Kelāsa,
and provided with a white parasol, a footstool, a walking-staff,
and hand-guards; it was a supreme vehicle fit for a king.
“The Sivis are angry with me, and my father is displeased;
the king has imprisoned me. I shall go to the crooked mountain;
please find a suitable place in the forest where we may dwell.”

In that context, "in this" means for this reason my sons are angry with me. "One whose mind is wounded" means one whose heart is wounded; being angry, he has banished me from the kingdom. "Where" means in whichever forest we might dwell, please know that as our place of residence.
Those kings said:
"Welcome to you, O Great King, and a most gracious welcome to you."
“You have arrived as a lord; declare what there is here:
‘Eat vegetables, lotus roots, honey, meat, and pure rice-gruel;
enjoy them, O Great King, for you have come as our guest.’”
In this context, *pavedaya* means "speak"; we shall prepare everything and give it to you. *Bhisa* refers to the root of the lotus, or any kind of bulbous plant.
Vessantara said:
"Whatever has been given has been accepted, and for all of it, a respectful offering has been made."
"The king has imprisoned me; I am going to the crooked mountain.
Know well the place where we shall dwell in the forest.
In this context, "accepted" means: let all this given by you be indeed accepted by me; of everything—
"You have offered me a respectful greeting and an invitation; however, the king has imprisoned me and banished me from the kingdom.
Therefore, I shall go to Vaṅka itself; please let me know my dwelling place in that forest.
Those kings said:
“Stay right here for now, O bull among charioteers, in the kingdom of Ceti,
until the people of Ceti go into the presence of the king to make their request—
to persuade the Great King, the prosperer of the Sivi realm.”
"Placing this or that person at their head, joyful and having gained their support, they go forth surrounding them—know this to be the way of the khattiyas.

In this context, "to go into the presence of the king" means they will go for the purpose of petitioning the king. "To convince" means to make him know your innocence. "Having gained their support" means having obtained a firm footing. "They go" means they will depart.
The Great Being said:
"Do not let it please you to go to the presence of the king to make a request;
to persuade the great king, even the king himself would have no power there."
“The Sivis who have risen up, and the leaders of the guilds—these wish to destroy the king on my account.

Regarding that, “there and there” means that even the king has no power in causing me to be seen as innocent. “Risen up” means exceedingly enraged. “Leaders of the forces” means the military units. “To destroy” means to expel from the kingdom. “The king” means even the monarch himself.
Those kings said:
"If she shall rule here, O Increaser of the Realm,
then exercise sovereignty right here, surrounded by the Cetis."
“This kingdom is prosperous and flourishing; this great country is thriving.
O King, apply your mind to governing the realm.

In this context, “if this [state] prevails here” means if this condition prevails in this kingdom. “To govern the realm” means to rule over the kingdom; or rather, this is simply the reading of the text.
Vessantara said:
"I have no desire, nor do I have the mind, to rule over a kingdom;
O sons of the Cetis, hear me as I have been exiled from the realm."
“The Sivis were dissatisfied, as were the leaders of the army and the merchants;
because he had been banished from the kingdom, they consecrated Cetā as king.
‘Even though you may not have social intercourse with me, it shall be for my sake forever.’”
I do not like quarreling with the Śivīs, nor do I like conflict.
"For my sake alone, many people might inflict terrible quarrels and much violence upon him."
“What has been given has been accepted, and for all of it, honor has been rendered.
The king has imprisoned me; I shall go to the crooked mountain.
Know well the place, where we may dwell in the forest.”
In that context, "If they were to consecrate him to the kingdom" means that when the inhabitants of Ceta reportedly consecrated Vessantara to the kingdom, you too were dissatisfied with them.
"Asammodiyaṃ" means discord. "Assa" means it would come to pass. "Atha assa" means:
"Then, because of me alone, there will be quarreling among you."
Thus, although the Great Being was entreated in many ways, he did not desire the kingdom.
Then those neighboring kings paid him great honor. He did not wish to enter the city;
therefore, they decorated the very same sala tree, surrounded it with a curtain, prepared a great couch, and provided full protection for him. There he stayed for one night with them.
Having been provided with protection and having slept in the hall, he bathed early the following morning,
ate various kinds of choice food, and set out surrounded by them. Sixty thousand nobles traveled fifteen yojanas with him,
stopped at the edge of the forest, and, pointing out the remaining fifteen yojanas of the road ahead, said:
“Truly, O King, we shall explain to you as those who are skilled would;
where the royal seers, having offered the fire-sacrifice, dwell in composure.
This, O Great King, is the mountain Gandhamādana.”
“Where you dwell together with your sons and your wife—
if they have exhorted you thus, with tearful eyes and weeping faces:
‘Go from here, O Great King, straight toward the north.’”
“Then, O Blessed One, you will see the mountain named Vepulla,
strewn with various groves of trees, cool-shaded and delightful.
Having passed beyond that, O Blessed One, you will then see a river.”
There was a river named Ketumatī, deep and nestled within a mountain cleft.
It was filled with large-scaled fish, possessed excellent landing places, and abounded in water.
Having bathed there, drunk, and refreshed myself along with my sons, I remained.
“Then you shall see, O venerable one, the Nigrodha tree with its honey-sweet fruit,
grown upon a delightful peak, cool-shaded and enchanting.
Then you shall see, O venerable one, the mountain named Nāḷika.”
The mountain was strewn with various kinds of creatures and inhabited by *kimpurisa* beings.
To its northeast was the lake named Mucalinda,
covered with white lotuses and fragrant white water lilies.
“Thus the forest, resembling a cloud, with its grass always lush and green;
like a lion eyeing his prey, he plunged into the woodland thicket,
which was covered on both sides by flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees.”
“There, birds of many colors and various kinds, sweet-voiced and lovely,
warble in response to one another as they perch upon trees in full bloom due to the season.
Having traveled through the mountain fastnesses and to the sources of rivers,”
Thus you saw the lotus pond, filled with *karañja* and *kakudha* trees;
strewn with fish having broad scales, with excellent landing-stairs,
abundant water, level and square, sweet and free from foul odor.
“Build a leaf-hut to the northeast of that [place];
having built the leaf-hut, strive for the practice of gleaning.
In this context, *rājisī* refers to those who have gone forth after having been kings. *Samāhitā* means those with one-pointed minds. *Esa* refers to the right hand.
"Having lifted [the boat], go by way of this mountain foot," they say, pointing it out. "Acchasi" means you will dwell.
"Āpaga" refers to a river that carries water. "Girigabbhara" means occurring from within the womb of the mountains.
"Madhupipphala" means sweet fruit. "Rammake" means in a delightful place. "Kimpurisāyuta" means frequented or surrounded by *kimpurisas*.
"Covered with various kinds of white water-lilies (*seta-uppalāni*) and *sogandhika* lilies" means it was overspread with these diverse types of white lotuses and *sogandhika* flowers.
"Like a lion looking for meat" means like a lion gazing at prey.
"With a lowing sound" means with a blended, resonant voice. "Charming" means sweet-voiced. "Warbling and warbling along" refers first to...
"Other birds warble after the warbling bird. This means that when a tree has blossomed in season, they settle upon that tree blooming in its proper time and warble after it as it warbles.

"You shall see him" means that you yourself will see him. "Surrounded by *karañja* and *kakudha* trees" means encircled by *karañja* trees and *kakudha* trees. "Free from offensive odors" means devoid of any disagreeable smells.
"Surrounded by sweet water and covered with various kinds of lotuses, such as padumas and uppalas.
"Build a leaf-hut" means you should have a leaf-hut constructed. "Having built it" means after having had it built.
"Strive for a livelihood by gleaning" means: "Then, O King, while maintaining yourselves by gleaning, strive heedfully; the meaning is that you should dwell having aroused energy."
Thus those kings, having pointed out to him the fifteen-league road and sent him on his way,

called upon a clever and well-trained village youth and said to him, "Go and keep watch over him as he goes and as he comes, so that no enemy whatsoever may find an opportunity to cause Vessantara harm."
Having stationed [guards] at the entrance of the forest for the sake of protection, they departed for their own city.
Vessantara, too, having reached Mount Gandhamādana with his sons and wife, stayed there on that day;
then, proceeding northward along the foothills of Mount Vepulla, he sat down on the bank of a river named Ketumatī and ate the honey and meat provided by a forest-dweller.
Having given him a golden needle, he bathed and drank there;
his fatigue allayed, he crossed over from the river and sat for a short while at the foot of a banyan tree standing on a mountain ridge.
After eating some banyan fruits, he rose and proceeded until he reached the mountain named Nāḷika. Passing by that, he went to the Mucalinda Lake.
Having reached the northeastern corner on the bank of the Sarassati River, he entered a forest thicket by a narrow footpath;
having passed through it, he reached a square lotus pond situated in front of the mountain passes that form the source of the river.
At that moment, Sakka, reflecting and perceiving that "the Great Being has entered the Himālayas," [considered] his dwelling place.
Thinking, "It is right that I obtain [this]," he summoned Vissakamma and sent him forth, saying, "Go, dear one;
having constructed a hermitage in a delightful spot within a cave on Vaṅka Mountain, return.

He replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and descending from the world of the gods, he constructed there two leaf-huts, two walking-paths, and places for standing by night and day, and at the end of one walking-path—
Having displayed various fruit-bearing trees and plantain groves in those various places, and having prepared all the requisites for the ordained, he wrote the words:
"Whoever desires to go forth, let them take these. Then, after causing non-human beings to utter terrifying sounds and driving away the wild animals and birds, he returned to his own place.
Seeing a footpath, the Great Being thought, "This must be the dwelling place of those who have gone forth.
He stationed Maddī and his two sons at the entrance of the hermitage, entered the hermitage grounds, and upon examining the inscriptions, realized, "I have been seen by Sakka.
He then entered the leaf-hut, removed his sword and bow, and took off his garments.

Having dressed himself in red bark garments, draped a deerskin over his shoulder, bound his matted locks into a circlet, and assumed the appearance of an ascetic, he took up a walking staff, emerged from the leaf hut, and, bearing the glory of one who has gone forth, uttered this inspired exclamation: "Oh, what happiness!
Oh, what happiness! I have attained the state of renunciation! Then, ascending the walkway, he paced back and forth.
Accompanied by a tranquility like that of a *paccekabuddha*, he went into the presence of his wife and children.
Maddī too, having fallen at the feet of the Great Being and wept, entered the hermitage with him; she went to her own leaf-hut and assumed the garb of an ascetic.
Subsequently, they made their two sons into young ascetics as well. [Meanwhile,] the four Khattiyas were on the slopes of Mount Vaṅka.
They lived there. Then Maddī requested a boon from the Great Being:
"Your Majesty, instead of going to the forest for fruits, please stay right here with our children; I shall bring back the fruits.
From that time on, she would gather fruits from the forest and look after the three of them.
The Bodhisatta also requested that boon: "Bhadde Maddi, from this day forth we are called 'those who have gone forth.
Now, womanhood is indeed a stain upon the holy life; from now on, do not come into my presence at an improper time.
She accepted, saying, "Very well. Through the power of the Great Being’s loving-kindness (*mettā*), even all the animals within three *yojanas* around...
They attained mutual thoughts of loving-kindness. Queen Maddī, too, rising early in the morning, prepared drinking water and water for washing;
she brought water for rinsing the mouth, gave him a tooth-stick, and swept the hermitage grounds.
Having placed her two sons beside their father, she entered the forest with a basket, a hoe, and a hook in her hands, [to gather] roots and various fruits from the woods.
Having taken her basket and filled it, she returned from the forest at the time of evening;
having set the various fruits down in the leaf-hut and bathed, she bathed her children. Then all four people sat at the door of the leaf-hut and partook of the fruits.
Thereafter, Maddī took her children and entered her own leaf-hut. In this manner, they [lived] on the mountain slopes.
"They dwelt for seven months.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Entry into the Forest is finished.
The commentary on the Jūjaka Chapter.

At that time, in the kingdom of Kāliṅga, a brahmin named Jūjaka, a resident of a poorly situated brahmin village, having obtained a hundred kahāpaṇas while wandering for alms, deposited them in a certain brahmin family and went away again to seek further wealth.
While he was away for a long time, the brahmin family spent those hundred kahāpaṇas; subsequently, when the other [Jūjaka] returned, they began to press him for repayment.
Being unable to give him the kahāpaṇas, they gave him their daughter named Amittatāpanā.
Taking her with him, he went and lived in a poorly situated brahmin village in the kingdom of Kāliṅga. Amittatāpanā served the brahmin properly.
Then, other young brahmins, seeing the excellence of her conduct, remarked, "She attends properly to this elderly brahmin."
"But what have you forgotten about us? they said, rebuking their respective wives.
Thinking, "We shall drive this scorner of his enemies away from this village," they gathered at river fords and other places and reviled him.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“In Kaliṅga there was a brahmin named Jūjaka;
he had a young wife named Amitatāpanā.
When she went there to fetch water from the river, they said to her:”
People gathered together out of curiosity and reviled her, saying:
"Surely your mother is an enemy, and surely your father is an enemy,
who have given you away while you are so young and they themselves are old."
“Alas, your kinsmen have acted for your harm, deliberating in secret;
they who, while you are old, have given you such youthful counsel.
Alas, your kinsmen have acted as enemies, deliberating in secret!”
“Those who gave you away when you were old, though you were so young and mindful—
‘What a wicked deed your kinsmen have plotted in secret,’ they must have thought,
‘those who gave you away when you were old, though you were so young and mindful.’”
“Alas, your kinsmen have deliberated wickedly when they met in secret,
they who gave such a young bride to you in your old age. Alas,
your kinsmen have deliberated what is truly unpleasant when they met in secret!”
Those who gave their feet to one who was old, even so is this youthful mindfulness [of yours].
You have lived a life of unpleasant dwelling together with an aged husband;
you who live for an old man—for you, death would be better than life.
“Surely it was not your father or mother,
O beautiful one, who gave you to an old man as a husband when you were so young and possessed of such mindfulness.”
“Twice have you seen this on the ninth day: that no fire-sacrifice was performed for you when they placed you upon the funeral pyre while you were so young.
Surely, it must be toward the recluses and brahmins devoted to the holy life [that you should turn].”
"You, who dwell with an old man while you yourself are so young, bring a curse upon yourself in this world— upon the virtuous and the learned.
There is no suffering from being bitten by a snake, nor is there suffering from being struck by a spear."
And that suffering is intense, as one sees her husband grown old:
"There is no play, there is no delight with an aged husband;
there is no conversation or discourse, and even laughter does not shine."
“When young women, being young themselves, deliberate in secret,
all sorrows whatsoever that reside in the heart perish.
You are young and beautiful, desired by men.”
"Go and stay with your kinsmen; what will an old man do with pleasures?
Therein, *ahū* means "there was. *Vāsī Kaliṅgesu* means "a resident of a poorly situated brahmin village in the Kaliṅga kingdom.
*Tā naṃ tattha gatā vocuṃ* means that those women who had gone there to fetch water at the river ford spoke to him.
They said to him: "The women reviled him" means that the women said nothing else at all, but rather they reviled him.
"With curiosity" means as if they had become filled with curiosity. "Having gathered together" means having surrounded him on all sides.
"A young woman" means one who was young, fresh, and possessed of the height of beauty. "Of the old man" means of one worn out by old age.
“In your house. “Your *navamiya* sacrifice will be ill-performed (*duyiṭṭha*);
that sacrificial morsel of yours will first be seized by an old crow. There is also a reading, “Your *navamiya* will be ill-performed,” meaning it will be ill-performed by you.
“The fire-sacrifice (*aggihutta*) was not performed” means that even the offering of the fire was not performed by you.
"It will come to pass. "Cursing" means that they spoke with the very intention:
"This is the fruit of that evil deed," while reviling ascetics or brahmins who have stilled their evil or cast out their evil.
"Even laughing does not become him" means that even the laughter of an old man who laughs by showing his broken teeth does not become him. "The sorrows of all shall perish."
"The sorrows of all these will perish. 'What, he is old!'—how will this old man delight you with the five strands of sensual pleasure?

Having received this reproach from them, she took a water-jar and went home weeping. When asked by the brahmin, "Why are you weeping, lady?", she related what had happened to him and spoke this verse:
"I did not go to the river to fetch water for you, O brahmin; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
"The women revile me because of you, an old man, O Brahmin.
The meaning of this is: "Brahmin, the women revile me because of you, who are old; therefore, from now on, I shall no longer go to the river to fetch water for you.
Jūjaka said:
“Do not do work for me; do not fetch water for me. I shall fetch the water myself; do not be angry with me.
In this context, “I shall fetch the water, lady,” means: “I, lady, will bring the water.”
The brahmin woman said:
“I was not born in that family from which you have brought this water;
know this, O brahmin, I am not your daughter-in-law in this house.”
“If you do not bring me a male or female slave, O Brahmin, know this, O Brahmin: I will not go near you.
In this context, “I am not born in that family, O Brahmin, where the master himself performs the labor. And as for “that water which you shall bring,” I have no need of it.
Jūjaka said:
"I have no craft or profession, nor wealth or grain, O Brāhmaṇī;
from where could I bring a male or female slave for my lady?"
“I will attend upon you, ladies; do not be angry with me.
The brahmin woman said:
“Come, I will tell you how my words were heard.”
"This King Vessantara dwells on Mount Vaṅka.
Go to him, O Brahmin, and ask for a male slave and a female slave;
when entreated, that Kṣatriya will give you a male slave and a female slave."
Therein, "Come, I will tell you" and "I will explain it to you"—this was said by that deity who had taken possession of him.
Jūjaka said:
"I am old and weak; the road is long and very difficult to traverse."
"Do not lament, O lady, and do not be despondent;
I shall attend upon you, O lady, so do not be angry.
In this context, "I am old, O Bhaddā" means: "I am old; how shall I go?"
The Brahmin woman said:
"Just as one who has not gone into battle is defeated even without fighting,
so too, O Brahmā, have you been defeated without even going."
“If you do not bring me a male or female slave, O Brahmin, know this, O Brahmin: I shall not remain in your house.
I will do what is displeasing to you, and that will be your suffering.”
“When, during the festival or at the change of seasons,
you see me sitting on the stone slab enjoying myself with others, that will be your sorrow.
From not seeing me, as you lament in your old age— ”
“Furthermore, there will be many brahmins who are crooked and deceitful.
In this context, “I shall do what is disagreeable to you” means: “I shall perform an act that is not pleasing to you, such as bringing a male or female slave to Vessantara.
“Under the constellations and at the proper seasons” means either by way of the conjunction of the constellations...
On festive occasions occurring during the various seasons according to their respective precedents.
Having heard that, the brahmin became afraid. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then that brahmin, terrified and subservient to his wife,”
Distressed by sensual desire, he said this to the brahmin woman:
“Prepare provisions for my journey,
O brahmin woman— mixed rice with sugar-candy, well-made honey-balls, and grain-meal.”
“I will bring two young male slaves who are sexually experienced;
they will attend upon you day and night without weariness.
In this context, *aṭṭito* means afflicted, oppressed, or tormented. *Saguḷāni* means cakes made with flour. *Sattubhattaṃ* refers to both prepared grain-meal and unprepared grain-meal.

And food for the journey. "In similar [circumstances]" means in those resembling each other by way of birth, clan, family, or region. "A young man who is a slave" means a boy intended for the purpose of being your slave.
She quickly prepared provisions for the journey and informed the brahmin.
He strengthened the weak spots of the house, repaired the door, brought firewood from the forest, fetched water in a jar, and [arranged] all the vessels in the house.
Having filled [the bag] and assumed the guise of an ascetic right there, he instructed her, saying, "My dear, from now on do not go out at improper times;

remain vigilant until my return. Then, mounting his sandals and slinging the shoulder-bag of provisions over his shoulder, he circumambulated Amittatāpana, wept with eyes full of tears, and departed. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
Having said this, that wretched Brahmin put on his sandals;
then, after consulting with his wife and circumambulating her,
he departed with a tearful face, having abandoned his companionship.
“The city of the Sivi people is prosperous; go forth in search of a slave.

Therein, *ruṇṇamukho* means with a weeping face. *Sahitabbato* means from one who has undertaken [the vow], that is to say, having assumed the guise of an ascetic. “He goes about searching for a slave” means that while wandering in search of a slave, he set out toward the city of the Sivi people.
Having gone to that city, he asked the assembled crowd, “Where is Vessantara? To explain this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having gone there, he spoke to those who were assembled there:
‘Where is King Vessantara? Where may we see the Kshatriya?
Those people who were assembled there replied to him:”
“O Brahmā, it was by you that the kṣatriya was provoked with excessive generosity;
he was banished from his own kingdom and now dwells on the Vaṅka mountain.
“O Brahmā, it was by you that the kṣatriya was provoked with excessive generosity...”
“Having taken his sons and wife, he now dwells on Mount Vaṅka.
In this context, “distressed” means that being afflicted and oppressed, having been unable to dwell in his own city, he now dwells on Mount Vaṅka.
Thus, [the people said]: “Having destroyed our king, you have come back again; stay here!”—and with clods of earth, sticks, and other weapons in their hands, they [attacked them].
They followed after the brahmin. Being possessed by a deity, he took only the path to Vaṅka Mountain.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Thus urged by the brahmin woman, the brahmin, greedy for sensual pleasures,”
He practiced that evil in the forest teeming with wild beasts,
frequented by rhinoceroses and leopards.
Taking up a *beḷuva* staff, a sacrificial fire, and a water-pot;
Thus he entered the vast forest where he had heard of Kāmada.
Once he had entered that vast forest, the kokas surrounded him;
lost and crying out, he departed onto a distant path.
“Then that brahmin, having gone there— greedy for wealth and unrestrained—
spoke these verses when he had lost his way on the ascent of Vaṅka.
In this context, *aghaṃ* refers to both the suffering of being pursued by the great multitude and the suffering of wandering through the forest.

"Aggihutta" means a ladle for pouring oblations into the fire. "The cocks surrounded him" means that after he had entered the forest, not knowing the path to the village of Vaṅkapabbata, he wandered lost in the wilderness;
then the dogs of the Cetaputta, who was sitting there for the purpose of guarding him, surrounded him. "He cried out" means that he [climbed] a single tree.
Having climbed up, he cried out with a great roar. "Vippanaṭṭho" means one whose path is lost.
"Dūre panthā" means he departed far from the path leading to Vaṅka Mountain. "Bhogaluddho" means greedy for wealth. "Asaññato" means immoral.
"Vaṅkassorohaṇe naṭṭhe" means when the way of going to Vaṅka Mountain was lost.
Surrounded by his hounds, while sitting beneath a tree, he spoke these verses:
“Who knows my Vessantara, the prince Nisabha, the unconquered victor, the giver of safety in times of fear? Who knows me?”
“Who knows of that Vessantara, O Great King, who was like the earth, the supporter of all beings for those who came to him as supplicants?
He who was the refuge for those who asked, just as the ocean is for rivers.”
“Who among the wise knows my Vessantara, that great king who is like the ocean?
He is a beautiful landing-place, pure, with cool and delightful waters,
covered with white lotuses and strewn with the pollen of their filaments.”
“Who among the wise would not know my Vessantara, O Great King, who was like a lake?
He was like a *assattha* tree grown by the road—cool-shaded and delightful;
a bringer of peace to those on uneven paths, a refuge for the weary.”
“Who, O wise one, knows my Vessantara, who is like that great king—
like a banyan tree grown by the roadside, cool-shaded and delightful,
a refuge for those weary and a recipient for those in need?”
“Who, O wise one, knows my Vessantara, who is like that great king?
Like a mango tree grown by the road— cool-shaded, delightful, calming,
a deliverer from unevenness, and a refuge for those who are weary.”
“Who among the wise, O King, would know my Vessantara to be like that?
Like a sal tree grown by the wayside, cool-shaded and delightful;
a refuge for those weary, a supporter who rescues them from uneven paths.”
“Who among the wise, O Great King, would know my Vessantara to be like that?
Like a tree grown by the roadside, cool-shaded and delightful;
a protector for those weary, a refuge for those on uneven paths.”
“Who among my wise men knows that Great King Vessantara was like that?
And while I am thus lamenting, having entered the Brahma Forest,
whoever might say, ‘I know him,’ would bring me joy.”
“And while I was thus lamenting, having entered the Great Forest,
whoever should say, ‘I know him,’ would by that single utterance produce no small merit.”
In this context, *jayantaṃ* means overcoming the mind of stinginess (*maccharacitta*). "Who knows my Vessantara? he says, meaning "Who might explain Vessantara to me?
*Paṭiṭṭhāsī* means there was a support (*paṭiṭṭhā*). *Santānaṃ* means of those who are exhausted. *Kilantānaṃ* means of those weary from the road.
*Paṭiggahaṃ* means a recipient who has become a support. *Ahaṃ jānanti yo vajjā* means "I know him who would speak."
The meaning is: "Whoever should say, 'I know the dwelling place of Vessantara.
Having heard that sound of lamentation, the Cetaputta who had been stationed there for the purpose of guarding him went about in the forest as a deer-hunter and thought:
"This brahmin is lamenting for the sake of Vessantara’s dwelling place; indeed..."
"He has come here by the very nature of things; he will ask for Maddī or the children. I shall kill him right here!
Having thought this, he went into his presence and, stringing his bow and drawing it back, threatened him, saying, "Brāhmaṇa, I will not grant you your life!
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
The hunter wandering in the forest heard his mind’s response:
“O Brahmā, this khattiya has been treated by you with excessive generosity;
banished from his own kingdom, he dwells on the Vanka mountain.”
“O Brahmā, by your excessive giving, the khattiya has been ruined;
taking his wife and children, he dwells on a mountain in the bend.
This foolish man, having done what was not his duty, has come from the kingdom to the forest.”
Seeking the prince like a heron seeking fish in the water, he said:
“I will not give you life here, O brahmin;
for this arrow, shot by me, shall drink your blood.”
“Having cut off your head and severed your heart along with its attachments,
O Brahmin, I shall sacrifice the ‘path-bird’ for you with your own flesh.
With your flesh, your fat, and your skull, O Brahmin...”
“I shall offer an oblation, having cut out your heart:
‘This has been well-offered and well-poured by me for you with your flesh, O Brahmin;
and you shall not lead away the king’s son’s wife and children.’”
In this context, "one who does what should not be done" means you are a doer of improper acts. "Dull-witted" means lacking wisdom.
"Come from the kingdom to the forest" means come from the realm to the great wilderness. "He shall drink your blood" means this arrow shall drink your blood.
"Having struck you down" means having killed you; then, having stripped the head from you as you fall from the tree like a palm fruit, [he shall take] your heart-flesh along with its attachments.
"Having cut it down, I shall sacrifice the bird named Panthasakuṇa to the deity of the path.
And not you—this being the case, you will not carry off the wife or children of the prince.
Having heard his words, terrified by the fear of death, he spoke a falsehood, saying:
“A brahmin messenger is inviolable; listen to me, son of a Cetī!
Therefore, they do not kill a messenger; this is the eternal law.
All the Śivis are appeased, and your father wishes to see you.”
"And his mother was weak; soon his eyes grew dim.
'I have been sent as a messenger to you; listen to me, Cetaputta!
I shall lead away the prince—if you know him, tell me.'"
In this context, *nijjhattā* means conciliated. "Before long their eyes will fail" means that because of constant weeping, their eyes will soon become impaired.

Then Cetaputta, filled with joy at the thought, "They have come, it seems, to bring Vessantara back," tied up his dogs, helped the brahmin down, seated him on a bed of branches, gave him food, and spoke this verse:
"The messenger of one dear to me is dear to me; I give you a full bowl."
"And this jar of honey, O Brahmin, and the deer's haunch;
I shall tell you the place where the Giver of Desires is at peace.
Therein, "dear to me" means you are a dear messenger to my dear Vessantara. "Full bowl" means I give you a full bowl that fulfills your heart's desire.
The commentary on the Jūjaka chapter is finished.
The commentary on the Cūḷavana chapter:

Thus, having fed the brahmin, the son of a Cetan gave him a jar of honey and the leg of a wild deer for provisions on the journey; standing on the path, he raised his right hand and, pointing out the dwelling place of the Great Being, said:
“O Great Brahmā, that is Mount Sela, the Gandhamādana mountain,
where King Vessantara dwells together with his sons.
Assuming the guise of a brahmin, he carries a water-strainer, a razor, and matted hair.”
The leather-clad dweller on the ground lies upon the earth and pays homage to the fire-god:
“These blue forms appear, trees bearing various fruits;
they rise up like masses of clouds, like blue mountains of collyrium.”
“The Dhava, Asoka, Khadira, Sāla, Phandana, and Māluva trees tremble in the wind,
just as young men do when they have drunk but once.
Upon the high branches of the trees, sounds like those of a musical concert are heard.”
Flocks of cuckoos cry out as they fly from tree to tree.
Stirred by their branches and leaves, they seem to call out to him as he departs;
they seem to delight him as he approaches, and they gladden those who dwell there.
