“Where King Vessantara dwells together with his sons—
assuming the guise of a brahmin, bearing a staff, a water-pot, and matted hair, clothed in skins,
he lies upon the bare ground, paying homage to the fire.”
In that context, "Gandhamādana" refers to the Gandhamādana mountain. The meaning is:
"As you proceed northward along its slope, you will see the hermitage of Sakka where King Vessantara dwells together with his children and wife.
"The guise of a brahmin" means the dress of a noble renunciant. Having pulled out the beard, the flesh, and the matted hair, [he ate] of the fruits.
He carries a hook for the purpose of gathering [food], a ladle for offering fire, and a circle of matted hair. "Dressed in skins" means wearing a deerskin.
"He sleeps on the ground" means he lies upon the earth with a bed of leaves. "The *dhava*, *assakaṇṇa*, and *khadira* trees" refers to the *dhava*, the *assakaṇṇa*, and the *khadira*.
"Young men who have drunk but once" refers to those intoxicated by liquor after drinking it only a single time.
"Upon the branches of the trees" means on the boughs of the trees. "Chants as it were are heard" means that the cries of various birds singing are heard like celestial choruses.
"Najjuha" refers to the *najjuha* bird. "Flying about" means they move about warbling.
"Agitated by the leaves of the branches" refers to the birds warbling after being struck by the leaves of the branches.
"Or like a leaf on a branch stirred by the wind. "Āgacchantam" means people coming. "Yattha" means:
having gone to that hermitage where Vessantara dwells, you will see this excellence of the hermitage grounds.
Then, further describing the hermitage grounds, he said:
“Mangoes, wood-apples, breadfruit trees, sal trees, rose-apples, and marking-nut trees;
Terminalia chebula, emblic myrobalans, *assattha* trees, and jujubes.
And here are beautiful *timbaru* trees, as well as banyan and wood-apple trees.”
Honeybees hum there, and ripe udumbara fruits hang low.
There are pigeons and honey-thick grapes; they take their own pure, unadulterated honey and eat it there.
“Some mango trees here are in bloom, others stand as mere buds;
some are unripe and some are ripe, and both of these have the color of frogs.
Then, beneath them, a man gathers the ripe mangoes.”
“Both raw and ripe fruits, supreme in color, fragrance, and taste—this is truly a marvel to me!
The sound of the *hiṅkāra* strikes my mind;
like the abode of the gods, it shines like the Nandana grove.”
“Vibhedikā and nāḷikerā trees, and dates in the Great Forest;
garlands woven like those in Mālava stand there, appearing like the tops of victory banners;
with flowers of many colors, the sky is as if strewn with stars.”
“*Kuṭaja* and *kuṭṭha-tagara* trees, and *pāṭali* trees in full bloom;
*punnāga* and mountain *punnāga* trees, and *koviḷāra* trees in full bloom.
*Uddālaka* and *somarukkha* trees, and many *agaru-phalliya* trees.”
Putrajīvas and kakudhas, and asanas were in bloom there.
Kuṭajas, salaḷas, nīpas, kosambas, labujas, dhavas,
and sāl trees were flowering there, appearing like heaps of straw.
“Not far from that, on a delightful stretch of ground, was a lotus pond,
covered with pink and blue lotuses, like the Nandana grove of the gods.
And there, cuckoos sweet-voiced, intoxicated by the flavor of the flowers, [were singing].”
The trees, blossoming in season, resound with the wind.
"Honey flows from the nectars in every lotus;
then the winds blow here—southerly and westerly."
The hermitage was strewn with the pollen from the filaments of lotuses.
There were large crocodiles, both *saṃsādiya* and *pasādiya* species;
many fish and turtles were tossed about, and there were many water-fowl there as well.
Honey flows from the roots with stalks, and milk and ghee from the tubers.
"That forest wafts forth a fragrant scent, blended with various aromas;
indeed, that forest is massaged by the fragrance of its flowering branches."
Bees hummed all around, drawn by the fragrance of the flowers.
"And here there are many birds of various colors,
winged creatures who rejoice together with their mates, warbling to one another."
“Nandikā and Jīvaputtā, our dear Jīvaputtā;
dear sons, dear Nandā, the birds dwelling in the lotus pond.
Like woven garlands they stand, their crests alone are visible.”
With flowers of many colors, fragrant and well-prepared,
where King Vessantara dwells together with his sons.
Wearing the guise of a brahmin, carrying a water-pot, a meat-sickle, and matted hair;
“The leather-clad one lies on the ground, worshipping the fire.
In this context, *cārutimbarukkha* means beautiful *timbaru* trees. *Madhumadhuka* means sweet-tasting *madhuka* trees.
*Thevanti* means they shine. *Pārevata* refers to trees resembling the feet of pigeons (*pārevata*). *Bhaveyya* refers to plantains with long fruit.
*Madhutthikā* means those that drip honey-like fluid; or, because of their sweetness, they resemble honey-drops.
*Sakamādāya* means having taken them themselves, they consume them. *Dovilā* refers to those where fruits are produced from fallen flowers and leaves.
*Bhekavaṇṇā tadubhayaṃ* means both of these—whether raw or ripe—are indeed the color of a frog’s back. Now, herein...
"Below, a man": here, while standing right beneath those mango trees in the hermitage, a man picks the mango fruits;
there is no need for him to climb up. "Supreme in color, fragrance, and taste": they are supreme by virtue of these qualities, such as color and so forth.
"It is truly wonderful to me": it is exceedingly wonderful to me. "The sound 'hiṅ'": the making of the sound "hiṅ. "A divider": [it causes] separation.
*Tālā*: Like garlands strung upon trees in full bloom, the flowers remain suspended as if they were wreaths tied above the trees.
*Dhajaggāneva dissare*: Those trees appear as if their tops were adorned with victory banners. *Kuṭajī kuṭṭhatagarā*: *Kuṭajī* is a species of tree;
*kuṭṭha* refers to shrubs, and *tagara* refers to shrubs as well. *Giripunnāgā*: Great *punnāga* trees.
*Koviḷāra* means *koviḷāra* trees. *Uddālaka* means *uddālaka* trees. *Somarukkha* means royal trees with yellow-colored flowers.
*Phalliya* means *phalliya* trees. *Puttajīva* means great banyan trees. *Labuja* means *labuja* trees.
"Resembling a heap of straw" refers to the clusters of flowers that have fallen beneath them, which resemble a heap of straw.
"Lotus pond" (*pokkharaṇī*) means a square lotus pond. "In Nandana" means like the Nandā lotus pond in the Nandana Grove.
"Intoxicated by the juice of flowers" means intoxicated and stirred by the floral nectar. "With the nectars" means with the filaments. "Upon each lotus" means upon each lotus leaf;
for from the filaments upon those leaves, pollen falls and becomes what is called "lotus honey. *Dakkhiṇā*.
Now, by the phrase "the western," all the cardinal and intermediate directions have been shown.
"Large crossroads" means great junctions. "Samsadiya" refers to rice that grows spontaneously; it is also called *sukasali*.
"Pasadiya" refers to those very same plants fallen upon the ground. "Byaviddha" refers to those growing in clear water, spreading out and moving in rows.
They are seen. *Mupayānakā* means crabs. *Madhuṃ* means that when the root of the *bhisaka* plant is split open, the exuding juice is like honey.
*Khīrasappi muḷālibhī* means that the exuding juice from the lotus roots is like fresh butter mixed with milk.
*Sammaddateva* means as if it intoxicates those who have come near. *Samantā mabhināditā* means resounding on all sides.
They wander about. “Nandikā,” and so forth, are their names. Among them, the first says, “Master Vessantara, while dwelling in this forest, may you be happy.
The second says, “May you live happily, and may your sons as well.
The third says, “May you live, and may your dear sons as well. The fourth says, “May you be happy, and may your dear sons...”
And so they say. Therefore, these were their names. "Lotus-pool dwellers" (*pokkharaṇīgharā*) means those who live by the lotus pool.
When the son of the Cetan had thus described Vessantara’s dwelling place, Jūjaka was satisfied and, offering a greeting, spoke this verse:
"And this rice for my enemies, mixed with honey;..."
"And well-prepared honey-cakes; I give you this rice mixed with honey.
In this context, "rice mixed with honey" refers to rice known as *sattu*, which resembles cooked honey. This is what is meant: "This I have; I give it to you; please accept it.
Having heard that, the son of the Cetan said:
“Let the provisions be yours alone; I do not desire the provisions.
Take them from here as well, O Brahmā; go, Brahmā, as you please.
This one-footed path comes straight toward the hermitage.”
Even though he had passed away from that state, with mud on his teeth and dust on his head,
wearing the guise of a brahmin, carrying a water-pot, a lump of meat, and matted hair; clothed in skins,
he slept upon the ground and paid homage to the sacrificial fire.
“Go to him and ask; he will tell you the way.

In this context, *sambala* means provisions for the journey. As for the word *eti*: that single-path track which comes toward us goes straight to the hermitage. *Accuta* is the name of the seer who dwells there.
Having heard this, the kinsman of Brahmā, having made a respectful circumambulation, set out.
With an uplifted mind he departed for the place where the seer Accuta was.
Therein, "for the place where" means that he went to that location where the seer Accuta was.
The commentary on the Cūḷavana Sutta is finished.
The Description of the Great Forest:
“As he was going along, Bhāradvāja saw the seer Accuta.
Having seen him, Bhāradvāja exchanged greetings with the seer.”
“I hope it is well with you, sir; I hope you are free from illness.
I hope you manage to subsist by gleaning, and that roots and fruits are plentiful.
I hope gadflies and mosquitoes are few, as are reptiles.”
“In the forest teeming with wild beasts, is there no violence?
Therein, “Bhāradvāja” refers to the sacrificer. “Appam eva” means very little. “Hiṃsā” means injury to you caused by them.
The ascetic said:
“O Brahmā, my state is indeed wholesome, and moreover, O Brahmā, it is free from affliction;
furthermore, I subsist by gleaning, and I have many roots and fruits.
Moreover, there are gadflies and mosquitoes, and very few creeping reptiles.”
"In the forest teeming with predatory beasts, no violence exists for me.
For many a series of years, while dwelling in this hermitage,
I do not recall the arising of any unpleasant affliction."
“Welcome to you, Great Brahmā; indeed, you have come from afar.
Enter within, O Blessed One; wash your feet.
Here are *tinduka* fruits, *piyāla* nuts, *madhuka* flowers, and *kāsumārī* berries.”
“Eat the various small fruits, O Brahmā, the finest of the fine.
This cool water too has been brought from the mountain caves;
drink from it, Great Brahmā, if you so desire.”
Jūjaka said:
"Whatever was given has been accepted, and for all of it, a great honor has been performed;
[I have received] Sañjaya’s own son, who had been separated from the Sivi people."
“I have come here to see him; if you know him, tell me.
Therein, “I have come here to see him” means: I have come for the purpose of seeing him. The ascetic said:
“Your Honor does not come here for the sake of merit, but to see the King of the Śivis.”
"I think you desire the consort of a king as your wife;
I think you wish for the black antelope skin, the handmaid, and Jāli as your slave.
Or perhaps you have come from the forest to take away these three—a mother and her two sons."
“O Brahmin, there are no possessions for him—neither wealth nor grain—for that Vessantara dwelling in the forest;
he lives in poverty. What will you achieve by going to his presence?”
Having heard that, Jūjaka said:
“I am not one to be angry with you, sir; I have not come to beg.
It is good to see the Noble Ones; living together with them is always happy.”
“King Sivi has never been seen before, having been separated from his people;
I have come here for the sake of seeing him—if you know of him, tell me.
The meaning of this is: “O ascetic, I am not a rogue; enough of this much [talk]. But as for me, I do not know anything of Vessantara.”
"I have come to ask for him; however, it is good to see the Noble Ones, and dwelling together with them is pleasant.
I am that brahmin teacher, and since he was separated from the Sivi people by me, he has not been seen by me since then;
therefore, I have come for the purpose of seeing him. If you know his place of residence, please tell me."

Having heard his words and having placed faith in them, [Vessantara] said, "Very well, I shall go with you tomorrow; for now, stay right here. After satisfying him with various fruits, on the following day, pointing out the way, he extended his right hand and said:
"O Great Brahmā, this is Mount Gandhamādana, Where King Vessantara dwells together with his sons."
“Bearing the appearance of a brahmin, with a water-strainer, a lump of meat, and matted hair;
clothed in skins, he sleeps on the ground and pays homage to the fire.
These blue trees are seen, bearing various fruits.”
Towering like masses of clouds, they are blue as mountains of collyrium.
The dhava, assakaṇṇa, and khadira trees, along with the sāla, phandana, and māluva vines,
tremble in the wind like young men once intoxicated.
“In the upper reaches of the trees, only songs are heard;
flocks of *nandana* and cuckoos fly from tree to tree.
Stirred by their branches and leaves, they seem to call out as they go.”
They delight as if welcoming a guest,
gladdening the inhabitants wherever King Vessantara dwells together with his sons.
Bearing the guise of a brahmin, carrying a water-pot, a meat-sack, and matted hair;
The leather-clad dweller sleeps on the ground and pays homage to the fire.
"A canopy of garlands is spread out upon a delightful stretch of earth;
the ground is lush and green, where no dust rises."
“Resembling the neck of a peacock, and comparable to the touch of cotton;
the grasses do not exceed [the ground] by more than four finger-breadths on all sides.
Mangoes, rose-apples, wood-apples, and low-hanging ripe udumbara fruits [fall there].”
With trees providing all enjoyments, that forest increases delight.
There, water flows— pure and fragrant— resembling the color of beryl and frequented by schools of fish.
“Not far from that place, on a delightful stretch of ground, was a lotus pond,
covered with pink and blue lotuses,
like the Nandana grove of the gods. O Brahmin, in that lake there were three kinds of lotuses:”
“Variegated with many blues, and white and red as well.
Its meaning is exactly as stated below. “A canopy of *kareri* garlands spread out” means it was covered with *kareri* flowers. “Green with fresh shoots” means it was verdant with evergreen foliage.
“No dust rises there” means that not even the slightest speck of dust arises in that forest.
It rises upward. "Resembling the touch of cotton" means they are like the touch of cotton due to their softness.

"The grasses do not overgrow" means that those grasses on that ground, which are the color of a peacock's neck, grow to a height of exactly four finger-breadths all around and do not increase beyond that.
"Mangoes, rose-apples, and wood-apples" means mangoes, rose-apples, and wood-apples.
"By means of enjoyments" means by various kinds of trees that provide enjoyment, such as those bearing flowers and fruits.
"It flows" means that in that forest grove on Vaṅka Mountain, water flows down from the mountain streams; the meaning is that it moves along.
"Variegated with many blues, whites, and reds" means some are blue, some are white, and some are red.
By these three kinds of lotus flowers, that lake is variegated; it shows that it shines like a well-arranged flower basket.
Having thus described the square lotus pond, he spoke again while describing Lake Mucalinda:
"There, the lotuses are like fine linen, and there are white *sogandhika* [lotuses];"
Covered with *kālamba* trees, that lake is named Mucalinda.
There, lotuses in full bloom are seen on all sides;
blooming from summer through winter, they form a carpet reaching as high as the knees.
“They waft forth a fragrant scent, strewn with variegated flowers;
bees hum all around, drawn by the fragrance of the blossoms.
In that context, *khomāva* means as white as if made of *khoma* cloth. *Setasogandhikehi ca* means with white water-lilies (*setuppala*) and *sogandhika* lilies.
And that lake was covered with *kalambaka* flowers. "Appearing as if boundless" means they appear as if immeasurable.

"The summer and winter [lotuses]" refers to the lotuses blooming in both summer and winter. "Spread out as high as the knees" means that in water reaching the depth of the knees, the flowers are spread out;
they appear as if carpeted. "Carpeted with variegated flowers" means variegated...
Having been offered as oblations, they are always strewn with flowers and emit a fragrant scent.
"Furthermore, O Brahmin, at the edge of this water stand trees:
kadamba trees in full bloom, trumpet-flowers, and flowering kovidāra trees."
“The *aṅkola* and *kacchikāra* trees, and the *pārijañña* in full bloom;
the *vāraṇa* and *vayana* trees, and the *mucalinda* on both sides of the lake.
The *sirīsa* and white *pārisa* trees, and the *paddhaka* trees blow forth their fragrance well.”
The *nigguṇḍī* and *sirīnigguṇḍī*, and the *asanā* tree are in bloom here.
The *paṅgurā*, *bahulā*, and *selā* trees, as well as the *sobhañjana*, are in bloom;
the *ketaka*, *kaṇikāra*, and *kaṇavera* are also in bloom.
“The *ajjunā* and *ajjukaṇṇā*, and the *mahānāmā* are in full bloom;
standing with their tips in perfect flower, the *kiṃsuka* trees seem as if they were ablaze.
The *setapaṇṇī*, the *sattapaṇṇā*, the plantains, and the *kusumbharā*—”
With *dhanutakkārī* flowers and *sīsapā* canopies;
with *acchiva*, *sallava*, and flowering *sallakī* trees;
and with white *tagara*, *tagara*, *maṃsikuṭṭha*, and *kulāvara* [trees].
“Both young and old trees, straight and in full bloom, stand on both sides of the hermitage, surrounding the fire-hall.
Therein, “they stand” means they stand surrounding the lake. “Kadambā” refers to kadamba trees. “Kacchikārā” [refers to...]
*Cāti* refers to trees of that name. *Pārijañña* means red jasmine (*rattamālā*). *Vāraṇā vayanā* refers to both *vāraṇa* trees and *vayana* trees.
*Mucalinda-mubhato saranti* means on both sides of the Mucalinda River. *Setapārisā* are white shrubs;
it is said that they have white trunks, large leaves, and flowers resembling those of the *kaṇikāra*. *Nigguṇḍī* and *sirīnigguṇḍī* [are types of jasmine].
*Pakatinigguṇḍī* and *kālanigguṇḍī*. *Paṅgurā* refers to the *paṅgura* trees. *Kusumbharā* refers to a single thicket.
"Adorned with the flowers of *dhanu* and *takkārī*" means beautified by the blossoms of the *dhanu* and *takkārī* trees.
"And adorned with *sīsapā* and *varaṇa*" means beautified by *sīsapā* and *varaṇa* trees. *Acchiva* and the others are also types of trees. *Setageru* and *tagara* [are likewise].
*Setageru* and *tagara*. *Maṃsikuṭṭhā kulāvarā* means *maṃsiga* shrubs, *kuṭṭha* shrubs, and *kulāvara* trees.
*Akuṭilā* means straight. *Agyāgāraṃ samantato* means standing surrounding the fire-hall; this is the meaning.
"And here, near the water's edge, much *phaṇijjaka* has grown."
There were many *muggatiya* and *karatiya* insects, and many with heads like seaweed.
There was the "flowing from the wall" (*uddāpavatta*), the "agitated" (*ulluḷita*), the "fly," and the "asafoetida-web" (*hiṅgujālikā*).
There was the "female slave" (*dāsimaka*) and the "ear-ornament" (*kañjaka*) there, as well as many "low-hanging" (*nīcekalambaka*) insects.
“O Brahmin, trees covered with *elā* and *phuraka* stand there;
even after being gathered for seven days, their fragrance does not fade.
On both sides of Lake Mucalinda, beautiful flowers remain in bloom.”
That forest, covered with blue lotuses, shines forth in splendor.
"The fragrance of those flowers, which have been borne for half a month, does not fade;
the blue-flowered *girikaṇṇikā* and the white *vārī* are in full bloom."
That forest was covered with *kālārū* trees and *tulasī* plants.
That forest was indeed crushed by the fragrance of its flowering branches;
it resounded on all sides with the humming of bees attracted by the scent of the flowers.
“There are three kinds of *kakkāru* plants in that lake, O brahmin:
some are the size of a water-jar, and both [other] types are the size of a drum.
In this context, *phaṇijjaka* means *bhūtanaka*. *Muggatiya* is a species of bean. *Karatiya* is the royal bean (*rājamāsa*). *Sevālasīsaka* refers to...
"These too go away," and furthermore, "lead" (*sīsaka*) refers to red sandalwood.
"The water of the embankment is agitated" means that the water, having been struck by the wind and its banks and boundaries broken, remains in a state of agitation.
"Flies on *hiṅgu*-nets" refers to five-colored honey-flies making a sweet humming sound among flowering shrubs known as *hiṅgu*-nets.
The meaning is "wandering there. "And here the *dāsimaka* and the *kañjaka*" refers to these two species of trees found there.
"Low-hanging" means hanging low. "Covered with *elamphuraka* creepers" means covered by a creeper of that name.
"Of them" refers to the flowers of those creepers, or indeed the flowers of all these [trees], such as the *dāsimaka*, the *kañjaka*, and so forth.
The fragrance does not fade for seven days. Thus, the flowers are endowed with fragrance, and the ground is filled with sand resembling silver plates.
"Their fragrance" means the scent of those blue lotuses (*indīvara*) and other such flowers does not fade for half a month.
"Blue-flowered ones," etc., refers to flowering creepers. And "with *tulasī* plants" means with *tulasī* shrubs. "Of the *kakkāru* species" means...
Creeper-fruits. Therein, the fruits of one creeper are the size of a large jar, those of two are the size of a *mudiṅga* drum.
Therefore it is said: "Both of them are the size of a *muraja* drum.
"And herein there is much mustard, with green stalks entwined."
There stand ponds where many blue lotuses grow,
fit to be plucked. There are the *apphoṭa*, the *sūriyavallī*, the *kāḷīyā*, the *madhugandhiyā*,
the *asoka*, the *mudayantī*, the *vallibha*, and the *khuddapupphiya*.
The *koraṇḍaka* and the *anojā*, and the blooming *nāgamallikā*;
having climbed the tree, they stand there, as do the flowering *kiṃsuka* creepers.
And the *kaṭeruhā*, the *vāsantī*, the *yūthikā*, and the honey-scented [flowers].
The *nīlī*, jasmine, and *bhaṇḍī* flowers shine, as does the *padumuttara*.
The *pāṭalī*, sea-cotton, and *kaṇikāra* trees are in full bloom;
they appear like nets of gold, resembling the beautiful crests of flames.
“Whatever flowers there are, both those born on land and those born in water—all of them are seen there;
thus delightful is the great ocean.
In this context, *sāsapo* means mustard seed (*siddhatthaka*). *Bahuko* means many. *Nādiyo haritāyuto* means the rivers are joined with greenery.
These two kinds of garlic; "that garlic also is abundant there" is the meaning.
"Eighty palm trees stand" means that trees named *asī* stand like palm trees upon the moist ground.
"Many blue lotuses to be plucked" means that many golden blue lotuses (*suvaṇṇaindīvara*) stand along the water's edge, ready to be gathered by the handful. *Apphoṭā*.
*Apphoṭavalliyo*: *Vallibho* and *khuddapupphiyo*, meaning both *vallibho* and *khuddapupphiyo*.
*Nāgamallikā*: *vallināgā* and *mallikā*. *Kiṃsukavalliyoti*: a species of creeper with fragrant leaves.
*Kaṭeruhā* and *vāsantī*: these two are flowering shrubs. *Madhugandhiyā*: having a fragrance like honey. *Niliyā*, *sumanā*, and *bhaṇḍī*.
The *nīlavallīsumanā*, the *pakatisumanā*, and the *bhaṇḍī*. The tree named *Padumuttara* is such a tree.
The *kaṇikāra*s are both the climbing *kaṇikāra* and the tree *kaṇikāra*. They appear like spread-out nets of gold, as it were.
The "Great Ocean" (*mahodadhi*) refers to the Mucalinda Lake, which serves as the receptacle for a vast mass of water.
“Then, in that lotus pond, there were many water-dwellers:
red fish, reed-eaters, horned fish, crocodiles, makaras, and susūs.
There was honey and honey-sticks, palm kernels, and priyaṅgu seeds.”
Kuṭaṇḍajas, bhaddamuttas, white-flowered lolupas;
Fragrant trees and tagaras, many with lofty stalks;
Paddhakas, naradas, kuṭṭhas, jhāmakas, and hareṇukas.
“Haliddaka, gandhasilā, hirivera, and guggula;
vibhedika, coraka, kuṭṭha, kappūra, and kaliṅguka.
Therein, regarding the phrase “of that lotus pond,” he speaks of the river itself as a “lotus pond” because it resembles a lotus pond.
*Roḥita*, *atīta*, and so forth are the names of those whose range is water. “And honey” means honey free from bees.
“And the madhulaṭṭhi” means the *laṭṭhika-madhuka*. “And the tālisa,” etc., refers to all varieties of fragrant substances.
“Now, here there are lions and tigers, and men-eaters and elephants;”
The black antelope, the spotted deer, the rohit deer,
and the sarabha deer— The house-dog and the wild dog, when weighed, are like blades of reed;
The yak-tail fan, the chowrie, and the leaping monkey, when burned, are like cotton-wool.
“Carpenter crabs and spider-mothers, iguanas and many horned lizards;
rhinoceroses, wild boars, mongooses, and black scorpions in great numbers.
Buffaloes, jackals, and wild cats, and *pampakas* all around.”
Jackals, bats, and leopards, as well as panthers;
scavengers and those who feed on scraps, lions and jackals that prey on herds of cattle;
eight-legged creatures and peacocks, and radiant pheasants.
“Caṅkoras, cuckoos, and nāgas warbled to one another;
Bakās, balākās, najjuhas, dindibhas, and kuñjavājitas;
Byagghinasas, lohapiṭṭhas, pampakas, and jīvajīvakas.”
Kapiñjaras, tittiras, and the kulā-paṭikutthakas;
mandālakas, celakeṭus, those named bhaṇḍutittiras;
celāvakas, piṅgalās, goṭakas, and aṅgahetukas.
“Karaviyas and swans, uhuṅkāras and cuckoos;
crowded with flocks of various birds, resounding with the warbling of diverse cranes.
Therein, *purisālū* refers to the *vaḷavāmukha* yakṣiṇīs. *Rohiccā sarabhā migā* means both *rohitā* deer and *sarabha* deer.
And deer. *Koṭṭhasukā* refers to jackals and dogs; there is also a reading as *koṭṭhusuṇā*.
And the *suṇa*—this is a species of small wild animal. *Tuliya* refers to birds and cats. *Naḷasannibhā* means tree-dogs, having the color of reed-flowers.
*Cāmarī*, *calanī*, and *laṅghī* refer to the yak (*cāmarī-miga*), the *calanī-miga*, and the *laṅghī-miga*. "The monkeys were burnt."
There were two species of monkeys. *Picu* refers to one monkey who, at the edge of the arrow’s range, took up his station.
*Kakkaṭā* and *Kaṭamāyā*: these were two large deer. *Ikkā* refers to bears (*acchā*). *Goṇasira* refers to wild oxen (*araññagoṇā*).
*Kāḷakettha bahūtasā* means that there were many black deer (*kāḷamiga*) there. *Soṇa-siṅgālā* refers to tree-dogs (*rukkhasunakhā*) and jackals. *Pampaka* refers to the hermitage site.
The great bamboo-crested birds stood surrounding [them]. The *ākucchi* are monitor lizards (*godhā*). The *pacalākā* are the elephant-headed deer (*gajakumbhamiga*).
The *citrakā* are both the leopard (*citramiga*) and the panther (*dīpimiga*).
The *pelakā* are hares (*sasa*). The *vighāsādā* are these vultures (*gijjhā-sakuṇā*). The *sīhā* are maned lions (*kesarasīha*). The *gogaṇisādakā* are...
Wild beasts are those whose nature it is to seize herds of cattle and eat them. *Aṭṭhapāda* refers to the *sarabha* deer. *Bhassara* refers to white swans.
*Kukutthaka* refers to the *kukutthaka* birds. *Caṅkora* refers to the *caṅkora* birds. *Kukkuṭa* refers to wild chickens.
*Dindibhā*, *kuñjavājita*—these three are also birds. *Byagghinasa* refers to leopards. *Lohapiṭṭha* refers to birds of red color.
"Pampakā" refers to *pampaṭaka* birds. "Kapiñjarā and tittirā" means both *kapiñjaras* and *tittiras*.
"Kulā and paṭikutthaka" refers to these two types of birds as well. "Mandālakā and celakeṭū" means both *mandālakas* and *celakeṭus*.
"Named bhaṇḍu and tittira" means those called *bhaṇḍus* and *tittiras*. "Celāvaka and piṅgalā" refers to two species of birds, as do "goṭakas."
The limbs are the cause. "Heavens" refers to the cātaka birds. "Hooting" refers to the owls.
"Now there are birds here, blue and sweet-voiced;
they rejoice with their mates, warbling to one another."
“Moreover, there are birds here, winged creatures with sweet voices,
perched upon white-topped peaks, auspicious-eyed, egg-born, and adorned with variegated plumage.
Moreover, there are birds here, winged creatures with sweet voices, perched...”
Sikhaṇḍī and Nīlagīvā cooed to one another:
“Kukutthakas, Kuḷīrakas, Koṭṭhas, Pokkharasātakas, Kālāmeyyas,
Balīyakkhas, Kadambas, and Suvasāḷikas.”
“Tawny, red, and white, and here many *nalaka* birds;
elephants and *bhiṅgarāja* birds, *kadamba* and beautiful cuckoos.
*Ukkusa*, ospreys, swans, *āṭa* and *parivadentikā* birds.”
The pākahaṃsa geese are exceedingly powerful, as are the najjuhas and the jīvajīvaka birds.
There are pigeons, ravishing haṃsas, ruddy geese, and river-dwelling birds;
there are elephants crying out in delight, lovely creatures that warble at both times of day.
“Furthermore, there are many birds here, variously colored,
winged creatures who rejoice together with their mates, warbling to one another. Furthermore,
there are many birds here, variously colored, winged creatures...”
All the birds warble sweetly on both sides of Lake Mucalinda.
Now there are certain birds here called karaviyas;
they rejoice together with their mates, warbling to one another.
“Now there are birds here, those winged creatures called karaviyas;
they all warble sweetly on both sides of Lake Mucalinda.
This forest is filled with deer and spotted deer, and is frequented by nāgas.”
It was covered with various creepers and frequented by plantains and deer.
"And here there was much mustard, much wild rice and millet;
there was rice that ripens without cultivation, and there was no small amount of sugarcane."
“This one-footed path comes straight to the hermitage;
having reached it, one finds no hunger, thirst, or discontent,
where King Vessantara dwells together with his sons.”
“Assuming the appearance of a brahmin, with a water-pot, a tuft of hair, and matted locks;
clothed in skins, he sleeps on the ground, paying homage to the fire.
In this context, *nīlakā* means having variegated streaks as their leaves. *Mañjūssarā sitā* means having a constantly sweet voice. *Setacchikūṭā* [means having white tips].
"Bhadrakkhā" refers to those with beautiful eyes, endowed with white eye-sockets on both sides. "Citrapekhuṇā" means those with variegated wing-feathers.
"Kuḷīrakā" refers to crabs. "Koṭṭhā" and so forth are indeed birds. "Vāraṇā" refers to birds with the characteristics of elephants.
"Kadambā" includes the great kadamba trees. "Suvakokilā" refers to both the suva-birds that roam together with cuckoos and the cuckoos themselves.
*Ukkusa* means black *kurara* birds. *Kurarā* means white *kurara* birds. *Haṃsa* refers to the *haṃsa* birds. *Āṭa* refers to birds with mouths shaped like a deer’s antlers.
*Parivadentikā* is a species of bird. *Vāraṇābhirudā rammā* means delightful *vāraṇa* birds that cry out beautifully.
*Ubho kālūpakūjino* means they warble together, making a single sound at the foot of the mountain both evening and morning. *Eṇeyyapasadākiṇṇaṃ* means crowded with *eṇeyya* deer.

It was crowded with deer and wild animals. "One who has arrived there finds nothing," O Brahmin—meaning that a person who has reached Vessantara’s hermitage does not encounter hunger, thirst, or distress there.
Having heard this, O kinsman of Brahmā, pay homage to the seer by keeping him to your right.
With an uplifted heart, he departed for where Vessantara was.
Regarding the phrase "where Vessantara was": he went to that place where Vessantara had been.
The commentary on the Great Forest is concluded.
The Commentary on the Birth of the Boy:
Jūjaka, too, traveling by the path described by the truthful ascetic, reached the square lotus pond and thought:
"It is already very late today; Maddī will now be returning from the forest. For a woman is indeed an obstacle to giving."
"Tomorrow, when she has gone to the forest, I will go to the hermitage, approach Vessantara, ask for the children, and once she has not yet returned, I shall take them and depart.
Then, having climbed a certain mountain ridge not far from there, he lay down in a comfortable spot. That night, at the time of dawn, Maddī saw a dream.
Such was the dream that occurred: a man, black in complexion, wearing two saffron-colored robes and red garlands on both ears, came brandishing weapons and threateningly entered the leaf-hut;
seizing Maddī by her matted locks, he dragged her down and threw her flat upon the ground, and while she was crying out, he gouged out both her eyes and [seized] her arms.
“Having cut through my chest and pierced it, he took the heart-flesh, with drops of blood streaming forth, and departed.
Upon waking, she became terrified and anxious, thinking, “I have seen a terrible dream, yet there is no dream-interpreter equal to Vessantara;
I shall ask him. Having thought this, she went to the leaf-hut and approached the door of the Great Being’s leaf-hut.
She knocked. The Great Being asked, "Who is this? "O Lord, it is I, Maddī," she replied.
"My dear lady, why have you come at an improper time, breaking our agreement? "Lord, I do not come under the influence of defilement;
rather, I have had a bad dream. "In that case, tell me about it, Maddī," he said. She related it exactly according to what she had seen.
The Great Being, having reflected upon his dream, thought: "My perfection of giving will be fulfilled; tomorrow a supplicant will come and ask for my children.

I shall comfort Maddī and dismiss her. Having thus deluded and reassured her with the words, "Maddī, your mind must be agitated by thoughts of fine clothing and food; do not fear," he sent her away. When dawn had broken, she—
Having performed all his duties for the night, he embraced his two sons, kissed them on the head, and exhorted them, saying, "Dear ones, today I have seen a bad dream; you must be heedful.
Then, having entrusted his sons to the Great Being, saying, "Your Majesty, be heedful regarding these two princes," he took his cloak, scissors, and other items, and shed tears.
While she was cleaning herself, she entered the forest for the sake of roots and fruits.
At that time, Jūjaka, thinking, “Maddī must have gone into the wilderness now,” descended from the mountain and set out toward the hermitage by a narrow footpath.
The Great Being also emerged from the leaf-hut and sat upon a stone slab at the door of the hut like a golden statue; then—
Thinking, “A beggar will come,” he sat watching the path of his arrival like a drunkard parched with thirst.

His sons were playing at his feet. As he watched the road and saw the brahmin approaching, he felt a surge of joy as if lifting up the burden of giving that he had set aside for seven months, and cried out, “Come, good brahmin!”
Addressing Jālikumāra, he spoke this verse:
“Arise, Jāli, stand firm! It appears as it did of old;
I see you like a brahmin. Let not joy overwhelm you.”
In this context, "it appears as if it were ancient" means that just as there was formerly the arrival of beggars from various directions at the city of Jetuttara,
so too is the arrival of beggars seen today. "Nandiyo mābhikīrare" means that from the moment this brahmin saw me,
gladdening joys have showered upon me, like a thousand jars of cold water poured over the head of a man scorched by the heat.
"It has become like the time for his consecration.
Having heard this, the prince said:
"I too, father, see him who appears like Brahmā himself."
"He approaches like one on a long journey; he will be our guest.
Having said this, the prince rose from his seat, paid homage to the Great Being, and went out to meet the brahmin, asking for permission to take his belongings.
The brahmin, looking at him, [recognized]: "This is Jāli-kumāra, the son of Vessantara."
Thinking, "I shall speak harsh words from the very beginning," he snapped his fingers, saying, "Get away! Get away!
The prince stepped back and, wondering, "This brahmin is exceedingly harsh; what could be the reason?
stood observing his body and saw eighteen faults of a man. The brahmin then approached the Bodhisatta.
Offering a hospitable greeting, he said:
“I hope you are well, sir; I hope you are free from illness.
I hope you are getting by with what you glean, and I hope roots and fruits are plentiful.”
“I hope there are no gadflies or mosquitoes, and very few creeping reptiles;
in this forest teeming with wild beasts, I trust that no harm is found?
The Bodhisatta, exchanging greetings with him, said:
“O Brahmā, it is wholesome indeed, and moreover, O Brahmā, it is free from affliction;
thus we shall subsist by gleaning, and there will be many roots and fruits.
Moreover, there are only a few gadflies and mosquitoes, and very few creeping reptiles.”
“In this forest teeming with predatory beasts, no harm exists for us.
Having lived for seven months in the wilderness, grieving for our lives,
we now behold for the first time this brahmin who has the appearance of a god.”
Taking up his bamboo staff, the sacrificial fire, and his water-pot:
“Welcome to you, Great Brahmā! You have come from afar;
enter within, O Blessed One, and wash your feet.”
“Tiṇḍuka fruits, piyāla fruits, madhuka, and kāsumārī;
eat these small fruits, O Brahmā, one by one.
This too is cool water, brought from the heart of the mountain.”
“Then drink, Great Brahmā, if you so desire.
Having spoken thus, the Great Being thought, “This brahmin has not come to this great forest for no reason; I shall ask him the reason for his coming without making a delay,” and he spoke this verse:
“But by what appearance, or for what cause, have you come?”
“You have arrived at the great forest; explain that to me when asked.
In this context, “by way of appearance” means by way of cause; “by way of reason” means by way of condition.
Jūjaka said:
"Just as a full river of water never runs dry at any time, so have I come at your request:
'Give me your sons,' as I was asked.
In this context, "river of water" refers to the flow of water in the five great rivers. "Does not run dry" means that even when thirsty people come and [take water] with their hands...
Even when poured out from the vessels and drunk, it is not exhausted. Thinking, "Thus they come to beg;
you too are just like this because you are filled with faith," I have come to beg of you. When I said, "Give me your sons, I beg," I meant:
"Give your sons to me for the purpose of being my slaves."
Hearing this, the Great Being was filled with joy. As if placing a thousand-piece purse into outstretched hands, he spoke these verses while making the mountain foot resound:
“I give; I do not waver. O Brahmin, take it as your lord!
The princess departed in the morning; she shall return from her alms-gathering this evening.”
“Having stayed for one night, you depart in the morning, O brahmin;
[you leave] them after they have bathed and adorned themselves, and then wearing garlands.
Having stayed for one night, you depart in the morning, O brahmin.”
“Covered with various flowers, adorned with various scents, strewn with various roots and fruits—go, O Brahmin, to gather what you please.
In this context, “lord” means: being the lord and master over my sons, lead them away; moreover, however, one...
There is a reason. Their mother, a princess, went out early in the morning for the sake of gathering fruits and will return from the forest in the evening;
after you have eaten the sweet fruits brought by her and stayed right here for this one night, you shall take the children and depart early in the morning.
*Tassā nhāteti*: she has been bathed by her. *Upaghāteti*: she has had her head anointed with fragrant unguents.
"Atha ne māladhārino" means "then [he saw] them wearing various garlands," that is, adorned with diverse garlands and carrying those garlands.
However, in the manuscript copies, it is written as "atha ne māladhārino," the meaning of which has not been investigated.
"Nānāmūlaphalākiṇṇe" means strewn with various roots and fruits given for the purpose of provisions on the road.
Jūjaka said:
“I do not delight in staying; going is what pleases me.
Let there be obstacles for me as well, O bull among charioteers, yet I would rather go.”
“Women are not practitioners of asceticism; they do not create obstacles for him.
Women know the spells; they take everything from the left side.
While he was giving a gift out of faith, he did not see his mother for a month.”
She might even create an obstacle as you go along, O bull among charioteers.
"Address your sons: 'Do not devour your mother!
For one giving a gift with faith, merit increases in this way.'"
“Command your sons: ‘Let them not devour your mother!
Having given wealth to one such as me, O King, you shall go to heaven.
In this context, the word *na* in the phrase *na hetā yācayogī* is a mere particle (*nipātamatta*). This is what is meant: “O Great King!”
These so-called women are not indeed those who practice begging;
they are not suitable for begging, but rather act as obstacles, creating an obstruction to the merit of the givers and an obstruction to the gains of the supplicants.
They are called "women" because they know deception (*māyā*). From the left, they take everything from the left, not from the right. With faith...
"Of one giving a gift" means of one who gives a gift having faith in both the action and its fruit. "Māsaṃ" means "do not see their mother.
"Kayirā" means "he should do. "Āmantayassu" means "inform [her]" or "send her along with me," he says.
"Dadato" means "of one who is giving."
Vessantara said:
"If you wish to see my devoted and faithful wife,
show her both Jāli and Kaṇhājinā to your grandfather as well."
“Having seen these two boys, who are charming and speak so sweetly, he will be thrilled, joyful, and delighted, and he will give you much wealth.
In this context, “of the grandfather” means of my father, King Sañjaya, the grandfather of the two boys. “He will give you wealth” means that the king will give you much wealth.
Jūjaka said:
“I fear being cut to pieces; O prince, listen to me!
You might give me to the king’s punishment, or sell me, or even kill me.”
“The Victor [takes] wealth and slaves from the one who is censurable, that wretched Brahmin.
In this context, “from the one who seizes” means I fear being seized after having been robbed.
“He would give me over to royal punishment” means he would hand me over to the ministers for the sake of punishment, saying, “This Brahmin is a child-thief; give him his due penalty.”
"‘A censurable Brahmin-pretender’—he thought, ‘I shall be censured by the Brāhmaṇīs alone.
Vessantara said:
‘Having seen these two boys, so charming and sweet-spoken;’"
"Established in the Dhamma, O Great King, you who increase the kingdom of the Sivi people,
having attained joy and gladness, will give much wealth to you.
Thus spoke Jūjaka.
“I will not do even that which you instruct me; I shall take these children as attendants for my brahmin wife.
In this context, “I shall take these children as attendants for my brahmin wife” means: “Enough for me with other wealth; I shall take these very children as attendants for my own brahmin wife.”
Hearing those harsh words of his, the children fled in fear; they went to the leaf-hut at the back, but fleeing from there as well, they hid in a dense thicket.

There too, seeing themselves as if seized by a hunter who had come upon them, trembling and unable to remain still anywhere, they ran hither and thither until they reached the bank of the square lotus pond.
Having gone there and firmly donned bark garments, they descended into the water, placed lotus leaves upon their heads, and stood there concealed by the water.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then the princes, distressed upon hearing the hunter’s words, ...”
"Both Jālī and Kaṇhājinā ran hither and thither.
But even when he did not see the two boys, Jūjaka reproached the Bodhisatta: "O Vessantara, you have just now given me your children;
yet you say, 'I will not go to the city of Jetuttara,' and that the children are to be attendants for my Brahmin wife!"

When he said, "I shall bring them," [the other] gave a sign with his eyebrows and, having caused the sons to flee, sat there as if unaware, thinking, "There is likely no liar in the world equal to you. Hearing this, the Great Being’s heart trembled;
thinking, "The children must have fled," he said, "O Brahmin, do not worry; I will bring the princes back to you."
Having risen and gone to the leaf-hut on the ridge, and knowing that they had entered the forest thicket, he followed their footprints to the edge of the lotus pond.

Seeing the tracks where they had stepped into the water, and realizing that "the princes must have descended into the water and are standing there," he called out, "Dear Jālī! and spoke these two verses:
“Come, dear father, beloved son, fulfill my perfections;
sprinkle my heart with [the water of] consecration, and do as I say.
Be for me a vehicle and a ship, immovable in the ocean of existence.”
“I shall cross to the further shore of birth; I shall ferry across the world together with its gods.
Having heard his father’s words, the prince thought, “Let the brahmin do as he pleases; I will not engage in two conversations at once with my father.
He then emerged from the water, shaking off the lotus leaves like a head emerging from beneath them, and approached the Great Being.
Falling on his right knee and firmly grasping her ankle-joint, he wept.
Then the Great Being said to him, "Dear one, where is your sister? "Dear one, when danger arises, these beings protect only themselves.
Then the Great Being, realizing that an agreement must have been made with his sons, called out, "Come, my dear Kanhā," and spoke these two verses:
“Come, dear mother Piyadhīti, fulfill my perfections;
sprinkle my heart with water, and do as I say.
Be for me a vehicle and a ship, unshakable in the ocean of existence.”
"I shall cross to the further shore of birth; I shall uplift the world together with its gods.

She too, thinking, "I will not speak two words with my father," likewise emerged from the water, fell at the Great Being’s left foot, gripped his ankle-joint firmly, and wept. Their tears [fell upon] the Great Being...
They fell upon the soles of his feet, which were the color of full-blown lotuses; his tears fell upon their backs, which resembled golden plates.
Then the Great Being, having raised the princes and comforted them, said, "Dear Jāli, do you not know my state as one who has given away his wealth?
Dear son, fulfill my intention to the very end," and there, as if driving oxen, he urged them forward.
He had the boy brought before him. Having summoned his son, he said, "Dear Jāli, if you wish to become a free man, you may do so by giving a thousand *nikkhas* to the brahmin;
for your sister possesses the most excellent beauty, and some person of low birth might give the brahmin some small amount of wealth and thereby make your sister a free woman."
"He would cause the confusion of castes; indeed, there is no one other than a king who is a giver of all things to beings.

Therefore, sister, if you desire to be free, give a hundred male slaves, a hundred female slaves, a hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred bulls, and a hundred gold coins—having thus given away all these hundreds, you shall be free.
Having thus caused the prince to be valued and having comforted her, [he spoke].
Having gone to the hermitage, he took water in his water-pot, addressed them saying, "Come, O Brahmins!
and made a resolution that it might become a condition for the attainment of omniscience.
Then, pouring out the water, he said, "O Brahmin, omniscience alone is dearer to me than my sons—hundredfold, thousandfold, and even hundred-thousandfold."
Making the earth resound with his cry, he gave the gift of his beloved sons to the brahmin. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then, taking both the princes, Jāli and Kaṇhājina, the one who increased the prosperity of the Śivi kingdom gave them as a gift to the brahmin.”
“Then, taking both the princes Jāli and Kaṇhājinā, the delighted [king] gave his two little sons as a supreme gift to the brahmin.
That was a terrifying thing; that was hair-raising.”
When the prince was given away, the earth trembled all over.
That was a terrifying thing; that was hair-raising, when the king, with palms joined in reverence, [gave] the prince who was cherished for his happiness.
“The King who increases the realm of the Sivis gave a gift to the brahmin.
In this context, *vitta* means having become filled with joy and gladness. Regarding the phrase “then there was that which was terrifying”:
at that time, through the power of the gift, the great earth—four hundred and twenty-four thousand yojanas in thickness—roared like an elephant in rut.
As he roared, the earth trembled and the ocean was agitated. Sineru, the king of mountains, bent over like a well-watered bamboo shoot and stood facing the Vaṅka mountain.
Sakka, the king of the gods, clapped his hands, and Mahābrahmā gave a cry of "Well done!
A great clamor arose as far as the Brahma-world. With the sound of the earth, the sky thundered and a brief rain fell.
Unseasonable flashes of lightning burst forth. Lions and other creatures dwelling in the Himalayas let out a single roar throughout the entire Himalayan range;
such was the terrifying spectacle. However, in the Pāḷi, only this much is stated: "The earth shook and trembled. *Yaṃ* means "when.
*Sukhavacchitā* means "dwelling in happiness" or "reared in happiness. *Adā dānaṃ* means "O, give the gift! [Ambho]...
"O Brahmin, all-knowing wisdom (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is indeed dearer to me than my sons by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and a hundred-thousandfold.
For that purpose he gave it away.
Having given the gift, the Great Being, generating joy at the thought, "Truly well-given is this gift of mine," looked upon the princes.
He stood there. Jūjaka, too, having entered the thicket of trees, bit through the creeper with his teeth and took it;
he then bound the prince’s right hand together with the maiden’s left hand, and grasping the very end of that creeper, he set off, lashing them along.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
Then that greedy brahmin, having cut the creeper with his teeth,
bound the elephant’s trunk to the creeper and rubbed it back and forth along the creeper.
Then that brahmin, taking a rope and taking a staff, [proceeded].
“Beating them, they lead them away while the King of Sivi looks on.
In this context, “the King of Sivi” refers to Vessantara.
At every spot where they were struck, their skin was torn and blood flowed. While they were being beaten, [they would call out] to one another—
They gave him their backs. Then, at a certain uneven spot, the brahmin slipped and fell.
The creepers bound by the princes' tender hands broke and came loose. Weeping, they fled and came into the presence of the Great Being.
Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
Then the princes departed, having released the brahmin;
with eyes filled with tears, he gazed upon his father.
Like a *vedhamassa* tree laden with fruit, he bowed at his father’s feet.
Having prostrated at his father’s feet, he spoke these words:
“Mother and father have already departed; you will see us, father.
Let us first see our mother, and then, father, you shall see us.”
“Mother and father have gone out, and you, father, will show us [the way].
Do not give us away, father, until our mother has also returned.
Then let this brahmin do as he pleases—sell us or kill us.”
“With feet like a balance-scale, with dark nails, and moreover with a protruding belly;
with long upper lips, fickle, with reddish-brown skin, and a broken nose.
With a pot-like belly, a broken back, and moreover with uneven eyes.”
With copper-colored hair and greenish locks, covered with wrinkles and freckles;
tawny, stooped, misshapen, tall, and harsh;
clad in skins, he was a non-human being, terrifying to behold.
“Are you a human or a *yakkha*, a consumer of flesh and blood?
Having come from the village to the forest, dear father, you beg for that wealth.
While being led away by a *pisāca*, why indeed, dear father, do you look back?”
“Surely your heart must be made of iron, bound with firm fetters,
you who do not realize that we are bound by this Brahmin seeking wealth—
a man in great haste and cruelty who slaughters us like cattle.”
“Stay right here, O Kanhā; she knows nothing at all.
Like a doe intoxicated by milk, she cries out, having been separated from the herd.
Therein, *udikkhati* means that having gone to her father’s presence, she looks about while trembling. *Vedhanti* means trembling (*vedhamāna*).
"And you, dear father, will give us"—meaning, "you will give us to the brahmin even before she has arrived.
Do not do this; please wait until we have seen our mother. Then, once she has been seen, you may give us to him.
"Let him sell us or kill us," dear father—once our mother has arrived, let him sell us or kill us.
"Or rather, let him do whatever he wishes. However, he is harsh and cruel, and is possessed of the eighteen faults of a man"—thus he spoke of the eighteen faults of a man.
In that context, "bald-footed" means one whose feet are splayed; "blind-nailed" means one with putrid nails; "with drooping calves" means one whose calf-muscle flesh has sagged downward.
*Dīghuttaroṭṭho* means one who possesses a long upper lip that protrudes when the mouth is closed. *Capalo* means one whose saliva drips.
*Kaḷāro* means one who possesses teeth that protrude like the tusks of a boar. *Bhagganāsako* means one who possesses a broken and uneven nose.
*Lohamassū* means one with hair on the face the color of copper-red metal. *Haritakeso* means... [one with green hair].
One with hair grown golden-colored. "Valīna" means his body skin is wrinkled. "Tilakāhata" means covered with black moles.
"Piṅgala" means having protruding yellowish-brown eyes, endowed with eyes like those of a cat.
"Vinata" means crooked in three places: the waist, the back, and the shoulders. "Vikaṭa" means having deformed feet. Also, "one with loose joints."
It was said: "He is possessed of bone-joints that creak. *Brahā* means tall. *Amanusso* means not a human;
even though he wanders in human guise, he is a *yakkha*. "Terrifying" means extremely frightening.
"Is this a human or a *yakkha*, dear?"—if anyone were to see this brahmin and ask thus: "Is this a human..."
“Is he a brahmin, or is he a *yakkha*? “He is not a human; rather, it is fitting to say he is a *yakkha* who feeds on flesh and blood.
“He asks for that wealth, dear one”—that is, dear one, this one desires to eat our flesh and asks you for the wealth of our children.
“Do you look on?”—that is, do you remain indifferent? “Surely your heart is made of stone, dear one”—the heart of a mother and father.
The heart is tender toward one's children; it cannot endure the suffering of one's children.
You remain as if you did not know this, yet your heart seems like stone, or perhaps like iron with firm bonds.
Therefore, when such suffering has arisen for us, it does not break it.
"You do not know" means you remain as if unaware. "By one who is exceedingly greedy" means by one who is excessively avaricious and has transgressed all bounds.
"Who is this? means, O Brahmin, you who do not know that we, your younger brothers, have been bound and imprisoned.
"He beats" means he strikes. "Stay right here, dear father; this black antelope skin knows nothing of suffering. Just as, for example...
"A young fawn, deprived of her herd and separated from her mother, cries out for milk;
likewise, not seeing her mother, she will cry, wither away, and die. Therefore, give me alone to the brahmin;
I shall go, but let this black antelope skin remain right here."
Even when this was said, the Great Being did not say anything at all. Then the prince, lamenting with reference to his parents, said:
“This is not such a sorrow for me as that which can be found by a man;
but that I do not see my mother—that is a sorrow for me even greater than this.”
“This suffering of mine is not so great, for such a thing may indeed befall a man;
but that I do not see my father—that is a sorrow greater than this.
Surely my poor mother must be weeping for a long time.”
Not seeing the black antelope skin and the girl of lovely appearance, [he thought]:
"Surely that poor father of mine will pine away for a long time,
not seeing the black antelope skin and the girl of lovely appearance."
“Surely that poor mother is grieving long in the hermitage,
not seeing the black antelope skin and the girl of lovely appearance.
Surely that poor father is grieving long in the hermitage.”
Not seeing the black antelope skin nor the girl of lovely appearance, [he thought]:
"Surely that poor mother longs for me for a long time;
whether at midnight or at nightfall, she yearns for me like a river in spate."
“Thus surely my poor father weeps for a long time;
like a river at midnight or at night, he weeps incessantly.
These are those *jambuka* trees, the *vedisa* and *sinduvāraka* trees.”
“Various kinds of trees, those we shall abandon today.
‘These are *assattha* and *panasa* trees, and *nigrodha* and *kapittha* trees;
various kinds of fruits, those we shall abandon today.’”
“Here stand these monasteries, and here is this river of cool water;
where we used to play in the past, there today we must leave behind.
On this mountain above, there are various kinds of flowers.”

“‘These elephants and horses are ours, and these oxen are ours;
those with which we used to play in the past, today we must abandon them.
In this context, ‘by one’ means by a person wandering through existence. ‘To be obtained’ means that which ought to be obtained. That [loss] is more painful for me.”
"Iti" means: that suffering of mine from not being able to see my mother is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, even a hundred-thousandfold more painful than this suffering of being beaten.
"Rucchatī" means she will weep. "Aḍḍharatte vā ratte vā" means either at midnight or throughout the entire night, remembering us, she will weep for a long time. "Avasucchati" means...
"A small stream with little water dries up; just as it dries up quickly, so too, at the very moment the sun rises, it will dry up and perish"—this was said with this intention.
"Vedisā" means hanging branches. "Those" refers to those whose roots, flowers, and fruits we have long enjoyed gathering;
today we both shall abandon them. "Elephants" refers to [those given] by our father to us.
The elephant was made for the purpose of play.
While it was thus lamenting, Jūjaka arrived with its sister, seized it while beating it, and departed. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"As they were being led away, those boys spoke thus to their father:"
“May you wish health for our mother, and may you yourself, dear father, be happy.
‘These elephants and horses are ours, and these oxen are ours;
give them to our mother, and she will dispel her grief with them.’”
"These elephants and horses are ours, and these oxen are ours;
looking after them, mother will dispel her sorrow.
Then, on account of the Bodhisatta’s sons, a powerful sorrow arose, and the flesh of his heart grew hot. He—
Trembling like an intoxicated elephant seized by a lion with a mane, or like the moon that has entered the mouth of Rāhu,
unable to remain in his natural state, he entered the leaf-hut with eyes full of tears and lamented piteously.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then King Vessantara, the Kshatriya, having given his gift,
entered the leaf-hut and lamented piteously.
Following this are the verses of the Great Being’s lamentation:
“Whom will these hungry and thirsty children approach today?
At the time of evening rest, who will give them food?
Whom will these hungry and thirsty children approach today?”
At the time of going to bed in the evening, [the children] said, "Mother, we are hungry, give us food.
"How indeed do they travel the road on foot, without sandals?
With feet that are weary and bare, who will take them by the hand?"
“How could he not feel shame for striking me in my very presence?
Shameless indeed is that brahmin, who strikes his own innocent sons!
Even toward my slave or servant, or anyone else who is dependent on me...”
Who, being a person of shame, would strike one such as he, who has utterly lost his sense?
While I am like a fish held in a net, bound at the mouth of the trap,
he reviles and strikes me, unable to see his own dear sons.
In this context: *kaṃ nvajja* means "what indeed today? *Uparucchanti* means they will arrive after traveling a road of sixty yojanas.
*Saṃvesanākāle* means at the time when the great multitude is being served food. *Kone dassati* means who will give them food?
*Kathaṃ nu pathaṃ gacchanti* means how indeed will they travel the road of sixty yojanas? *Pattikā* means on foot, [not by] elephant-vehicles and so forth.
"Deprived. "Without sandals" means one who is separated even from the mere presence of sandals, having delicate feet. "Will take it" means who will take it for the purpose of dispelling fatigue?

"Of a female slave's slave" means he is the slave of a female slave; or else, "another servant," meaning the slave of that one, and the slave of that one as well—thus, in this succession of slaves and sub-slaves, "he who is my fourth servant, a messenger to be sent."
"Even though he has thus utterly lost [his senses], knowing that 'this is the slave of the slave of Vessantara,' who would strike?
Who endowed with shame (*lajjā*) would strike? Is it not fitting for that shameless one to strike my sons?
'As of one in water' means as if I were a fish caught at the mouth of a net. In the word *apassato*, the letter *a* is merely a grammatical particle."
As he was passing by, the man reviled and struck his own dear sons, crying out, "Alas, what a cruel man!
Then, out of affection for his children, a reflection arose in him: "This brahmin is tormenting my sons excessively;
I cannot bear this grief. I shall follow this brahmin and bring about his death."
“I will bring the princes back to you. Then he thought: “It is not right that the princes should suffer such extreme pain;
it is not the way of the virtuous to feel regret after having given a gift. To illustrate this meaning, there are these two verses of reflection:
“Having taken up that bow, and having fastened the sword on my left side...”
“I shall bring back my own sons, for the slaughter of sons is painful.
This is an impossible situation, this form of suffering: that young princes should be slain.
Having understood the Dhamma of the virtuous, who would repent after giving [them away]?”
In this context, "mindfulness" refers to the traditional practice of former Bodhisattvas.
It is said that at that moment he recollected the lineage of the Bodhisattvas. Then [he thought]:
"The renunciation of wealth by all Bodhisattvas, the renunciation of limbs, the renunciation of children, the renunciation of wives, and the renunciation of life—these five..."
"There has never been anyone who became a Buddha without having practiced great renunciation. I too was among them;
it would not have been possible for me to become a Buddha without giving away my beloved sons and daughters. Having thought thus, [he said]:
"Vessantara, do you not know the suffering of those children given away to be slaves for others, that you [gave] to the brahmin..."
Having pursued him, he formed the intention, "I shall bring about his end," [thinking], "It is not fitting for you to feel regret after having given a gift.
Having thus reproached himself and made a firm resolve, thinking, "Even if he should kill the princes,
nothing belongs to me from the moment it was given," he departed from the leaf-hut.
He sat upon a stone slab at the door of the leaf-hut like a golden statue.
Jūjaka, too, beat the princes before the Bodhisatta and led them away. Then the prince, lamenting, said:
“Truly, as some men here have said:”
He who has no mother of his own is just as if he did not exist.
“Come, Kaṇha, let us die; there is no purpose for us in living.
We have been given away by the Lord of Men to a Brahmin seeking wealth.”
“Of the hunter who is in great haste, he who slaughters our cows—
these are your rose-apple trees, the *vedisa* and *sinduvāraka* trees;
various species of trees are these, O Kṛṣṇa, which we shall abandon.”
“Here are these *assattha* and *panasa* trees, and *nigrodha* and *kapittha* trees;
various kinds of fruits—these we leave behind for Kaṇha.
These groves stand here, and here is this river with cool water.”
“Those places where we used to play in the past, O Kanhā, those we now abandon.
The various kinds of flowers that grew on this upper mountain,
which we used to carry in the past, O Kanhā, those we now abandon.”
“Various kinds of fruit are found on this upper mountain;
those which we used to eat before, Kāḷa, we now abandon.
These are our elephants and horses, and these are our oxen.”
“We used to play together in the past; we shall abandon those [pleasures] in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
Therein, “yassa” means in whose presence one’s own mother does not exist. Although a father exists, he is as if non-existent.
Again, the brahmin stumbled and fell in a rugged place. From their hands, the binding creeper—
Having been released, they departed. Trembling like beaten cocks, they fled and came with one swift motion into the presence of their father.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Those princes being led away, having been released by the brahmin;”
“They both ran hither and thither, Jālī and Kaṇhājinā.

In this context, “hither and thither” means that at the very moment they were released, they ran toward the direction where their father was; having run, they came right into their father’s presence—this is the meaning.

Jūjaka, rising up with speed and a creeper-staff in hand, came rushing along like the fire at the end of an eon, and saying, “You two are extremely clever at running away,” he bound them by the hands and led them back again. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then that brahmin, taking a rope and taking a staff, led them away while striking them, even as King Sivi looked on.
While they were being led away in this manner, Kaṇhājinā turned back, looked [at her father], and conversed with him. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
To each of them Kaṇhājinā said: "Father, this brahmin is poking me with his staff as if I were a slave-girl born in the house.
Father, this man is not a true brahmin; for brahmins are those who live according to the Dhamma."
"A yakkha, in the guise of a brahmin, is leading us away, dear father, to devour us.
While we are being led away by this demon, why indeed, dear father, do you look on?
Therein, "him" (taṃ) refers to the father, King Sivi, who was sitting watching them. "Dāsiyaṃ" means "the female slave. "Khādituṃ" means "to devour."

"Even before we have reached Giridvāra, he leads us away for the purpose of eating us, with both our eyes streaming with drops of red blood, saying, 'I shall eat you. While you are being led away to be eaten or cooked, why do you look on at us?
May you always be happy! Thus she lamented.
As the young girl walked along, lamenting and trembling, a powerful sorrow arose within the Great Being;
his heart grew hot. Unable to breathe through his nose, he emitted hot sighs and gasps through his mouth.
Tears issued from his eyes like drops of blood. He thought: "This suffering of such a kind has arisen because of the fault of affection."
"It was born [of this cause], not from any other reason. Without forming an attachment, one must remain equanimous.
Having dispelled such grief by the power of his own knowledge, he sat down in his usual manner.
Before she had even reached Giridvāra, the young woman went on lamenting.
“These feet of ours are painful, and the path is long and very difficult to traverse;
the sun hangs low, and the brahmin still carries us.
We cry out to the beings, to the mountains, and to the forests.
“We pay homage with our heads to the Sarasī and to the waters at Supatiṭṭha.
‘O grasses, creepers, herbs, mountains, and forests:
may you grant health to our mother; this brahmin is leading her away.’”
“Go, sirs, and bring our mother, Queen Maddī;
if you wish to follow us, come quickly after us.
This one-legged woman comes straight toward the hermitage.”
"You should follow right after him; perhaps you will see him quickly.
Alas for you, O matted-hair ascetic, gatherer of forest roots and fruits!
When you see the hermitage empty, that shall bring you suffering."
“Mother, surely you have gathered a great deal of gleaned grain,
that you do not know us who are bound by a Brahmin seeking wealth—
a greedy man who slaughters us like cattle.”
"Let us go see our mother when she has returned from her alms round in the evening.
'Mother, give this fruit mixed with poison to the brahmin;
then this Asita, being nourished by it, will not carry us too heavily.'"
“The soles of our feet are indeed a slaughterhouse; the brahmin bears us heavily!
Thus did the youths, lustful for women, lament there.
In this context, *pādaka* means small soles. *Okandāmasa* means we wailed, showing our lack of respect and humble conduct.
"Let us announce it. Regarding the words "of the lake": we pay homage with our heads to the families of *nāgas* who are the guardians of this lotus-lake.
And regarding the words "and of the river Supatiṭṭhā": we also pay homage to the deities dwelling in the river Supatiṭṭhā.

Regarding the words "grasses and creepers": these are the grasses and the hanging creepers. Regarding the word "herbs": these are the medicinal herbs. In all these cases, he spoke thus with reference to the deities dwelling therein.
"Anupatitukāmāsī" means: "Even if she were desirous of following upon our footsteps. "Api passesi ne lahuṃ" means:
"Perhaps, by following along this narrow path, you might see your little sons quickly"—thus one should speak to her.
"Jaṭinī" refers to the mother, addressing her with words behind her back regarding her bound hair. "Ativelaṃ" means...
"Having made it exceed the measure. "Gleaning" means by the practice of gleaning. "Fruit" means forest roots and various fruits.
"Mixed with honey" means mixed with small-bee honey. "Eaten" means having eaten and consumed the fruit. "Satisfied" means well-fed.
"He should not carry it too heavily" means he should not carry it with excessive force. "Lusting after his mother" means by one who is greedy for his mother.
"Endowed with great affection, they lamented thus.
The commentary on the children is finished.
The commentary on Maddī begins.
Furthermore, when the king had caused the earth to resound and bestowed his beloved children upon the Brahmin, a great clamor arose as far as the Brahma-world;

hearing that lamentation of theirs as they were being led away by the Brahmin, the deities dwelling in the Himalayas felt as if their hearts were breaking and deliberated: "If Maddī should come to the hermitage even now..."

"In that case, not seeing her children there, she will ask Vessantara; and upon hearing that they have been given to the brahmin, she will run after them step by step with intense affection and experience great suffering.
Then those three sons of the gods said, "Having assumed the disguises of lions, tigers, and leopards, block the queen's path of approach so that even when she begs for them, [you may take them]."

"Without allowing the sun to set, you must ensure that the hermitage is well-guarded so that she may enter it by the light of the moon, and so that she will not be harmed by lions and other wild beasts," they commanded. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"Hearing their lamentation, three wild animals in the forest..."
The lion, the tiger, and the leopard spoke these words:
“May the princess not return from her alms-gathering this evening;
may she not thus distress us, the forest deer, who are without our usual provisions.”
“If a lion were to harm her, or a tiger or a leopard,
Lakkhaṇā would not belong to Prince Jālī, much less to Kaṇhājinā;
she would be lost to both— her husband and her son.”
In this context, the statement "you three persons, namely the lion, the tiger, and the leopard—thus you three wild forest animals shall be" was spoken by those deities to the three sons of the gods.
"Mā heva no" means that Queen Maddī said, "Do not come back in the evening from your search for gleaned food; let her return in the evening by the light of the moon. Do not...
"Thus, while we are away from our home, in our domain, in this forest grove, let no wild beast harass her in the woods.

Guard her so that no one may harass her"—thus they say. "If a lion," they mean, "if anyone among the lions or other predators should harass her while she is unprotected, then when her life has come to an end, [there will be no blame for us]."
“If he were a prince, where would there be black antelope skins? Thus, though she is endowed with auspicious marks, she will be deprived of both her husband and her sons”;
thus she is indeed deprived by two portions. Therefore, “you must provide well-guarded protection for her.
Then those three sons of gods, saying “Very well,” assented to the words of those deities and [became] lions, tigers, and leopards.
Having offered the sacrifice and returned, they lay down one after another along the path by which she would come. Maddī, thinking, "Today I have had a bad dream;
I shall take roots and fruits early and go to the hermitage," set out gathering roots and fruits while trembling.
Then the spade fell from her hand, and likewise the hoe and the shoulder-scraper fell from her shoulder, and her right eye...
The trees quivered; those that were once fruitful appeared as if fruitless, and those that were fruitless appeared as if laden with fruit.
The ten directions could no longer be distinguished. She thought, "What is this? Never before has such a thing happened to me today. What will come of it?
Will there be some misfortune for me, or for my sons, or perhaps for Vessantara? Having reflected thus, she said:
“My spade has fallen, and my right eye throbs;
the fruit-bearing trees are fruitless, and all the directions are bewildering to me.
Thus she departed, lamenting.
“In the evening, as she was returning to the hermitage,
when the sun had set, wild beasts appeared on the path.
‘The sun has sunk low, and the hermitage is indeed far away.’”
And whatever food they have left over from this meal, they would surely eat.
"Surely that nobleman sits alone in the leaf-hut,
comforting his hungry children as he sees me coming without provisions."
“Surely those sons of mine, my poor and wretched one,
must still be here at the time of evening rest, drinking milk.
“Surely those sons of mine, my poor and wretched one...”
In the evening, at the time of going to bed, they were like water-dripping fawns.
"Surely these are my poor, wretched little sons,
standing there to meet me like young calves meeting their mother."
“Surely those are my little sons, of me, the wretched and forlorn;
they stand waiting for me like swans upon a pond.
“Surely those are my little sons, of me, the wretched and forlorn;”
"They stand waiting for me, not far from the hermitage:
'A one-way path, a single track, with lakes and ravines on either side;
I see no other road by which one might reach the hermitage.'"
“May it be well with you, O kings of the deer, mighty in the forest!
Be brothers in righteousness; grant me passage when I ask.
I am the wife of the illustrious prince who was imprisoned.”
And I do not despise him, Rāma, who follows Sītā.
"May you both see your sons when they go to bed at evening;
and may I too see my two sons, Jāli and Kaṇhājinā."
“There is much root and fruit here, and this food is not small;
I will give you half of it, so I beg you, grant me passage.
Our mother is a princess, and our father is a prince.”
“Be brothers according to the Dhamma; grant me the way when asked.
Therein, “to her” means to me. “In relation to the arrival at the hermitage” means with reference to her coming toward the hermitage.
“They stood up” means they rose and remained standing. It is said that they had first lain down in a row, and at the time of her arrival—
Having risen and stretched, they stood across the path in a row, blocking the way. "And whatever of theirs" means:

whatever roots, fruits, or other produce I have here, I shall bring for them; then Vessantara, his two sons, and I—these three people together—shall eat that, for they have no other food. "Not coming" (*anāyanti*) means not approaching me.
Having understood this, he must surely be sitting alone, gladdening the children.
At the time of going to sleep—meaning at a time other than those days when he was feeding and watering them—he thought, "They have drunk milk.

Just as fawn-cubs who have drunk milk cry out for the sake of more milk and fall asleep while still crying because they do not obtain it, so too my little sons cried out for the sake of fruits and [other food].
He says that not having obtained it, they will fall asleep while still weeping.

"Having drunk water" means that just as thirsty fawns, having cried out for the sake of water and not obtaining it, fall asleep while still crying—this is how the meaning should be understood. "Accharā" means they move; they have gone forth to meet [him].
"Maṃ tiṭṭhanti" means they stand having come out to meet me. There is also the reading "paccuggantunā," which has the same meaning as "having come out to meet.
"Ekāyana" means the path of one alone, a track for a single person. "Ekapatha" means that it is indeed one;
there is no second, and it is impossible to go by descending [into a fork]. Why? Because on both sides there are lakes and ravines. "Migā namatthu" means may animals... [sā]... protect him.

Seeing no other way, thinking, "Having entreated them, I shall make them turn back," she lowered her fruit-basket from her head, raised her hands in añjali, and while paying homage, spoke thus: "O brothers!
I am the daughter of a human king, and you are the sons of the king of beasts; thus, by right, be my brothers."
“Of one who is confined” means of one who has been banished from the kingdom. “As Sītā followed Rāma”:

just as Queen Sītā, the younger sister of King Daśaratha’s son Rāma, became his chief queen and followed him, serving him with vigilance as one for whom her husband is a deity, so too do I serve Vessantara; I do not despise him—thus she speaks.
“You both give me the path, and at evening time when you go out for alms, you shall see your sons;
and I too shall see my own sons. Give me the path,” she entreated them.
Then those three sons of the gods, observing the time and realizing that it was now the hour to give her the path, rose up and departed. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having heard her lamenting, uttering many words full of piteousness—her speech that was *nelapati*—the wild beasts departed from the path.
Therein, *nelapati* means not faltering (*na elapati*); it refers to clear, sweet speech free from stammering.
