When the beasts of prey had departed, she too went to the hermitage. It was then the full-moon Uposatha day. Having reached the end of the walking path, not seeing her sons in those various places where she had previously seen them, she said:
"In this very spot, my little sons, covered in dust, Used to stand up to meet me, like young calves meeting their mother."
“In this very place, my little sons, covered in dust,
stand before me like swans upon a lake.
“In this very place, my little sons, covered in dust...”
“They stand waiting for me, not far from my hermitage.
Like two deer with high-ridged backs, they run toward me from all sides;
joyful and delighted, they leap about as if trembling.”
“Leaving my two sons behind— I see neither Jāli nor Kaṇhājinaka—
I have gone forth, abandoning my children like a doe leaving her fawn, like a bird leaving its young from the cage, or like a lioness greedy for meat.”
“Leave the two sons; I do not see Jāli or Kaṇhājinā here.
“This is their path of departure, like elephants on a mountain;
The funeral pyres are strewn about, not far from the hermitage.”
"Leave them, my son; I do not see Jāli or Kaṇhājinā, both of them.
Though strewn with sand, my little children, covered in dust, are running about on all sides—I do not see those boys."
“Those who formerly used to rise up for me when I returned from far away in the forest—
I do not see them here today, neither my son Jāli nor Kaṇhājinā.
Like young fawns following their mother, the Chakalī deer, they did not go out to meet me.”
“They look for me from afar, yet I do not see those children.
This is their plaything, a fallen pale wood-apple;
today I do not see my sons, neither Jāli nor Kaṇhājina.”
“My breasts are full and my chest heaves;
yet here I see neither my sons, Jāli nor Kaṇhājina.
One searches in my lap, while the other clings to my breast.”
"Abandon them, my son; I see neither Jāli nor Kaṇhājinā.
Those children of mine, who in the evening time, covered in dust, used to roll about on my lap—I do not see those boys now."
“This hermitage was once filled with people; it appears to me as it did before.
Yet today, not seeing my sons, this hermitage seems to me as if it were empty.
Why is it that this hermitage now appears to me so silent?”
“Even the crows do not cry out; surely my children must be dead.
Why does this hermitage appear so silent to me?
Even the birds do not call; surely my children must be dead.”
In that context, *taṃ* is a mere particle. *Paṃsukuṇṭhitā* means covered with dust.
*Paccuggatā maṃ* means having come out to meet me. There is also the reading *paccuggantunā*, which has the same meaning as "having come out to meet.
*Ukkaṇṇā* means just as young fawns, upon seeing their mother, lift up their ears, stretch out their necks, and approach their mother with joy and delight all around.
"Running toward me, as if struggling and trembling, they seemed to shake the very flesh of my heart—such were my sons in the past.
Today I do not see them. Like a doe with her fawns, or as a doe and her fawns have been released from their cage-like nest, and like a lioness greedy for meat [releasing] her own [cubs]."
"Just as they leave their lairs to go foraging, so too do I leave my sons and set out for foraging"—this is what he says.
This "turning about" (*padakkanta*) of theirs is like the tracks of elephants on a mountain slope during the rainy season;
it is perceived as their running back and forth and turning about at their place of play. "Piles" (*citaka*) refers to heaps of sand that have been gathered and heaped up.
*Parikiṇṇāyo* means scattered about. *Samantā abhidhāvanti* means they run about on all sides on other days.
*Paccuṭṭhenti* means they go out to meet them. *Dūramāyantiṃ* means coming from afar.
*Chakaliṃ va migiṃ chāpā* means young fawns [behave] like a spotted doe, their own mother, or like a doe; this is their play.
"While they were playing with elephant-figures and such, this golden-colored *velu* plaything fell from their hands and dropped here.
'These breasts of mine are full of milk,' [she says]. 'And my chest heaves' means her heart throbs.
'They roll about in my lap' means they turn over and toss about in my lap. A festival appears to me."
It appears to me like a place for a sacrificial feast. "Tyajjāti" means "today they. "Apassantīti" means "not seeing," [referring to] me.
"Bhamate viyā" means it revolves like a potter’s wheel. "Kākolā" refers to wild crows.
"Matā nūnā" means they have certainly either died or been carried off by someone. "Sakuṇā" refers to the remaining birds.
Thus lamenting, she went into the presence of the Great Being; having set down her fruit-basket and seeing the Great Being sitting in silence, and not seeing the children near him, she said:
“What is this that you have become silent? Surely my heart is as if dead.
Even the crows do not cry out; surely my children are dead.”
"Why are you silent? My heart is as if pierced by arrows.
Even the birds do not sing; surely my children must be dead.
I wonder, noble son, have wild beasts devoured my children?"
“In the forest, in the wilderness, in the open glade—by whom have my children been led away?
Have messengers been sent for you? Or perhaps those sweet-spoken ones are asleep?
Or have they gone outside, absorbed in their play?”
“Not even hair is seen, nor hands and feet with webbed fingers;
like the nest of birds—by whom have my children been carried off?
Therein, “Even now my mind is as if stained” means: even at this powerful dawn, my mind is as if it were seeing a dream. “The deer”—[refers to the following:]
"Lions and other wild beasts" refers to predatory animals. "In a desert" means in a place devoid of moisture. "In a secluded place" means in a solitary spot.
"Messengers" refers to those sent by you as messengers to King Sivi in the city of Jetuttara. "Asleep" means having entered the inner leaf-hut and lain down. "Or not outside?
he asks this to inquire whether those children, having become absorbed in play, have gone outside. "Nor are their hair-locks seen."
"Lord Vessantara, their hair does not appear black like that of the Añjana trees.
'Jālino' means their hands and feet are variegated with golden nets. And 'the swoop of birds': in the Himalayan regions there are birds called *hatthiliṅga-sakuṇa*;
they swoop down, seize [their prey], and travel through the air. Therefore I ask you: have they been carried away by those birds? From here..."
“Has a pitfall been set for some others as well, like those birds? Tell me, by whom have my children been carried off?
Even when this was said, the Great Being said nothing. Then she said to him, “My lord, why do you not speak with me? What fault is mine? And she spoke:
“This is even more painful than a wound pierced by an arrow.”
“I do not see my two sons, Jāli and Kaṇhājina;
this is the second arrow that makes my heart tremble:
that I do not see my sons, and you do not speak to me.”
“Prince, it does not occur to me that this night will pass for me today;
I think you will see me in the morning as one who has entered into peace, or else as one who is dead.
In this context, “this is even more painful than that,” O Lord Vessantara, refers to [the suffering] when I was exiled from the kingdom and [dwelt] in the forest.
The suffering of Vasanti not seeing her son, and this failure of yours to speak with me—this is even more painful for me than that.

For you have tormented me through your silence, as if you were burning me again after I had already been consumed by fire, as if striking me with a staff after I had fallen into a precipice, or as if piercing a wound with an arrow. Indeed, my heart is pierced by an arrow.
Just as a wound, so too does it throb and cause pain. There is also a reading, *sampaviddho*, meaning "pierced through.
Regarding the phrase *okkantasantaṃ maṃ*: it means "me who have entered into peace," or "me whose life has departed.
In the expression *dakkhisi no mataṃ*, the word *no* is merely a particle; the meaning is, "You will see me dead very soon."
Then the Great Being, thinking, "I shall cause her to abandon her grief for her son by means of a harsh discourse," spoke this verse:
"Surely Maddī, the noble daughter of high renown, set out early for alms; why has she returned now at evening?"
In that regard, as for the question, "Why have you come back now? [he said]: "Maddī, you are beautiful and lovely;
moreover, many forest-dwellers such as ascetics, masters of spells, and others roam about in the Himalayas. Who knows what might happen? What have you done?
Why do you come back in the evening when you should have gone early in the morning? You have left behind young children—women who have gone into the forest."
“Women with husbands do not act like this; even such thoughts as ‘What is the state of my children?
What will my husband think? did not occur to you at all. You go out early in the morning and return by the light of the moon.
This is the fault of my own misfortune,” she said, speaking thus after having threatened and deceived her.
Having heard his words, she said:
"Did you not hear the sound of those who have come to discharge their arrows,
and even the roar of the lion and the growl of the tiger?"
“A foretoken has appeared to me as I was wandering in the Great Forest:
the spade fell from my hand and slipped from my shoulder.
Then, trembling and afraid, I joined my palms together in reverence.”
I shall pay homage to all directions; may there be safety from this place.
"May the prince not be slain by a lion or a leopard;
nor may the children be seized by a bear, a hyena, or a jackal."
“The lion, the tiger, and the leopard—these three wild beasts of the forest—they have blocked my path, and thus I have come here this evening.
In that passage, “those who have come to drink from the lake” means those who have come to this lake to drink water. “And of the tiger” means of the tiger.
"And did you not hear the single, uniform sound of the trumpeting of other four-footed creatures such as elephants, and the warbling of the flocks of birds?
he asked. "It was the sound at the time my sons were given away by the Great Being," [the other replied].
"O King, it was an omen for me; it was an omen for the experience of this suffering."
They will raise their shoulders, leaning back against their shoulder-blades. "Puthu" means individually.
"They shall pay homage to all directions" means they have paid homage to all ten directions. "May it not be so" means: "May our prince not be killed by lions and the like;
may the children also not be seized by bears and the like"—thus, praying, they shall pay homage. They surrounded me and searched for me.
"Master Vessantara, thinking, 'These things are terrifying and vast, and I have had a bad dream;
I shall depart very early today,' I gathered roots and fruits while trembling.

Then even the fruit-bearing trees appeared as if they were fruitless, and those that were fruitless appeared as if they were laden with fruit. With great difficulty I gathered the roots and fruits and reached the mountain gate."
"I have arrived. Then those lions and other animals, seeing me, stood blocking the path one after another.
"Therefore, I have come this evening; forgive me, my lord," she said.
Having spoken only these few words with her, the Great Being said nothing at all until the rising of the dawn. From that time on, Maddī spoke, lamenting in various ways:
“Like a student to his teacher, I attended upon my husband and sons,
day and night unwearied, wearing matted hair and living the life of celibacy.
Clad in deerskins, I gathered roots and fruits from the forest.”
"I brood day and night, my dear sons, for it is your desires that consume me.
I ate yellow turmeric, imported pale beluva fruit, and the fruits that ripen on trees;
these, my sons, were your playthings."
“O Kṣatriya, eat this lotus-root, the *mūḷāli*, the *vattaka*, the *sāluka*,
and the *ciñcabhedaka*, together with these small creatures and your sons.
Give the *paduma* to Jālinī and the *kumuda* to the young girl.”
“Behold Mālinī dancing as she calls out for her sons, O Sivi!
Then, O bull among chariot-warriors, listen also to Kaṇhājinā as she approaches the hermitage with her sweet voice and warbling song.”
“Exiled from the kingdom where both shared the same joys and sorrows,
do you still see both your sons, Sivi’s Jāli and Kaṇhājina?
Surely you see those ascetics and brahmins who are devoted to the holy life?”
“I have sought out in the world those who are virtuous and learned;
yet here today I do not see my two sons, Jāli and Kaṇhājina.
In this context, “like a student to his teacher” means that a pupil endowed with proper conduct attends upon his teacher just as he would. “Anuṭṭhitā” means... [the rest of the passage follows].
"Having performed my service, I have attended to you with diligence and looked after you.
'By your desire' means longing for you through your wish. 'O children,' she laments while addressing the princes.
'O children, golden turmeric! she says, "I have come bringing golden-colored turmeric ground for the purpose of bathing you."
"Paṇḍubeluvanti: 'I have brought this golden-colored beluva fruit for you to play with. 'Rukkhapakkāni': I also brought other delightful tree fruits for you to play with.
'Ime vo puttakā ime vo kīḷanā': he says, 'These are your little sons; these are your toys.
'Mūḷālivattakaṃ' means a coil of mūḷāla [grass]. 'Sālukaṃ' refers here to the bulbous root of the blue lotus (*utpala*) and so forth."
"I have brought much. Ciñcābhedaka is the crossroads.
'Eat'—she laments all this, saying, 'Eat together with your sons, along with the honey-cakes.
'Sivi, call your sons!'—O Lord King Sivi, quickly summon your little sons from the place where they are lying in the leaf-hut. 'Perhaps, O Sivi, you will see your sons.'"
"O King of the Śivis, do you see your children? If you see them, show them to me; why do you distress me so excessively?
You must be cursing me, surely reviling me by saying, 'May you never see your sons and daughters!
Even as she lamented thus, the Great Being did not say anything to her. While he remained silent toward her—
Trembling in the light of the moon, searching for her sons among the various jambu trees and others where they had previously played,
she reached each of those places and, lamenting, said:
"These are those jambu trees, the *vedisa* and *sinduvāra* trees;"
Various kinds of trees—those young princes are not to be seen.
These *assattha* and *panasa* trees, and these *nigrodha* and *kapittha* trees;
various kinds of fruits—those young princes are not to be seen.
“Here stand these monasteries, and here flows this river of cool water;
where they once used to play, those young princes are no longer seen.
Various kinds of flowers grow upon this upper mountain;”
Those princes who formerly used to ride in vehicles are no longer seen.
Those princes who formerly used to eat various kinds of fruits on this upper mountain are no longer seen.
“Here are your elephants and horses, and these are your oxen;
those boys who used to play with them are nowhere to be seen.

Therein, “Here are your elephants”: not seeing the children on top of the mountain, she lamented; then, having descended from there and returned again to the hermitage, she searched for them there and, seeing their toys, spoke thus.
Then, by the sound of her lamentation and the sound of her footsteps, the deer and birds were stirred. Seeing them, she said:
"These deer with their fawns, and many kadalī-deer, who used to play here before—those young princes are nowhere to be seen."
“Here are these swans and cranes, peacocks with variegated plumage;
those princes who used to sport here are no longer seen.
In this context, *sāmā* refers to small golden deer; *sasolūkā* refers to hares and owls.
Not seeing her beloved sons in the hermitage, she departed and entered a flowering grove of trees. Surveying various places, she said:
"These are those forest thickets, flowering in all seasons, where formerly those boys used to play; yet they are not to be seen."
“Delightful are these lotus ponds, resounding with the cries of ruddy geese,
covered with mandārava flowers and with pink and blue lotuses;
there it was that those princes used to play in the past, yet they are not to be seen.”
In that context, "forest thickets" refers to clusters of forest trees.
Having failed to find her beloved son anywhere, she returned once more to the presence of the Great Being. Seeing him sitting there with a dejected face, she said:
"Have you not split the firewood? Have you not brought water?"
“Even the foremost fire has not been neglected;
why then do you meditate like one who is dull-witted? “When the beloved meets with the beloved, my grief is allayed.
But today I see neither my sons, Jāli nor Kaṇhājina—neither of them.”
In this context, *na hāpito* means "not kindled. This is what is meant:
"Master, formerly you would split wood, bring water and set it aside, and make a fire on the charcoal brazier;
today, having done none of those things, why do you sit meditating like one who is dull? Your activity does not please me. *Piyo piyena*: Vessantara is dear to me.
"He is dear; there is no one dearer to me than him. By meeting and coming together with this beloved one, my former distress was dispelled and my suffering vanished.
But today, even though I see him, my grief does not vanish. What could be the reason for this?
"Let that be as it may; I have seen the reason. Today I do not see your sons; that is why [I am grieving]."
"Even though she looks on, her grief does not depart.
Although she spoke thus, the Great Being remained seated in silence.
As he did not speak, she, overwhelmed with sorrow and trembling like a beaten hen, again wandered through the places where they had previously roamed, [and came to] the Great Being.
Having returned to his presence, he said:
"O King, I do not see anyone by whom your sons were carried off dead;
even the crows do not descend upon them. Surely my children must be dead."
“Indeed, O King, I do not see by whom they have been carried off dead;
even the birds do not cry out—surely my children must be dead.
Therein, “Indeed, O King, I do not see” means: “I do not see our sons. He spoke thus with the intention: “I do not know by whom they have been carried off.”
Even when this was said, the Great Being did not say anything at all.

Afflicted by grief for her sons, searching for them, she wandered through various places with the speed of the wind even for a third time. The area she covered wandering for a single night measured fifteen yojanas.
Then the night brightened and dawn broke. She went back once more to where the Great Being—
Standing nearby, she lamented. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having lamented there among the mountains and forests, she returned once more to the level ground and wept in the presence of her husband.”
“O King, I do not see anyone by whom those dead ones have been carried away;
even the crows do not descend upon them. Surely my children must be dead.
“O King, I do not see anyone by whom those dead ones have been carried away.”
"Even the birds do not cry out; surely my children must be dead.
O King, shall I see them now—those who were carried away dead—as they wander at the roots of trees, on mountains, and in caves?"
“Thus Maddī of the noble form, the illustrious princess, raising her arms and weeping, fell right there upon the ground.
In that regard, monks, “in the presence of her husband”: there, in the interior of Vaṅka Mountain, among the mountain ridges, Maddī—

Wandering through the forests and lamenting, she returned once more and, relying upon her husband, stood by his side and wept for the sake of her sons, lamenting, saying, "It is not so for us," and so forth;

this is the meaning. Thus, monks, Maddī of the noble limbs—meaning that Maddī of the noble limbs, who possessed the most excellent form, while wandering at the foot of trees and other places, not seeing her children, [thought], "Without a doubt..."
"She must have died! Raising his arms and wailing, he fell right there at the feet of Vessantara like a golden plantain tree cut down, collapsing upon the ground.
Then the Great Being, trembling with the conviction that "Maddī is dead," thought: "Maddī has died in an improper place.
Had her passing occurred in the city of Jetuttara, she would have had a vast retinue; two kingdoms..."
"Let them go. But as for me, being all alone in the forest, what indeed shall I do?
Although he was overcome by intense grief, he established mindfulness and thought, "I shall first find out. Rising up, he placed his hand upon her heart;

perceiving the state of her feverish distress, he fetched water with his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). Although he had never before engaged in physical contact with her for seven months, due to his intense grief—
Unable to recognize his state of having gone forth, he raised her head with eyes full of tears,
placed it upon his thighs, sprinkled it with water, and sat there stroking both her face and her heart.
Maddī, after a short while, regained her mindfulness, established a sense of shame and moral dread, and rose up toward the Great Being.
Having paid homage, he said, "Lord Vessantara, where have your children gone? "Queen, they were given away as slaves to a brahmin.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"Sprinkle with water the princess who has reached that middle state."
“Having perceived that she had reached him, he then spoke this to her.

In this context, *ajjhapattaṃ* means having come into his presence; the sense is that she fell at the base of his feet and lost consciousness. *Etadabravī* means he spoke these words: “I have been given as a slave to a certain brahmin.
Then, when she said, “O Lord, having given your children to the brahmin, why do you not tell me what to do as I wander about lamenting all night long? the Great Being replied:
“Maddī, it was precisely because of my poverty that I did not wish to reveal my suffering:
an old brahmin, a beggar, had come to our house.
Maddī, do not fear; take heart; I gave my sons to him.”
“Look at me, Maddī; do not mourn excessively for your sons.
We shall regain our sons while still living, and we shall remain free from illness.
“Sons, cattle, grain, and whatever other wealth there is in the house—”
“A good person should give a gift upon seeing a beggar arrive;
rejoice in my gift, Maddī, for these two little sons are the supreme gift.
Therein, “by the very beginning” means by the very first part. This is what is meant: if I had explained that matter to you at the very outset.
Then, unable to bear your grief, your heart might break; therefore, Maddi, they will not wish to tell you of your suffering at the very outset.
"He has come home" means he has come to this dwelling place of ours.
"And may we be free from illness" means that we remain healthy in every way; while we are alive, [the Brahmin] will certainly [take] the children.
"Even when it has been taken away, we shall see [what remains]. And 'whatever else' means whatever other animate wealth there may be in the house.
'A good man would give as a gift' means that a good man, aspiring to the supreme goal, would give a gift even by breaking his chest and taking out his heart's flesh.
Thus spoke Maddī.
“I rejoice in you, O King, for this supreme gift to your children;
having given, gladden your heart, and become one who gives even more.
You who, O Lord of Men, amidst people possessed by stinginess...”
“The King who increases the realm of the Sivis gave a gift to the brahmin.

Regarding that, “I rejoice in you”: this refers to the Bodhisatta himself, among the sons whom he had nurtured for ten months in his womb, bathed, fed, given drink, and laid upon his breast two or three times a day.
Rejoicing in the gift of her son, she spoke thus: "By this reason it should be known that the father alone is the master of his children.
"Furthermore, O Great King, be a giver of gifts; continue to give gifts again and again.
Set your heart at ease with the thought, 'My gift is well-bestowed,' you who gave your beloved son to beings who were full of stinginess."

When this was said, the Great Being replied, "Maddī, what are you saying? For if my heart had not been gladdened by giving away my children, these wonders would not have occurred," and he recounted all the events beginning with the quaking of the earth.
Then Maddī, having praised those wonders, spoke while expressing her appreciation for the gift:
“The earth resounds with your voice, and your sound has reached the triple heaven;
flashes of lightning have appeared on all sides, like echoes from the mountains.

In this context, “flashes of lightning have appeared” means that unseasonable lightning bolts burst forth on all sides in the regions of the Himālaya. “Like echoes from the mountains” means that cries arose like the sounds of echoes rebounding from the mountains.
“Both Nārada and Pabbata rejoice in you;
so too do Indra, Brahmā, Pajāpati, Soma, Yama, and Vessavaṇa.
All the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, together with Sakka, rejoice.”
“Thus Maddī of the noble form, the illustrious daughter of a king, rejoiced in Vessantara’s supreme gift of his two sons.
Therein, “both Nārada and Pabbata”—these two classes of deities, standing at the doors of their own celestial mansions, [exclaimed]: “Well given!”...
“They rejoice in that gift. The Tāvatiṃsa gods, with Indra as their leader, also rejoiced in that gift.

Thus, when the Great Being had praised his own giving, Maddī likewise praised the gift in the same manner, saying, “Great King Vessantara, well given indeed is your gift,” and sat there expressing her appreciation. By that—
The Teacher spoke the verse beginning, "Thus was Maddī of the noble loins.
The commentary on the origin of Maddī is concluded.
Now begins the commentary on the origin of Sakka.
While they were thus exchanging friendly greetings with one another, Sakka thought to himself:
"Yesterday, King Vessantara, having made the earth resound, gave his children to Jūjaka;
now some base man might approach him, request Maddī—who is endowed with every auspicious mark—and, leaving the king alone, take Maddī away."

"Then he would become helpless and destitute. I shall approach him in the guise of a brahmin, ask for Maddī, have him take the peak of the mountain as a price for her, ensure that it cannot be given away to anyone else, and then, having returned it to him, I will come back.
At the time of sunrise, he went into his presence. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then, at the end of the night, as the sun was rising,
Sakka appeared before them in the guise of a brahmin at dawn.
Therein, “he appeared before them at dawn” means that at dawn he stood before both those people, his form becoming visible, and having stood there, he spoke while performing a friendly greeting:
“Is it well with you, sir? Are you free from illness?
Do you subsist on gleaned food? Are roots and fruits abundant?
Are gadflies and mosquitoes few, and are there but few creeping reptiles?”
“In this forest teeming with predatory beasts, is there indeed no violence?
The Great Being replied:
“O Brahmā, we are indeed well; moreover, O Brahmā, we are free from affliction.”
“Furthermore, we shall subsist by gleaning; furthermore, there are many roots and fruits.
Moreover, though there are gadflies and mosquitoes, and very few reptiles, and the forest is teeming with wild beasts, no harm exists for me.”
“Having lived for seven months in the forest, grieving for our lives,
this is the second time we have seen a brahmin of divine appearance,
carrying a bamboo staff and wearing a deerskin cloak.”
“Welcome to you, Great Brahmā; indeed, you have come from afar.
Enter within, O auspicious one, and wash your feet.
Here are *tinduka* fruits, *piyāla* nuts, *madhuka* flowers, and *kāsumārī* fruits.”
“Eat these small fruits, O Brahmā, the finest of the fine.
This cool water too has been brought from the heart of the mountain;
drink from it, Great Brahmā, if you so desire.”
Having thus exchanged greetings with him, the Great Being asked:
"By what appearance, or for what reason, have you come to this vast forest? Tell me that when you are questioned."
He asked the reason for his arrival. Then Sakka said to him, “Great King, I am an old man; having come here, I have come to ask for your wife Maddī. Give her to me,” and he spoke this verse:
“Just as a full river’s flow never runs dry at any time, So have I come to you with a request:
give me your wife, as I have been asked.”
When this was said, the Great Being did not say, "Yesterday I gave my children to the brahmin; being all alone in the forest, how can I give Maddī to you?

Instead, as if placing a purse of a thousand coins into an outstretched hand, without clinging, without attachment, and with a mind free from dejection, he cried out to the mountain and spoke this verse:
“I give and I do not waver, O Brahmin, regarding that which you ask of me;
I do not conceal what exists, for my mind delights in giving.
In this context, “I do not conceal what exists” means I do not hide that which is actually present.
Having spoken thus, he quickly fetched water with his water-pot, poured the water into his hands, and gave it to his beloved wife.
At that very moment, all the wonders described below appeared.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Taking Maddī by the hand and a water-pot, the increaser of the Śivi kingdom gave this gift to the brahmin.
At that time there was a terrifying event; at that time there was a hair-raising occurrence.”
As he was renouncing Maddī, the earth trembled all around.
“Maddī showed no frown, nor did she cling to him or weep;
she simply looked at him in silence, for she knew what was best.”
In that regard, "he gave a gift" means that he spoke thus: "O Brahmin, omniscient knowledge itself is dearer to me than my kingdom by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and a hundred-thousandfold;
may this gift of mine be a condition for the penetration of omniscient knowledge," and having said this, he gave the gift. And this has also been said:
“Though I was giving away my son Jāli, clad in a black antelope skin, and my daughter-in-law Queen Maddī,
who was devoted to her husband, I did not feel grief, solely for the sake of awakening.
Neither were both my sons to be given up by me, nor was Queen Maddī to be given up.”
“Omniscience is dear to me; therefore, you have given what is dear.
In that context, “the earth shook all around” means the earth trembled as far as the ocean’s edge.
“There was no frown on Maddī’s face,” monks, is said because at that moment Maddī, out of anger at the thought, “The king is giving me to an old brahmin,” [did not show any sign of displeasure].
She did not frown. "She was neither dejected nor weeping" means she was not distressed, nor did she stand with eyes filled with tears and weeping;
rather, remaining silent, she thought, "One who gives away a woman-treasure such as I would not do so without cause;
he knows what is best," and she simply gazed at his face, which was like the color of a full-blown lotus—the meaning is that she stood looking right at him.
Then the Great Being looked at her face, wondering, "What kind of woman is Maddī? She too, saying, "Husband, why do you look at me?", let out a lion’s roar and spoke this verse:
"I am a maiden who has been his wife; my husband is my lord.
To whomever he wishes, he may give me away, sell me, or even kill me."
In this context, "I am his wife" means: "He to whom I, your young wife, belong—he, you yourself, is my master and husband.
"To whomever he wishes" means: he who is called the master may give me, a slave woman, to whomever he desires;
or he may sell me when there is need for wealth, or [dispose of me] with meat when there is need for it.
“...he might even kill you; therefore, do whatever pleases you, for I am not angry.
Knowing their noble disposition, Sakka offered them praise. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having understood their intention, the Lord of Devas spoke thus:”
“All obstacles have been conquered by you—those that are divine and those that are human.
The earth resounds with your fame, and your renown has reached the triple heaven.
Lightnings have appeared on all sides, like echoes from the mountains.”
“Both Nārada and Pabbata rejoice in him,
as do Indra, Brahmā, Pajāpati, Soma, Yama, and Vessavaṇa;
all the gods rejoice, for he performs what is difficult to do.”
“To those who give what is hard to give, who perform what is difficult to do—the wicked do not follow their example;
the Dhamma of the virtuous is hard to emulate.
Therefore, the destination after death is different for the virtuous and the wicked.”
“The wicked go to hell, while the virtuous are destined for heaven.
‘Since you gave this maiden as a wife to one dwelling in the forest,
may that merit of yours ripen in heaven, even though you have not yet ascended the Brahma-vehicle.’”

In this context, *paccūhā* means adversaries. *Dibbā* means those that obstruct divine prosperity; *mānusā* means those that obstruct human prosperity. But what are they? They are the qualities of stinginess (*macchariya*).
All of these were conquered by the Great Being when he gave away his wife and children. Therefore it is said: "All those adversaries have been conquered by you.
For he, King Vessantara, performed what is difficult to do, being all alone in the forest.

"Vasanto" means dwelling in the forest; "vasanto" means while dwelling in the forest. "Brahmayānam" means the supreme vehicle. For the threefold dharma of good conduct and such a dharma of giving are conditions for the Noble Path. Thus he says that all the gods rejoice, thinking, "The one named Vasanta is performing a difficult task by giving his wife to the brahmin.

Speaking thus, he uttered the verse beginning with "Yam etam," expressing his appreciation. He said this while offering his rejoicing. "In the forest" (vane) means dwelling in the forest. "Brahmayānam" means the best vehicle.
Indeed, the dharma of good conduct in its three forms and such a dharma of giving are the requisites for the Noble Path.

Because it leads [to the Brahma-world], it is called the "Brahma-vehicle. Therefore, may this Brahma-vehicle—which has been accomplished even by one giving this gift today—ripen for you in heaven without descending to the planes of misery, and at the conclusion of its ripening, may it become the giver of omniscient knowledge.
Having thus offered his thanksgiving, Sakka thought, "Now, it is fitting that I should go after giving this to him here without further delay," and he said:
“I give you my wife Maddī, who is beautiful in every limb;
you shall be united with Maddī, and Maddī with her husband.
Just as milk and a conch shell are both of the same color,” so it was said.
Thus you and Maddī, with minds of one accord,
both dwell together in this forest hermitage.
You are kṣatriyas of noble lineage, well-born on the side of both mother and father.
"Just as one who performs meritorious deeds, giving again and again.
In this context, "suitable" means appropriate. "Both of equal appearance" means that both are indeed equally pure in appearance.
"Possessing minds of equal intention" means being endowed with a mind characterized by intention that is identical through actions such as conduct and so forth.
"Avaruddhe'ttha" means: having been banished from the kingdom, dwell here in this forest. "Yathā puññāni" means:
just as many meritorious deeds were performed by you in the city of Jetuttara—both those done yesterday for your sons and today for your wife—do not be satisfied with only that much;
rather, giving further and further beyond this, perform deeds appropriate to the occasion.
"You should perform meritorious deeds.
Having spoken thus, Sakka entrusted Maddī to the Great Being and, announcing himself in order to grant her a boon, said:
"I am Sakka, the lord of the gods; I have come into your presence."
“Choose a boon, O Chief of Kings; I grant you eight boons.
And even as he spoke, blazing with his divine form like the young sun, he stood in the sky. Then the Bodhisatta, choosing his boon, said:
“If you would grant me a boon, Sakka, Lord of all beings:”
“May my father give his consent for me to go from here to my own home;
may he invite me with a seat—this is the first boon I choose.
‘I would not approve of the execution of a man, even one who has committed a crime.’”
“I would release them from execution— this I choose as my second boon.
‘May those who are old, those who are young, and those of middle age all depend upon me alone for their livelihood’— this I choose as my third boon.”
“I would not go to another’s wife; I would be devoted to my own wife;
I would not fall under the power of women—this I choose as the fourth boon, O Sakka.
May a son be born to me, O Sakka, and may he be long-lived.”
“May he conquer the earth through righteousness; this is the fifth boon I choose.
‘Then, at the end of the night, at the rising of the sun, may divine foods appear; this is the sixth boon I choose.’”
“May my giving never be exhausted; having given, may I have no regret;
while giving, may I gladden my mind—this is the seventh boon I choose.
Released from here, may I go to heaven and attain distinction.”
"I would not turn back from that; this is the eighth boon I choose.
Therein, "should he rejoice" means he should accept it and not be angry. "Arrived from here" means having reached his own home from this forest.
"With a seat" means with the royal throne. He says, "May he grant me the kingdom. "Even though he be a doer of evil"—
"Having become a king, I would release even a criminal deserving of death from execution;
even for such a person, I would not approve of execution. 'May they all depend on me' means that they should all live depending on me alone.

'May he conquer by Dhamma' means that he should conquer by Dhamma, that he should exercise sovereignty according to Dhamma. 'One who has attained distinction' means having gone to a distinguished state, [he dwelt] in the Tusita city."

"I shall be reborn," he says. "There shall be no turning back from there" means that having passed away from the Tusita heaven and come to the human state, there shall be no turning back in a future existence; he says, "I shall attain omniscience.
Having heard those words of his, the Lord of Devas spoke thus:
"Before long, indeed, your father will come from there to see you.
In this context, "he will come to see you" means: O Great King, both your mother and father, desiring to see you, will come here before long;
and having arrived, they will grant you the white parasol and hand over the kingdom, [and you shall go] back to the city of Jetuttara itself.
"Everything you desire will reach its fulfillment; do not worry, O Great King, remain heedful.
Having thus given this exhortation to the Great Being, Sakka returned to his own abode. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"Having spoken these words, Maghavā, the king of the gods and lord of the Sujā, departed."
"Having granted the boon to Vessantara, he departed for the heavenly realm.
In this context, "Vessantara" refers to Vessantara. "Departed" means that he went and arrived [there].
The commentary on the Sakka-pabbava is finished.
The commentary on the Great King’s departure:
The Bodhisatta and Maddī dwelt in the hermitage given by Sakka, greeting one another with joy.
Jūjaka, having taken the two princes, set out on a journey of sixty yojanas. Deities provided protection for the princes. When the sun had set, Jūjaka—
Having bound the prince and laid him upon the ground, he himself climbed a tree out of fear of fierce wild beasts and lay among the branches.
At that moment, a son of the gods came in the form of Vessantara and a daughter of the gods in the form of my own self;
they released the prince, massaged his hands and feet, bathed him, adorned him, and [offered] divine food.
Having fed him and laid him upon a celestial bed, [the deity] vanished while he was still lying there in a bound state at the time of sunrise.
Thus, through the assistance of the deities, they proceeded free from illness.
Jūjaka, too, being possessed by a deity, set out saying, "I am going to the kingdom of Kaliṅga," and after half a month, he arrived at the city of Jetuttara. On that day, at the hour of dawn—
Great King, Sañjaya saw a dream. Such was the dream:
while the king was seated at the great court of justice, a man who was dark-complexioned brought two lotuses and placed them in the king’s hands. The king fastened them on his two ears.
Their pollen fell away and landed upon the king’s chest. Having woken up, he questioned the brahmins early in the morning.
They declared, "Your relatives, O King, who have been away for a long time, are arriving.
Early in the morning, he washed his head, ate various kinds of choice food, adorned himself, and sat down in the court of justice.
At that moment, the deities brought the Brahmin along with the two boys and placed them in the royal courtyard. At that instant, the king, looking along the road, saw the boys and said:
“Whose face is this that shines forth, like gold refined by fire,
like a coin of pure gold polished in the furnace?
Both have limbs of equal beauty, both possess identical marks.”
“One is like Jāli, and the other is like Kaṇhājinā.
‘Two lions have emerged from their lairs; both are perfectly matched.
These children appear as if they were made of pure gold.’”
In that context, *hemantatamagginā* means "like gold heated by fire. *Sīhā bilāva nikkhantā* means "like lions emerging from their caves," that is, like lions coming out from a golden cave.

Thus, having praised the princes with these three verses, the king commanded a minister: "Go and bring this brahmin here along with the children. He went quickly and brought the brahmin. Then the king said to the brahmin:
"From where, indeed, did you bring these children, O Bhāradvāja?"
"Today you have arrived in the kingdom; where are you going, O Brahmin?
Jūjaka replied:
"Those children of mine, O King, were given to me by Sañjaya for a price."
"Today is the fifteenth night since I obtained these children.
In this context, "with wealth" means with a mind satisfied and serene. "Today is the fifteenth night" means he says that today is the fifteenth night counting from the day they were obtained.
The king said:
“By what kind of pleasant speech, or by what right method, did you gain [this] from him?
Who gave you that gift, that supreme gift for your children?
In this context, “by what kind of pleasant speech” means, O Brahmin, by what kind of endearing words were they obtained by you? By what right method...
"Believe us; without speaking falsehood, you should cause us to believe through right knowledge and reason. "O son!
[she said], referring to her own dear son, after having made an excellent gift: "Who would give this gift to you?
Jūjaka replied:
“He who was the refuge for those who asked, like the earth for all beings—
that King Vessantara gave away his two sons to dwell in the forest.
He who was the destination for those who sought him, like the ocean for rivers— ”
"Thus King Vessantara, having given away his children, dwells in the forest.
Regarding that, "he was established" means he became established there.
Having heard this, the ministers spoke, censuring Vessantara:
“Alas, sir, what a wicked deed has been done by the king, who seeks a home for his son!
How indeed could he give away his two little sons while they were confined in the forest?
Listen to this, sirs, you who have gathered here!”
"How did King Vessantara dwell in the forest with his children and wife?
He would give away a female slave and a male slave, a chariot drawn by a stallion and a mare, and he would give away an elephant and a tusker; how could he have given away his two children?"
In this context, "by one endowed with faith" means even by a king living at home who is possessed of faith [thinking]: "Alas, this is a misdeed;
alas, what has been done is improper. "A forest-dweller" means one who has been banished from the kingdom and is living in the wilderness.
"May you all" means: "O worthy city-dwellers, as many as have gathered here, may you all attend to this and consider it—how..."
They spoke thus with the intention: "How indeed has anyone ever done such a thing as to make these little sons his slaves and give them away?

Regarding the word *dajjā*, it means "let him give whatever wealth," such as slaves and so forth. As for the phrase "how could he give away these children?", they asked for what reason he gave away these two children.
Having heard this, the prince, unable to endure his father’s reproach, spoke this verse like one stretching out an arm against Mount Sineru when struck by the wind:
“In whose house there is no slave, nor horse, nor mare, nor chariot,
Nor elephant, nor tusker, nor great bull— what could such a grandfather give?”
The king said:
“We praise his generosity, my sons, and do not criticize it;
but how did your hearts feel after you had given to that mendicant?”
In that regard, "we praise his giving" means: "O children, we praise your father's giving, we do not revile it.
Having heard this, the prince said:
"It was the very heart of suffering, and yet you see it as something warm."
“O Rohinī, with eyes like copper, my father shed tears.
In this context, “the heart was filled with suffering” means that upon hearing these words spoken by his grandfather Kaṇhājinā, his heart was overcome with grief.
“O Rohinī, with eyes like copper” refers to my father’s eyes, which were as red as the color of copper.
At that moment, she shed tears.
Now, showing him those words of hers, he said:
"O dear father, this brahmin who spoke to me as Kaṇhājinā did—"
He strikes her with a staff, like a maidservant born in the house.
"This is not a brahmin, dear father; brahmins are righteous.
This is a yakkha in the guise of a brahmin who leads us away, dear father, to devour us."
“While being led away by a *piśāca*, my dear, why indeed do you look back?
Then, seeing that the princes were not releasing the brahmin, the king spoke this verse:
“The princess is your mother, and the prince is your father.”
“In the past you used to climb onto my lap; why do you now stand so far away?
Regarding this, “In the past, me” means: seeing me from here in the past, you would come running with speed and climb onto my lap; why then do you now stand at a distance?
The prince said:
“The princess is our mother, and the prince is our father;
we are the slaves of the brahmin, therefore we stand far away.
In this context, “we are the slaves” means that now we have become the slaves of the brahmin.
The king said:
"Do not speak thus to me, for my heart is burning;
my body is like a funeral pyre, and I find no comfort on my seat."
"Do not speak thus to me; do not increase my grief further.
I shall ransom you with wealth; you shall no longer be slaves to them.
For what gift did your father give to the brahmin, my dear?"
"Tell me as it truly is, O Brahmin, and instruct me.
In this context, *samma* is a term of endearment. "My body is like a heap of embers": now my body has become as if placed upon a heap of burning coals.
"Produce [fire] for me" (*janetha maṃ*); or rather, the reading is simply *janetha me*. "I shall redeem it with goods": I shall pay for it with material wealth.
“Having given wealth, I shall release him. “How much is he worth? means “having fixed what price. “Let them pay it” means “let them hand over the wealth.
The prince said:
“Father, my father gave me to the brahmin for a price of one thousand [pieces of gold].”
"Then a black antelope skin, a maiden, and a hundred elephants.
Regarding that, "worth a thousand" means, O King, my father at that time had it appraised at a thousand *nikkhas* and gave it to me.
"Then a black antelope skin" refers to my youngest sister, Kaṇhājinā. "And with a hundred elephants" refers to both elephants and horses.
"Of bulls and coins"—he had everything valued at a hundred each, including even beds, stools, and sandals;
thus he caused the entire amount to be appraised.
As the king was causing the price for the princes to be paid out, he said:
“Arise, Kattiya, and quickly give to the brahmin:
a hundred female slaves and a hundred male slaves, a hundred cows with a bull as the hundredth,
and a thousand measures of gold— give these as the price for your sons.”
Therein, "avākārā" means "give.
Then the giver, hurrying, gave to the brahmin:
a hundred female slaves, a hundred male slaves, a hundred cows, and a hundred bulls.
"And he gave a thousand pieces of gold as the price for his sons.
In this context, *avākari* means "he gave. *Nikkayaṃ* means the price or value.
Thus, he gave the Brahmin all one hundred [pieces of gold] and a thousand *nikkhas* as the price for the princes, as well as a seven-storied [palace].
The palace was large, and the brahmin’s retinue was great.
Having secured his wealth, he ascended the palace, partook of delicious food, and lay down upon a great couch. They bathed the prince’s head, fed him, and adorned him;
then they seated both his grandfather and grandmother on their laps, one on each side. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having bought [them], having bathed them, and having fed the children;
having adorned them with ornaments, they set them upon their laps.
With heads washed, dressed in clean clothes, and adorned with all kinds of jewelry;”
Taking him on his lap, the king questioned his grandfather:
“O you who are adorned with earrings, perfumes, and garlands, and decked out in every ornament—
taking you upon my lap, the king spoke these words.”
“Are both your mother and father well, Jāli?
Are they able to sustain themselves by gleaning? Is there plenty of roots and fruits?
Are there few gadflies and mosquitoes, and few creeping reptiles?”
“In the forest teeming with wild beasts, is there no danger of harm?

Therein, “having adorned with earrings” means having caused them to wear earrings. “Having proclaimed” means having made a proclamation while uttering a delightful sound. “Having adorned with garlands” means having caused them to wear flowers. “Having taken onto his lap” means having caused Prince Jāli to sit upon his lap.
The prince said:
“Moreover, both my mother and father, O King, are free from illness;
they sustain themselves by gleaning, and there is an abundance of roots and fruits.
Furthermore, there are few gadflies and mosquitoes, and very few creeping reptiles.”
In the forest teeming with predatory beasts, no violence exists among them.
Digging up the *āluka*, *kalamba*, and *takka* tubers, as well as the *kola*,
*bhallātaka*, and *bella* fruits, our mother brings them back and nourishes us.
“Whatever she brings back from gathering roots and fruits in the forest,
let us all gather together and eat it at night, not by day.
Mother, she is indeed thin and pale from bringing back the fruit of trees.”
“By the wind and the sun, she who was so delicate is like a lotus held in the hand.
O mother, her hair has fallen away as she wanders in the great forest—
forests teeming with wild beasts, frequented by rhinoceroses and leopards.”
“Tying his matted hair on his head, he bore filth on his shoulders;
clad in skins, he slept upon the ground, worshipping the fire.
In this context, *khaṇantālukalambānī* means digging for yams (*ālū*) and lotus roots (*kalamba*). By this, the difficult livelihood of his parents is indicated.
He praises it. Regarding the phrase *taṃ no*: here *no* is merely a particle. "Like a lotus fallen into the hand"—it became like a lotus crushed by the hand.

"O King, my hair has fallen out": while I was wandering in the great forest, those black hairs of mine, which were the color of bees' wings, were stripped away by the branches of trees and so forth, and thus they fell out. "She bore filth": filth from both her armpits.
"He bears [the child] and moves about in a state of defilement.
Having thus described the mother's state of suffering, he spoke this verse while reproaching his grandfather:
"Dear sons have arisen for men in this world..."
"Surely no affection for our noble master’s sons has arisen in you.
Therein, "udapajjisuṃ" means they arose.
Then the king, revealing his own fault, said:
“Indeed, my son, a transgression and a heinous crime has been committed by me;
for it was at the word of the Sivi people that I caused this innocent man to be banished.
Whatever wealth and grain I possess here in this world—”
"Let King Vessantara come; let him rule over the kingdom of Sivi.
In this context, "O son, O Jāli, this was our misdeed. "The slaughter of beings" means an act that destroys growth.
"Whatever I have here, dear one, all that I give to you, my father. "Let him rule over the kingdom of Sivi."
"May that king rule over this city.
The prince said:
"O King, it is not by my word that the supreme lord of the Śivis will come."
"Let the King himself go and sprinkle [him] with wealth, O son.
Therein, "Sivisutta" means the most excellent Sivi, Vessantara. "Sprinkle" means: like a great cloud with rain, sprinkle him with wealth.
Then King Sañjaya addressed the general:
"Let elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—let the army arm itself for me;
let the townspeople follow me, as well as the brahmins and the chaplains.
Then let sixty thousand warriors of handsome appearance [follow]."
“Let those who are armored and adorned with various colors come quickly!
Some wear blue garments, some are clothed in yellow;
others have red turbans, and some are dressed in pure white.”
"Let those who are armored and adorned with various colors come quickly!
Just as Mount Gandhamādana in the Himavat, the bearer of fragrance,
is covered with various trees and is the abode of great hosts of beings."
“By means of divine herbs, let the quarters shine and waft forth;
let those who are armored come quickly, and let the quarters shine and waft forth.
Then, let fourteen thousand elephants be harnessed.”
The Mātaṅgas with golden girths, dressed in garments of refined gold,
mounted by village chiefs holding spears and goads in their hands—
let them come quickly, armored and displayed upon the backs of elephants.
“Then let fourteen thousand horses be harnessed—
noble Sindhu-bred steeds, swift of pace like thoroughbreds by birth—
and mounted by village chiefs bearing quivers and bows.”
“Let the armored men, adorned with golden ornaments, mount their horses quickly!
Then let fourteen thousand chariots be harnessed—
chariots with iron-forged rims and wheels inlaid with gold.”
“Let them raise their banners there, and their shields and armor;
let the firm-handed archers string their bows;
let the chariot-drivers, equipped and ready, mount their chariots quickly.”
In that context, "let them arm themselves" means let them prepare for battle. "Sixty thousand" refers to the sixty thousand ministers born together with my son.
"Wearing blue garments, some of them" means let some come having dressed themselves in blue robes. "The abode of great hosts of beings" means the dwelling place of many hosts of *yakkhas*.
"Let the quarters be filled and blow forth" means like the aforementioned Himālaya mountain, [adorned] with ornaments, ointments, and so forth.
"Let them shine and let them blow. "Upon the backs of elephants" means those elephant-drivers should quickly mount upon the backs of the elephants.
"Adorned" means having displayed their ornaments. "With rims well-bound with iron" means having rims that are thoroughly encircled with iron.
"With golden-studded fenders" means having fenders inlaid with gold. "Let them yoke fourteen thousand such chariots"—this is what was said.
He spoke thus: "Let them level it" means let them raise it up.

Having thus inspected his army divisions, the king gave orders, saying: "Prepare my son’s road for his journey from the city of Jetuttara as far as Mount Vaṅka, making it eight usabhas wide and level;
and for the sake of adorning the road, perform this and that. Thus he spoke.
“Let parched grain, scattered flowers, garlands, perfumes, and ointments,
as well as offerings, remain on whichever path he shall come.
In every village, let there be a hundred jars of *meraya* and *surā* liquor.”
"May they stand by the road along which he shall come.
May there be meat, cakes, and saṅkuli bread, rice-porridge accompanied by fish;
may they stand by the road along which he shall come."
“Ghee, oil, curd, milk, much millet-seed, and liquor—
let these fall upon the path by which he shall come. Let cooks, kitchen-stewards,
actors, dancers, and singers [also fall there].”
“Let the *pāṇissara* lutes, the *kumbhathūṇī* drums,
the *mandaka* and *sokajjhāyika* instruments all be struck!
Let the *vīṇās* be played, and let the *bherīs*, *dindimas*, *kharamukhas*, and *ekapokkharas* resound!”
“Let the mudiṅgas, paṇavas, and conchs, the godhas and parivadentikas,
the dindimas and the kutumpadindimas be struck!
Therein, “lājā, olopiyā, and flowers” refers to those who scatter flowers together with parched grain— namely, the five kinds of flowers beginning with parched grain.
He commands, "Prepare flowers for sprinkling. "Garlands, perfumes, and ointments" refers both to the garlands hanging from the canopy over the road and to the perfumes and ointments.
"And offerings" refers to both flower-offerings and jewel-offerings;
let them stand wherever my son shall come along that road. "In every village" means at the gate of every village.
"Let them stand firm" means: let the jars of *surā*, *meraya*, and *majja* prepared for the thirsty to drink remain standing.
"Provided with fish" means: supplied with fish. "Made of *kaṅgu* seed" means: made from *kaṅgu* flour. "Singing softly" means: those who sing softly.
"Meditating on sorrow" refers to magicians, or anyone else capable of removing arisen sorrow; they are called "meditators on sorrow."
They are called "weeping" because they cause the people who grieve to cease their lamentation when the succession of the lineage’s sounds is made to dance;
that is the meaning. "Kharamukhāni" refers to the great sea-conchs. "Saṅkha" refers to two types of conchs:
the right-spiraled *muṭṭhisaṅkha* and the *nāḷisaṅkha*. "Godhā," "parivadentikā," "dindimāni," and "kutumpadindimāni"—these four are likewise musical instruments.
In this way, the king examined the ornaments on the road. Jūjaka, too, having eaten beyond his capacity and being unable to digest it, passed away right there.

After the king had performed the funeral rites for him, he caused a drum to be beaten, proclaiming: "If there is any kinsman of this brahmin in the city, let him take this. Not finding any kinsman of his, the wealth returned once more to the king.

It came to pass. Then, on the seventh day, the entire army assembled. Thereupon the king, accompanied by a great retinue and making Jāli his guide, set forth. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“That army was vast, a host set out for the conquest of Śivi.”
With the guide Jālin, he set out for Mount Vaṅka:
"The elephant, the sixty-year-old tusker, cries out like a crane;
bound by his girth-straps, the war-elephant cries out like a crane."
“The noble steeds neighed, and the sound of the chariot wheels arose;
a cloud of dust covered the sky as the auspicious army set forth.
That great host was formidable, setting out with a captivating splendor.”
With his net as a guide, he went to Mount Vaṅka.
They reached a vast wilderness, thick with many branches and abundant water,
covered with flowering trees and likewise with fruit-bearing trees.
“Therein, birds of various colors and many kinds, sweet-voiced with their warbling notes,
warble in response to one another on trees blossoming in season.
Having traveled a long distance, at the passing of days and nights, they arrive.”
“They approached that region where Vessantara was.
Therein, “great” refers to an army consisting of twelve akkhobhaṇīs. “Mobilized” means set out on its march. “It trumpets like a crane”:
at that time, when it had rained in their own kingdom, the brahmins dwelling in the Kāliṅga country brought that nāga and [presented it] to Sañjaya.
They gave them. The elephant, delighted with the thought, "I shall indeed be able to see my master," let out a cry like a crane;
it was with reference to this that it was said. Regarding the phrase *kacchāya*: even when being bound by a golden girth, he cries out like a crane out of satisfaction.
*Hasiyantī* means they made a sound like laughter. *Hārahārinī* means capable of carrying what is to be carried. *Pāviṃsu* means they entered.
"Bahusākha" means having many branches, like the branches of a great tree. "Dīgham addhānaṃ" means a road of sixty yojanas.
"Upāgacchuṃ" means they arrived at that region where Vessantara was.
The commentary on the Great King is finished.
The Commentary on the Sixty-Two Kinds of Action:

Prince Jāli, having caused his camp to be pitched on the bank of Lake Mucalinda and having stationed fourteen thousand chariots facing the path by which [the enemy] might come, arranged for protection against lions, tigers, leopards, and other beasts in various locations. [He likewise provided for] elephants and so forth...
A great sound arose. Then, hearing that sound, the Great Being thought, "Have my enemies come for my sake after having slain my father?
Terrified by the fear of death, he took Maddī and climbed a mountain, from which he surveyed the army.
To explain this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having heard their outcry, Vessantara became afraid;
having climbed a mountain, he looked upon the army in fear.
‘Come now, Maddī, observe what kind of outcry there is in the forest.’”
“Excellent thoroughbred horses are being laughed at, and the tops of banners are visible.
Surely these hunters in the forest have surrounded herds of deer with snares and immediately caused them to fall into a pit.”
“Striking out fiercely, they kill the best among them,
saying: ‘See how we, though innocent and confined in the forest,
have fallen into the hands of our enemies— look at those who slay the weak!’”
In this context, *iṅgha* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation. *Nisāmehi* means "look upon" or "examine," as in whether it be one's own army or an enemy army.
The connection of the meaning for these two and a half verses beginning with "Surely these [beings] in the forest... should be understood as follows:
"Maddi, just as hunters, having surrounded herds of deer in the forest with snares, or else having caused them to fall into a pit..."
"Kill them right now! You wicked deer! they cried out, striking down the best and fattest of those deer with sharp weapons for killing game.
"Surely these men will likewise strike us with harsh words and sharp weapons while we cry out;
yet we are innocent, confined here in the forest, having been driven from our kingdom."
"Having been ordained, we dwell in the forest; even so, we have fallen into the hands of our enemies. Look upon us, O slayer of the weak!
Thus he lamented out of fear of death.
Having heard his words, she looked at the army and, thinking, "This must be our own army," spoke this verse to comfort the Great Being:
“May enemies not overpower you, like fire upon the waters of the ocean;
contemplate that very thing so that there may be safety from this.
In this context, “like fire upon the waters of the ocean” means just as a fire brought forth by means of grass, fuel, and so forth [might be extinguished] upon what is called the ocean...
Just as shallow and deep waters cannot overwhelm one and are unable to scorch them, so too enemies shall not overcome or prevail over you.
"That very thing" refers to what Sakka said to you after granting you the boon: "Great King, before long your father will come.
Reflect upon that alone: perhaps there may be safety for us from this military force.
"May it be so," he said, comforting the Great Being.

Then the Great Being, having lessened his grief, descended from the mountain with her and sat at the door of his leaf-hut; she too sat at the door of her own leaf-hut. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
"Then King Vessantara, having descended from the mountain..."
He sat in the leaf-hut, having made his mind firm.
Therein, "having made his mind firm" means he sat down after making his heart steadfast, thinking: "We are indeed called renunciants; what can anyone do to us?
At that moment, King Sañjaya addressed the queen: "My dear, Phussati is among all of us together..."
"There will be great sorrow at the gates; first, I shall go there. Then, perceiving that 'they will now be sitting having dispelled their sorrow,' you may arrive with a large retinue.
After some time has passed, let Jāli, Kaṇha, and Ajina follow after. Having said this, he turned the chariot back.

Having turned the chariot back toward the path he had come and having stationed guards here and there, he descended from the back of his decorated elephant and went into the presence of his son. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having turned back the chariot and dismissed the troops,”
While he was dwelling alone in the forest, his father approached him.
Having dismounted from the back of an elephant, with his robe arranged over one shoulder and palms joined in reverence,
surrounded by his ministers, the father came to sprinkle water upon his son.
“There he saw the prince, of lovely form, composed, sitting in the leaf-hut, meditating, fearless from every side.

In that context, *vuṭṭhapetvāna seniya* means having stationed a body of troops for the purpose of guarding him. *Ekaṃso* means with his upper robe draped over one shoulder. *Siñcitumāgamī* means he came to consecrate him in the kingdom. *Rammarūpaṃ* means unanointed and unadorned.
“Seeing him approaching, his father who was longing for his son,
Vessantara and Maddī went out to meet him and paid him homage.
And Maddī bowed her head at the feet of her father-in-law.”
"Maddī said: 'O King, I am indeed your daughter-in-law; I bow at your feet.
Having spoken thus, she bowed down, and he there embraced her and stroked her with his hand. In this passage, "I am indeed your daughter-in-law;
I bow at your feet" means: "O King, I, your daughter-in-law, bow at your feet"—having said this, she paid homage.

"Te su tattha" means: both those people, having embraced him there in that hermitage given by Sakka, having laid him down upon their hearts and kissed his head, rubbed him all over with gentle hands; they also rubbed their own backs.
Then, after weeping and lamenting, the king, as the sorrow was extinguished, spoke while exchanging greetings with them:
“I hope you are well, my son; I hope you are free from illness.
I hope you sustain yourself by gleaning, and that roots and fruits are plentiful.
I hope there are few gadflies and mosquitoes, and very few creeping reptiles.”
“In this forest teeming with predatory beasts, is there indeed no violence?
Having heard his father’s words, the Great Being said:
“We have our livelihood, O King, and it is of such a kind as that.”
“Let our livelihood be easy, living by the gleaning of grains.
Like a charioteer taming one who is not yet broken, O Great King, we are untamed;
therefore, being untamed ourselves, we tame those who are not yet broken.”
“Indeed, our flesh has become emaciated, O Great King, because we have not seen our father or mother, being confined in the forest and grieving for our lives.
In this context, *yādisakīdisā* means “of whatever kind,” that is, “of any sort whatsoever”; *kasirā jīvikā* means “our livelihood is difficult. O dear one, [we are thus].
"Living by the practice of gleaning is indeed difficult; our livelihood was one of suffering.

'Aniddhi,' O Great King, means a man who is without success, lacking prosperity—a poor man. Yet even such a man, being 'aniddhi,' a skillful charioteer tames like a horse, making him free from wickedness.
While living here, we—though ourselves 'aniddhi'—have been tamed and made free from wickedness; we remain truly without prosperity."
“Do not tame us. There is also a reading, “Tame us,” which means “you have tamed us.
He says, “What happiness indeed can there be for us who dwell in the forest with sorrow not yet departed?
Having spoken thus, he spoke again, asking about the condition of his sons:
“Jālī and Kaṇhājinā, both of whom were devoted to their father Sivisetha, followed the will of the brahmin,
even as he slaughtered them like cattle for the sake of a greedy man in urgent need.”
“Those sons of the princesses—if you know them, speak of them;
let us master them quickly, as one would a youth bitten by a snake.

In this context, “those whose minds have not attained their inheritance,” O Great King, refers to those who are your heirs, yet whose minds have not attained [the status of] the most excellent of the Sivis.
Having had their desires unfulfilled, they became subject to the will of the brahmin;
those two princes whom the brahmin slaughters like cattle—strike them down—if you know them by sight or by report, speak out!
Like a young man bitten by a snake, they are being treated for the sake of neutralizing the poison.
He said, "Master, you do not master it quickly; teach it to us.
The King replied:
"Both princes have been ransomed—both Jālī and Kaṇhājinā."
“Having given wealth to the brahmin, my son, do not fear;
take heart. Therein, “bought” means taken after giving a price.
Having heard this, the Great Being, finding his breath again, exchanged greetings with his father.
“Is it well with you, dear one?
Is it free from ailment, dear one? Is my mother’s sight not failing her?
In this context, “is her sight not failing” means that her sight does not fail as she weeps out of grief for her son.
The king said:
“It is well with me, my son, and likewise, my son, I am free from illness;
and furthermore, my son, your mother’s sight does not fail.”
The Bodhisatta said:
“I hope you are free from illness and fit for work; I hope your draft animals are capable of carrying their loads;
I hope the countryside is prosperous; and I hope the rains do not fail.”
In that context, "rain" means a downpour of rain.
The king said:
"Furthermore, my [body] is healthy and fit; furthermore, my vehicle carries [me]."
“Furthermore, the countryside is prosperous, and furthermore, the rain does not cease.

While they were thus conversing, Queen Phussatī, observing that they would now sit with their grief diminished, went into her son’s presence accompanied by a great retinue. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
While they were thus deliberating, their mother appeared to them—
the king’s daughter at the mountain gate, on foot and without sandals.
And seeing her approaching, their mother who was longing for her sons, [they rose].
Both Vessantara and Maddī went out to meet them and paid homage.
Maddī bowed her head at the feet of her mother-in-law and said:
"O noble lady, I, Maddī, your daughter-in-law, pay homage at your feet."
While they stood there having paid homage to Queen Phussatī, their children—sons and daughters—arrived, surrounded by their companions.
Maddī remained standing, watching the path along which they were coming.
Seeing them arrive safely, she was unable to maintain her composure; like a cow with a young calf, she set out from that spot, lamenting.
Seeing the shore, they ran toward their mother while lamenting. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Seeing Maddī and their children, who had returned safely from afar, they ran toward them crying out, like young calves toward their mother.”
“Seeing her two little sons, who had arrived safely from afar, Maddī, trembling like a woman possessed by the spirit Vāruṇī, showered them with streams from her breasts.

Therein, “weeping, they ran toward them” means weeping, they ran toward them. “Like a woman possessed by the spirit Vāruṇī” means like a female fortune-teller possessed by a *yakkha*, trembling, she showered them with streams from her breasts.
It is said that after lamenting with a great cry, she fell to the ground from a height, trembling and unconscious.
The princes also came running with speed and, falling unconscious themselves, collapsed right upon their mother.
At that moment, two streams of milk issued from her two breasts and entered their mouths. If indeed this much—
If there had been no consolation, the two princes, their hearts becoming parched with grief, would surely have perished.
Vessantara, too, upon seeing his beloved sons, being unable to restrain his sorrow, fell unconscious right there.
His parents also fell unconscious and lay down in that very spot, as did the sixty thousand ministers born together with them. Such was that compassion.
Not even a single passerby was able to stand his ground.

The entire hermitage became like a grove of sal trees crushed by the winds at the end of an eon. At that moment, the mountains roared, the great earth quaked, the great ocean was agitated, and Sineru, the king of mountains, tilted.
The six celestial realms of the sense-sphere devas were filled with a single tumultuous uproar.
Sakka, the king of the gods, thought: "The six kshatriyas and their retinues have become unconscious;
not even one among them is capable of rising to sprinkle water on anyone's body. Now, I shall cause a rain of lotuses to fall upon this assembly of the six kshatriyas.
Having thought thus, he caused a rain of lotuses to fall at that gathering of the six kshatriyas. There, those who wished to be wetted were wetted.
Not even a single drop fell upon those who desired to be wet; like water from a lotus leaf, it turned back and passed away.
Thus, that rain was like rain fallen upon a bed of lotuses. The six kṣatriyas regained their composure.
Seeing this, the great multitude exclaimed, "Oh, how wonderful! Oh, how marvelous! Such a reunion of kinsmen!"
"A rain of lotuses fell and the great earth trembled," he proclaimed as a marvel. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"A great roar arose among the assembled kinsmen;
the mountains resounded and the earth was shaken."
“While the rain-god poured down a continuous stream of rain,
King Vessantara was reunited with his kinsmen. His grandsons,
daughters-in-law, son, the king, and the queen were all together.”
When they had all assembled, there was a hair-raising scene.
With palms joined, they entreated him while weeping in the terrifying forest—
all those who had gathered from the kingdom, including Vessantara and Maddī.
“You are our lord and king; let both of us rule the kingdom together.
In this context, “shout” refers to a cry of compassion. “With palms joined” means that all the city-dwellers, merchants, and country-folk stood with their hands raised in reverence.
“Entreat him” means falling at his feet, weeping and crying out, “O King!”
“Sir, you are our lord; your father wishes to lead you back to the city after consecrating you right here.
Please accept the white parasol belonging to your family,” they entreated him.
The commentary on the six khattiya rites is finished.
The Explanation of the Section on the City:
Having heard that, the Great Being, conversing with his father, spoke this verse:
“They have banished me from the kingdom while I was ruling according to the Dhamma.”
“You, as well as the countryfolk and the guildsmen, have all assembled here.
Then the king, seeking forgiveness for his son’s transgression, said:
“Indeed, my son, we have committed a wrong; I have perpetrated a heinous act of violence.”
"Since I, at the word of the Sivi people,
have caused this innocent man to go forth," having spoken this verse, he spoke the following verse while requesting his son for the sake of removing his own suffering:
"By whatever means possible, one should dispel the suffering of a father."
"And even for one's mother and sister, [one should act] even at the cost of one's own life.
In this context, "udabbaheti" means he should remove [the grief]. "Api pāṇehi" means that, dear son, even by renouncing one's own life, the sorrow and suffering of one's parents must be removed;
therefore, do not harbor malice toward me in your heart, but carry out my word.
"Dear brother, remove this female characteristic and take on the guise of a king"—this was said to him, it is said, with this underlying intention.
Although the Bodhisatta desired to exercise sovereignty, he spoke thus, thinking, "If only this much were said, it would not be a grave matter.
The Great Being consented, saying, "Very well. Then, perceiving his acceptance, the sixty thousand who were born together with him...
The ministers said, “It is time for bathing, Great King; wash away the dust and dirt.
Then the Great Being, saying to them, “Wait a little longer,” entered the leaf-hut, removed his hermit’s rags, and set them aside.
He put on a conch-colored robe, emerged from the leaf-hut, and [reflected]: “This is the fruit of the ascetic life which I have lived for nine months and a half-month...”
"This is the place where, while striving for the summit of the perfections, I gave a gift and caused the great earth to tremble.
Having circumambulated the leaf-hut three times clockwise, he prostrated himself with the fivefold salutation and stood there.
Then his barber and others performed his hair and beard grooming and other services. Adorned with all his ornaments, he appeared like a king of the gods.
They consecrated him as king while he was shining with splendor. Therefore it is said:
“Then King Vessantara washed away the dust and dirt;
having washed away the dust and dirt, he put on the color of conch-shell.”
In that context, "he caused it to flow away" means he removed it; and having removed it, he assumed the royal attire—this is the meaning.
Then his glory became great. Every place he looked upon trembled;
bards proclaimed auspicious verses, all musical instruments were sounded, and it was like the roar of thunder within the belly of the great ocean.
The sound of musical instruments arose. Having adorned the elephant-treasure, they brought it forward. He fastened the sword-treasure and mounted the elephant-treasure.
At that very moment, sixty thousand ministers born together with him, adorned with all ornaments, surrounded him;
and all the maidens, having bathed and adorned Maddī-devī as well, consecrated her on his head.
And as they were sprinkling her with the consecration water, they recited auspicious verses, beginning with, "May Vessantara protect you!
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"Her head bathed, dressed in clean garments, adorned with all kinds of ornaments,"
Without mounting his chariot, he girded on a sword that struck fear into his enemies.
Then sixty thousand warriors of handsome appearance, born together with him,
surrounded the bull among charioteers, bringing him joy.
“Then the assembled women of the city bathed Maddi as well.
May Vessantara protect her, and both Jālī and Kaṇhājinā;
furthermore, may the great king Sañjaya guard her.”
In that context, "not having mounted the elephant-king" refers to the elephant-king that appeared on the day of his birth.
"Scorching the enemy" means tormenting his foes. "They surrounded him" means they encircled him. "Rejoicing" means gladdening him.
"The daughters of Sivi" refers to the wives of King Sivi who, having assembled, bathed him with scented water. "Jālī, Kaṇhājinā, and Cubhā"—these were his sons as well.
"May they protect their mothers.
And having obtained this requisite, they experienced joy in the delightful Giribbaja, delighting in what was previously a source of defilement for themselves.
“Having obtained this condition, which previously was a source of defilement for herself,
Lakkhaṇā was joyful, exultant, and glad at heart upon meeting her sons.
