Having obtained this condition, which previously was a source of defilement for herself...”
“Ānandī, Vittā, Patītā, and Lakkhaṇā together with their sons.

In this context, “having obtained this condition, monks,” means that Vessantara and Maddī, having obtained this condition and having gained this foundation—namely, being established in the kingdom—[acted].
“In the past” means prior to this, [regarding] his own affliction during the forest dwelling.

Having remembered, they celebrated with joy in the delightful Giribbaja—that is, in the lovely interior of Vaṅka Mountain—beating the golden-lattice-covered drum of rejoicing, crying out, “This is the command of King Vessantara!
and thus they held a festival of joy. Maddī, joyful and well-disposed, endowed with auspicious marks, gathered her sons together and attained them.
"Vittā" means having become joyful, the sense being "exceedingly glad. "Patītā" means having become elated with happiness.
And having thus become elated, she said to her sons:
"Formerly I ate but one meal a day, and I always slept on the bare ground."
Such was the vow I made, for you, my children, were indeed my desires.
"That vow of mine has been fulfilled today, O children, having come together;
may it protect both your mother and your father, my children."
"Furthermore, O Great King, let Sañjaya protect you.
By whatever merit has been performed by me, my father, and you—
by all that wholesome deed, may you become ageless and immortal."
In this context, she says: "O children, you are indeed my desires. She means: "O children, I am your desire;
longing for you, when you were formerly taken away by the brahmin, I ate but a single meal and lay upon the ground—such was my vow for the sake of you, my desires.
"Samiddha" means that this vow of mine has today been fulfilled. This applies to her mother as well.

"May it protect... may it protect both the father and the son"—the meaning is that the joy born of the son may protect the joy born of the mother, and may the merit belonging to the parents protect that [merit]. For this very reason, he said: "Whatever merit has been performed.

Queen Phussatī also, saying, "From now on, let my daughter-in-law wear these very clothes and let her wear these ornaments," sent them after filling golden caskets [with the gifts]. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Cotton cloth and silk, linen and fine wool—
these her mother-in-law sent to her daughter-in-law, with which Maddī was adorned.
Then there were golden armlets and necklaces made of jewels.”
The mother-in-law sent to her daughter-in-law those things with which Maddī had shone:
"Then gold, armlets, bracelets, gems, and girdles—
the mother-in-law sent these to her daughter-in-law, with which Maddī had shone."
“Her high head-dress and blooming face, and her many-colored jewels—
these the mother-in-law sent to her daughter-in-law, with which Maddī shone. The lofty crown,
the neck-ornament, the girdle, and the foot-ornaments;”
The mother-in-law sent to her daughter-in-law those things with which Maddī had shone:
"Examine well the thread and the flaws in the thread when you lie down;
thus did the princess shine like a celestial maiden in the Nandana grove."
“With heads bathed, dressed in clean garments, and adorned with every ornament,
the princesses shone like celestial nymphs in Tāvatiṃsa. Like plantain trees shaken by the wind,
they grew up in the grove of wish-fulfilling creepers.”
Endowed with the most excellent ornaments, the princess shone resplendent.
“Like a female bird born among humans, with wings of thought,
and with lips like the fruit of the banyan tree, the princess shone resplendent.”
In this context, *hemañca kāyūraṃ* refers specifically to a golden neck-ornament shaped like the fruit of the wild date palm.
*Ratanamayaṃ* refers to another neck-ornament made of jewels. *Aṅgadaṃ maṇimekhalan* refers to both an armlet ornament and a jeweled girdle.
*Uṇṇataṃ* is a single forehead ornament. *Mukhaphullaṃ* is a decorative mark (*tilaka*) on the edge of the forehead.
“Of various colors” (*nānāratta*) means of diverse hues. “Māṇika” means made of gems. “Uggatthana” and “giṅgamaka”—these two are also ornaments.
“Mekhala” means a girdle made of gold or silver. “Pāṭipādaka” means an ornament for the feet.
“Sutta” and “suttavajja”—these are ornaments mounted on thread and those not mounted on thread. In the text, however, it says “suppa” and “suppavajja.”
It is written: "Upanijjhāya seyyasī" (Beholding the most excellent). This refers to the ornament, both that which is fixed upon the Sutta and that which is not;
having looked at each deficient place and adorned herself, the most excellent one, possessing supreme beauty, shone like Maddī, a daughter of the gods, in the Nandana grove.
"Vātacchupitā" means she was born in the Cittalatā grove and, touched by the wind, was like a golden plantain tree.
Stretching her limbs throughout the day, she shone. "Endowed with ivory tusks" means she was possessed of red ivory tusks resembling *bimba* fruits.

"Like a bird born of a human woman, with variegated wings" means that just as a bird born from a human woman’s body—known as a "human-born bird"—shines as it flies through the air with outspread variegated wings, so did she.
Thus she shone with lips like ripe *bimba* fruits, red as if stained with lac.

Sixty thousand ministers brought a young elephant, adorned with every ornament, neither too large nor too small, and capable of enduring the strike of a spear-head, for the purpose of mounting Maddī. Therefore it is said:
"And they brought for her an elephant, not too large, like a young bull."
“Enduring weapons, enduring arrows, with tusks like plow-poles, and grown large—
Maddī mounted that elephant, which was not yet overgrown,
enduring weapons, enduring arrows, with tusks like plow-poles, and grown large.”
In that regard, monks, they brought for her a young elephant, adorned with every ornament, not too large, and capable of enduring the blows of swords and arrows;
she mounted it—that is, she ascended the back of the noble elephant.
Thus, both of them went to the royal camp with great splendor. King Sañjaya [was accompanied] by twelve *akṣauhiṇīs*.
For about a month he engaged in mountain sports and forest sports.
By the power of the Great Being’s majesty, no predatory beast or bird in that vast wilderness harmed anyone. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“In all that wilderness, whatever beasts were there;”
By the power of Vessantara, they did not harm one another.
"In all that forest, as many birds as there were here,
by the power of Vessantara, they did not harm one another."
“In that entire forest, as many deer as were there gathered together in one place when Vessantara had set out for the increase of the kingdom of the Sivis.”
“In that entire forest, as many birds as were there,
all gathered together when Vessantara had set out for the increase of the kingdom of the Sivis.”
“In that entire forest, as many wild animals as there were,
none failed to utter sweet cries when Vessantara set forth,
increasing the prosperity of the kingdom of the Sivi people.”
“In all that forest, as many birds as there were,
none failed to warble sweetly when Vessantara set out,
increasing the prosperity of the kingdom of the Sivi people.”
In that context, "as many as there were here" means however many were there. "They gathered together in one place" means they assembled at a single location;

and having assembled, they fell into dejection, thinking, "From this point on, we shall no longer have mutual shame, moral dread, or self-restraint. "They did not warble sweetly" refers to the Great Being.
Distressed by separation, they did not sing their sweet songs as they had done before.

King Sañjaya, having spent about a month enjoying mountain sports and forest sports, summoned his general and asked, "Dear son, we have dwelt long in the forest; has the path for my son's departure been decorated?"
When he replied, “Yes, Your Majesty, it is time for you to go,” [the king] had Vessantara informed and set out, taking his army with him.
From the side of Vaṅkagiri to the city of Jetuttara, the Great Being traveled along a sixty-yojana decorated road together with a vast retinue. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“The royal highway was prepared, variegated and strewn with flowers,
as far as Jetuttara where Vessantara dwelt.
Then sixty thousand warriors of beautiful appearance [set out].”
They surrounded him on all sides when Vessantara had set out for the increase of the kingdom of the Sivis:
"Eunuchs and princes, merchants and brahmins," they said.
They surrounded him on all sides when Vessantara had set out,
increasing the prosperity of the Śivis’ kingdom:
elephant-riders, cavalrymen, chariot-warriors, and infantrymen.
They surrounded him on all sides when Vessantara had set out,
increasing the prosperity of the Śivis’ kingdom.
“The people of the countryside have gathered, and the town-dwellers have also gathered.”
They surrounded him on all sides when Vessantara had set out to increase the kingdom of the Sivi people— those with skull-bowls,
those carrying shields, those with spears in hand, and those with excellent quivers.
“They marched in front as Vessantara, the increaser of the kingdom of the Sivi people, set forth.
In that context, “prepared” means adorned, like at the time of the Visākha full-moon festival. “Variegated” means [adorned] with plantain trees, full water-jars, banners, flags, and so forth.
*Vicitto*: "Spread with flowers" means strewn with flowers having fried grain as the fifth [type]. *Yattha*:
From the Vaṅka mountain where Vessantara dwelt, all the way to the city of Jetuttara, it was continuously adorned and prepared.
*Karoṭiyā*: Warriors who had placed skull-bowls (*karoṭika*) upon their heads—so they were named "Skull-heads. *Cammadharā*: Those bearing shields made of hide.
"Suvammī" means well-fortified with various kinds of defensive works.
"They marched ahead" means that heroic warriors, who did not turn back even when intoxicated elephants approached, marched in front of King Vessantara.

Having traversed a road of sixty *yojanas* in two months, the king reached the city of Jetuttara; entering the city which was fully adorned and prepared, he ascended the palace. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“They entered that delightful city, which had great walls and gateways,
and was well-supplied with both food and drink, as well as with both dance and song.
The country folk were joyful, and the merchants gathered together.”
When the prince, the increaser of the Śivi kingdom,
had arrived, there was a waving of garments as the bringer of wealth entered;
he brought joy into the city, and the proclamation of release from bonds resounded.
In that context, "with great walls and gateways" means endowed with large walls and gateways.
"With both dance and song" means endowed with both dance and song. "The people were joyful" means they were satisfied and attained a state of gladness.
"When the giver of wealth to the multitude arrived" means when the Great Being, who bestows wealth upon the masses, had arrived. "He caused delight to enter" [refers to] Vessantara’s...
“By order of the Great King,” they proclaimed, and the drum of joy (*nandibherī*) resounded throughout the city. The release from bonds was announced;
it was proclaimed that all beings were to be freed from their fetters. Even down to a mere cat, Great King Vessantara caused all living creatures to be released from bondage.
On the very day he entered the city, at the time of dawn, he thought: “Those who, when night has turned to morning, shall hear of my arrival...”
“Having heard this, supplicants will arrive; what shall I give them? At that moment, Sakka’s palace manifested a sign of heat.

Reflecting on it, he understood the reason and immediately caused a rain of the seven treasures to fall like a thick cloud, filling the eastern and western grounds of the royal residence to the depth of a man's waist.

He caused it to rain knee-deep throughout the entire city. On the following day, the Great Being had the wealth that had fallen on the first and last plots of land belonging to various families returned to those very families;

having had the remainder brought back, he had it poured into storehouses together with his own property upon his own house-site and established it as a source for gifts. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“For as long as it rained gold, the god poured down that rain while Vessantara was entered into the kingdom of the Sivis, increasing their prosperity.
Then King Vessantara, the kshatriya, having given his gift,”
"With the breakup of the body, the wise one was reborn in heaven.
Therein, "he was reborn in heaven" means that, having passed away from there, he arose in the Tusita city with his second moment of consciousness.
The commentary on the *Nagarakaṇḍa* is finished.
Having delivered this Great Vessantara Dhamma Teaching adorned with a thousand stanzas, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying:
"At that time, Jūjaka was Devadatta; Amittatāpanā was the young woman Ciñca;
Cetaputta was Channa; the ascetic Accuta was Sāriputta; Sakka was Anuruddha; and King Sañjaya was the Great King Suddhodana."
“Queen Phussatī was Sirimā Mahāmāyā; Queen Maddī was Rāhula’s mother; Prince Jāli was Rāhula; Kaṇhājinā was Uppalavaṇṇā;
the rest of the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly; and as for King Mahāvessantara, he was none other than myself, the Sammasambuddha.
This is the tenth, the commentary on the Vessantara Jātaka.
The commentary on the Mahānipāta is finished.
The Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā is complete.
